The phrase “from their Lord” also identifies the source of the forgiveness, mercy, and guidance: these are gifts God grants to the patient, not claims that the afflicted person can impose upon Him. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī explains that God’s blessing can include pardon, mercy, blessing, and honor, while the separate mention of mercy emphasizes the breadth of that favor. **[Qurṭubī]** His discussion distinguishes the divine blessing from a human prayer for another person; the wording here describes God’s favor upon His servants. **[Study Quran]**

Guidance in this passage includes recognizing the truth of human dependence and returning to God, then acting on that recognition through patience. **[Saʿdī]** The person who says the words but refuses their meaning has not yet embodied the response described by the verse. **[Ṭabarī]** Conversely, a person who grieves while remaining faithful is not excluded from the promise merely for feeling sorrow. **[Qurṭubī]** The blessing, mercy, and right guidance together describe a way of passing through trial with God’s aid. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

As-Saʿdī notes that these verses prepare people for hardship before it comes, identify the response to make when it arrives, and describe the reward of those who meet it with patience. **[Saʿdī]** That preparation does not eliminate the trial; it gives believers a framework for understanding and enduring it. **[Study Quran]** The promise is therefore both consoling and instructive: patience is a chosen act of faith, and God’s mercy accompanies those who practice it. **[Jalālayn]**

**Reflection.** Guidance appears here in the practice of remembering God’s ownership and returning to Him in faith when life hurts. **[Saʿdī]** The believer may feel loss, but does not have to face it without hope of mercy or judgment. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse closes the passage with a promise that patient trust is seen and honored by God. **[Jalālayn]**
## 2:158

158158
*“Truly Ṣafā and Marwah are among the rituals of God; so whoever performs the ḥajj to the House, or makes the ʿumrah, there is no blame on him in going to and fro between them. And whoever volunteers good, truly God is Thankful, Knowing.”*

**Meaning.** The verse names Ṣafā and Marwah, the two hills beside the Sacred Mosque, as “among the rituals of God.” Al-Qurṭubī explains *shaʿāʾir* as signs and appointed places of worship; as-Saʿdī calls them visible markers of the religion through which God has instructed His servants. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran notes that the term can refer both to sacred symbols and to ritual actions. **[Study Quran]** The verse thus restores the hills to their revealed religious meaning, rather than leaving them associated with the pagan practices that had once taken place there. **[Maʿārif]**

The historical reports describe more than one reason for hesitation about the ritual. ʿĀʾishah corrected ʿUrwah when he thought “there is no blame” meant that pilgrims could omit the passage between the hills: she explained that the verse answered people who were uneasy because some pre-Islamic pilgrims connected the practice with Manāt, while others feared that the rite itself had no sanction. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī records reports about the Ansar’s reluctance and about idols called Isāf and Nāʾilah that had been placed on the hills and touched by pagan pilgrims. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran likewise notes both the concern that the rite was a survival from idolatry and the question whether only circumambulation of the Kaʿbah had been commanded. **[Study Quran]**

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān concluded that the verse could address both groups: those who had avoided the ritual in the pre-Islamic period and those who later hesitated because the Qur’an had mentioned circumambulation of the House without yet naming Ṣafā and Marwah. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The shared answer is that the hills are God’s signs and the rite, when performed as God has prescribed, is not tainted by the idolatrous actions that once accompanied it. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse rejects guilt by association: an act of worship is judged by its revealed purpose, not by the false beliefs of people who once performed it. **[Maʿārif]**

The expression “no blame on him in going to and fro between them” reassures the hesitant; it is not a declaration that a pilgrim may freely omit the rite. ʿĀʾishah points out that if omission were intended, the wording would have said there was no blame in not going between them. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī makes the same grammatical point, distinguishing permission to perform an act from permission to leave it. **[Qurṭubī]** The Prophet’s practice and instruction then clarify how the rite is observed: he began at Ṣafā, as God mentions it first, and the reports describe the saʿy as a prescribed part of pilgrimage. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The jurists differ on the precise legal classification of saʿy. As-Saʿdī regards it as an obligatory rite of ḥajj and ʿumrah, supported by the Prophet’s practice and instruction to learn the pilgrimage rites from him. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī reports that al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, and the well-known Mālikī position treat it as a pillar, while the Ḥanafī position treats it as necessary but compensable if omitted. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran also notes the difference between schools that call it a pillar and those that regard it as recommended or otherwise non-pillar, while observing that all schools practice it. **[Study Quran]** These disagreements concern the legal category and consequence of omission, not whether saʿy is an established pilgrimage ritual. **[Maʿārif]**

The traditional account associates the movement between the hills with Hājar’s search for water for her son Ismāʿīl, when she ran between them in distress and God relieved her through the spring of Zamzam. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran reports this account as the traditional explanation for the rite’s origin. **[Study Quran]** Its spiritual lesson in Ibn Kathīr’s commentary is humility and reliance: the pilgrim remembers need, seeks God’s guidance and forgiveness, and asks to be kept firm on the straight path. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The account is not a substitute for the verse’s own legal explanation, which grounds the rite in God’s designation of these places. **[Ṭabarī]**

“Whoever volunteers good” is interpreted in several ways. Ibn Kathīr reports that it may mean extra circuits, voluntary ḥajj or ʿumrah, or good works more generally. **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī includes pilgrimage, circumambulation, prayer, fasting, and other acts done sincerely for God. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Jalālayn likewise understands the phrase as voluntary good beyond what is obligatory. **[Jalālayn]** The wording does not undo the preceding ritual command; it encourages additional goodness while leaving the juristic discussion of saʿy’s status visible. **[Qurṭubī]**

God is “Thankful, Knowing”: the commentaries explain that He recognizes even a small act and rewards it generously, while knowing the intention and quality behind it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran notes that gratitude here describes God’s rewarding response, not a need in God for human service. **[Study Quran]** The verse therefore assures pilgrims that the sincere effort of worship is neither overlooked nor wasted. **[Ṭabarī]**

Al-Ṭabarī emphasizes that the definite names Ṣafā and Marwah identify the two familiar hills within the sanctuary, rather than every rocky rise that might fit the words’ lexical roots. **[Ṭabarī]** He explains “rituals of God” as appointed signs at which people worship through supplication, remembrance, and prescribed acts. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī likewise treats the hills as known ritual places and connects the term *shaʿāʾir* with the marks of worship established for pilgrims. **[Qurṭubī]**

The wording “whoever performs ḥajj or ʿumrah” places the saʿy within a pilgrimage to the House. Al-Qurṭubī notes that ḥajj has the basic sense of intending or aiming for a destination, while ʿumrah has the sense of visiting; in religious use each refers to a defined set of rites. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Jalālayn also notes those lexical roots before explaining the ritual meaning. **[Jalālayn]** This helps distinguish the verse’s prescribed worship from an ordinary walk between two hills. **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** The rite turns a location once clouded by idolatrous associations into a sign of worship directed to God alone. **[Maʿārif]** The pilgrim’s movement is not an empty repetition; it recalls dependence, obedience, and the search for divine help. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The final promise broadens the lesson: every sincere act of good is known and generously received by God. **[Jalālayn]**
## 2:159

159159
*“Truly those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance—after We made it clear to mankind in the Book—are those who are cursed by God and cursed by the cursers,”*

**Meaning.** The verse warns people who deliberately conceal clear revelation after God has made it known. Al-Ṭabarī identifies the immediate referents as Jewish and Christian scholars who hid what their scriptures said about Muḥammad, his prophethood, and the truth of the religion he brought. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Jalālayn mentions the concealment of the Prophet’s description and of the ruling on stoning as examples associated with the verse. **[Jalālayn]** The Study Quran preserves both a specific reading about some People of the Book around the Prophet and a general reading that applies to anyone who obscures religious truth. **[Study Quran]**

“Clear proofs” and “guidance” include what God revealed to show the truth and direct people toward it. Al-Ṭabarī emphasizes the signs of Muḥammad’s mission described in the earlier scriptures and the evidence for the religion he was sent with. **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī extends the ruling to every person who conceals revealed knowledge that clarifies the straight path and distinguishes the way of salvation from error. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī likewise records both the specific reference to scriptural scholars and the general principle concerning anyone who hides religious knowledge that needs to be conveyed. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse therefore addresses a historical concealment while establishing a broader ethical responsibility. **[Maʿārif]**

The phrase “after We made it clear” makes the offense deliberate. The warning is not aimed at someone who does not know an answer or who honestly finds a matter uncertain; it concerns information made clear and then suppressed. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī describes the concealment as refusing to tell people what had been disclosed in the revealed books. **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī calls this a double wrong: withholding God’s guidance and deceiving those who need it. **[Saʿdī]** The seriousness lies not only in a speaker’s private failure but in the harm done to others’ understanding and religious choices. **[Maʿārif]**

The sources also distinguish concealment of clear guidance from the judgment that every piece of religious information must be announced indiscriminately to every audience. Al-Qurṭubī discusses the duty to teach needed truth, while also noting that difficult or potentially misunderstood material must be taught with discernment and in a manner suited to the hearer. **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif makes the same distinction: withholding a clear required truth is not the same as declining to burden an unprepared audience with intricate material likely to confuse it. **[Maʿārif]** This qualification does not excuse self-serving concealment; it concerns responsible teaching, not suppressing evidence to protect status or win an argument. **[Study Quran]**

“God curses them” means that He removes them from His mercy and favor. Al-Ṭabarī explains the root sense of the curse as expulsion and distance. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī similarly describes it as being distanced from divine reward. **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī relates the punishment to the harm done: those who push people away from guidance are themselves distanced from mercy. **[Saʿdī]** The statement is severe because the concealed material concerns people’s access to truth, not a trivial omission. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The “cursers” are identified differently in the transmitted explanations. Al-Ṭabarī records interpretations that include angels, believers, and creatures of the earth; al-Qurṭubī prefers angels and believers while also citing a report that includes animals. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran likewise notes these alternatives and also mentions the possibility that the inhabitants of Hell curse those who misled them. **[Study Quran]** These are reported interpretations of the phrase, not a license to claim that every creature’s response can be observed or described with certainty. **[Jalālayn]** The central sense remains that concealment provokes condemnation beyond the wrongdoer’s own community. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The duty to communicate knowledge appears in the warning reported about a person asked for knowledge that he possesses but conceals: such a person is threatened with a bridle of fire on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Ṭabarī notes that the report is authentic, and Ibn Kathīr cites it as a warning against hiding knowledge. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī uses the verse to support the obligation to convey truth when a person is asked about knowledge that should be made clear. **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif further notes that Abū Hurayrah invoked this verse when explaining why he transmitted prophetic reports. **[Maʿārif]**

The warning should not be narrowed to one ancient community, nor applied carelessly to every disagreement. **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī says the rule is general for anyone who hides clear revealed guidance, while the immediate occasion concerns concealment about the Messenger. **[Saʿdī]** The verse calls teachers and custodians of knowledge to honesty, and listeners to seek clarity without mistaking uncertainty or responsible explanation for deliberate concealment. **[Jalālayn]**

The earlier passage at 2:146 says that some among the People of the Book recognized the Prophet as they recognized their own sons, yet concealed the truth knowingly. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī connects the present warning to that concealment of the Messenger’s description and mission in the revealed books. **[Ṭabarī]** The Study Quran observes that the wording can apply to a particular group around the Prophet while retaining a general import for anyone who conceals religious truth. **[Study Quran]**

Al-Qurṭubī further explains that “clear proofs and guidance” can include both explicit revealed texts and guidance established through sound interpretation. **[Qurṭubī]** His discussion grounds the duty in the need for people to receive truth that they are entitled to know, while preserving discernment about how complex material is taught. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse’s “Book” can refer to the revealed scriptures as a whole, not merely one physical volume. **[Qurṭubī]** This broadens the ethical lesson beyond the immediate dispute without erasing its historical setting. **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** Knowledge entrusted to a person can become a means of guidance or a means of misguidance, depending on whether it is communicated truthfully. **[Maʿārif]** Concealing a clear proof for personal advantage harms both faith and community. **[Ṭabarī]** The next verse will show that even this grave wrong is not beyond repentance when the offender returns, repairs the damage, and makes the truth clear. **[Saʿdī]**
## 2:160

160160
*“Save such as repent, and make amends, and make clear. They are those unto whom I relent. And I am the Relenting, the Merciful.”*

**Meaning.** The exception follows the severe warning against concealing revealed guidance. It shows that the door of repentance remains open: those who repent, make amends, and make clear are not left under the condemnation stated in the previous verse. Al-Ṭabarī explains the immediate case as people who had hidden the signs of Muḥammad’s prophethood, then returned to faith, affirmed his message, repaired their conduct, and disclosed what their scriptures said about him. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr likewise says that the exception includes those who regret concealment, correct their behavior, and explain to people what they had hidden. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The three verbs name connected parts of a real change. “Repent” means to turn back from the wrong with regret and a decision to leave it. As-Saʿdī describes it as remorse, cessation, and resolve not to return. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī says the claim “I have repented” is not enough if later conduct shows no difference from the earlier state. **[Qurṭubī]** Jalālayn similarly links repentance with turning away from those deeds. **[Jalālayn]** The verse asks for a changed direction, not a verbal formula that leaves the offense untouched. **[Maʿārif]**

“Make amends” adds positive reform. As-Saʿdī stresses that stopping an evil is not the whole of repentance; the person must also restore what was damaged through good action. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī gives examples: a person who abandoned faith returns to Islam openly, while a sinner shows righteous conduct and leaves corrupt practices. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr understands the phrase as correcting one’s behavior after the concealment. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The repair should correspond to the wrong: where people were misled, private regret alone cannot give them back the truth that was withheld. **[Maʿārif]**

That is why the verse adds “and make clear.” In the immediate context, al-Ṭabarī says the repentant must explain what God revealed about the Messenger and the duty to follow him, instead of continuing to hide it. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records the interpretation that they should disclose what was in the Torah concerning Muḥammad, while preferring the broader sense of showing the opposite of the concealment they practiced. **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī likewise says that a former concealer must make known the truth previously hidden and openly reverse the earlier deception. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran notes that “make clear” is understood to mean addressing and clarifying what had been concealed. **[Study Quran]**

This requirement protects the verse from being read as a purely private transaction. If the harm involved misleading a community, repentance includes a public correction proportionate to that harm. **[Maʿārif]** A person who once obscured the evidence must now help restore people’s access to it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** This does not require disclosing every complex detail to every listener: the commentaries on the prior verse distinguish clear guidance that must be communicated from intricate material requiring judgment about how it is taught. **[Qurṭubī]** But such prudence cannot be used as a pretext to continue hiding a clear truth for advantage. **[Saʿdī]**

“Those are the ones toward whom I relent” describes God’s acceptance of their return. Al-Ṭabarī notes the apparent reciprocity: how can God turn toward those who have already turned back? He explains that the servant’s repentance and God’s acceptance occur together, and the wording assures the repentant of divine welcome. **[Ṭabarī]** The Study Quran observes that the same root is used for the human act of repentance and the divine act of relenting, with different prepositions. **[Study Quran]** God’s acceptance is described as mercy and pardon for the one who truly returns, not as a reward that a human act can compel. **[Ṭabarī]**

The names “the Relenting, the Merciful” reinforce that assurance. Al-Qurṭubī explains that God repeatedly accepts those who turn back and shows mercy to them. **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī says God guides the sinner toward repentance and then accepts that repentance through generosity and kindness. **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr notes that even those who previously called people toward innovation or disbelief can be forgiven if they sincerely repent. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The passage condemns concealment firmly without declaring that the wrongdoer is permanently beyond forgiveness. **[Jalālayn]**

The order of the exception is also important: repentance is accompanied by reform and clarification. **[Ṭabarī]** Belief alone does not erase the duty to correct the effects of a public wrong, and a bare announcement of regret does not equal a reformed life. **[Saʿdī]** At the same time, the verse does not deny the possibility of change; its promise is explicit for those who undertake it. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The three-part response also explains what makes the exception meaningful: a person turns away from the concealment, repairs the conduct that enabled it, and reverses the silence by making the truth clear. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī says that the general reading is preferable: people should show the opposite of what they previously did. **[Qurṭubī]** In the immediate setting, al-Ṭabarī names ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and other People of the Book who accepted the Messenger and disclosed what they had formerly hidden as examples of those who returned. **[Ṭabarī]**

Al-Ṭabarī explains “I turn toward them” as God returning the hearts of His servants who had turned away, guiding them back to obedience, then covering their former wrong with pardon. **[Ṭabarī]** The promise looks beyond the first moment of regret to a restored relationship: the servant returns to God, and God receives that return with mercy. **[Maʿārif]** The next verse’s warning concerns those who persist in disbelief until death, which makes clear that the exception here is a genuine alternative to remaining under the condemnation. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Reflection.** The verse joins accountability with hope. **[Maʿārif]** One who has hidden the truth can return, repair what was damaged, and become a source of clarity rather than confusion. **[Study Quran]** God’s mercy is presented not as approval of concealment but as the welcome offered to a sincere and constructive repentance. **[Qurṭubī]**

## 2:161

161161
*“Truly, those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers—the curse of God, the angels, and mankind, all together, is upon them.”*

**Meaning.** This verse completes the warning about people who conceal revealed guidance and then refuse it. Its decisive phrase is “and die as disbelievers”: the condemnation describes those who persist in unbelief through death, not everyone who has ever been an unbeliever regardless of what they later do. Al-Ṭabarī reads it in continuity with the preceding account of concealment, while Ibn Kathīr likewise explains that the exception in 2:160 belongs to those who repent and reform, and this threat concerns those who do not return. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The placement therefore holds together two truths: the warning is severe, but the call to repent remains open during life. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The sources give more than one account of whom “those who disbelieve” describes in the immediate setting. Al-Ṭabarī records that it can include Jews, Christians, and the idolaters who rejected the Messenger, and also preserves explanations tied more specifically to the People of the Book who concealed what they knew. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī similarly reports that the verse may concern Jews and Christians, while its wording is general enough to include all who die in disbelief. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran notes the relation to the previous warning against concealing signs and guidance, but does not confine the moral scope to a single historical group. **[Study Quran]** These readings are compatible if the historical occasion is distinguished from the verse’s wider description. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The Arabic expression for being cursed, *laʿnah*, is explained by the commentators as being driven away or excluded from divine mercy. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī notes the same core sense, and Maʿārif emphasizes that the verse describes a grave distance from God’s mercy rather than a passing rebuke. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The repetition of the word “curse” in the following verse will stress the lasting consequence for those who die in that state. **[Jalālayn]** The verse does not describe a curse as a human power to determine someone’s final standing; its subject is God’s judgment, accompanied by the testimony of the angels and people. **[Study Quran]**

The three groups named—God, the angels, and mankind—make the condemnation comprehensive. **[Ṭabarī]** The phrase “all together” has been understood in several ways: that all people on the Day of Resurrection curse them, that believers do so, or that people in general call down condemnation upon those who oppress and corrupt. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records multiple explanations of “mankind” and discusses whether the wording refers to all people or the people of faith. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran likewise notes a range of explanations rather than requiring one narrow identification. **[Study Quran]** Al-Jalālayn takes the phrase as the curse of all people, while Ibn Kathīr underscores that the curse includes God, angels, and believers. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

Al-Ṭabarī prefers an expansive reading in which people generally curse those whose wrongdoing becomes manifest; this helps explain the universal language without asserting that every individual has uttered a curse in this world. **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī reads the verse as a declaration that the curse reaches them from God and from the angels and believers. **[Saʿdī]** The shared point is that their rejection is not a private disagreement that leaves the moral order untouched. **[Maʿārif]** It is an offense against the truth that God revealed, and its consequences are recognized in the judgment of the unseen and the judgment of those who see its full effects. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The word “upon them” pictures the curse as settled upon the people described, not as a momentary feeling that they can dismiss. **[Jalālayn]** The following verse clarifies the force of that image by describing their abiding in the curse and receiving no respite. **[Ṭabarī]** At the same time, the condition “die as disbelievers” prevents the warning from being turned into a claim that repentance is impossible. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The previous verse explicitly names those who repent, repair, and make clear as people whom God accepts. **[Saʿdī]** The contrast is between two trajectories—persistent concealment and return—not between fixed ethnic communities. **[Maʿārif]**

**Context.** The immediate passage has moved from concealment of guidance (2:159), through the possibility of repentance and clarification (2:160), to the fate of those who refuse that return. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī says the verse’s severity is connected with suppressing revealed evidence, though the general wording encompasses disbelievers more broadly. **[Qurṭubī]** This sequence keeps the accusation historically intelligible while making the warning relevant wherever people knowingly reject guidance. **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The verse speaks of the end of a life’s response to truth, not of the first moment of doubt or of a person’s status as judged by other humans. **[Saʿdī]** A reader is directed to the distinction the passage itself makes: concealment and disbelief call for repentance, and sincere repentance must be joined with repair and truth-telling. **[Maʿārif]** The warning is serious precisely because the opportunity to return is meaningful while a person is alive. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Its final horizon is God’s judgment, beyond the incomplete verdicts of worldly communities. **[Ṭabarī]**

The disagreement about “mankind, all together” is a reminder to separate the certainty of the verse’s judgment from uncertainty about every human response to it. **[Qurṭubī]** Some explanations take the curse to be voiced by all people on the Day of Resurrection, while others understand it as the condemnation of believers or of people who recognize wrongdoing. **[Ṭabarī]** These are ways of explaining the scope of the expression; they do not change the central claim that rejection ending in death without faith places a person under divine condemnation. **[Study Quran]** The passage also prevents a reader from confusing the communal recognition of wrongdoing with a personal license to declare a named person’s final fate. **[Maʿārif]**
## 2:162

162162
*“Abiding therein. The punishment shall not be lightened for them, nor shall they be granted respite.”*

**Meaning.** This verse continues the sentence begun in 2:161 and describes the lasting consequence for those who die in disbelief. “Abiding therein” is read by the commentators with more than one possible antecedent: it may refer to remaining under the curse, or to abiding in the Fire that is the consequence of that curse. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records both readings, and al-Jalālayn makes the connection explicit by mentioning both the curse and the Fire. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that the curse is joined to the punishment of Hell, so the phrase communicates a real and continuing penalty rather than an abstract denunciation. **[Ṭabarī]**

The word translated “abiding” conveys continuance, not a short interval after which the warning expires. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr similarly reads the verse as a description of the disbelievers’ enduring punishment, while the Study Quran links it to the unrelieved curse announced in the previous verse. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The passage’s scope remains governed by the preceding condition: these are people who die rejecting faith, not people who repent during life. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** That qualification matters because 2:160 has just held out divine acceptance for those who turn back and make amends. **[Ṭabarī]**

“They shall not be lightened from the punishment” denies relief in its intensity. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that their chastisement is not reduced so that they can find rest; al-Qurṭubī likewise treats the line as a denial of any lessening of the punishment. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr emphasizes that the verse describes no easing for the people who persist to death in disbelief. **[Ibn Kathīr]** This is not a measure of every experience of distress in the world but a statement about the final judgment described in the passage. **[Study Quran]**

The second clause, “nor shall they be granted respite,” can be rendered as no delay or no postponement. **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators explain that they will not be given a period in which to escape the consequence, offer a plea that reverses their state, or begin a new life of repentance after the judgment has arrived. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Saʿdī says the sentence removes hope of a later reprieve, while Ibn Kathīr relates it to the punishment continuing without a break. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Maʿārif stresses that worldly postponement must not be mistaken for divine neglect: the verse’s point is that the final reckoning will not be indefinitely deferred. **[Maʿārif]**

There is a difference between God allowing a person time in this life and granting a respite after the final judgment. **[Study Quran]** The former can be an opportunity to reflect, repent, and correct conduct; the latter is what the verse denies to those who meet death in persistent disbelief. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** This distinction prevents the verse from being read as though the call to repentance in the previous verse were insincere or pointless. **[Qurṭubī]** The passage sets out a genuine alternative: return while the opportunity remains, or face the outcome of refusing it. **[Maʿārif]**

The commentators also connect the verse to the wording of 2:161. Al-Ṭabarī explains the pronoun as referring to the people under the curse; al-Qurṭubī observes that the same language may be understood of those abiding in the Fire. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Either way, the relation between curse and punishment is close: exclusion from divine mercy is made concrete in the lasting chastisement described here. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran notes the continuity of the two verses and the way 2:162 completes the warning rather than introducing a separate group. **[Study Quran]**

The verse’s short clauses make its point by removing both forms of imagined relief: neither the severity nor the duration is reduced. **[Jalālayn]** One clause addresses the degree of the punishment; the other denies a pause that could be mistaken for release. **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī reads them as a comprehensive statement of the punishment’s permanence for those described. **[Saʿdī]** This is why the qualification in 2:161 must stay in view: the verse is not a license to announce an individual’s fate, but a warning about dying in unbelief. **[Qurṭubī]**

**Reflection.** The two verses together oppose both complacency and despair. **[Maʿārif]** They warn against assuming that a person can safely postpone every response to revelation, while the preceding exception preserves hope for the one who truly repents. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The text directs attention to the seriousness of a final, unrepented rejection, not to speculation about the unseen status of particular people. **[Study Quran]** The opportunity that remains in life should be used for truthful return and repair. **[Saʿdī]**

The two denials in the verse answer different imagined escapes. **[Qurṭubī]** A person might hope that a punishment described as lasting could at least become easier, or that a pause would eventually allow a new appeal; the wording rejects both hopes for those described. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Jalālayn explains “they shall not be granted respite” as there being no delay that would permit another plea or apology after the judgment has come. **[Jalālayn]** The verse therefore closes the future opening that its preceding exception leaves open in earthly life: repentance belongs to the time when a person can still turn back, not to an imagined interval after the final consequence. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

This closure also clarifies why the phrase “abiding therein” is joined to the two statements about punishment. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The duration is not presented apart from its quality: there is no relief in intensity and no postponement in time. **[Study Quran]** Al-Qurṭubī’s note that the pronoun may refer to the curse or to the Fire keeps the image tied to the preceding verse, where divine condemnation and punishment are placed together. **[Qurṭubī]** The commentary thus explains the sentence’s continuity without changing its subject. **[Ṭabarī]**
## 2:163

163163
*“Your God is One God; there is no god but He, the Compassionate, the Merciful.”*

**Meaning.** After describing the fate of persistent disbelief, the passage returns to the central truth that grounds the whole chapter: the one whom people are commanded to worship is the only true God. Al-Ṭabarī explains “your God” as the one worthy of worship and obedience, not merely a deity whom people happen to acknowledge. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī likewise reads “there is no god but He” as negating every claim to divinity apart from God. **[Qurṭubī]** The statement therefore joins two affirmations: God is one, and worship belongs to Him alone. **[Jalālayn]**

The word *ilāh* carries the sense of one who is worshipped; the verse does not say that no created thing can ever be called a god by its worshippers, but that no one besides God possesses the right to divine worship. **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī stresses that nothing in creation shares God’s right to be worshipped, because all created beings depend upon Him. **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif explains the uniqueness in relation to God’s essence, attributes, and acts, while the Study Quran emphasizes the verse’s force as a proclamation of divine unity. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** This distinction helps explain why the Qur’an can speak of people taking rivals while denying that those rivals possess any real divine status. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The declaration of oneness is not an isolated slogan. The following verse points to the created world as a set of signs for reflective people, so that the confession of one God is joined to contemplation of the order and provision of the universe. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī connects the signs in 2:164 with the proof of the Creator’s oneness announced here. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī says that the verse answers those who wondered how one God could suffice for all people, and reports that the Quraysh asked for a sign of the claim. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran records the relationship between the challenge of monotheism and the signs that follow, while noting reports that the opponents asked for a miraculous demonstration. **[Study Quran]** The varied reports are background explanations, not a reason to restrict the verse’s argument to one occasion. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The description “One God” is then reinforced by the exclusive phrase “there is no god but He.” **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that this denies partners and equals in worship, while al-Qurṭubī notes that the construction combines a general negation with the affirmation of God alone. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The point is not that other beings do not exist, but that none of them is a deity entitled to worship. **[Maʿārif]** The statement dismantles the logic of seeking intermediaries as independent powers, a theme developed when the next verse describes people taking rivals and loving them as they should love God. **[Saʿdī]**

The two divine names at the end of the verse—*al-Raḥmān* and *al-Raḥīm*, “the Compassionate” and “the Merciful”—place the affirmation of unity beside mercy. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī explains the names through God’s extensive and continuing mercy, while Ibn Kathīr notes that the verse gathers the proclamation of oneness with the names of compassion. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī describes God as the source of blessings and care for creation, so that His mercy is not a remote abstraction but is known through the gifts that sustain life. **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif similarly relates the names to the mercy that reaches creatures, while affirming that divine mercy is not simply identical to the limited affection of created beings. **[Maʿārif]**

The placement of mercy after oneness also corrects the idea that exclusive worship means a distant or indifferent God. **[Study Quran]** The verse presents the one God as merciful, and the signs in 2:164 include rain, provision, and the sustaining order of life. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** These gifts do not turn nature into a deity; they point beyond themselves to the one who brings them into being and directs them. **[Saʿdī]** The believer’s response is therefore gratitude and worship of the Giver rather than attachment to created means as independent powers. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

Al-Qurṭubī records an account in which the claim that God is one was challenged by the many objects of worship in Arabia; his point is that numerical abundance among idols does not establish divine reality. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran notes that the Qur’an’s insistence on divine unity is not merely a denial of statues but an argument against assigning divine power or ultimate devotion to any created being. **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī explains that the created world itself cannot be a set of equal gods, because its creatures are needy while God alone is complete and independent. **[Saʿdī]** The verse’s singular pronouns repeatedly return attention to the one who is truly worshipped. **[Maʿārif]**

**Belief.** The verse establishes *tawḥīd*: God alone is worthy of worship, and His unity is not shared by partners. **[Ṭabarī]** It also places mercy among the attributes by which God is known, so that worship is grounded in recognition of both His exclusive divinity and His care for creation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The following catalogue of signs elaborates the first claim by directing reason toward the one Creator and Sustainer. **[Jalālayn]**

**Reflection.** The verse compresses a complete orientation into a few words: recognize the one God, reject rivals, and remember that the one worshipped is merciful. **[Saʿdī]** Its affirmation prepares the reader to see the world not as an independent source of power but as a field of signs pointing to its Creator. **[Study Quran]**
## 2:164

164164
*“Truly, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, the ships that sail upon the sea with what benefits mankind, the water God sends down from the sky with which He revives the earth after its death and scatters every kind of creature upon it, the turning of the winds, and the clouds compelled between heaven and earth—surely there are signs for a people who understand.”*

**Meaning.** This verse follows the declaration that God alone is divine by presenting signs in the created world that direct reflection toward the Creator and Sustainer. Al-Ṭabarī explains that these phenomena are proofs of God’s oneness and power for people who use their understanding. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī calls attention to the many signs gathered into one sentence, while as-Saʿdī says that they show God’s knowledge, wisdom, mercy, and care. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse does not ask the reader to worship nature; it asks the reader to notice what the natural order indicates about the one who creates and directs it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The first sign is “the creation of the heavens and the earth.” **[Jalālayn]** The commentators take this as the vast created order above and below, including its size, arrangement, and benefits. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that the heavens and earth are signs in themselves through their structure and the order God has established in them. **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī emphasizes that their creation from nothing, their magnitude, and their continuing arrangement point to the Creator’s perfect power and wisdom. **[Saʿdī]** The language is broad rather than a technical account of physical origins; its invitation is to reflect on creation as a whole. **[Maʿārif]**

The alternation of night and day is a second sign. **[Ṭabarī]** The verse points to their repeated succession and the different conditions each brings: darkness and rest in one part of the cycle, light and activity in another. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī notes the regularity and variation in the duration of night and day across times and places, which make them useful for rest, work, and measuring time. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran likewise understands the cycle as an ordered sign in which contrasts are governed rather than random. **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī links the arrangement to the needs and well-being of creatures. **[Saʿdī]**

The ships sailing at sea carry “what benefits mankind.” **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī explains the phrase as cargo and goods that people transport for their livelihood, while Ibn Kathīr also notes that vessels travel from region to region and serve human needs. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī observes that ships are human-made means of travel, yet their movement depends on the water and conditions God has created and subjected to use. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran points out that the verse includes human commerce among its signs, not only phenomena untouched by human activity. **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī adds that navigation and the transport of provisions are blessings made possible by a world whose elements are fitted to human life. **[Saʿdī]**

Rain is described as water sent down from the sky. **[Ṭabarī]** The verse stresses what follows: God revives the earth after its apparent death. **[Qurṭubī]** The earth’s barrenness gives way to vegetation and provision, which Ibn Kathīr presents as a sign of both divine mercy and the possibility of resurrection. **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī says that the revival of land after rain resembles the revival of the dead, while showing God’s power to restore life. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran notes the recurring Qur’anic use of rain and revived earth as an analogy for resurrection. **[Study Quran]** The verse does not claim that every dry field has the same cause or outcome; it directs attention to the renewing process as a sign. **[Maʿārif]**

The phrase “and scatters every kind of creature upon it” extends the sign from vegetation to living beings. **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators understand *dābbah* as creatures that move or live upon the earth, whose variety and provision display the breadth of divine creation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** Ibn Kathīr explains that God brings forth creatures of many kinds and sustains them through what the earth produces. **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī adds that their different forms, needs, and modes of life invite recognition of the Creator’s wisdom. **[Saʿdī]** The wording is expansive without requiring readers to supply an exhaustive inventory of every species. **[Study Quran]**

The “turning of the winds” is another sign of divine direction. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records interpretations that describe winds by their directions, qualities, or effects, including winds that bring benefit and winds associated with hardship. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran notes that the Arabic can encompass variation in direction and character. **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī says the winds carry rain, move clouds, and serve other purposes that sustain life, while their changing conditions also show that they are subject to command rather than independent powers. **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr connects the winds with the movement and delivery of rain-bearing clouds. **[Ibn Kathīr]** These examples illustrate the sign; they are not a fixed exhaustive classification of every wind. **[Maʿārif]**

Finally, the verse describes clouds “compelled between heaven and earth.” **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that clouds are directed and held in their course by God. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that *musakhkhar* means subjected or directed, not that clouds are motionless; they move while remaining under the order God has established. **[Qurṭubī]** The clouds carry water and travel through the atmosphere in ways that people cannot command at will. **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī sees in their gathering, movement, and release of rain a sign of wisdom and mercy. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran emphasizes their place between sky and earth as a visible link in the cycle of rainfall and terrestrial life. **[Study Quran]**

The verse ends by specifying the audience: “a people who understand.” **[Ṭabarī]** The signs are present to sight, but their theological meaning becomes clear through reflection. **[Maʿārif]** As-Saʿdī says that the verse calls people to consider these phenomena and recognize that the one who created and directs them alone deserves worship. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī reads the phrase as praise for those who use reason to infer the Creator from what has been created. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran notes the connection with 2:163: the signs that follow the declaration of one God furnish a reasoned response to those who reject it. **[Study Quran]**

**Context.** Al-Qurṭubī and other commentators report that people challenged the proclamation of one God and asked for a sign; reports differ about the precise occasion, and some connect it with demands for a visible miracle. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī does not make the verse’s proof depend on a single report: its wording itself calls attention to the signs available in the world. **[Ṭabarī]** Whether or not one accepts a particular occasion report, the passage moves from the affirmation of divine unity to a series of reasons for recognizing it. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Reflection.** The catalogue ranges from cosmic order to trade, rain, living creatures, winds, and clouds. **[Saʿdī]** It therefore trains attention to see both vast patterns and ordinary benefits as signs, without confusing the means with the Giver. **[Maʿārif]** Reasoned reflection is presented as a path to worship and gratitude, not as a substitute for them. **[Jalālayn]**
## 2:165

165165
*“Yet among mankind are those who take rivals apart from God, loving them as they should love God. But those who believe are stronger in love for God. If only those who do wrong could see, when they see the punishment, that all power belongs to God, and that God is severe in punishment.”*

**Meaning.** The verse turns from signs that point to one God to the human response that contradicts them: some people take *andād*, rivals or equals, apart from God. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī reports that these rivals may be idols, but also records explanations that include human leaders obeyed in disobedience to God. **[Qurṭubī]** likewise relates the phrase to idols and to people who are followed as if their authority could compete with revelation. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran notes that the term can encompass any object of devotion or obedience treated as a rival to God. **[Study Quran]** The verse does not claim that these created beings truly share God’s power; it describes the status people assign them. **[Saʿdī]**

As-Saʿdī emphasizes the verb “take”: no actual equal to God exists, but people can designate a creature as a rival through their worship and attachment. **[Saʿdī]** A creature cannot be God’s equal in creating, providing, or governing, because it is itself created and dependent. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Maʿārif similarly explains that the verse condemns assigning partners in worship, not an equality in the work of creation. **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran distinguishes the real Creator from the rivals that human beings construct in belief and practice. **[Study Quran]** This keeps the verse’s accusation focused on misplaced devotion rather than on the metaphysical existence of a second god. **[Ṭabarī]**

“They love them as they should love God” has been interpreted in more than one related way. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī records that idolaters love their objects of worship with a love comparable to the believers’ love for God; he also gives the interpretation that they divide the love due to God between Him and the rivals. **[Qurṭubī]** notes both explanations and observes that the next clause, praising believers’ stronger love for God, supports the comparison of the two kinds of attachment. **[Study Quran]** describes this love as involving reverence and devotion, not merely an inward feeling. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The word “love” here therefore concerns where a person places ultimate allegiance and worship. **[Jalālayn]**

The verse contrasts that divided devotion with the believers, who are “stronger in love for God.” **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī explains this as a more intense and enduring attachment to God than the polytheists’ attachment to their rivals. **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī says believers direct their love to the one who truly deserves it, whereas the idolaters attach themselves to what cannot provide the good they seek. **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif emphasizes that faith gathers the heart’s love upon God rather than scattering it among dependent beings. **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran notes that this contrast is not a denial of ordinary affection for family or creation; it concerns the love that becomes worshipful or ultimate. **[Study Quran]**

The verse then asks the hearer to imagine the wrongdoers seeing the punishment. **[Qurṭubī]** The Arabic reading may be rendered as “if only those who did wrong could see” or “if you could see those who did wrong,” and the commentators discuss the difference. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records readings that address the Prophet directly and readings that state the wrongdoers’ own seeing; al-Jalālayn explains the clause as a counterfactual whose consequence is left for the listener to infer. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** The Study Quran notes the alternate grammatical possibilities while preserving the shared scene of punishment becoming visible. **[Study Quran]**

At that moment, they will know that “all power belongs to God.” **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that the power, command, and ability they imagined their rivals possessed belong to God alone. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The idols and leaders cannot shield their followers or alter the judgment. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī reads the clause as a disclosure of God’s complete power when the punishment is witnessed. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran relates it to the collapse of the false confidence that rivals could mediate independently or rescue their devotees. **[Study Quran]**

“God is severe in punishment” completes the warning. **[Jalālayn]** As-Saʿdī says the severity becomes manifest when the wrongdoers see what their misplaced love has brought about. **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr explains that the verse warns those who associate partners with God and refuse the truth. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Maʿārif connects the warning with the failure of the rivals to provide any benefit at the very point when their followers most need help. **[Maʿārif]** The verse does not invite speculation about the details of punishment; it emphasizes that no rival can reduce it. **[Ṭabarī]**

**Belief.** The passage distinguishes loving created beings in ordinary, lawful ways from assigning them the devotion and obedience that belong to God. **[Qurṭubī]** A love that becomes worship, or that treats a creature’s claim as overriding God’s guidance, is the kind of rival-making the verse condemns. **[Saʿdī]** Believers’ stronger love is rooted in recognizing God as the true source of benefit and the only possessor of ultimate power. **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks what receives a person’s deepest trust when competing claims arise. **[Study Quran]** A created being may be loved, respected, or followed in what is right, but it cannot replace the Creator or promise rescue apart from Him. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The imagined scene of punishment strips away the false security of rivals and exposes where power always lay. **[Ṭabarī]**

The contrast in “stronger in love” is not a command to measure private feeling against another person’s. **[Study Quran]** It contrasts the believers’ devotion to God with the idolaters’ attachment to rivals, which could be expressed through worship, reliance, or obedience. **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī explains that the believer’s love is better directed because its object truly deserves complete love and leads to the person’s well-being, whereas attachment to false rivals harms their followers. **[Saʿdī]** This reading keeps the comparison within the verse’s argument about worship, while leaving ordinary affection for family and other created beings outside its accusation. **[Maʿārif]**
## 2:166

166166
*“When those who were followed disavow those who followed them, and they see the punishment, and all bonds between them are cut off.”*

**Meaning.** This verse depicts the collapse of the relationships described in 2:165 when the people who trusted rivals confront the punishment. Al-Ṭabarī explains “those who were followed” as leaders and chiefs who were obeyed in disbelief; he also reports an interpretation involving devils who misled people. **[Ṭabarī]** He prefers a wording broad enough to include all who were followed in disbelief, rather than limiting it to one class of leader. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī likewise mentions human chiefs and devils among the possible referents. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran presents the same range—leaders, satans, or all who led others into error. **[Study Quran]** Ibn Kathīr illustrates the scope with angels and jinn who, according to other Qur’anic passages, disavow those who claimed to worship them (28:63; 34:41); these examples are not the verse’s only possible referent. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

“The followers” are those who accepted the guidance or example of such leaders. **[Jalālayn]** Ibn Kathīr explains that the leaders disown their adherents after having misled them, while Maʿārif pictures both groups seeing the punishment and repudiating the relationship that once joined them. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The text can describe a broad pattern of following error, not just one historical group or one specific form of idolatry. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** What united them was a bond formed around a path that could not survive the disclosure of its consequences. **[Saʿdī]**

The phrase “they disavow them” can include a denial of responsibility: the leaders reject those who had followed them, and the followers discover that their supposed patrons will not stand by them. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī reads the separation as a mutual abandonment when both sides see the punishment. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr stresses the reversal of worldly allegiance: the leaders no longer claim the followers, and the followers cannot obtain help from the leaders. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran notes that the scene exposes the failure of relationships built on error. **[Study Quran]** The verse does not present the leaders’ denial as an exoneration of their followers; the next verse shows the followers taking responsibility through regret, even as they wish they could return. **[Saʿdī]**

“They see the punishment” explains the moment when the former ties collapse. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Qurṭubī records that the scene may be understood as occurring when the punishment is witnessed after resurrection, though commentators also discuss the timing of the separation. **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif emphasizes that the reality of punishment strips away the confidence and cooperation that had held the relationship together. **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran frames the sight of punishment as the point at which recourse to human or satanic guides is revealed to be futile. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī’s broader interpretation avoids making the verse depend on a single chronology or class of misleader. **[Ṭabarī]**

The final phrase, “all bonds between them are cut off,” translates *al-asbāb*, a word with several related meanings. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī records explanations that include affection, kinship, connections, and the means by which one might obtain help; he concludes broadly that the causes on which they relied are severed. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī describes the ties of love and alliance that joined them in the world. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Jalālayn identifies the broken ties as affection and kinship, while Ibn Kathīr emphasizes friendships that had been formed apart from God’s obedience. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The range of meanings matters because the verse’s point is not limited to one social relation. **[Study Quran]** Family connection, political loyalty, affection, and other worldly ties cannot provide rescue when they were treated as a substitute for truth. **[Maʿārif]** As-Saʿdī says that the bonds disappear because they were established on falsehood and not on obedience to God. **[Saʿdī]** The text does not condemn every human relationship; it distinguishes bonds that serve good from alliances that invite people into error. **[Qurṭubī]** The Qur’an elsewhere describes faithful friends as enemies to one another on that Day except for the God-conscious (43:67), a contrast noted by the commentators. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

A second explanation of *asbāb* concerns the deeds or means by which people expected to benefit. **[Ṭabarī]** The Study Quran notes that the word can refer to deeds that remain effective when righteous, but are cut off when evil. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī’s broad formulation includes the failure of every relied-upon cause that cannot avert the punishment. **[Ṭabarī]** This keeps the phrase connected to the previous verse: idols, leaders, and loyalties all fail when their followers discover that they possess no independent power. **[Saʿdī]**

**Context.** The scene follows the warning that people gave rivals a share of the love due to God. **[Qurṭubī]** The relationships once treated as proof of security are now tested by the reality of judgment. **[Maʿārif]** The followers cannot transfer their accountability to the leaders, and the leaders cannot make their false teachings effective by disowning those who accepted them. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Reflection.** A relationship is not a refuge merely because it is powerful or long-standing. **[Study Quran]** The verse asks whether the bonds that shape a person’s life lead toward truth and accountability, or merely reinforce a shared error. **[Saʿdī]** Whatever is founded on falsehood cannot serve as an ultimate means of rescue. **[Ṭabarī]**

The commentators also consider when the disavowal takes place. **[Qurṭubī]** Some explanations locate the breaking of the relationship at death, when the person leaves the worldly attachments on which he relied; others place the scene at the resurrection, when the leaders and followers see the punishment together. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse itself emphasizes the result rather than requiring a single timetable: the ties no longer function as means of protection. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī’s broad reading of “those who were followed” supports this emphasis, since many kinds of worldly guide and follower can discover that their alliance has no power in the Hereafter. **[Ṭabarī]**

The image of severed bonds is especially sharp because the same *asbāb* that once seemed to connect people to security are now visibly ineffective. **[Maʿārif]** It does not say that every memory of affection disappears, but that affection, kinship, leadership, and other causes cannot purchase escape from judgment when they were treated as a substitute for obedience to God. **[Qurṭubī]** This reading allows the verse to warn against false allegiance without declaring family affection or companionship intrinsically blameworthy. **[Saʿdī]**
## 2:167

167167
*“Those who followed will say, ‘If only we could return once more, then we would disavow them as they have disavowed us.’ Thus God will show them their deeds as regrets for them, and they will not come out of the Fire.”*

**Meaning.** The followers speak after the leaders have disowned them and their worldly bonds have been severed. **[Ṭabarī]** Their wish—“if only we could return”—is a desire to go back to earthly life, where they imagine they could reject the leaders who misled them. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Qurṭubī explains the conditional phrase as an optative wish, not as a promise that return will be granted. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr likewise understands it as regret voiced after the truth of the punishment has become visible. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran connects the wish with the followers’ desire to disown the people they once obeyed. **[Study Quran]**

Their proposed reversal does not undo their responsibility. **[Saʿdī]** As-Saʿdī says that the followers’ regret comes too late and that their wish should not be mistaken for proof that they would truly reform if returned; elsewhere the Qur’an says that people returned to worldly life would go back to what they had been forbidden (6:28). **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī records the wish as part of the scene of regret, while Maʿārif describes it as anger and disappointment at the leaders who have abandoned them. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse exposes the painful recognition that blaming a guide does not erase one’s own choice to follow. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The promise “thus God will show them their deeds as regrets” has received more than one explanation. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī prefers the reading that God shows them the evil deeds they committed, which then become a source of grief and remorse. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records this view and also mentions interpretations in which they are shown the good deeds they failed to perform, or the reward they have lost. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran likewise preserves alternatives: the deeds may be their actual misdeeds, or the good works they neglected and can no longer recover. **[Study Quran]** These readings converge on the regret of seeing one’s former choices clearly when it is too late to change them. **[Saʿdī]**

The wording may also be understood as God showing them the consequences of their actions, so that what they expected to help them becomes a source of anguish. **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī says that the works they hoped would bring benefit turn into regret because they were attached to false objects of devotion and cannot deliver the promised outcome. **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif stresses the painful contrast between the followers’ worldly expectations and the reality they now see. **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran notes that the phrase links the experience of remorse to the deeds themselves rather than to an arbitrary punishment unrelated to their choices. **[Study Quran]**

Al-Jalālayn explains the verse’s “thus” as a comparison: just as God shows them the severity of punishment and their mutual disavowal, He will show them the deeds that become regrets. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that the expression can describe the way the consequences are made visible to them. **[Qurṭubī]** Their regret is not merely a passing emotion; it is recognition of an irretrievable loss. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī’s preferred explanation keeps the focus on the evil actions they performed, while the alternative readings underscore the same finality from the perspective of omitted good. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

“They will not come out of the Fire” closes the scene with the fate of the disbelievers being described. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī connects the pronoun to those who rejected God and followed the false path under discussion. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr says they will remain in the punishment, and al-Qurṭubī treats the statement as the end of the passage’s warning about the consequences of disbelief. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The line should be read with the stated condition of dying in disbelief, rather than generalized to every person who has sinned or who experiences regret. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

The three verses form a connected account: the rivals fail, leaders and followers separate, and the followers wish they could undo their allegiance. **[Ṭabarī]** The connection shows why the false attachments are described as *andād*: they received a kind of love and reliance that could not survive judgment. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran points to the wider Qur’anic theme that people who followed one another in error dispute and disavow each other in the Hereafter. **[Study Quran]** The scene is therefore not an isolated story about ancient idols but a warning about any allegiance that encourages disobedience and claims to replace God’s guidance. **[Qurṭubī]**

**Reflection.** The followers’ words reveal a wish to be different only once the consequences are unavoidable. **[Maʿārif]** The verse encourages a person to examine commitments before they become irreversible, and to take responsibility rather than wait for a failed leader to admit fault. **[Saʿdī]** The regret described here is not a substitute for repentance in life; it is the result of having refused the chance to return when it was still open. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The alternatives for “their deeds” should be kept distinct rather than combined into a claim that the commentators all identify the same objects. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī’s preferred explanation concerns evil deeds already committed, now displayed as a source of remorse. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī also records the interpretation that people regret the good deeds they left undone or the reward they lost. **[Qurṭubī]** In the first reading the anguish comes from seeing what one did; in the second it comes from seeing what one failed to do. **[Maʿārif]** Both readings fit the verse’s larger scene of irreversible loss, but the first is the preference explicitly given by al-Ṭabarī. **[Ṭabarī]**

The structure of the verse makes the contrast between a wish and a settled outcome especially stark. **[Jalālayn]** The followers voice a hypothetical return, but the final clause immediately states that they will not leave the Fire. **[Jalālayn]** Their imagined chance to disown the leaders is therefore not a new opportunity granted to them; it is part of the regret the scene exposes. **[Saʿdī]** The verse names the missed opportunity without allowing the wish to undo the earlier choice. **[Ibn Kathīr]**
## 2:168

168168
*“O mankind, eat of what is lawful and good on earth, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Truly, he is an open enemy to you.”*

**Meaning.** The address “O mankind” makes the instruction broad rather than limiting it to the believers already named in the surrounding passage. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī says the command concerns people generally, while the Study Quran notes that the following verses narrow the immediate discussion toward food customs and claims about what God has forbidden. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The verse tells people to eat from the provisions of the earth that God has made lawful and good. **[Jalālayn]** As-Saʿdī explains that this encompasses grains, fruits, and animals, while reminding readers that lawful consumption does not include what is stolen, acquired through a forbidden transaction, or used to assist wrongdoing. **[Saʿdī]**

The two terms “lawful” and “good” are related but not identical in every commentary. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains *ḥalāl* as permitted by God and *ṭayyib* as pure rather than impure or prohibited. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records the view that *ṭayyib* means pleasant or wholesome, while another interpretation treats it as close in meaning to lawful. **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif likewise notes the lexical range and does not reduce the pair to a single gloss. **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran presents the command as one to partake of good things God has allowed, not to impose arbitrary prohibitions on oneself. **[Study Quran]**

As-Saʿdī draws a distinction between what is forbidden in itself, such as carrion, blood, and swine, and what becomes unlawful because of how it was acquired or because it violates another person’s right. **[Saʿdī]** This distinction helps preserve the verse’s positive force: lawful provision is a gift, but the permission to eat does not erase questions of justice or lawful acquisition. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī points to the next verse’s list of prohibited foods as a clarification of the limits, while the present verse warns against inventing further prohibitions. **[Qurṭubī]** These are general principles drawn from the commentaries, not a substitute for the detailed rulings that apply to particular foods or circumstances. **[Study Quran]**

Al-Ṭabarī connects the immediate context with pre-Islamic food taboos: people had declared certain animals forbidden, including *baḥīrah*, *sāʾibah*, *waṣīlah*, and *ḥām*, without authority from God. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī explains that the Arabs treated such customs as religious law and then attributed their prohibitions to God. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr also links the “footsteps of Satan” with the invented restrictions and customs that made lawful things forbidden. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse’s general command is therefore set against a concrete example of superstition and false attribution. **[Jalālayn]**

“Do not follow the footsteps of Satan” is an image of following a path step by step. **[Ṭabarī]** The phrase is not limited to a single dramatic act: as-Saʿdī says it includes the routes of unbelief, wrongdoing, and disobedience, including forbidden food and invented taboos. **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr cites reports from Qatādah and al-Suddī that every act of disobedience to God belongs among Satan’s steps. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran similarly explains the expression as following Satan’s ways and practices. **[Study Quran]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that a person may begin by accepting one false custom and then follow it into further claims about religion. **[Qurṭubī]**

The verse calls Satan an “open enemy.” **[Jalālayn]** Ibn Kathīr connects this description with other Qur’anic commands to treat Satan as an enemy rather than obey his invitation (35:6; 18:50). **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that following the invented prohibitions amounts to following Satan and the errors of earlier generations. **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī says the enemy’s apparent commands serve to deceive people and lead them toward ruin. **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif points to Satanic suggestion as an inward prompting that can make an attractive advantage out of wrongdoing and draw a person away from truth. **[Maʿārif]** This helps explain why the next verse describes Satan’s commands as evil, indecency, and speaking about God without knowledge. **[Study Quran]**

A report cited by Ibn Kathīr from Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim says that God created His servants upright, but devils came and turned them away from their religion, including by forbidding what God had made lawful. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The report illustrates the verse’s contrast between divine permission and humanly invented restriction. **[Ibn Kathīr]** It is not a replacement for the Qur’an’s own argument: the text itself condemns the practice of calling a prohibition divine without warrant. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

**Rulings.** The verse establishes a general permission to benefit from lawful, wholesome provisions, while the surrounding verses identify limits and prohibit fabricated restrictions. **[Saʿdī]** Its warning also reaches the means by which food is obtained: a thing permitted in itself does not become lawful when taken by theft or a forbidden transaction. **[Saʿdī]** Because the sources discuss legal details in broader contexts, this entry preserves the general principle without turning the verse into an exhaustive contemporary food code. **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** The verse joins gratitude for provision with discernment about authority. **[Study Quran]** Enjoyment of what God has made good is not disobedience, and piety does not consist of declaring lawful things forbidden without knowledge. **[Ṭabarī]** Following Satan can begin with an inherited custom that seems familiar; the believer is asked to measure custom against revelation. **[Qurṭubī]**

As-Saʿdī draws from the wording a general principle that the starting point for created things is permission, while recognizing that particular items may be forbidden in themselves or become unlawful through a violation of God’s or another person’s right. **[Saʿdī]** This is an exegetical legal inference, not permission to disregard the specific prohibitions stated elsewhere in the Qur’an. **[Qurṭubī]** The balance is important: the verse rejects the invention of religious restrictions while the following verses preserve the boundaries God actually revealed. **[Ṭabarī]** It therefore opposes both arbitrary austerity and the claim that divine permission removes responsibility for how a person obtains or uses what is consumed. **[Maʿārif]**

The two halves of the command work together: *ḥalāl* rules out what revelation has forbidden, while *ṭayyib* directs people toward what is wholesome and not repugnant. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Since the commentators preserve more than one gloss for *ṭayyib*, the safest synthesis is not to force a single narrow translation but to retain the shared sense of good, pure, or wholesome provision. **[Maʿārif]** The permission to eat is therefore affirmative without being indiscriminate. **[Saʿdī]** It allows people to receive the earth’s provisions gratefully while keeping revealed limits and the rights of others in view. **[Study Quran]**

The metaphor of “footsteps” also suggests a path made up of successive choices rather than a single isolated temptation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The commentators use it broadly for Satan’s ways, including disobedience and fabricated religious rules. **[Saʿdī]** Following an inherited taboo may train a person to trust human invention over revelation, which is why the verse joins food permission with a warning about the source of religious authority. **[Qurṭubī]**
## 2:169

169169
*“He only commands you to evil and indecency, and to say about God what you do not know.”*

**Meaning.** The pronoun “he” refers to Satan, whose footsteps people have just been told not to follow. **[Ṭabarī]** The statement describes the direction of his prompting: it leads toward evil, shameful conduct, and false claims about God. **[Jalālayn]** As-Saʿdī explains that the warning names broad classes of wrongdoing rather than a narrow list of isolated acts. **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr says that it includes Satan’s efforts to make disobedience attractive and to draw people into disbelief and innovation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse describes temptation and command, not a compulsion that removes human responsibility. **[Maʿārif]**

Al-Ṭabarī glosses *al-sūʾ* as sin or evil that harms its doer, and *al-faḥshāʾ* as what is grossly ugly or shameful. **[Ṭabarī]** He transmits a report from al-Suddī that *sūʾ* means disobedience and *faḥshāʾ* means fornication, while making clear that these are reported applications of the terms. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī explains that *faḥshāʾ* originally has a sense of ugliness and comes to mean acts that the revealed law treats as indecent. **[Qurṭubī]** He also cites the view that the word can particularly refer to sexual immorality, and discusses a distinction between sins with prescribed penalties and those without them. **[Qurṭubī]**

The commentators do not all restrict “indecency” to the same example. **[Study Quran]** Ibn Kathīr treats adultery as a clear instance but understands the verse to include wider forms of serious wrongdoing. **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī lists such matters as unlawful sexual conduct, intoxicants, killing, slander, and miserliness as examples of acts that sound reason recognizes as vile. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran connects the verse with other passages in which God or prayer forbids indecency (7:28; 16:90; 29:45), showing that the term belongs to a broader moral vocabulary. **[Study Quran]** These examples illuminate the category without claiming that every commentator gives one identical definition. **[Maʿārif]**

The last clause raises the warning to a further level: Satan urges people to “say about God what you do not know.” **[Ṭabarī]** In the immediate context, al-Ṭabarī relates this to the pre-Islamic claim that God had forbidden *baḥīrah*, *sāʾibah*, and similar animals when He had not done so. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī likewise connects the clause with treating invented taboos as divine law. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran notes the connection to 5:103, where God rejects the people’s false claims about these animals. **[Study Quran]** The example is specific, but the wording reaches any unsupported attribution of a command or prohibition to God. **[Jalālayn]**

As-Saʿdī expands the principle to claims about God’s law and, where relevant, His attributes and decree: one must not affirm or deny something about God without sound knowledge. **[Saʿdī]** He cautions against declaring a thing lawful or forbidden, commanded or prohibited, merely on personal assertion. **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif explains Satanic command as a prompting that can promise immediate advantage while opening a path away from truth. **[Maʿārif]** This makes the danger both intellectual and practical: false religious claims can legitimize misconduct, and misconduct can in turn make a false claim attractive. **[Ibn Kathīr]**
