Maʿārif explains the verb “commands” through the idea of an inward suggestion rather than requiring an audible order: a temptation may enter the heart and make a harmful action seem advantageous. **[Maʿārif]** It cites a report from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd contrasting a satanic suggestion, which encourages evil and can open the way to denial of truth, with an angelic suggestion that encourages good and leaves the heart at peace. **[Maʿārif]** This explanation is offered as a way to understand the experience of temptation; the verse itself remains a warning about the direction of Satan’s prompting. **[Ṭabarī]** A suggestion does not make the person helpless: the command to avoid Satan’s steps assumes the possibility and responsibility of refusing them. **[Saʿdī]**

The progression from evil to indecency to speaking about God without knowledge intensifies the warning. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī presents the first terms as covering sinful conduct, with indecency as a particularly grave form; the final clause then identifies an especially serious offense against revelation. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Jalālayn gives examples of speaking against God by forbidding what He has not forbidden. **[Jalālayn]** As-Saʿdī says that unsupported assertions about divine law are among the broadest routes by which Satan misleads people. **[Saʿdī]** The wording warns both against knowingly fabricating doctrine and against careless certainty where knowledge is lacking. **[Study Quran]**

The close of the clause echoes 2:168: the false prohibitions of pagan custom were not merely a dietary mistake, but a claim about what God had decreed. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr connects the verses through Satan’s efforts to make unlawful what God permitted and to present the error as religion. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that the phrase “what you do not know” fits the prohibition of attributing invented rules to God. **[Qurṭubī]** The same standard applies to anyone who announces what God has commanded without evidence, regardless of whether the claim supports a permissive or restrictive conclusion. **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks readers to be alert not only to obvious evil but also to the authority claimed for it. **[Maʿārif]** A harmful practice can be made to seem sacred when people falsely say that God requires it; humility before revelation is therefore part of moral integrity. **[Study Quran]** The proper response is to seek knowledge and avoid presenting conjecture as divine command. **[Ṭabarī]**

The verse’s final warning is especially relevant to anyone who teaches or repeats religious claims. **[Saʿdī]** A person should distinguish what revelation states from what is an interpretation, a report, or a personal inference, rather than attributing every conclusion directly to God. **[Qurṭubī]** The commentaries do not use the verse to prohibit all interpretation; they warn against speaking without knowledge or asserting a divine ruling without evidence. **[Maʿārif]** This distinction preserves both the seriousness of the prohibition and the need for careful explanation when scholars disagree. **[Study Quran]**

The clause also shows why the earlier prohibition of arbitrary dietary taboos is spiritually serious. **[Ṭabarī]** Such a rule can appear to concern only food, yet when it is attributed to God it becomes a false statement about revelation itself. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The error combines conduct with a claim of religious authority, placing it under both the warning against wrongdoing and the warning against saying of God what one does not know. **[Saʿdī]**
## 2:170

170170
*“When it is said to them, ‘Follow what God has sent down,’ they say, ‘Rather, we follow what we found our fathers doing.’ What—even if their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?”*

**Meaning.** The verse gives a direct example of the resistance described in 2:168–169. People are called to follow what God has revealed, including His guidance about worship and what is lawful, but reply that they will remain with the practice they found among their ancestors. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains “follow what God has sent down” as accepting and acting upon His revelation, making it a guide for what is permitted and forbidden. **[Jalālayn]** The Study Quran relates the verse to the preceding discussion of food customs, while noting that its address can include idolaters, the People of the Book, or people generally. **[Study Quran]** The verse thus addresses a recurring argument, not only a single community. **[Maʿārif]**

The expression “what we found our fathers doing” describes inherited custom. **[Ṭabarī]** The verb translated “found” means to encounter or discover something already being practiced, and al-Qurṭubī notes the same plain sense. **[Qurṭubī]** The reply presents ancestry as sufficient authority: because the practice is old and familiar, they refuse to test it against revelation. **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr says the particular example includes idol worship and the false dietary customs of the pre-Islamic period. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Jalālayn similarly connects it with worship of idols and declaring certain camels forbidden. **[Jalālayn]**

The rhetorical question—“even if their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?”—exposes the weakness in that appeal. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī explains the interrogative as a repudiation: would they follow their ancestors even under the very conditions named? **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī says the fathers lacked understanding of God’s religion and were not guided to the right path, so their customs could not serve as proof against revelation. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr likewise explains that the ancestors had neither sound knowledge nor guidance in the matter at issue. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse does not require the claim that every ancestor was ignorant in every aspect of life; it identifies the absence of religious knowledge and guidance as the decisive defect in this argument. **[Maʿārif]**

The context matters. The previous verse condemned inventing rules about what God had made lawful, and this verse shows that people defended those rules by appealing to inherited practice. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verses are connected: the Arabs restricted animals according to custom and then justified the restrictions by saying they had found their fathers doing the same. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran compares other Qur’anic passages where communities use the same answer, including 5:104 and 31:21. **[Study Quran]** The repeated pattern shows that tradition by itself is not proof of truth. **[Saʿdī]**

This criticism is not a blanket rejection of learning from earlier generations. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī warns against using the verse to condemn every form of following or reliance on another person’s knowledge *(digression)*. **[Qurṭubī]** In his interpretation, the censure here concerns following forebears in false belief and wrongdoing. He distinguishes that from following what is true, and says that a person who lacks the ability to derive religious rulings should consult a qualified scholar. **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif makes a similar distinction between blind adherence to ancestors who lack revelation and guidance, and seeking the judgment of a learned jurist who works from recognized sources. **[Maʿārif]** The detailed theories of legal authority differ among scholars and are not all settled by this single verse. **[Study Quran]**

The key test is the content and warrant of the inherited practice. **[Saʿdī]** If an ancestral teaching accords with revelation and sound guidance, this verse does not condemn it merely because it was inherited. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī cites Joseph’s praise of following the monotheistic way of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (12:37–38) to show that following righteous prophets differs from defending error. **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif likewise says the verse condemns following those who lack revealed guidance, not the practice of accepting truth from a qualified source. **[Maʿārif]** The issue is whether a person remains loyal to a custom after it has been shown to contradict God’s guidance. **[Ṭabarī]**

The verse’s scope of address is also discussed. Al-Ṭabarī considers whether “them” refers back to the people who take rivals in 2:165 or more broadly to “mankind” in 2:168. **[Ṭabarī]** He prefers the broader connection with the address to all people, while acknowledging reports that associate the verse with Jewish interlocutors who rejected the Prophet’s invitation. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records both the view that it concerns the Arab idolaters and the report from Ibn ʿAbbās that it was revealed about Jews. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr also transmits the report concerning Jews who were invited to Islam and answered that they would follow their forefathers. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse’s wording remains broader than any one occasion report. **[Study Quran]**

The command to “follow what God has sent down” is not a demand for novelty for its own sake. **[Jalālayn]** It asks the hearer to measure belief and practice by revealed guidance, rather than assume that age or social acceptance makes a custom true. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī says revelation is to be accepted, acted upon, and made a guide for decisions. **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī describes the appeal to ancestors as a weak excuse when a person has the ability to examine the evidence and follow the truth. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran’s cross-references show that this response recurs in varied communities, making self-examination relevant to every generation. **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks whether a practice is followed because it is true or merely because it is familiar. **[Maʿārif]** Respect for ancestors does not require preserving their errors, and correction need not entail contempt for them. **[Qurṭubī]** Revelation provides a criterion by which inherited beliefs can be assessed, while learned guidance helps those who cannot examine every detail independently. **[Saʿdī]** The warning is against allowing custom to silence evidence and accountability. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]**

## 2:171

171171
*“The likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who calls to what hears nothing but a call and a cry: deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not understand.”*

**Meaning.** The verse continues the challenge to unexamined resistance in the preceding passage, but shifts from the words of those who follow inherited custom to an image of failed communication. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī explain the principal comparison as a caller addressing livestock: the animals hear the shepherd’s voice, yet do not grasp the meaning of his words. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Jalālayn likewise describes people who hear an admonition as cattle hear a shepherd’s cry, without understanding what is said. **[Jalālayn]** The point is not that the message is absent or inaudible; it is that hearing its sound has not become comprehension, reflection, or response. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The Arabic verb *yanʿiqu* is associated with calling out or driving livestock by a voice, and the paired terms *duʿāʾ* and *nidāʾ* can be rendered as a call and a louder cry. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran notes that the image can be understood as a caller whose audience hears only the sound, not the sense. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī reports the grammatical compression behind the parable: the comparison concerns the disbelievers’ response to their admonisher, even though the wording evokes the person who calls and the animal being called. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī similarly explains that the listener, rather than the caller alone, is the relevant side of the comparison. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr paraphrases the scene as a shepherd calling animals toward what benefits them, while they register only an unintelligible noise. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The commentators also preserve a different reading of the image. **[Ṭabarī]** On this interpretation, the disbelievers call upon idols or other supposed deities that cannot hear or answer them; their appeal is like shouting into a distance and receiving only an echo. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī records this view but prefers the comparison of a preacher and people who do not understand, reasoning from the surrounding discussion and from his view that the passage addresses people who were not idol-worshippers. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī presents several versions of the animal-call and idol-call readings without making them identical. **[Qurṭubī]** The alternatives share a central image of speech that fails to convey guidance, but they differ over who is calling and who cannot understand. **[Maʿārif]**

“Deaf, dumb, and blind” describes a spiritual failure to receive and act on truth, not a literal claim about people with hearing, speech, or sight disabilities. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that the people in view do not hear the truth in a receptive way, do not speak what is true, and do not see the path of guidance. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr gives the same figurative sense: they do not hear or acknowledge truth, utter it, or recognize its way. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Jalālayn connects these descriptions to their inability to benefit from admonition. **[Jalālayn]** As-Saʿdī says they hear the words as sounds but do not comprehend them in a way that benefits them; they do not look with reflection or speak words that would help them. **[Saʿdī]** The verse therefore criticizes a chosen refusal to understand, not an involuntary physical condition. **[Study Quran]**

The final clause, “so they do not understand,” gathers the image into a judgment about the use of reason. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī interprets the failure as lack of understanding of the divine address, while al-Saʿdī stresses that the disbelievers have heard a call toward what benefits them and away from harm but have not used their minds to accept it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif describes them as hearing the correction without taking in its intended meaning. **[Maʿārif]** The verse does not suggest that the message is obscure; it locates the failure in the response of those who refuse its guidance. **[Study Quran]**

The immediate audience is discussed in relation to the surrounding verses. Al-Ṭabarī prefers an address to the People of the Book in this verse, while acknowledging how the surrounding passage also discusses the polytheists’ inherited customs. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records both the reading about the Prophet calling people to guidance and the reading about idolaters calling to unhearing idols. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr places the image in a broader warning to disbelievers and polytheists who reject revelation and persist in misguided practices. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran likewise presents the two possible referents, rather than treating one occasion report as a limit on the verse’s wider lesson. **[Study Quran]** The descriptions can therefore apply wherever people hear revealed guidance but refuse to understand or follow it. **[Saʿdī]**

The Qur’an uses similar language elsewhere for moral deafness and blindness, including 2:18 and 8:22; the Study Quran also points to 17:97. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī’s explanation of the three terms as failures toward truth helps connect this verse with those passages. **[Ṭabarī]** The comparison with an animal that hears a sound but not its meaning is a focused illustration of one aspect of heedlessness, not an exhaustive definition of human nature. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Its force depends on the contrast between receiving a warning and benefiting from it. **[Qurṭubī]**

**Reflection.** Hearing religious language is not yet the same as understanding it; understanding is shown by taking its call seriously and letting it redirect conduct. **[Saʿdī]** The verse warns against becoming accustomed to admonition while leaving one’s choices unchanged. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī’s preferred reading keeps the focus on the relationship between a truthful caller and listeners who do not heed him. **[Ṭabarī]** The alternative idol reading adds that appeals to powerless objects cannot provide the guidance or help their worshippers seek. **[Qurṭubī]** In either reading, the invitation to reflect remains open to the hearer: one can move from merely receiving words to understanding and responding to them. **[Study Quran]**
## 2:172

172172
*“O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided you, and give thanks to God, if it is Him you worship.”*

**Meaning.** After the general address in 2:168 to all people about eating what is lawful and good, this verse addresses believers in particular. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī calls it a renewed emphasis on the earlier instruction and says the believers are singled out in honor. **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif explains that the believers are warned not to imitate the polytheists by inventing prohibitions for things God has allowed. **[Maʿārif]** The command is positive: receive the provision God grants, use it lawfully, and respond with gratitude rather than treating lawful sustenance as something to be rejected without warrant. **[Study Quran]**

Al-Ṭabarī glosses “the good things” as lawful provision that God has made wholesome by permitting it, including foods people had wrongly declared forbidden. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Jalālayn similarly explains the phrase as good and lawful things from the provision God has given. **[Jalālayn]** As-Saʿdī notes that the instruction is directed to believers because faith should lead them to use permitted provision without taking what belongs to others or violating God’s limits. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī observes that “eat” can refer to ordinary eating or more broadly to benefiting from God’s gifts. **[Qurṭubī]** The immediate subject is food, but the language also encourages a grateful use of provision rather than waste or false asceticism. **[Maʿārif]**

The command to give thanks is joined directly to the permission to eat. **[Ṭabarī]** He explains gratitude as praising God for the provision and recognizing that it came from Him. **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī makes the response practical: use the food and strength it provides in obedience and righteous action. **[Saʿdī]** In this reading, gratitude is not confined to a spoken formula after a meal; it includes acknowledging the Giver and directing His gifts toward good. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse’s closing condition—“if it is Him you worship”—links exclusive worship with obedience to the One who provides. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī paraphrases it as being willing to follow God’s command and avoid the restrictions invented by Satan or inherited custom. **[Ṭabarī]**

A well-known report cited by Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī reinforces the relation between lawful nourishment and worship. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Prophet says that God is good and accepts only what is good, then describes a traveler who raises his hands in supplication while his food, drink, clothing, and nourishment are unlawful, asking how his prayer could be answered. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The report is presented in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and connects the command to eat lawful provision with a person’s spiritual life, not merely with outward dietary classification. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran cites the same principle in its discussion of the good things God provides. **[Study Quran]**

Maʿārif describes lawful provision as supporting a person’s readiness for worship, while unlawful nourishment can dull the heart’s appetite for good and compromise the sincerity of supplication. **[Maʿārif]** As-Saʿdī likewise says that eating good provision is a cause for righteous work and its acceptance. **[Saʿdī]** These are spiritual observations in the commentaries, not a claim that one can judge another person’s prayer from outward circumstances. **[Study Quran]** Their practical point is that worship involves the whole person: what one consumes and how one acquires it matter alongside formal acts of devotion. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The verse also preserves the balance established by 2:168–169. **[Maʿārif]** Believers should neither treat forbidden things as lawful nor create new religious taboos about what God has permitted. **[Ṭabarī]** The next verse names several prohibited foods, but the list there must be read alongside the Qur’an’s other legal passages; it is not a license to ignore further guidance or to claim that every forbidden matter appears in a single list. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī connects the command to the earlier discussion of food customs, and the Study Quran likewise reads 2:172–173 as a connected passage. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The believer’s enjoyment of lawful provision is therefore compatible with reverence. **[Jalālayn]** The verse does not invite heedless consumption; it couples permission with thanks and worship. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī emphasizes that believers should eat what God has made lawful rather than follow fabricated prohibitions. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr highlights the link between provision and the ability to perform righteous deeds. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Maʿārif adds that remembering the divine source of one’s food can protect a person from arrogance and ingratitude. **[Maʿārif]**

**Cross-references.** The command echoes the address to the messengers in 23:51: “Eat of the good things and do righteous deeds.” Ibn Kathīr cites that parallel to show that lawful nourishment and right action are presented together, not as competing concerns. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran also notes that the good things are what God has not forbidden, placing the permission within the wider Qur’anic distinction between wholesome provision and sin. **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī adds that gratitude after a blessing preserves the blessings already present and is a cause for further good. **[Saʿdī]** He reads the believers’ faith as a protection from consuming what is unlawful, which helps explain why the verse can focus on thanks and worship rather than repeat every dietary limit in the same sentence. **[Saʿdī]** The connection reinforces that receiving provision gratefully includes acting in a way that honors its Giver. **[Maʿārif]**

The permission also corrects any assumption that devotion requires refusing ordinary, lawful provision. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Saʿdī reads the command as an instruction to use God’s gifts while remaining within the limits that faith teaches, so material nourishment can assist worship rather than distract from it. **[Saʿdī]** The link with the messengers in 23:51 further places lawful eating alongside righteous work as a shared religious principle. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse therefore values both the gift and the response: eating is permitted, but gratitude and obedience determine whether the recipient recognizes the Giver. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

**Reflection.** Gratitude turns provision into a reminder of dependence: the believer receives what is good, recognizes its source, and uses it in a way consistent with worship. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse also asks readers to distinguish revealed limits from humanly invented ones. **[Ṭabarī]** Eating lawfully is part of a broader integrity in which outward choices, prayer, and the heart’s orientation reinforce one another. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**
## 2:173

173173
*“He has forbidden you only carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which a name other than God’s has been invoked. But whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him. Truly, God is Forgiving, Merciful.”*

**Meaning.** The verse names four categories of food prohibited in the immediate context: carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and an animal dedicated or slaughtered in the name of a being other than God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The wording answers customs that treated unlawful food as acceptable or declared permitted food forbidden, but the list should not be read as an exhaustive inventory of every dietary rule in the Qur’an. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** As-Saʿdī explains that other prohibitions are established by further texts and by the wider contrast between wholesome and impure things. **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif likewise reads *innamā* in its particular dietary setting, rather than as a claim that no other food is ever forbidden. **[Maʿārif]**

Carrion is an animal that dies without the prescribed slaughter, and the commentators discuss its impurity and the reason it is excluded from ordinary consumption. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī connects the Qur’anic qualification “poured forth” in 6:145 with the blood forbidden here: it distinguishes flowing blood from the traces remaining in meat, and from the liver and spleen, which are not treated as poured blood. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr also cites reports distinguishing the prohibited blood from the liver and spleen, while noting that separate texts address exceptions such as sea food. **[Ibn Kathīr]** These details show why the phrase should not be used carelessly to classify every trace of blood as the same legal category. **[Study Quran]**

The wording “flesh of swine” is explained broadly by al-Qurṭubī, who says that the mention of flesh covers the animal more generally rather than permitting its other parts. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr similarly understands the prohibition to include the animal’s fat as well as its meat. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The fourth category concerns what is slaughtered or offered in devotion to other than God, including offerings to idols or other objects of worship. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Qurṭubī discusses the intention behind sacrifices made in another’s name and cites reports about food offered for non-Muslim festivals; those discussions are attached to the legal context and should not be converted into an unqualified rule about every modern food-sharing situation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The permission for a person “compelled by necessity” qualifies the prohibition without cancelling it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī reports that the majority understand the necessity here as hunger severe enough to create danger, while commentators also discuss the limits of what may be eaten. **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī says that when abstaining would bring death, eating what is needed becomes obligatory, since a person is not to destroy himself. **[Saʿdī]** The exception therefore protects life in a genuine emergency; it is not a convenience clause for someone who merely prefers a forbidden food. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The phrase *ghayra bāghin wa-lā ʿādin* has several reported explanations. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī records interpretations such as not seeking forbidden food when lawful food is available, not exceeding the amount needed, and not transgressing by using the dispensation as a pretext for disobedience. **[Ṭabarī]** He favors the interpretation that the person does not seek the forbidden food when lawful provision is accessible and does not exceed the limits of its use. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr reports readings that focus on continuing to eat the prohibited food or believing it to be permitted, while al-Saʿdī stresses that the person is genuinely unable to find lawful food and takes only what necessity allows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran likewise summarizes the condition as neither coveting the prohibited nor crossing the limit. **[Study Quran]**

The commentators differ over how much a person may eat once necessity is established. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī records a dispute between limiting the person to enough to ward off immediate danger and allowing enough to satisfy the need more fully, including during travel. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī’s preferred explanation retains the paired restraints against seeking forbidden food unnecessarily and transgressing in the use of the exception. **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī treats the allowance as a protection from sin and, where abstention would cause death, a duty to preserve life. **[Saʿdī]** The verse gives a principle of necessity; the sources’ detailed applications should not be turned into a single modern ruling without their legal contexts. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The closing names, “Forgiving, Merciful,” suit the exceptional permission. **[Jalālayn]** God removes culpability from the person who eats what is normally forbidden under real compulsion and within the stated bounds. **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī explains that the mercy includes the allowance itself and forgiveness for a person whose senses may be overwhelmed by the hardship of hunger. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī emphasizes that the exception is part of the revealed rule, not a rebellion against it. **[Ṭabarī]**

**Cross-references.** Ibn Kathīr notes that the general description of carrion is qualified elsewhere: 5:96 permits the food of the sea, and he cites the report that its water is pure and its dead are lawful. **[Ibn Kathīr]** He also cites the report distinguishing two permitted dead things, fish and locusts, and two permitted kinds of blood, liver and spleen. **[Ibn Kathīr]** These are examples of how separate Qur’anic and prophetic texts clarify the application of the broad wording; they do not cancel the ordinary prohibition of carrion or blood. **[Study Quran]** Al-Qurṭubī’s discussion of blood similarly relies on the qualification “poured forth” in 6:145 rather than treating every trace in prepared meat as the same thing. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse’s legal teaching is therefore read in conjunction with other revealed evidence, as the commentators repeatedly emphasize. **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse holds two responsibilities together: respect the ordinary prohibition, and do not let scrupulosity destroy a life when God has provided a lawful dispensation. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** Necessity is real and bounded, not an excuse to treat a limit as meaningless. **[Saʿdī]** The provision of an exception is itself a sign of mercy, while the obligation to observe its conditions protects the integrity of the rule. **[Study Quran]**
## 2:174

174174
*“Those who conceal what God has sent down of the Book and sell it for a small price—they consume nothing but fire in their bellies. God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and theirs is a painful punishment.”*

**Meaning.** The verse turns from the dietary rules to people who conceal revealed knowledge for worldly advantage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Several commentators place the immediate warning in the context of People of the Book who concealed passages or descriptions concerning the Messenger, then exchanged silence or distortion for material gain. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** The wording is not limited to one transaction: al-Qurṭubī says its warning can include anyone who knowingly hides truth in order to obtain a worldly benefit. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran likewise emphasizes the danger of concealing scripture for profit. **[Study Quran]**

“To sell it for a small price” describes treating divine guidance as a commodity. **[Ṭabarī]** The price may be money, status, influence, or another temporary advantage; its smallness is measured against the loss of truth and the consequence that follows. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Jalālayn glosses the transaction as the taking of a worldly payment in return for concealment. **[Jalālayn]** Ibn Kathīr connects it with altering or suppressing what was revealed. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse condemns the conscious choice to let a transient gain outweigh an obligation to make knowledge clear. **[Saʿdī]** It does not say that every failure to know or every mistake in interpretation is deliberate concealment. **[Study Quran]**

“They consume nothing but fire in their bellies” is commonly explained as a vivid description of unlawful earnings and the punishment to which they lead. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī records both the metaphorical reading—unlawful gain becomes a cause of fire in the Hereafter—and a more literal afterlife reading in which the consumed wealth is transformed into punishment. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran also notes the image’s force: a gain that looks consumable and profitable in this life is, in its true consequence, fire. **[Study Quran]** The metaphor does not require readers to claim that the physical substance of every coin is literally flame in this world. **[Maʿārif]**

The statement that God “will not speak to them” is also interpreted with care. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī explain it as God not addressing them with favorable, welcome, or merciful speech, rather than as a claim that no speech or questioning occurs anywhere on the Day of Resurrection. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran points out that other Qur’anic passages describe questioning and speech on that Day, so this threat should not be flattened into absolute silence. **[Study Quran]** Al-Jalālayn connects the denial to speech that would please or benefit them. **[Jalālayn]**

“Nor will He purify them” may mean that God will not cleanse them of their wrongdoing, praise them, or declare them purified. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī explains the denial in terms of not purifying them from their sins, while the Study Quran records the related sense of withholding praise. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī treats the phrase as an aspect of their disgrace and exclusion from divine favor. **[Saʿdī]** The sequence thus describes more than a financial loss: it names a moral corruption, an unfavorable judgment, and a painful end. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]**

The context makes the contrast with genuine religious learning especially sharp. **[Ṭabarī]** Those who hide guidance for profit do not merely remain silent about an inconsequential detail; they place people’s access to truth at risk for their own benefit. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr links the warning to the preceding verses about those who conceal revelation, and the Study Quran notes that the verses form a connected denunciation of concealment. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Saʿdī says the threat is directed at those whose knowledge should have led them to explain the truth rather than exchange it for gain. **[Saʿdī]** The passage invites readers to distinguish deliberate suppression from honest scholarly disagreement. **[Maʿārif]**

The “small price” also warns that the apparent scale of a worldly reward is irrelevant beside the value of truthful guidance. **[Jalālayn]** **[Qurṭubī]** A person may receive a benefit that seems substantial to him, but the verse calls it small because it is temporary and purchased at the cost of accountability before God. **[Ṭabarī]** The Study Quran emphasizes that the image of consuming fire exposes the final character of the bargain, while Ibn Kathīr relates it to punishment in the Hereafter. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Context.** The commentators connect the concealed revelation with information the People of the Book had received but did not disclose, especially passages that bore on the prophetic message. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī’s surrounding discussion emphasizes that the matter hidden from people was guidance God had made clear, while al-Qurṭubī extends the principle to anyone who conceals a truth he knows. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The text does not condemn scholarship, interpretation, or careful qualification; the offense is suppressing what one knows in order to gain a price. **[Study Quran]** This distinction is important because the severe warning describes an intentional betrayal of knowledge, not the ordinary limits of a person’s learning. **[Saʿdī]**

The sequence of images moves from what concealment does to the concealer, to the relation between that person and God, and finally to the announced punishment. **[Jalālayn]** **[Qurṭubī]** The image of fire in the belly makes the worldly gain appear already marked by its final consequence; the next two clauses describe the loss of favorable divine address and purification, and the last names the painful punishment openly. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran likewise reads the verse’s severe images as a unified warning rather than as separate, unrelated threats. **[Study Quran]** The progression underscores why the bargain is called small: its temporary payment cannot compensate for the spiritual and ultimate loss. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** Knowledge carries a trust: those who possess it must not manipulate or conceal it for advantage. **[Saʿdī]** The warning is severe because the concealed truth concerns guidance, not merely private information. **[Maʿārif]** The verse does not license accusations against individuals whenever they disagree; its subject is knowing concealment and the deliberate sale of revelation. **[Study Quran]** It asks both teachers and hearers to value truth above temporary reward. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**
## 2:175

175175
*“Those are the ones who have purchased error in exchange for guidance, and punishment in exchange for forgiveness. How patient they are in facing the Fire!”*

**Meaning.** The opening phrase continues the warning about those who conceal revelation and choose a worldly price over truth. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** “They have purchased error for guidance” describes an exchange in which a person gives up the way that could lead to right guidance and chooses misguidance instead. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that they have preferred error over the guidance God made clear, and al-Qurṭubī similarly treats the language of purchase as a deliberate choice. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The phrase “punishment for forgiveness” completes the contrast: they choose a course that merits punishment instead of seeking forgiveness through faith and repentance. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The two exchanges are not ordinary bargains but a moral description of what their choice produces. **[Qurṭubī]** They do not literally purchase punishment from another seller; by concealing and rejecting truth, they exchange the prospect of guidance and forgiveness for the consequence of error. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī stresses the depth of the loss: they turn away from what would benefit them in this world and the next. **[Saʿdī]** The verse therefore describes culpable preference, not a person who lacks access to knowledge or makes an honest mistake. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The expression translated “How patient they are in facing the Fire!” is unusual, and al-Ṭabarī preserves several interpretations. **[Ṭabarī]** He prefers an exclamation of astonishment: how boldly or persistently they perform deeds that lead them to the Fire, as though they show remarkable endurance in approaching its cause. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records the same astonishment reading and also reports interpretations that take the words as a question about what makes them endure the Fire or what has made them so patient in it. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr presents the phrase as wonder at their readiness to face punishment after choosing the path that leads there. **[Ibn Kathīr]** These are alternative grammatical and rhetorical explanations, not one single literal description of their emotional state. **[Study Quran]**

Al-Jalālayn renders the phrase as astonishment at how enduring they are in the Fire, while also explaining their choice of error and punishment. **[Jalālayn]** As-Saʿdī uses the verse to underscore how far their actions carry them from forgiveness. **[Saʿdī]** The force of al-Ṭabarī’s preferred reading is that people can act with striking boldness toward consequences they would never willingly choose if they saw them clearly. **[Ṭabarī]** The phrase is a rebuke of the folly of their course, not praise for suffering or patience in wrongdoing. **[Maʿārif]**

The following clause says that God sent down the Book in truth. **[Ṭabarī]** The revelation is not itself the source of their error; it came with truth, while they chose to conceal or dispute it. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Jalālayn explains that the Book was sent down with truth, and the Study Quran connects this affirmation to the contrast between revealed guidance and the misguidance they chose. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** The verse therefore places responsibility for their exchange on their response, not on any defect in the guidance. **[Saʿdī]**

The final phrase, “those who differ concerning the Book are in far-reaching schism,” prepares for the next verse’s explicit statement about disagreement. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī treats the Book as revelation whose truth the people under discussion opposed; other commentators identify the Book more specifically with scripture given to the People of the Book or with the Qur’an. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The verse’s description of schism emphasizes separation from the truth, rather than condemning every careful interpretive difference among sincere readers. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī links the division to their rejection of the revealed guidance and the consequences described in the preceding clause. **[Qurṭubī]**

The verse’s language of exchange also recalls the “small price” in 2:174. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** What they receive in worldly advantage is set beside what they forfeit: guidance and forgiveness. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Saʿdī says their choice is a sign of the corruption of their aim, while Maʿārif draws attention to the disproportion between a transient gain and lasting accountability. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The image does not make repentance impossible for others; it exposes the path of those who knowingly persist in concealment and error. **[Qurṭubī]**

**Language.** The parallel structure makes the moral reversal explicit: error is chosen in place of guidance, and punishment in place of forgiveness. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī treats “purchase” as a figure for preferring one course and its consequence over another, rather than an ordinary exchange in a market. **[Ṭabarī]** That imagery connects this verse with the “small price” in the preceding verse: temporary advantage is accepted while the lasting benefit of guidance is relinquished. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The exclamation about facing the Fire is not a commendation of endurance; in al-Ṭabarī’s preferred reading it expresses wonder at their boldness in doing what leads there. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī’s alternative interrogative readings likewise expose the irrationality of the choice, asking what could make a person endure such a consequence. **[Qurṭubī]**

The question-like rendering, “What has made them endure the Fire?”, should not be mistaken for a request for information; in its rhetorical setting it exposes the absurdity of the choice. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī’s preferred exclamation likewise expresses astonishment at people acting so boldly toward a punishment they would not choose if they considered its reality. **[Ṭabarī]** The alternative readings—wonder at their apparent patience or a question about what caused them to bear the Fire—are recorded because the Arabic permits more than one rhetorical force. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The common point remains a rebuke: their conduct is so heedless that it looks as though they willingly face the consequence. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** People can treat a damaging choice as if it were a profitable purchase when the immediate reward hides the long-term cost. **[Saʿdī]** The verse calls that distortion by its proper name: choosing error over guidance and punishment over forgiveness. **[Ṭabarī]** Its astonished question warns against confusing boldness with wisdom. **[Qurṭubī]** The next verse will identify the roots of the division as rejection of the Book’s truth, urging the reader to return to revelation rather than defend a harmful bargain. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**
## 2:176

176176
*“That is because God sent down the Book in truth, and those who differ concerning the Book are in far-reaching schism.”*

**Meaning.** “That is because” links the painful consequence in the preceding verse to the fact that God sent down the Book in truth and to the people’s response to it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The Book is not presented as uncertain or internally false; the separation described here arises when people differ over revealed guidance in a way that turns them away from the truth. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī explains that the revelation was sent with truth and that those who oppose it have moved far from the straight path. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran reads the verse as the conclusion to the warning about concealment and the choice of error in 2:174–175. **[Study Quran]**

The commentators do not identify “the Book” in only one way. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī favors the People of the Book in the immediate setting, since the previous verses speak about those who conceal what was revealed to them; within that context, the Book may refer to scripture more broadly. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī and other exegetes also record readings that identify it with the Qur’an or with the Torah and other revealed scripture. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Ibn Kathīr connects the phrase with the revelation that establishes truth and the rejection of those who dispute it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** These identifications are related but should not be collapsed into the claim that every commentator names precisely the same scripture. **[Maʿārif]**

Al-Ṭabarī prefers to understand those who differ as Jews and Christians disputing about the scripture and the message in the context of the passage. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records that some instead take the group to be the Quraysh disputing about the Qur’an, while other reports connect the disagreement with the People of the Book. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran likewise notes the alternatives and observes that “the Book” can refer to different revealed texts in the reports. **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī emphasizes the general warning: anyone who turns away from the revealed truth and divides from it falls under the description of distant schism. **[Saʿdī]** The specific historical identifications are therefore reported readings, while the verse’s moral warning is expressed broadly. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The word *shiqāq* suggests opposition and separation, and “far-reaching” intensifies the distance from the truth. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** It is not merely that people hold different views; the verse condemns a division that arises from rejecting or obscuring what God has made clear. **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī explains that this opposition leaves them on a path far removed from guidance. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran’s treatment keeps the focus on disagreement over revelation and the consequences of turning away from it. **[Study Quran]** This distinction matters: the passage should not be used to brand every sincere interpretive disagreement as the culpable schism it condemns. **[Maʿārif]**

Read together, 2:174–176 present a connected sequence. **[Ibn Kathīr]** First, people conceal revealed knowledge for a worldly price; then they are described as choosing error and punishment over guidance and forgiveness; finally, the text states that the Book was sent in truth and that those who oppose it are divided from that truth. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The order places responsibility on the human response rather than on revelation itself. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Saʿdī notes that the passage exposes the danger of treating divine guidance as something to manipulate for worldly aims. **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif likewise links the verses through concealment, rejection, and the resulting separation. **[Maʿārif]**

The phrase “sent down in truth” also grounds the warning in God’s authority. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī reads it as confirmation that the scripture is true in what it teaches and commands, while Ibn Kathīr emphasizes that the divine Book is a true revelation rather than an invention. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran notes that truth in this context is not simply a partisan label; it is the standard against which concealment and dispute are judged. **[Study Quran]** Al-Jalālayn’s concise gloss likewise places the source of the Book in God’s truthful revelation. **[Jalālayn]**

The passage has a particular historical setting in the disputes around scripture and the prophetic message, but its warning extends to any situation in which people recognize guidance and then suppress or distort it for advantage. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī’s preference for the People of the Book preserves the immediate context, while the alternatives he records caution against claiming that the verse can have only one historical referent. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The universal lesson does not erase the original audience; rather, it draws from their example a rule about accountability before revelation. **[Study Quran]**

**Language.** Al-Qurṭubī explains *shiqāq* as opposition and separation, an image of people moving apart from the revealed truth rather than simply disagreeing about a minor detail. **[Qurṭubī]** The adjective “far-reaching” intensifies the distance, and al-Jalālayn renders it as a schism far from the truth. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī’s preferred historical reading places the division among the People of the Book, while the alternative reports about Quraysh show that the phrase was also understood in connection with rejection of the Qur’an. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The wording thus connects the specific disputes around revelation with a general warning against opposition that arises from deliberate rejection. **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** A disagreement becomes spiritually dangerous when it is used to hide truth or to protect an advantage, not simply because readers ask questions or interpret carefully. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse calls the reader to approach revelation honestly, acknowledging what it says rather than using it as a tool for gain. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī’s contextual reading reminds us that the warning was spoken into real disputes over scripture, while al-Qurṭubī’s alternatives preserve the breadth of the exegetical record. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**
## 2:177

177177
*“Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west. Rather, righteousness is to believe in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets; to give wealth, despite loving it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask, and for freeing people from bondage; to establish prayer and give zakah; to fulfill covenants when made; and to be patient in hardship, illness, and at the time of battle. Those are the truthful, and those are the God-fearing.”*

**Meaning.** The verse does not make the direction of prayer unimportant; it rejects reducing righteousness to orientation alone. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī and al-Jalālayn connect the opening to disputes over whether the east or west should be faced, including the Jewish and Christian directions of prayer. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Ibn Kathīr stresses that facing the direction God has commanded is part of obedience, but the direction itself is not the whole of *birr*; the aim is to follow God’s command. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī records related contexts and calls the verse a comprehensive account of foundational virtues. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran describes *birr* as a broad term for inward and outward obedience that draws a person near to God. **[Study Quran]**

The verse begins with belief in God, the Last Day, angels, the Book, and the prophets. **[Jalālayn]** These clauses set the foundation of faith before listing acts of charity, worship, social responsibility, and patience. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Saʿdī explains belief in the Last Day as accepting what God and His Messenger have revealed about what follows death; belief in the Book includes the scriptures God sent, with the Qur’an as their culmination. **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif sees the verse as gathering the main dimensions of religion: creed, action, and character. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī likewise counts within it belief in God, resurrection, angels, revealed books, and prophets. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran notes that the list echoes the principal articles of faith found elsewhere in the Qur’an. **[Study Quran]**

“Giving wealth, despite loving it,” praises generosity when a person still values and may need what is given. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī reads the pronoun as referring to the wealth: the giver parts with something cherished, rather than giving only what is unwanted. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records other possibilities, including that the giving is done for love of God or that the phrase describes the act of giving while the giver’s heart remains attached to wealth. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran similarly notes that the phrase can refer to loving wealth or, in another reading, to love of God. **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī includes giving while healthy and reluctant, giving from limited means, and giving what one values most. **[Saʿdī]**

The recipients are named in a sequence that directs care toward vulnerable people and those with claims on one’s help. **[Qurṭubī]** Relatives are mentioned first, since kinship adds the duty of maintaining family ties to the merit of charity. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Orphans are children who lack a father’s protection and provision, while the poor are people whose needs are not adequately met. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The wayfarer is commonly explained as a traveler cut off from resources away from home; al-Ṭabarī records a further interpretation that includes a guest. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī urges assistance suited to the traveler’s actual need, such as help to continue the journey. **[Saʿdī]**

“Those who ask” includes people who seek help when a need arises; the sources caution against assuming that every asker fits one narrow category of destitution. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Saʿdī mentions that some may ask because of an urgent obligation or for a public benefit, and he does not make wealth alone the sole test of whether the request has a claim. **[Saʿdī]** “For freeing people from bondage” is explained as spending to emancipate enslaved people, helping a contracted servant pay for freedom, or ransoming captives. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī connects the phrase with freeing slaves and says the legal details are treated elsewhere. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse thus directs wealth toward both personal needs and release from coercive dependency. **[Study Quran]**

The verse then names the regular duties of establishing prayer and giving zakah. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Prayer is not merely an outward turn toward a direction; it is a maintained act of worship, while zakah is the prescribed financial duty. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The relationship between the earlier giving of wealth and the later mention of zakah is disputed. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī records one view that the first spending is distinct from obligatory zakah and another that it can include the prescribed alms; al-Qurṭubī and Maʿārif favor a distinction, in part because zakah is named separately. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The report al-Qurṭubī cites from Fāṭimah bint Qays asserting a right in wealth beyond zakah is described in his discussion as weak and should not be treated as decisive proof *(weak)*. **[Qurṭubī]**

“Those who fulfill their covenant when they make it” covers commitments to God and obligations undertaken with other people. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī includes the duties God has imposed, people’s rights, and obligations a person takes upon himself through oaths or vows. **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr connects covenant-keeping with the opposite traits of hypocrisy, such as breaking promises and betraying trusts. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse then praises patience in *baʾsāʾ* (poverty or hardship), *ḍarrāʾ* (illness or affliction), and *ḥīn al-baʾs* (the time of battle). **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Qurṭubī and al-Saʿdī also explain the first two as financial hardship and bodily illness, with the final phrase referring to meeting the enemy in battle. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The description is steadfastness through difficulty, not a demand to seek suffering. **[Maʿārif]**

The word *al-ṣābirīn* appears in the accusative where the preceding description is in the nominative; al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī explain it as a construction of praise that gives patience particular emphasis. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The conclusion calls these people truthful because their conduct confirms their faith, and God-fearing because they carry out obligations and avoid what is forbidden. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī says the listed beliefs, acts, and moral qualities contain many of the central virtues of religion. **[Saʿdī]** The verse therefore answers a narrow debate with a broad account of what faithful life looks like. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** Orientation, belief, generosity, worship, fidelity, and patience belong together; no single outward marker can replace the whole pattern. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse invites readers to test claims of righteousness against care for people and steadiness under pressure. **[Ibn Kathīr]** It praises giving while wealth is still loved, not only giving after it has become irrelevant to the giver. **[Ṭabarī]** Its final description places sincerity and God-consciousness in lived practice rather than in self-description alone. **[Study Quran]**
## 2:178

178178
*“O you who believe, prescribed for you is just retribution concerning those killed: a free person for a free person, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. But whoever is granted pardon by his brother for something, then let there be fair pursuit and good payment to him. That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy. Whoever transgresses after that shall have a painful punishment.”*

**Meaning.** The verse establishes *qiṣāṣ*, a measured legal response to intentional killing, and places it within limits rather than leaving blood vengeance to private anger. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains “prescribed” as establishing the rule that the responsible killer, not an unrelated person, is the one against whom retaliation may be sought. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī describes *qiṣāṣ* as an equal response and explains the term through the idea of following or matching an act. **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif likewise stresses that “like for like” is the principle and that the innocent must not be punished in place of the offender. **[Maʿārif]** The verse is not permission for a victim’s family to exact punishment on its own: al-Qurṭubī says the execution of *qiṣāṣ* belongs to the public authority or its appointed agent. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran also identifies this rule as a prohibition on vigilantism. **[Study Quran]**

The clauses “free for free, slave for slave, female for female” are explained against reports of pre-Islamic and tribal retaliation that could exceed the original killing. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** In some accounts, a powerful group demanded a socially higher-status person in return for a person of lower status, or a man in return for a woman; the reports differ over the precise historical setting. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Ibn Kathīr relates the account of Banu Naḍīr and Qurayẓah, while al-Ṭabarī records versions involving Arab tribes and other groups. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** Their shared point is that retaliation must not target an innocent person merely to make a group appear powerful. **[Maʿārif]**

The legal implications of these status clauses were debated by jurists. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Qurṭubī records disagreements over whether differences of status affect the conditions for *qiṣāṣ*, alongside arguments that the broader principle of “a life for a life” applies across those categories. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr notes that some later scholars treated part of the wording as superseded by 5:45, while other readings understand it as a restriction on over-retaliation rather than a denial of protection to a person killed by someone of another status. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī’s preferred explanation is that the verse bars taking anyone other than the killer, including a person of greater status who did not commit the act. **[Ṭabarī]** The commentaries preserve legal debate; this entry does not turn those historical arguments into a ruling for private application. **[Maʿārif]**

The next clause opens the possibility of pardon. **[Jalālayn]** “Whoever is granted pardon by his brother” is commonly understood as the killer being forgiven by the victim’s heir or family, often in return for compensation rather than execution. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** The word “brother” preserves a relation of human or religious kinship even in the context of a grave crime and is also read as an appeal toward restraint and reconciliation. **[Jalālayn]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī record more than one grammatical interpretation of who is the subject of the pardon, but the familiar reading is that the injured party waives retaliation and accepts a settlement. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]**

“Fair pursuit” directs the claimant to seek the agreed right without harassment, excess, or demands beyond what is due. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** “Good payment” directs the person who has been pardoned to meet the obligation honestly and promptly, without delay, denial, or reduction. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī generalizes the two instructions: the one with a claim should ask in a decent manner, and the one who owes should discharge it with good conduct. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran describes the options of retaliation, compensation, and pardon as distinct routes that cannot be combined once one has been settled. **[Study Quran]** The precise legal question of whether the heirs can require compensation without the killer’s agreement is disputed in the sources. **[Qurṭubī]**

The description “an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy” refers to the range of responses granted in cases of intentional homicide. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The early exegetical reports compare this flexibility with rules they associate with earlier communities, while the verse itself emphasizes God’s easing of the matter for this community. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran cautions that comparison with earlier legal traditions is part of the commentators’ explanation, not the only point of the verse. **[Study Quran]** Al-Saʿdī highlights the moral invitation toward pardon, while making clear that the injured party’s right to seek lawful justice remains recognized. **[Saʿdī]**

“Whoever transgresses after that” is most commonly read as a warning against killing the offender after a pardon or compensation has already been accepted. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī records disagreement over whether the painful punishment in the verse means execution, a sanction determined by the ruler, or punishment in the Hereafter; al-Saʿdī prefers the view that the offender is treated under the ordinary rules rather than made ineligible for pardon. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The shared prohibition is against reviving vengeance after the right has been settled. **[Study Quran]**

**Rulings.** Al-Qurṭubī cites reports that describe the victim’s heirs as having a choice between seeking retaliation and accepting compensation, and elsewhere records pardon as a further course. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse’s order does not mean that an heir must choose retaliation; al-Ṭabarī explicitly reasons that the option of pardon would otherwise have no place in the passage. **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators also differ over whether compensation can be demanded without the killer’s consent, so the broad principle of settlement should not be mistaken for unanimity on every procedural detail. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** In all cases, the rule is mediated through the proper authority and requires a just determination of responsibility; the text gives no support to an individual carrying out punishment by private decision. **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** Justice here is bounded by responsibility: the killer may be held accountable, but an innocent relative or member of a group cannot be made a substitute target. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse’s movement from retribution to pardon and then to fair conduct shows that legal justice can protect life while leaving room for mercy. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Its safeguards matter: punishment belongs to lawful authority, and an accepted settlement cannot be answered with private revenge. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**
## 2:179

179179
*“And in just retribution there is life for you, O people of understanding, so that you may be mindful.”*

**Meaning.** This verse states the wisdom of the rule just described: “in *qiṣāṣ* there is life for you.” **[Ṭabarī]** It may sound paradoxical because *qiṣāṣ* can involve taking the life of a killer, but the commentators explain that a fair and limited legal consequence can deter future killing and protect many lives. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī says the rule restrains people from killing one another, while reports from Qatādah describe the fear of retaliation stopping someone who was about to commit a grave act. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The potential aggressor may desist, the intended victim survives, and the retaliatory cycle is prevented from consuming more people. **[Saʿdī]**

The verse’s claim is not limited to deterrence of an individual offender. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that tribal revenge could provoke both groups to continue fighting, multiplying deaths after the first killing; a bounded rule of *qiṣāṣ* gives a defined response and can stop the wider feud. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran similarly explains that limiting revenge to the perpetrator and forbidding vendettas preserves life. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī also records the view that life is preserved because the law does not allow a person of higher status to be killed in place of the actual killer. **[Ṭabarī]** These explanations show how restraint and proportionality, rather than unlimited revenge, are central to the verse’s argument. **[Maʿārif]**

As-Saʿdī puts the deterrent logic plainly: a person who knows that killing may bring an equal legal consequence is less likely to commit murder, and others who see the rule applied are warned against doing the same. **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr also cites reports that a would-be killer may reconsider when reminded that his own life can be forfeit under the law. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Jalālayn describes the same effect: the prospect of retaliation can lead the would-be killer to refrain, preserving both the intended victim and himself. **[Jalālayn]** The claim concerns a legal rule applied under the conditions of justice; it does not authorize indiscriminate violence or private execution. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The address “O people of understanding” calls those with sound intellect to recognize the wisdom in the rule. **[Ṭabarī]** The Arabic *ulū al-albāb* is rendered by al-Ṭabarī as possessors of intellect, and the Study Quran explains the expression through the image of the inner “kernel” of understanding. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Qurṭubī takes the address as a summons to those capable of reflecting on God’s commands, while al-Saʿdī says that the wisdom of the law is clearest to people who consider its purposes rather than only its surface form. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

The closing “so that you may be mindful” can be read first in relation to avoiding murder and then more broadly as an invitation to *taqwā*. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that people may refrain from killing because they fear the consequence, while al-Qurṭubī says that avoiding the crime can lead to wider obedience. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī adds that reflecting on the wisdom and mercy of God’s law should lead a person to obey it and avoid what it forbids. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran likewise connects mindful restraint with the verse’s broader moral horizon. **[Study Quran]**

The phrase is concise but does substantial work. **[Qurṭubī]** It sets an enduring social result—life—beside a specific legal measure, and directs the reader to consider how the latter serves the former. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Maʿārif explains that *qiṣāṣ* is based on likeness and must remain proportionate; the verse’s reasoning depends on the limits explained in 2:178, not on punishment without measure. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī’s reports of “warning” and “restraint” likewise point to a rule that checks aggression rather than multiplying it. **[Ṭabarī]**

**Language.** Al-Ṭabarī explains “life” as the preservation of people through the restraint the law creates, and he records glosses such as warning, deterrence, and protection. **[Ṭabarī]** The verse’s concise wording places the means and its result side by side: *qiṣāṣ* is named, then “life” is the outcome it serves. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Jalālayn adds that the would-be killer may preserve both his own life and that of the intended victim by refraining. **[Jalālayn]** As-Saʿdī reads the life at issue socially as well as individually: the threat of a lawful consequence checks one person’s aggression and protects the community from further bloodshed. **[Saʿdī]** This reasoning also explains why the verse follows the permission to pardon and settle in 2:178; a system that limits revenge can stop a chain of killings rather than extend it. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The purpose is thus not death for its own sake, but security through proportionate justice and the restraint of vengeance. **[Maʿārif]**

The final phrase “so that you may be mindful” carries the argument from deterrence toward moral discipline. **[Ṭabarī]** One may first refrain from killing because of the immediate legal consequence, then learn to avoid wrongdoing more generally out of reverence for God. **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī says that recognizing the wisdom and mercy in divine law should lead people to obey it and avoid what it forbids. **[Saʿdī]** The addressees are called to use reason, not to substitute private opinions for the safeguards built into the rule. **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The verse invites reflection on why a just boundary can protect life: without a credible limit, the threat of vengeance can spread far beyond the person responsible. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī says the possessor of understanding is one who sees the law’s restraint and submits to it rather than exploiting it. **[Saʿdī]** The verse’s purpose is not to celebrate death, but to show how justice, when carefully limited, can prevent further deaths. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**
## 2:180

180180
*“Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is a bequest for parents and near relatives in a fair manner—a duty upon the God-fearing.”*

**Meaning.** The verse directs a person who sees death approaching and has property to consider a bequest for parents and close relatives. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** “When death approaches” is commonly explained as the arrival of its causes or signs, not only the final instant of life. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** The word *khayr* means wealth in this context, although early commentators differed over how much property counted as enough to trigger the instruction. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī prefers the plain sense that little or much wealth can be called good, while al-Qurṭubī records numerical thresholds reported from early authorities. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse places planning for death within responsibility toward one’s family rather than treating one’s property as entirely private. **[Maʿārif]**

The legal setting changed as the Qur’an established fixed shares of inheritance. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Before those shares were revealed, the commentators describe the bequest as a means of directing property to parents and relatives; later, Qur’an 4:11–12 assigned shares to inheriting relatives. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī records several views: that the verse was abrogated for heirs, that it remains for relatives who do not inherit, or that its instruction is now recommendatory. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī argues that the verse remains operative for non-inheriting parents and relatives and does not regard the whole command as cancelled. **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī seeks to reconcile the readings: fixed shares supply the fair due of inheritors, while care for excluded relatives remains within the verse’s concern. **[Saʿdī]**

The well-known report “there is no bequest for an heir” is cited by al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, and Maʿārif in explaining why a person cannot use a will simply to change the shares assigned by revelation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The sources present the verse’s interaction with that report and the inheritance verses as a question of legal scope: some call it partial abrogation, some emphasize the continuing instruction for non-heirs, and some speak of a recommendation rather than an obligation. **[Study Quran]** The existence of these interpretive differences should be stated rather than hidden behind a single claim that the verse is either wholly current or wholly irrelevant. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The command “in a fair manner” sets limits on the bequest. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Qurṭubī explains *maʿrūf* as justice and moderation, and he connects the later prophetic guidance to a limit of one-third of the estate in ordinary circumstances. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ibn Kathīr cites the report of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, who asked whether he could bequeath two-thirds, then half, and was permitted one-third, with the Prophet describing even a third as much and urging him to leave his heirs provided for. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Saʿdī says the bequest should be ordered by closeness and need, without extravagance or neglect of nearer relatives. **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif likewise notes that a bequest cannot be used to deprive rightful inheritors of the shares fixed for them. **[Maʿārif]**

The moral emphasis on parents and relatives does not mean that every bequest to a non-relative is invalid. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī records views that a needy relative should be preferred and that neglecting such kin is blameworthy, alongside the position that a permissible bequest to another person may still take effect. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Maʿārif explains that a bequest for non-inheriting relatives is desirable but not an unrestricted way to override inheritance rights. **[Maʿārif]** The verse’s focus is the duty of fair provision and family care; specific shares and limits are addressed in the wider inheritance law. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The force of “a duty upon the God-fearing” is also disputed. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī takes the verse as imposing a real obligation to bequeath to close relatives who do not inherit, while al-Qurṭubī reports that many later jurists regarded a general bequest as recommended, with a stronger obligation where debts, trusts, or rights would otherwise be lost. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif says the general obligation for relatives was later treated as abrogated, while a will remains necessary for documenting people’s claims and debts. **[Maʿārif]** As-Saʿdī reads the wording as evidence of obligation but also describes the current application to relatives excluded from inheritance. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran records these disagreements and cautions that the phrase does not settle every later juristic question by itself. **[Study Quran]**

Al-Qurṭubī notes the connection between this verse and the preceding one: the person whose death is near is also reminded to put his affairs in order, just as the earlier verse regulated claims after a killing. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** In both passages, a right is protected by setting it down fairly instead of leaving it to anger, confusion, or later dispute. **[Maʿārif]** Ibn Kathīr stresses that a will should not be manipulated by later alteration, a subject taken up in 2:181–182. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The bequest’s fairness is therefore part of a broader ethic of accountability after death. **[Study Quran]**

**Rulings.** The commentators distinguish a bequest for a person who already inherits from one made for a relative with no fixed share. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The report “no bequest for an heir” is used to explain why a will cannot simply add a preferred share to the portions assigned by revelation, although the heirs may consent to an arrangement in circumstances discussed by the jurists. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī’s continuing application of the verse focuses on close relatives who do not inherit, while other exegetes describe such a bequest as recommended rather than universally obligatory. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The sources separately note that a person who holds another’s property, owes a debt, or knows of a claim that might be lost has a responsibility to make that matter clear. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The purpose is to protect rightful claims, not to use a bequest to displace the inheritance framework. **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** Preparing a bequest is presented as care for those who may otherwise be overlooked, especially relatives who have no automatic share. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse also guards against favoritism that would harm rightful heirs or turn a final act into injustice. **[Qurṭubī]** A will is not a device for evading God’s allocation of inheritance; it is to be made within the limits and purposes that the wider revelation sets. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The disagreement over whether this instruction is obligatory or recommendatory is part of the exegetical record, while its call to fairness and care remains clear. **[Ṭabarī]**

## 2:181

181181
*“Then whoever alters it after hearing it—the sin thereof is only upon those who alter it. Truly God is Hearing, Knowing.”*

**Meaning.** Verse 181 follows the instruction to make a fair bequest in 2:180 by addressing what happens after a valid testament has been made known. A person who changes its terms after hearing them commits the wrongdoing described here; the deceased person is not charged with another person’s tampering. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse treats the bequest as a trust rather than an invitation for an executor, witness, or relative to substitute personal preference for the testator’s clear direction. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The concluding names, “Hearing, Knowing,” affirm that God knows both the spoken instruction and the motives concealed behind its alteration. **[Study Quran]**

The word “alter” includes changing, suppressing, or replacing what the testator actually directed. **[Ṭabarī]**  Commentators explain that a witness or guardian who heard the terms cannot later pretend that they were different, and one entrusted with carrying them out must not divert the property to himself or to someone he favors.   Al-Jalālayn describes the warning as directed at those who change the will after it has reached them, while al-Saʿdī stresses that the testator’s responsibility is distinct from the subsequent changer’s responsibility. **[Jalālayn]**   The legal and moral point is that a person who merely transmits or administers the instruction should not become its unauthorized author.  **[Ibn Kathīr]**
