The phrase “after hearing it” marks knowledge and deliberate interference, not an honest failure to understand an ambiguous statement.  **[Qurṭubī]** The sources discuss witnesses and those who take charge of a bequest because they may be positioned to alter its record or execution. **[Maʿārif]**  If a person knowingly substitutes a different beneficiary, conceals a portion, or falsely attributes a new instruction to the deceased, the sin belongs to the one who did so. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** This warning does not mean that every disagreement about how to interpret a will is automatically intentional fraud; the decisive concern is knowingly changing what was properly directed. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The sources distinguish such wrongful tampering from correcting a bequest that is itself invalid or unjust.  **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran gives examples: a direction exceeding the ordinary one-third limit may be reduced to the amount permitted without the heirs’ consent, and a bequest to provide a forbidden substance such as wine may be nullified. **[Study Quran]**  Maʿārif likewise explains that a will cannot be used to displace the inheritance shares God has established. **[Maʿārif]**   These are not changes made to steal from the testator or to reward oneself; they are adjustments made to prevent an instruction from violating the governing rules.    The distinction depends on the reason and authority for the intervention, not simply on whether the written wording remains untouched.

The relation to the previous verse is important. **[Qurṭubī]** Verse 180 calls for a bequest “in a fair manner,” while verse 181 condemns a person who later corrupts a valid instruction. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** A testator cannot claim that the word “bequest” authorizes injustice to rightful heirs, and an executor cannot claim that concern for fairness gives a private license to rewrite a just will. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Commentators therefore read the two verses together: the instruction must be just at its origin, and those who hear it must preserve it faithfully unless correction is required to restore a right or remove a forbidden provision.  **[Study Quran]**

The liability falls on the person who alters the instruction, even when that person tries to shift blame onto the deceased or onto the family’s later dispute.   The sources explain that God hears the words by which the bequest was made and knows what was changed afterward, including a concealed motive of self-enrichment or favoritism.   This gives the verse force beyond the public record: a manipulation that escapes human notice remains known to God. **[Qurṭubī]**  At the same time, its warning is carefully focused on the changer’s own act; it does not automatically condemn every person who benefits from a valid distribution or every heir who asks for clarification.

A will often concerns people who are absent, vulnerable, or unable to correct the record once the testator has died. **[Maʿārif]**  The verse consequently makes faithful testimony and responsible administration part of justice toward the dead and the living.  **[Saʿdī]** If witnesses preserve the terms, and those entrusted with property carry them out within the law, the family is less exposed to suspicion, coercion, and conflict. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** The verse does not supply a complete procedure for every inheritance dispute; rather, it establishes a moral boundary: do not intentionally change a valid instruction for personal advantage.

**Interpretive note.** The verse is especially concerned with what happens to a person’s rights when the person who made the bequest can no longer speak for himself. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** A witness may be the only person who heard the instruction, and an executor may be the only person who can ensure it is carried out; either role can become a means of protection or an opportunity for abuse. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The verse assigns the moral burden to the one who knowingly alters the bequest, not to the deceased whose words were changed. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The language therefore protects the testator’s lawful intention while holding the living accountable for how they handle it. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

This protection must be read alongside the inheritance rules, not against them. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Commentators relate the earlier instruction on bequests to the later fixed shares for heirs and the report that there is no bequest for an heir, while preserving discussion about bequests for relatives who do not inherit. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** A person cannot defend an unfair diversion of property by saying that the testator wanted it, if that instruction itself violates the legal limits; conversely, an administrator cannot change a fair direction simply because he prefers another distribution. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The duty is to distinguish a lawful bequest from an unlawful one and then act within that distinction. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]**

The sources’ examples of invalid provisions show why correction and corruption are different acts. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** Reducing a bequest that exceeds the permissible limit, or nullifying a direction to provide something forbidden, aims to prevent injustice; secretly changing beneficiaries for personal gain aims to cause it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The first may be a necessary correction under the governing rule, while the second is precisely the tampering condemned here. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Where terms are unclear, those responsible should seek clarification and preserve evidence rather than silently write their own version of what they think the deceased intended. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

God’s hearing and knowledge also mean that the distinction between a correctable instruction and a self-serving alteration is not hidden behind private intent. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The testator’s words, the witness’s memory, and the executor’s later account are all within divine knowledge, even when human evidence is incomplete. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** This gives the warning a serious inward dimension: a person may evade a family’s scrutiny, but not the One who heard the original direction and knows why it was changed. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** “Hearing, Knowing” closes the verse by making fidelity a matter of conscience as well as public evidence. **[Ṭabarī]**  A responsible witness or executor should distinguish a lawful correction from an opportunistic revision, preserve what was truly said, and seek clarification where the terms are uncertain. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The deceased’s instruction is not beyond review when it conflicts with justice, but neither may another person disguise self-interest as a correction. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The passage thus protects both the testator’s legitimate intention and the rights that the larger inheritance framework safeguards. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:182

182182
*“But whoever fears from a testator partiality or sin, and brings about a reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him. Truly God is Forgiving, Merciful.”*

**Meaning.** Verse 182 qualifies the warning of 2:181. The prohibition on altering a valid bequest does not require a person to stand by while an unjust or sinful instruction harms those entitled to fair treatment. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse describes someone who fears *janaf*—often explained as error, unintended leaning, or unfair bias—or *ithm*, deliberate wrongdoing, and who works to set matters right between the affected people. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The person who seeks a just reconciliation is not guilty merely because the resulting arrangement differs from the testator’s wording. **[Study Quran]**

The commentators do not collapse *janaf* and *ithm* into one kind of intention.   *Janaf* may describe an unintentional mistake or an unintended departure from fairness; *ithm* more readily points to a knowingly wrongful direction.   Al-Saʿdī emphasizes that the first may be a testator’s inadvertent bias, while the second is a sinful act; both can create a need for counsel or repair. **[Saʿdī]**   The distinction matters because a person who notices an unjust outcome should respond according to its character and timing, rather than presuming that every imperfect phrase proves deliberate malice.  **[Qurṭubī]**

There are two related applications in the commentaries. Al-Ṭabarī gives weight to the word “fears”: because the person anticipates injustice before it occurs, he reads the verse as encouraging advice to the testator while there is still time to make a fair bequest. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** One should counsel the person to remove an unintended bias or refrain from a sinful condition, not wait passively for the harm to be carried out.  **[Maʿārif]** Other commentators also discuss correction after death, when an executor, witness, or responsible authority discovers that the bequest prejudices the heirs or circumvents their rights.  **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** These readings differ over when the intervention occurs, but both direct it toward justice rather than private gain. **[Jalālayn]**

The phrase “between them” is commonly understood as referring to those whose interests are affected, especially the heirs.   The person who brings reconciliation may be the executor, witness, mediator, or another responsible person able to prevent the injustice.   The verse does not authorize that person to take the property or choose a favored beneficiary; it describes making peace by restoring a fair arrangement.  **[Qurṭubī]** If the testator is alive, this may mean persuading him to correct an unintended imbalance. If the testator has died, the sources describe repair through those entrusted with the estate or empowered to resolve the matter.

Examples help clarify the boundary. **[Ibn Kathīr]** A bequest that exceeds the permissible share, indirectly gives an extra benefit to an heir, or deprives another relative through a concealed device may require correction.  **[Study Quran]** Maʿārif notes that a bequest cannot be used to overturn the shares assigned by the inheritance verses. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]** Yet a person may not simply label an inconvenient but valid instruction “biased” and replace it with his own preference. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The remedy must address a genuine error or sin and should be limited to what is needed to remove the injustice.

The words “there is no sin upon him” relieve the mediator from the charge of wrongful alteration when the purpose is reconciliation.   This matters because verse 181’s warning could otherwise be misunderstood as forbidding every intervention, including the correction of a plainly unjust will. **[Ibn Kathīr]**  The two verses are therefore balanced: do not corrupt a valid bequest, but do not preserve wrongdoing merely because it was written down.   The person who acts should be careful, transparent, and directed by the rights at stake, rather than using the language of reconciliation to conceal an independent agenda.  **[Qurṭubī]**

The conclusion, “Forgiving, Merciful,” places the work of repair within a divine ethic of mercy. **[Ṭabarī]**  God’s forgiveness is not presented as indifference to injustice; the verse has just called for the wrong to be addressed. **[Maʿārif]**  Rather, the closing names encourage correction without despair and recognize the sincere effort to restore fairness.  **[Saʿdī]** They also restrain self-righteousness: the mediator must seek a just settlement with humility, knowing that human judgment can be mistaken even when the intention is good. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** Al-Ṭabarī’s attention to “fears” makes anticipatory counsel central: if an adviser sees that a testator is about to make an unfair or sinful bequest, the adviser may urge correction before the will takes effect. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** This reading gives the verse a preventive role, as well as a restorative one. **[Maʿārif]** Other commentators describe what an executor or responsible person may do after the testator’s death, when an unjust direction has become apparent and the heirs need a fair settlement. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** These applications are not identical in timing, but each is directed toward avoiding harm rather than taking advantage of it. **[Jalālayn]**

The wording “brings about a reconciliation between them” sets a positive standard for the intervention. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** It is not enough to remove one clause if doing so creates another injustice; the purpose is to reconcile the affected interests as fairly as possible. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The one who mediates should not take for himself what he removes from another, and should not use a genuine defect in the will as an excuse to alter unrelated provisions. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** In the reports concerning a bequest that indirectly favors an heir, the problem is not merely its wording but the way it is used to bypass the assigned shares. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]**

“Janaf” and “ithm” together cover a range from unintended partiality to deliberate sin. **[Jalālayn]** **[Qurṭubī]** A testator may make a mistake through ignorance, confusion, or an unbalanced preference without intending to harm anyone; another may knowingly try to exclude an heir or give an impermissible advantage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The person who notices the problem should respond proportionately to the evidence and not assume the worst about the testator. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** At the same time, a concealed plan does not become fair simply because its author describes it as affection, charity, or family peace. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The assurance “there is no sin upon him” is tied to the corrective purpose and does not cancel verse 181. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The former verse condemns a person who corrupts a valid instruction; this one absolves the person who intervenes to prevent or repair an actual injustice. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** The distinction protects conscientious mediation while denying a blanket power to rewrite a will. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** Its closing names, Forgiving and Merciful, encourage sincere repair without suggesting that justice is optional. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ṭabarī]**

The mediator’s good intention must be matched by care about whose right is being restored. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Advice before death gives the testator an opportunity to correct his own mistake; repair afterward requires the responsible people to understand the estate and the heirs’ claims. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** In neither case does the verse commend an impulsive intervention based on rumor. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The words “there is no sin upon him” describe the person who seeks a just reconciliation, not one who invokes reconciliation to secure a private benefit. **[Jalālayn]**

**Reflection.** The verse protects both fidelity and compassion. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** A faithful executor should not alter a fair bequest, but an ethical community should not let a clear injustice pass unchallenged. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The distinction rests on evidence, intention, and the rights involved: preservation guards the testator’s lawful instruction, while reconciliation prevents an error or sin from becoming another person’s injury. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The verse’s permission is therefore not a general license to rewrite a will; it is a carefully bounded path for restoring justice. **[Jalālayn]**

## 2:183

183183
*“O you who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, as it was prescribed for those before you, that haply you may be reverent.”*

**Meaning.** The address to believers introduces the obligation of fasting and places it within a history of worship that reaches beyond the Muslim community. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verb “is prescribed” conveys an obligation, while the comparison with earlier communities reminds believers that disciplined abstention is not an unfamiliar or uniquely imposed form of devotion. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** The commentators differ over who “those before you” are: some identify Christians, some the People of the Book more generally, and others earlier believing communities without limiting the phrase to one group. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The verse’s principal concern is not to settle every historical detail but to explain fasting’s purpose and its place among acts of obedience. **[Saʿdī]**

Reports about earlier fasting practices are not uniform.   Some exegetes connect the comparison to earlier communities’ fasts, while others understand it as a broad statement that God prescribed fasting to prophets and peoples before this community.   The Study Quran likewise records the range from Christians or the People of the Book to humanity more generally. **[Study Quran]**   The verse therefore supports continuity in the discipline of fasting without requiring the claim that every earlier community observed the same calendar, duration, or detailed rules as Muslims do.  **[Qurṭubī]**

The analogy may concern the obligation itself, the practice of fasting, or the fact that previous communities also received a command to abstain for a time. **[Ṭabarī]**  Commentators report differences about whether the earlier fasts resembled the Muslim fast in duration and timing or differed in their particular form. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** These historical possibilities should remain distinct rather than being combined into a single confident chronology. **[Maʿārif]** The comparison can still comfort the believer: fasting belongs to a long tradition of worship, even where the precise observance among earlier peoples is not fully known. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]**

The stated purpose is *taqwā*, reverent awareness of God expressed through restraint and obedience.   Fasting trains the believer to refrain from permitted food and drink during specified hours in response to a divine command; this discipline can strengthen the ability to avoid what is forbidden beyond those hours.   Al-Qurṭubī explains *taqwā* here as protection from wrongdoing, while al-Jalālayn connects it to obedience and avoidance of sin. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]**   The fast is not simply hunger or thirst: its religious meaning comes from intention and compliance with the limits God sets.

As-Saʿdī emphasizes that fasting involves restraining the self from appetite and desires that can distract from obedience. **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr likewise sees it as a means of purifying the soul and reducing the strength of temptation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** These are explanations of how the prescribed practice can cultivate *taqwā*, not a promise that every person who fasts automatically becomes righteous. **[Study Quran]** The verse names the aim; the believer must still carry the discipline into speech, conduct, and dealings with others. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** In this way, abstaining from lawful things for a limited period can rehearse a broader willingness to obey God even when appetite or habit pulls another way. **[Jalālayn]**

The surrounding verses unfold the obligation rather than leaving the believer to invent its details.  Verse 184 will speak of numbered days, illness, travel, and feeding; verse 185 will identify Ramadan and clarify the make-up fast.   This sequence matters: 2:183 gives the command and its purpose, while the following verses provide concessions and practical boundaries.   A reader should not lift the general call to fasting away from those later clarifications, nor should the concessions erase the verse’s affirmation that fasting is prescribed.

The opening “O you who believe” ties the practice to faith and communal responsibility. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The command is addressed to believers as a body, though later verses recognize individual circumstances and different capacities. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** That combination of shared obligation and personal concession will become important in 2:184–185: the practice is common, but the law does not treat illness or travel as though they were ordinary conditions. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]** The verse thus joins continuity, discipline, and mercy at the outset of the fasting passage. **[Ṭabarī]**

**Interpretive note.** The verse states the duty before specifying its days and concessions. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** This order first establishes fasting as a prescribed act, then allows the next verses to clarify how it is performed and when a person may make it up. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The later concessions should therefore be read as part of the structure of the duty, not as evidence that the command in this verse is merely optional. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** The reference to earlier communities similarly provides a frame of continuity without requiring identical legal forms across different revelations. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

Some transmitted explanations associate the pre-Ramadan practices of the early Muslim community with fasts on particular days, including reports about ʿĀshūrāʾ or several days each month. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Other commentators read the verse as referring to fasting prescribed for earlier peoples more generally, and the Study Quran records the possibility that “those before you” means Christians, the People of the Book, or people in general. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī cautions that the reports do not establish with certainty that an earlier fast was obligatory in the same way as Ramadan. **[Ṭabarī]** These accounts illuminate the background, but they do not alter the verse’s clear call to the believers addressed here. **[Saʿdī]**

Fasting trains the believer to observe a command even when the lawful appetite is present. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** That discipline can strengthen resistance to wrongful desire at other times, but the purpose clause remains *taqwā*, not bodily deprivation as an end in itself. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]** The sources connect reverence with obeying God, avoiding prohibited conduct, and cultivating self-restraint. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Someone who abstains from food yet persists in injustice has not exhausted the verse’s moral aim. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** The practice is a means of shaping the whole conduct of the worshipper. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The shared address also combines communal worship with different personal circumstances. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Believers receive a common command, while 2:184–185 recognize illness and travel and explain make-up days. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** The verse’s comparison with earlier peoples may comfort the community by placing its discipline within a broader prophetic tradition, but the detailed rules of Ramadan are made explicit in the verses that follow. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Read as a sequence, the passage joins duty, purpose, and mercy rather than setting them against one another. **[Saʿdī]**

The phrase “as it was prescribed for those before you” makes the duty intelligible through continuity, but the commentators’ range of interpretations cautions against assuming that all earlier communities fasted at the same time or under the same conditions. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Some reports describe a practice of fasting on particular days, while other explanations speak more generally of fasting as a command given to earlier believers. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse invokes a shared religious discipline, not a claim that the details of every community’s fast were identical. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Its comparison can encourage believers by showing that restraint belongs to a wider tradition of worship. **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** Fasting is presented as a means toward reverent awareness, not an end measured by hardship alone. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The believer’s restraint is meaningful because it answers a command and is meant to shape life beyond the hours of abstention. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The reference to earlier communities locates the practice within a wider history of devotion, even as the next verses define its particular form for this community. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse therefore invites a fast that is deliberate, God-conscious, and informed by the concessions as well as the duties that follow. **[Jalālayn]**

## 2:184

184184
*“For days numbered. So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days. And for those who can bear it, the ransom is feeding an indigent person. Whosoever volunteers good, that is better for him; and to fast is better for you, if you but knew.”*

**Meaning.** The phrase “days numbered” presents fasting as a bounded obligation, not an undefined burden. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Commentators differ over what these days first denoted: some take them as the days of Ramadan, while others connect them to an earlier fast before the Ramadan obligation was fully established. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī is cautious about reports that an earlier fast was obligatory and favors reading the passage in relation to the Ramadan fast, since he finds no decisive transmission establishing another required fast before it. **[Ṭabarī]**  The disagreement concerns the early chronology, not the verse’s clear provision for a sick person or traveler. **[Maʿārif]**

The sick and the traveler may make up later an equal number of days missed during the fast. **[Ṭabarī]**  The phrase “a number of other days” ties the make-up obligation to the days not observed, rather than replacing the fast with an unspecified act. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Commentaries discuss illness and travel in differing degrees of detail, including how much hardship is required and when the concession applies.   The general rule is stated here, but the verse alone does not settle every later juristic question about distance, severity, or the circumstances in which fasting while traveling is preferable.

The words translated “those who can bear it” have also been read in more than one way.  **[Study Quran]** Some early interpretation understands the phrase as allowing a person who could fast to choose either fasting or feeding a poor person for each day. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** In that account, the option for healthy residents was later replaced by the command in 2:185 to fast the month for those who are present and able. **[Qurṭubī]**  Another reading takes the phrase to mean people who are able only with severe difficulty, such as the elderly or those with a lasting condition; for them, feeding remains a concession rather than a temporary choice for every healthy person.

Al-Ṭabarī discusses reports about earlier fasting and the meaning of the feeding clause, while warning against treating a disputed historical report as conclusive. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī preserves multiple juristic interpretations of the clause and the relation of 2:184 to 2:185. **[Qurṭubī]**   The Study Quran explicitly notes both the earlier option and the continuing concession for those who can fast only with great hardship. **[Study Quran]**  Maʿārif also treats the elderly and people with enduring illness as a distinct case from the healthy resident who is able to fast. **[Maʿārif]** These positions should not be presented as though all commentators assign the same legal force to the clause. **[Saʿdī]**

“Whosoever volunteers good” is explained in several related ways.  It may refer to feeding more than one poor person, providing a fuller meal than the minimum, or undertaking additional good beyond the required amount.  **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Jalālayn associates the phrase with voluntary generosity in the feeding, and al-Saʿdī emphasizes that an additional good deed benefits the giver. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** The phrase broadens the verse’s moral horizon without making extra charity a substitute for the make-up fast when the latter is still required.  **[Ṭabarī]**

The statement “to fast is better for you” is read with attention to the audience under discussion. **[Qurṭubī]** For someone able to fast without undue hardship, fasting is better than choosing the former feeding option, according to the interpretation that treats that option as an early concession.   For a traveler or ill person, some commentators say fasting may be preferable if it causes no serious difficulty, while others stress that the concession itself is a mercy and should not be turned into a burden.   The verse’s closing “if you but knew” invites recognition of the spiritual benefit of fasting, not disregard for the exemptions that the same passage names.  **[Maʿārif]**

The commentaries also record disagreement about people who are pregnant or nursing, and about how the make-up fast or feeding obligation applies to them.  **[Ibn Kathīr]** Some distinguish fear for the mother from fear for the child, while reports differ over whether feeding accompanies make-up days.  **[Study Quran]** The verse’s broad categories—illness, travel, and ability to bear the fast—provide a framework, but the specific rulings were elaborated differently by jurists. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** It is therefore more accurate to report the existence of these distinctions than to claim that one detailed ruling is unanimously stated by the verse.

**Interpretive note.** The early reports about fasting before Ramadan are not uniform. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some narrations speak of a monthly fast or ʿĀshūrāʾ, while others attach “days numbered” directly to the Ramadan obligation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī does not consider the available reports decisive proof that a prior obligatory fast existed; the Study Quran likewise notes that the commentaries disagree about whether the early practice was itself obligatory. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** It is therefore more careful to describe the exegetical alternatives than to state a single chronology as certain. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]**

The feeding provision also has a history in the interpretation of the passage. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Some commentators describe an initial choice for an able resident between fasting and feeding an indigent person for each day, later replaced for those able to fast by the explicit command in 2:185. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** Others read the feeding clause as continuing for people who can fast only with severe hardship, such as the elderly or those with a lasting illness. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse’s phrase about bearing the fast is central to the disagreement, and the sources should not be compressed into a claim that the clause has only one application. **[Ṭabarī]**

Where the continuing concession applies, the feeding is linked to each day not fasted. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Commentators discuss the amount and form of feeding in legal detail, but the verse’s plain image is the provision of food to an indigent person rather than an unrelated substitute. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** The injunction also directs attention toward the poor person’s actual benefit; extra generosity is praised in the next phrase. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The sources differ over the precise boundary between someone able to make up a fast later and someone whose condition makes the fasting obligation enduringly difficult. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The terms “ill” and “on a journey” name broad grounds for concession, but their application was further specified by jurists. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Commentaries report different thresholds for illness and travel, and discuss whether a traveler who can fast without difficulty should fast or use the concession. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** Some regard fasting as better where it causes no hardship; others emphasize that the lawful alternative is a mercy and should not be treated as a failure of faith. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse’s make-up instruction remains a key part of the accommodation: missed days are completed later when the person is able. **[Jalālayn]**

The commentaries also record differing rulings for pregnancy and nursing. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Some distinguish whether a person fears harm for herself, for the child, or for both, and differ about whether feeding accompanies the later make-up fast. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** These details arise from juristic interpretation of the general categories of illness and capacity; they are not resolved in a single sentence here. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse should therefore be cited for its general structure—concession and make-up—without claiming unanimity on every special case. **[Ṭabarī]**

**Reflection.** “Days numbered” and the mention of concessions together hold discipline and mercy in view. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** Fasting is valued, yet illness and travel are recognized as real conditions that may change how the duty is performed. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The feeding clause preserves care for people who cannot sustain the fast, while the additional-good clause encourages generosity beyond a bare minimum. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** Read beside 2:185, the verse shows how the Qur’anic passage clarifies an early allowance and the continuing make-up duty without erasing legitimate hardship. **[Ṭabarī]**

## 2:185

185185
*“The month of Ramadan is that wherein the Quran was sent down as guidance to mankind, as clear proofs of guidance, and as the Criterion. Let him among you who is present fast during that month. And whosoever is ill or on a journey, it is a number of other days. God desires ease for you, and He does not desire hardship for you, so that you may complete the number and magnify God for having guided you, that haply you may give thanks.”*

**Meaning.** The verse identifies Ramadan as the month in which the Qur’an was sent down and describes the Revelation as guidance, clear proofs of guidance, and a criterion distinguishing truth from falsehood. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The commentators commonly report that the Qur’an’s initial descent occurred on Laylat al-Qadr, followed by its gradual revelation to the Prophet, while narrations differ about the precise account and chronology. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** This is an exegetical report explaining the verse’s language, not a reason to assert one uncontested timetable for every stage of revelation.

The three descriptions of the Qur’an are related but distinct. **[Ṭabarī]** *Hudan* presents it as guidance for people; *bayyināt* points to clear signs or proofs that make guidance recognizable; and *furqān* names its role as a criterion by which truth and falsehood are distinguished.   **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī explains that the clear proofs support the guidance, while al-Saʿdī stresses that the Qur’an’s explanations make the right path evident. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**   The Ramadan fast is thus set beside the revelation of the book that directs belief and conduct, not merely beside a calendar date.

The instruction “whoever among you is present” is interpreted in more than one way.  Some commentators understand it as being present in the month rather than away on a journey; others connect it to witnessing or establishing the month’s beginning. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The sources also discuss the case of someone who begins traveling after Ramadan has already started, and they do not all frame the application identically.  **[Maʿārif]** The central command remains clear: a person who is resident and able observes the fast, while illness and travel are expressly addressed by the following clause. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]**

The sick and traveler may fast a number of other days equal to those missed.   This repeats and clarifies the make-up principle in 2:184, now within the explicit setting of Ramadan.   Commentators differ over how severe an illness must be and how the travel concession applies in individual circumstances; al-Ṭabarī emphasizes hardship that becomes intolerable, while other authorities discuss a wider range of conditions. **[Ṭabarī]**   Fasting during travel can remain permissible when it is manageable, but the verse makes room for breaking the fast and making up the day later. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

“God desires ease for you, and He does not desire hardship for you” explains the concessions as part of the law, not as exceptions that a believer should feel ashamed to use. **[Qurṭubī]**  **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif and al-Jalālayn connect the wording to God’s facilitation of worship for those who are ill or traveling. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]** Ease does not mean that every demanding act is removed; it means that the obligation is structured with lawful alternatives when the named circumstances arise. **[Study Quran]**  The purpose is sincere worship within the limits God has set, not making hardship itself a measure of devotion.

“Complete the number” is explained in two principal ways.  It may mean making up the missed days after Ramadan until the required count is complete; al-Ṭabarī prefers this reading in the context of the preceding make-up instruction. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** It can also be connected with completing the lunar month, which contains twenty-nine or thirty days.   The phrase thus underscores the completion of the prescribed count, though commentators differ about which immediate count is meant.   It should not be used to erase the preceding concession: a person who made use of it completes the required number later according to the verse. **[Saʿdī]**

The command to magnify God for guiding the believers is linked by commentators to takbīr at the end of Ramadan.   **[Maʿārif]** The sources differ over the exact timing, formula, and occasions for these declarations, including whether they accompany the festival prayer or particular prayers near the end of the month. **[Study Quran]** The verse’s wording clearly joins the completion of the fast with praise of God for guidance, even where the later practice is described in more than one way.  **[Jalālayn]** The closing hope of gratitude brings the passage back to a recurrent Qur’anic theme: divine provision and guidance call for a thankful response. **[Saʿdī]**

**Interpretive note.** The verse gives the make-up command a clear context: the fast belongs to Ramadan, the month associated with the Qur’an’s descent. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse’s descriptions—guidance, clear proofs, and criterion—explain why revelation is central to the month rather than incidental to it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The sources commonly cite a report of the Qur’an’s initial descent to the lowest heaven and its subsequent gradual revelation to the Prophet, but they preserve different accounts about the details and duration. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** The report should therefore be attributed as an exegetical explanation, not presented as a universally agreed single chronology. **[Jalālayn]**

“Whoever among you is present” is commonly taken to mean the person who is resident in the month, in contrast to the traveler mentioned immediately afterward. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Some commentators also explain the wording in terms of witnessing the month or its beginning. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The sources discuss a person whose journey begins after Ramadan has started and differ about how that situation affects the fast; this is one reason not to flatten every travel case into a single rule. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The basic structure remains: the resident who is able fasts, and the sick or traveler may make up missed days. **[Saʿdī]**

The phrase “God desires ease for you” is paired with a real obligation, so ease is not the same as abolishing discipline. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** It means that the law makes room for illness and travel and allows missed days to be completed later. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Commentators differ over how severe an illness must be and what journeys qualify; al-Ṭabarī emphasizes hardship that becomes intolerable, while other authorities discuss a broader range. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The concession is therefore part of the divinely stated rule, not an exception invented by the worshipper to avoid the fast. **[Jalālayn]**

“Complete the number” may refer to making up days missed because of illness or travel, which al-Ṭabarī prefers in context, or to completing the lunar month, which can have twenty-nine or thirty days. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** The two readings keep attention on fulfillment of the prescribed count, although they identify the immediate count differently. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The following command to magnify God is linked by commentators to takbīr associated with the end of Ramadan and the festival, but they differ over timing, formulas, and the exact occasions. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** In either case, completion is accompanied by praise for the guidance God has given. **[Saʿdī]**

The takbīr associated with the end of Ramadan expresses gratitude for guidance, while the verse itself does not specify one exclusive formula or schedule for it. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Commentators describe different occasions for proclaiming God’s greatness around the festival and the conclusion of the fast. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Their shared point is the connection between completing worship and praising the One who made guidance possible. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]**

**Reflection.** Ramadan gathers the discipline of fasting and the remembrance of the Qur’an’s guidance into one month. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** Its concessions demonstrate that worship is measured by faithful obedience, not by ignoring the limits of the body. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Whether “complete the number” is read as making up missed days or completing the lunar month, the verse points toward fulfillment of the obligation without denying ease. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Its final movement—from guidance to magnification and thanks—shows how fasting is joined to recognition of the One who revealed the Book and made the path clear. **[Jalālayn]**

## 2:186

186186
*“When My servants ask thee concerning Me, truly I am near. I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me, that they may be led aright.”*

**Meaning.** The verse answers the question of God’s nearness with a direct assurance: “I am near.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The commentaries explain this nearness through God’s knowledge, hearing, mercy, and response to supplication, rather than as a statement that reduces God to a place or distance. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Saʿdī distinguishes God’s encompassing knowledge of all creation from His special nearness to those who worship and call upon Him through response, aid, and guidance.  **[Maʿārif]** The verse therefore reassures the servant that no intermediary or loudness is needed for God to hear. **[Study Quran]**

Reports about the occasion of revelation vary.  Some connect the verse to a question about whether God is near or far, others to when or how people should call upon Him, and another report describes a Bedouin asking whether to whisper or shout. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** The different accounts illuminate the same concern but should be presented as reported explanations rather than one certain historical narrative. Al-Ṭabarī’s notes mark one route for the near-or-far question as very weak and another report as mursal, so the occasion should remain a reported explanation rather than settled history. **[Ṭabarī]** The answer emphasizes nearness instead of giving a technical schedule for prayer: the caller can invoke God whenever the need arises.

“I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me” gives a promise of response, but the commentaries caution against reducing that promise to immediate delivery of every requested thing in exactly the form imagined.  **[Ibn Kathīr]** The request may be granted, its reward may be reserved, or harm may be turned away; these are among the explanations reported by exegetes. **[Maʿārif]** The verse assures the servant that supplication is heard and answered according to divine wisdom, not that the caller controls the timing or form of the outcome. **[Saʿdī]**  Al-Qurṭubī also warns against despair when an answer is not immediately visible and cites guidance against impatiently demanding a response. **[Qurṭubī]**

The word *duʿāʾ* includes calling upon God and asking Him for what one needs; the sources also link supplication with worship itself. **[Study Quran]**  A person who turns to God in need recognizes dependence and directs hope to the One able to answer.   The report “supplication is worship,” cited in the commentaries, makes this dimension explicit.  **[Ibn Kathīr]** Supplication is therefore not a technique for forcing a result but a form of devotion, trust, and humble request. **[Ṭabarī]**

The command “let them respond to Me” is generally understood as a command to answer God by obeying Him and accepting His guidance.   Some interpreters also explain it in terms of calling upon God, but al-Ṭabarī gives priority to responding to the divine call through faith and obedience. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** “And believe in Me” reinforces that relationship: the servant asks God while trusting His promise and responding to His commands.  **[Saʿdī]** The purpose clause, “that they may be led aright,” connects right guidance with both invoking God and following what He has revealed. **[Maʿārif]**

The fasting context gives the verse an especially intimate place in the passage.  **[Qurṭubī]** It appears between the rules of fasting in 2:185 and the nighttime permissions of 2:187, and some commentators connect that placement to prayer during Ramadan and supplication at the breaking of the fast. **[Maʿārif]** This link is a contextual interpretation, not a restriction of the verse’s promise to one hour or one ritual. **[Study Quran]**  Al-Qurṭubī lists moments traditionally regarded as favorable for supplication, including the pre-dawn and the time of breaking the fast, while the verse itself states the broader principle of God’s nearness.  **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The verse does not endorse every possible request. **[Qurṭubī]** Commentators note that one should not ask for sin or severing of family ties, and that a supplicant should not become impatient or speak as though God were compelled to grant the request.  **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī cites prophetic guidance to ask with firm hope rather than saying “if You will,” while keeping confidence in God’s wisdom. **[Qurṭubī]**   The proper manner combines earnest asking with obedience and trust; the servant may continue to pray without demanding that the answer match an immediate desire. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]**

**Interpretive note.** The verse’s different reported occasions—questions about God’s distance, when to call, or how loudly to call—should be presented as explanations preserved in the commentaries, not as mutually confirmed historical fact. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Their common concern is answered by the same assurance: God hears the servant without the caller needing to shout or locate Him in a direction. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Saʿdī’s distinction helps clarify the theological language: God’s knowledge encompasses all, while His special nearness to worshippers includes response, help, and guidance. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]**

The promise of response should not be reduced to the immediate granting of the exact object requested. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Exegetes cite explanations in which a request is granted, its reward is reserved, or a harm is turned away; this preserves the assurance of answer while acknowledging divine wisdom about its form. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The Qurṭubī discussion also encourages persistence rather than despair, and cites the instruction to ask with earnest confidence rather than impatiently demanding a sign of fulfillment. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** A delay that the servant cannot interpret does not prove that the call was unheard. **[Ṭabarī]**

The command to “respond to Me” is read by al-Ṭabarī primarily as obeying God’s call; a minority gloss understands it as calling upon God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The following words about believing in God support the obedience reading: the servant asks, trusts the answer, and responds to divine guidance. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse therefore binds supplication to faith and action instead of separating prayer from the life of obedience. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

Al-Qurṭubī’s discussion emphasizes that asking with hope is not presumptuous: the supplicant recognizes need and addresses the One who is generous, while accepting that the response may not be immediate. **[Qurṭubī]** He cites the counsel to persist rather than let awareness of one’s own faults become a reason to abandon supplication, since forgiveness and response belong to God. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse’s assurance therefore gives the sinner a path back to God as well as comfort to the worshipper already striving in obedience. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The two commands—to respond to God and to believe in Him—also prevent the promise of answered prayer from being detached from accountability. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The servant asks for help, but is also asked to answer God’s own call through obedience. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** This reciprocal structure keeps supplication from becoming a demand that God serve private wishes: faith entrusts the outcome to God, and response to His guidance shapes the one who asks. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The verse places a personal call within a relationship of nearness and response. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The believer is invited to ask openly, believe in God, and respond to His guidance, while leaving the wisdom and timing of the answer to Him. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Its promise is neither a denial of hardship nor a guarantee that every request will arrive unchanged; it is an assurance that sincere supplication is heard and met by God’s knowledge and mercy. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The passage’s movement from fasting to prayer makes disciplined worship and intimate reliance companions rather than opposites. **[Jalālayn]**

## 2:187

187187
*“Permitted to you, on the nights of the fast, is to go in unto your wives. They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them. God knew that you were betraying yourselves, so He relented unto you and pardoned you. So now lie with them and seek what God has prescribed for you. And eat and drink until the white thread and the black thread of the dawn become clear to you. Then complete the fast until nightfall, and do not lie with them while you are in retreat in the mosques. Those are the limits set by God, so approach them not. Thus does God make clear His signs to mankind, that haply they may be reverent.”*

**Meaning.** The verse opens by making nighttime intimacy lawful during Ramadan. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The commentators explain that an earlier restriction had made eating, drinking, or marital relations after sleep—or, in some reports, after the night prayer—unlawful until the next evening. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** Reports vary in how they describe the old rule and its occasion; accounts mention Qays ibn Ṣirmah’s exhaustion after labor and other Companions who found the restriction difficult.    The verse should not be made to depend on one embellished version of those reports.

“Betraying yourselves” describes people who violated the restriction then in force, not a permanent condemnation of marital intimacy.   God’s relenting and pardon accompany the new permission, and the address “now” marks the removal of the former hardship. **[Jalālayn]**   Commentaries relate the language of betrayal to both eating and sexual relations under the earlier rule, while reports differ about which incident prompted the revelation.  **[Study Quran]** The passage presents lawful intimacy as part of the ease granted to believers, not as something inherently blameworthy.

The image “they are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them” conveys mutual closeness. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some commentators emphasize the spouses’ physical nearness and covering of one another; others explain the garment as comfort, protection, or a dwelling in which each finds repose. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** The metaphor is reciprocal: it describes both spouses, rather than treating one as the sole giver or the other as merely the recipient.  **[Maʿārif]** It places marital intimacy within mutual companionship and lawful affection.

“Seek what God has prescribed for you” is interpreted in several ways.  Many early commentators take it to include seeking offspring through lawful marital relations, which fits the immediate mention of spouses.   Other explanations include seeking what God has permitted, following His revealed instruction, or seeking the Night of Power during Ramadan. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Saʿdī includes intending a good purpose through intimacy, such as chastity and children, while cautioning that pursuit of pleasure should not distract from the worshipful opportunities of the month. **[Saʿdī]** The interpretations need not be forced into a single narrow gloss.

The permission to eat and drink extends through the night “until the white thread is distinct from the black thread of the dawn.” **[Ṭabarī]**  The phrase is figurative: the white thread is the light of dawn and the black thread is the darkness of night, not two physical cords.  **[Jalālayn]** The addition “of the dawn” clarifies the image, and reports about ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim describe how the Prophet explained that it refers to daybreak and night.   Commentaries distinguish the true dawn that spreads across the horizon from an earlier vertical glow that does not mark the same boundary.  **[Maʿārif]**

The boundary of dawn gives a clear starting point for the daytime fast.  **[Ibn Kathīr]** The permission of a pre-dawn meal supports the practice of *suḥūr*, which the commentaries describe as recommended and best delayed within the night until the dawn boundary.    The verse does not license intentional eating after the true dawn has become clear, nor does it demand that people impose an unsupported early cutoff while night remains.  **[Study Quran]** Since marital relations remain permitted until dawn, the sources also infer that a person may enter the fast in a state of major ritual impurity and perform the washing afterward.  **[Qurṭubī]**

“Complete the fast until nightfall” sets its end at the arrival of night, identified with sunset. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The fasting period is therefore bounded at both ends: the true dawn begins abstention, and sunset ends it.  **[Saʿdī]** The verse does not commend extending the fast into the night without eating; al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī connect the stated endpoint to prophetic reports discouraging continuous fasting. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**   The commentaries describe the transition from day to night as the legal end, rather than requiring complete darkness before breaking the fast.

The exception for those “in retreat in the mosques” concerns *iʿtikāf*, a devotional retreat during which sexual relations are prohibited even at night.   **[Jalālayn]** The verse permits nighttime intimacy generally but expressly keeps this boundary for the person who remains in retreat. **[Maʿārif]**  Commentators discuss additional conditions of *iʿtikāf*, including which mosques qualify and when a person may leave, but those details are not all settled by this clause alone.   The image of retreat is one of sustained devotion, so the restriction protects the particular worship being undertaken. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Interpretive note.** The phrase “betraying yourselves” is explained through reports of people who ate, drank, or had relations after the old nighttime restriction had taken effect. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The accounts of Qays ibn Ṣirmah and ʿUmar are transmitted with differing details, and al-Ṭabarī preserves the status of several chains; they should not all be retold as one fully settled occasion. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** What the verse clearly establishes is that God removed the former restriction and granted permission for food, drink, and marital intimacy during the night. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The verb *rafath* is an indirect expression for sexual relations in this context, and *mubāsharah* likewise refers to intercourse in the verse’s permission. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The metaphor of garments adds a dimension beyond the legal allowance: spouses are close, mutually protective, and a source of rest for one another. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** The command to “seek what God has prescribed” is often glossed as seeking offspring, but the commentaries also record readings about seeking lawful permission, Qur’anic guidance, or the Night of Power. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The threshold for the fast is the true dawn, not an imagined literal thread. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Reports about ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim and the later phrase “of the dawn” explain that the image refers to the contrast between night’s darkness and daybreak’s spreading light. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The sources distinguish the true horizontal dawn from an earlier vertical glow and discuss the timing of *suḥūr*, without making every precautionary recommendation a separate Qur’anic command. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The mention of *iʿtikāf* makes a specific exception to nighttime permission: sexual relations remain prohibited while a person is in devotional retreat in the mosque. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The commentaries provide further differences about the qualifying mosque and the conditions of retreat; the verse itself marks the boundary without resolving every later legal detail. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The permission is also notable for its reciprocal language: both spouses are described as garments, and the lawful nighttime relationship is placed within mutual companionship rather than one-sided entitlement. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The source explanations of comfort, covering, and closeness add meaning to the legal change without replacing its plain permission for marital intimacy. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse thus frames the household as part of the ordinary life that the fast temporarily disciplines during daylight, not as something that must be denied throughout the month. **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** The concluding “limits of God” gathers the permissions and prohibitions into one framework.  **[Qurṭubī]** Nighttime eating and intimacy are permitted, the dawn-to-sunset fast is required, and the retreat has its own boundary. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** “Do not approach them” is a caution not only against crossing a stated line but against treating divine limits carelessly. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** The passage therefore combines mercy with precision: God removes an earlier hardship, makes the lawful clear, and teaches believers to observe the remaining limits so that fasting may cultivate *taqwā*. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]**

## 2:188

188188
*“And do not devour your property among yourselves falsely, nor proffer it to the judges that you may knowingly devour a part of the people’s property sinfully.”*

**Meaning.** The verse prohibits taking or using another person’s property by wrongful means. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The phrase “your property among yourselves” expresses mutual responsibility: another person’s wealth is not morally distant from one’s own, and the community is harmed when its members seize one another’s rights. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** “Devour” is a figurative expression for consuming or benefiting from wealth, not a restriction to food alone. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī explains *bāṭil* as acquiring property by a route God has not permitted. **[Ṭabarī]**

The commentaries apply the prohibition to theft, robbery, usurpation, betrayal of a trust, denial of a debt, deception in trade, gambling, usurious dealings, and other transactions treated as invalid or forbidden.    These examples illustrate the breadth of “wrongfully”; the verse is not a list limited to the named cases. **[Ṭabarī]**  Al-Qurṭubī includes property taken through false claims or by an unjust court action, while al-Saʿdī emphasizes that a transaction’s outward agreement does not by itself make it permissible if the exchange is inherently wrongful. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The central measure is whether the property is obtained through a lawful right rather than coercion, fraud, or an unlawful claim.

The phrase “nor proffer it to the judges” is explained in more than one related way.   Some commentators understand it as bringing property or a false claim before authorities in order to obtain another person’s wealth through a judgment; others emphasize bribing judges so they will rule in the claimant’s favor. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** Both readings concern using legal process or money to secure an unjust advantage. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Qurṭubī says the wording can include offering a bribe, while al-Ṭabarī focuses on a person who litigates while knowing that the right belongs to the other party. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The final words “while you know” place emphasis on deliberate wrongdoing. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr cites the example of a debtor who denies a debt when the creditor lacks proof, then uses a court case to retain money he knows is not his. **[Ibn Kathīr]**  A person who brings a claim in good faith because he sincerely believes it to be his is not the same as someone who knowingly lies or hides the truth.   The verse condemns conscious appropriation, not the mere act of asking a court to decide a genuine disagreement.  **[Jalālayn]**

A prophetic report cited by the commentators explains why a court ruling cannot erase a person’s inward knowledge. **[Ibn Kathīr]**  The Prophet says that disputants may present their arguments with unequal eloquence, and a judge may rule for one party on the basis of what he hears; whoever thereby receives another Muslim’s right has received a portion of Fire.  **[Study Quran]** A judgment is made from evidence available to the court and does not make a knowingly stolen property morally lawful for the person who knows the truth.  **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The sources also report an occasion involving a land dispute and a party who was about to swear an oath.   The details and identifications vary among the accounts, so they are best treated as reported contexts rather than as a single certain history.  The broader lesson does not depend on resolving those differences: a person should not use a false oath, witness, or legal argument to acquire what he knows belongs to someone else. **[Ibn Kathīr]**  The verse thus protects both property rights and the integrity of adjudication.

The mutual phrasing also warns that wrongful taking corrodes trust throughout society. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** When people assume that cleverness, pressure, or a favorable ruling can substitute for a rightful claim, the victim’s loss becomes a shared insecurity. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī’s explanation that one person’s wealth is spoken of as “your wealth” reflects the bonds of the believing community and the seriousness of harming another member. **[Ṭabarī]** The verse consequently addresses the possessor, the claimant, the witness, and the person who might facilitate a corrupt judgment.

**Interpretive note.** The image of “proffering” property to judges also evokes sending a bucket down a well, a lexical comparison al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī use to explain how a litigant offers a claim in hope of drawing out a ruling. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The wording can thus address both a false case presented through the court and a bribe offered to influence the judge; the commentaries give weight to both possibilities. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** The grammatical relationship between the clauses is also discussed, but either reading condemns using adjudication to take another person’s property knowingly. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

A truthful judge may be limited to the evidence and testimony placed before the court. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Prophet’s report makes clear that a persuasive argument can prevail outwardly even when the claimant knows that the disputed right belongs to someone else. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** Thus the court’s decision is not a moral permission to keep property acquired by false testimony, concealment, or a knowingly dishonest claim. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The commentaries note legal disagreements about the effects of some judgments in particular cases, but the moral warning against knowingly taking another’s wealth remains central. **[Qurṭubī]**

The commentaries report a dispute over land as one possible setting for the verse. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** In one account, a claimant lacking witnesses was asked to rely on an oath, and the verse’s warning turned attention to the danger of claiming what one knows belongs to another. **[Qurṭubī]** Other reports describe a debtor denying an obligation and attempting to win the matter before the authorities. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Since the accounts differ, the ethical principle is firmer than any one identification of the parties: a court case must not be used to dress deliberate appropriation as a lawful claim. **[Study Quran]**

“Your property among yourselves” also prevents the offender from imagining that only the victim bears the loss. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** If wrongful acquisition becomes ordinary, trust in exchange and testimony erodes, and everyone’s property becomes less secure. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse therefore addresses the social conditions that enable injustice as well as the individual who takes the disputed wealth. **[Jalālayn]** A judge’s ruling may resolve an outward case, but it cannot turn known falsehood into truth before God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The breadth of “wrongfully” reaches not only taking another’s property by force but also retaining what is owed or entrusted to someone else. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** As-Saʿdī includes betrayal of deposits, taking wages without doing the agreed work, and receiving charitable or endowed funds beyond one’s entitlement among examples of wrongful consumption. **[Saʿdī]** The common thread is that possession alone does not establish a right: an apparent opportunity, a persuasive claim, or another person’s inability to prove a debt does not convert the property into one’s own. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** A truthful claim may be brought to a judge for decision; the warning addresses the person who knowingly uses that process to consume another’s share. **[Study Quran]** **[Jalālayn]**

**Reflection.** The fasting passage immediately before this verse has emphasized restraint from lawful food for a limited time; this command turns attention to wealth that is not lawful to take at any time. **[Maʿārif]** The connection is a moral one: self-control in worship should deepen respect for others’ rights. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** A persuasive case or a technical victory does not relieve a person of accountability when he knows the claim is false. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The believer is called to seek only what is genuinely due and to leave another person’s property untouched, even when misuse of a court or transaction might appear to succeed. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]**

## 2:189

189189
*“They ask thee about the new moons. Say, ‘They are markers of time for mankind and for the Hajj.’ It is not piety that you should come to houses from their rear, but piety is he who is reverent and comes into houses by their doors. So reverence God, that haply you may prosper.”*

**Meaning.** The first part answers a question about the changing appearance of the moon by identifying the practical wisdom of its phases: the crescents are markers of time for people and for pilgrimage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Reports differ over whether the question came from Companions asking why the moon waxes and wanes or from another exchange about its changing form. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The Qur’anic answer does not attempt to give a physical account of lunar motion; it points to how the visible cycle serves human life. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]**

The Arabic *ahillah* refers to the visible crescents at the beginnings of lunar months, rather than only to the astronomical dark moon.   Their waxing and waning make the passage of months publicly recognizable.   The sources list times for fasting and breaking the fast, pilgrimage, women’s waiting periods, debts, leases, and other transactions as matters that can be reckoned by the lunar calendar. **[Ṭabarī]**   Al-Saʿdī emphasizes that this visible reckoning is accessible to people with different levels of learning. **[Saʿdī]** The verse presents the moon’s phases as a mercy and practical sign, not merely an object of observation.

The Hajj is singled out because its rites are tied to an appointed season, and the pilgrimage cannot simply be detached from the time God has set for it.  **[Qurṭubī]** The commentators relate the verse to the rejection of pre-Islamic manipulation of sacred months, though the detailed legal discussion belongs to the later passages on pilgrimage and sacred time.  **[Maʿārif]** The word “markers” therefore covers both ordinary arrangements and acts of worship; the same lunar cycle helps organize a debt’s due date and the timing of Hajj. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]**

The second part corrects a practice some Arabs treated as piety. Commentaries report that people in a state of *iḥrām* would enter their houses through the rear, a hole, or by climbing over a wall rather than using the door. **[Ibn Kathīr]**   Some reports focus on the Anṣār returning from pilgrimage or travel; others associate the practice with the *ḥums*, groups who followed particular customs during pilgrimage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** These accounts vary in detail, so the verse should not be tied to one story as the only certain occasion.  Al-Qurṭubī prefers the literal interpretation of entering houses, citing reports about the practice itself. **[Qurṭubī]**

The correction is not that a door has special spiritual power, but that a self-imposed hardship does not become worship merely because someone calls it pious.   “It is not piety” rejects a ritual restriction that God had not prescribed; “piety is he who is reverent” redirects attention to *taqwā* and obedience. **[Jalālayn]**  **[Maʿārif]** Al-Saʿdī generalizes the practical image: in ordinary affairs one should approach matters by the proper and straightforward means, while those who teach or correct others should use a wise and gentle approach. **[Saʿdī]** Other commentators offer metaphorical readings about approaching affairs by their proper “doors,” but al-Qurṭubī regards the literal house practice as the stronger immediate reading. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The prohibition of invented ritual does not mean that every difficult religious practice is invalid or that believers may dismiss established obligations.   Rather, the verse contrasts an uncommanded custom with genuine reverence shown by following God’s guidance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The reported custom turned an ordinary entrance into a supposed religious boundary, and the revelation removed that false burden. **[Jalālayn]**  The moral lesson must remain attached to the example: worship is not improved by declaring lawful conduct sinful or by inventing a hardship as a condition of devotion.  **[Maʿārif]**

The closing command, “reverence God, that haply you may prosper,” ties both halves together.   The lunar signs help people fulfill worship and manage obligations; genuine *taqwā* directs them to use those signs and obey the actual commands rather than follow unsupported taboos. **[Saʿdī]**  The verse’s movement from the moon to the doorway is therefore not a random change of subject: both passages distinguish useful guidance from unnecessary speculation or invented practice.  **[Study Quran]** Al-Jalālayn likewise closes by linking fear of disobedience with the prospect of success. **[Jalālayn]**

**Interpretive note.** The question about the crescents is answered in terms of benefit rather than a full physical explanation of why the moon changes shape. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran clarifies that the *hilāl* is the visible crescent marking the lunar month, rather than the invisible astronomical conjunction sometimes called the new moon. **[Study Quran]** **[Jalālayn]** Because the cycle is observable, the month can guide both communal worship and ordinary reckoning without specialized instruments. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The door custom is also explained in several forms: some reports describe a hole in the rear wall while in *iḥrām*, others climbing over a house, and still others a practice of avoiding a roof between the pilgrim and the sky. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The sources differ over the exact groups and circumstances, and some reports are not equally strong; al-Qurṭubī favors the literal explanation supported by reports of the Anṣār entering houses from the rear. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The lesson is not to reproduce every detail as certain but to see why the verse rejected a burdensome custom treated as an act of worship without divine command. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The verse also supports a broader analogy: approach an affair by the means properly appointed for it. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Saʿdī applies this to teaching and moral counsel, where a gentle, practical path is often more beneficial than an unnecessarily difficult one. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** This broader reading complements rather than replaces the literal correction of entering houses by their doors. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]**

The door custom illustrates how an inherited practice may acquire the appearance of religion even when it has no revealed basis. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The reports mention people in pilgrimage consecration avoiding the ordinary doorway, sometimes because they believed an obstruction between themselves and the sky was improper; the verse corrects that belief rather than demanding a more strenuous substitute. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The exact stories vary, including accounts involving the Anṣār and the pilgrimage customs of the *ḥums*. **[Study Quran]** Al-Qurṭubī’s preference for the literal reading rests on reports that describe houses and entrances directly. **[Qurṭubī]**

The correction also makes *birr* a matter of reverent obedience rather than outward spectacle. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Entering through a door is not condemned; what is rejected is treating an uncommanded avoidance of that door as a necessary act of devotion. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** The passage therefore restores ordinary lawful conduct and directs the pilgrim back to *taqwā* as the criterion of piety. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The visible crescent makes time legible for communal life and worship, while the doorway image makes a moral principle concrete. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** People should not confuse a custom’s apparent austerity with righteousness, nor mistake a question about the moon’s physical appearance for the only question the verse answers. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The passage directs attention to the benefit of God’s signs and to reverence expressed through what He actually commands. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Prosperity is attached not to a display of self-imposed difficulty, but to recognizing the appointed times and entering one’s affairs by the proper path. **[Jalālayn]**

## 2:190

190190
*“And fight in the way of God against those who fight against you, but do not transgress. Truly God loves not the transgressors.”*

**Meaning.** The verse introduces a command to fight “in the way of God” and immediately limits its scope to those who fight against the believers. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The commentators explain that the phrase directs the action toward God’s cause rather than display or factional strife. **[Saʿdī]**  Al-Saʿdī reads the reference to those who fight as including those prepared to engage in combat, while al-Ṭabarī emphasizes that the order does not include people who refrain from fighting. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**   The verse’s second command—“do not transgress”—makes clear that even a response to aggression remains bounded by moral limits. **[Jalālayn]**

Several commentators place the verse in the period after the migration to Medina, when permission to fight was given after an earlier period of restraint.  **[Maʿārif]**  Reports also connect the passage to the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyyah and the believers’ concern about returning to perform the lesser pilgrimage while facing possible aggression in the Sacred Precinct and sacred month.  **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** These are reported contexts that help explain the concern about fighting, not a reason to treat every detail of the narrative as equally certain. **[Ṭabarī]** Commentators differ over which verse was the first to permit fighting, with some naming this verse and others citing 22:39. **[Qurṭubī]**

The commentaries also preserve disagreement about whether the command was later abrogated.  Some early interpreters say that the initial restriction to those who fought was superseded by later commands concerning warfare; other authorities regard 2:190 as still operative in its prohibition of transgression and its restriction against harming noncombatants.  **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī rejects an unsupported claim of abrogation and favors the reading that the verse continues to limit fighting to combatants and to protect those who do not take part.  **[Study Quran]** It is important to preserve this interpretive disagreement instead of presenting one historical theory as though no other classical view existed. **[Maʿārif]**

In explaining “those who fight you,” al-Ṭabarī cites Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz on not killing women, children, the elderly, or people who have laid down their arms. **[Ṭabarī]**  Ibn Kathīr includes prohibitions on killing women and children, mutilating the dead, committing treachery, stealing from captured property, and killing people devoted to worship who do not fight.  **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī records a range of premodern juristic positions about other categories, including monks, laborers, and people with disabilities, and also records distinctions where individuals participate in fighting. **[Qurṭubī]**   These details are part of the sources’ classical legal discussions; the verse’s broad ethical point is that nonparticipation and restraint matter when identifying the limits of combat. **[Saʿdī]**
