The phrase “do not transgress” is not limited to refraining from striking first. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Commentators include among transgressions killing those outside the fighting, mutilation, betrayal, wrongful seizure, and needless destruction of trees or animals.  **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī also connects the command with avoiding combat for motives other than God’s cause and not harming those who are protected by a covenant or who have accepted peace. **[Saʿdī]**   The sources differ in the legal treatment of particular historical cases, so these examples should not be collapsed into an assertion that every jurist formulated every rule identically.  **[Study Quran]**

Al-Ṭabarī stresses that the words “those who fight you” allow restraint toward those who refrain, including women and children, while his preferred interpretation also mentions those who accept a protected status under the law then discussed by the commentators. **[Ṭabarī]**   The Study Quran highlights this distinction between combatants and noncombatants and notes that later verses continue to define conditions around the Sacred Mosque. **[Study Quran]**   Such later qualifications should not be imported into the first clause as though 2:190 alone settles every circumstance; the verse states the governing command and its prohibition on excess. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]**

The setting “in the way of God” is another limit on motive. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** A report cited by Ibn Kathīr distinguishes fighting for courage or display from fighting so that God’s word is upheld. **[Ibn Kathīr]**  The Study Quran likewise emphasizes that the passage treats fighting as subject to a stated purpose and rules, not as an unrestricted expression of hostility. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse’s final clause—“God loves not the transgressors”—places those limits under divine moral judgment: a claimed religious cause does not excuse conduct that exceeds them. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

**Interpretive note.** The phrase “do not transgress” has both a direct limit on whom to fight and a broader limit on how conflict is conducted. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī cites the interpretation that women, children, the elderly, and those who surrender or refrain from fighting are not to be treated as combatants. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī add examples from the classical legal discussion, including prohibitions on mutilation, treachery, looting, and killing people devoted to worship who do not participate in combat. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī includes unnecessary harm to animals and trees among forms of excess. **[Saʿdī]**

The disagreement about abrogation is substantive. **[Qurṭubī]** Some reports treat the limitation to those who fight as an early rule later superseded; al-Ṭabarī rejects that claim without evidence and reads the restriction as continuing. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr likewise argues that the phrase “those who fight you” has a meaningful scope and does not simply disappear under later verses. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran notes both positions and emphasizes that the adjacent verses continue to specify the Sacred Precinct and cessation of hostilities. **[Study Quran]** This interpretive history should be described, not converted into an unqualified present-day legal directive. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

Finally, “in the way of God” rules out making personal glory or display the purpose of fighting. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The sources link the phrase to sincerity and to action governed by divine limits; the closing statement that God does not love transgressors underscores that a claimed cause cannot sanctify excess. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The surrounding passage supplies context that 2:190 itself does not exhaust: the following verses address the Sacred Mosque, expulsion, the cessation of hostilities, and the limits on retaliation. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some commentaries connect the instruction with anxiety about returning to Mecca after Ḥudaybiyyah and the possibility of being attacked during a sacred time. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** Other exegetes foreground the broader transition from restraint before the migration to permission to fight in Medina. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** Those contexts explain why the verse combines a command with an immediate warning against transgression. **[Saʿdī]**

The reported dispute over abrogation shows why the limitation must be kept visible. **[Qurṭubī]** Some authorities connect later verses to a wider command, while al-Ṭabarī argues that an abrogation should not be asserted without evidence and preserves the ban on targeting those who do not fight. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** Ibn Kathīr likewise reads the clause as addressing those actively engaged against the believers, not as a phrase emptied of meaning by later revelation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The exegetical history is complex, but all discussion remains framed by the explicit condemnation of transgression. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]**

**Reflection.** The verse holds response and restraint together. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** It does not describe conflict as a free-standing virtue; it directs the believers to act for God’s cause, addresses those who fight them, and forbids crossing the limits. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The exegetes’ disagreement over abrogation and over the application to particular groups should remain visible, while their shared concern with prohibiting excess is central to the verse. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Its warning that God does not love transgressors means that moral restraint is not suspended in conflict. **[Maʿārif]**
## 2:191

191191
*“And kill them wherever you encounter them, and expel them from where they expelled you, for persecution is more grievous than killing. But do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you there. If they fight you, then kill them; such is the requital of the disbelievers.”*

**Meaning.** Read directly after the command to fight those who fight the believers and not to transgress in 2:190, this verse speaks within a conflict marked by aggression, expulsion, and obstruction of worship. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Its opening command is not a free-standing instruction detached from that setting: the following words recall the believers’ expulsion from their homes, and the verse itself immediately places a special restriction on fighting at the Sacred Mosque. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** The forceful language must therefore be read with both the preceding limit against transgression and the conditions stated in the verse, rather than taken as a license to attack people indiscriminately. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The phrase “from where they expelled you” points to the displacement of the early Muslim community from Mecca. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Commentators explain the command to expel in light of that prior expulsion: the verse answers a history of being driven from home and prevented from worship, not a private grievance or a general permission to dispossess others. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif connects the passage with the believers’ anticipated return to Mecca after Ḥudaybiyyah, when they feared that the Meccans might break the truce and attack them. **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran likewise treats the reported Ḥudaybiyyah setting as context for the concern about aggression in a place and season ordinarily held sacred, while keeping the report identified as a contextual account. **[Study Quran]** **[Jalālayn]**

“Persecution is more grievous than killing” translates *al-fitnatu ashaddu min al-qatl*, a phrase the early commentaries explain in more than one related way. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Many early authorities gloss *fitna* as idolatry or disbelief, while others stress the coercion by which believers were tortured, driven from Mecca, or prevented from carrying out their religious obligations. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** These readings share an emphasis on the harm of persecution and religious coercion, but they are not identical: a gloss of *fitna* as shirk should not erase the concrete pressure and expulsion described in the surrounding verses. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The Study Quran cautions against turning the phrase into an unqualified argument that forcible conversion is the goal; it points readers to the Qur’anic protection given to those who seek safety, including 9:6. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The verse singles out the precinct of the Sacred Mosque: the believers are not to initiate fighting there, unless they are attacked there. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** The commentators understand the sanctuary as having a special inviolability, while recognizing the stated exception for defense if an opponent begins hostilities inside it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** This clause is not redundant with the general command at the start of the verse; it narrows how that command applies at a sacred location. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The immediate sequence thus holds two concerns together: the community may resist aggression, yet the sanctuary is not to become a place where believers begin violence. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The commentators do not agree on whether the restriction on initiating combat at the Sacred Mosque remained in force or was later superseded by broader permissions. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī records arguments that the exception was abrogated by later verses, alongside readings that retain the defensive qualification; al-Qurṭubī reports the disagreement and favors preserving the sanctuary’s protection, while Ibn Kathīr argues that the clause remains meaningful and is not abrogated. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Maʿārif likewise explains the exception in terms of answering an attack rather than initiating one at the sanctuary. **[Maʿārif]** This is a real exegetical and legal disagreement, so a summary should disclose it instead of presenting one position as the uncontested view of all the commentators. **[Study Quran]** **[Jalālayn]**

The broader discussion of “those who fight you” also leads commentators to distinguish combatants from people who do not participate in fighting. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī cites early authorities on sparing women, children, and others who do not fight; Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī discuss further classical limits, including prohibitions on treachery and mutilation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Their reports and legal categories are not identical in every detail, but the shared exegetical concern is that the permission to resist aggression does not cancel the prohibition on transgression announced in 2:190. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran emphasizes the need to read the verse with its immediate restrictions and the broader Qur’anic treatment of protected persons. **[Study Quran]**

The historical account does not itself answer every question later jurists debated about sacred territory, truces, or the scope of warfare. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** It does, however, make the verse’s sequence intelligible: the believers are told to resist those who expelled them, are reminded that persecution and religious obstruction are grave harms, and are specifically forbidden to initiate combat at the Sacred Mosque. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** The concluding phrase “such is the requital of the disbelievers” belongs to this encounter with active opposition in the verse’s setting; it should not be detached from the preceding conditional language and read as a command against every person outside the faith. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Reflection.** The verse’s severity is paired with limits: it speaks of expulsion and persecution, marks the sanctuary as inviolable except in response to attack, and remains under the command not to transgress. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Its classical interpreters differ over abrogation and over the precise scope of the terms, but they do not all read it as an unrestricted warrant. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran’s caution about conversion as the sole endpoint is especially relevant when *fitna* is translated only as disbelief, without attending to coercion, protection, and the surrounding verses. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The passage calls for a contextual reading that preserves both the reality of persecution and the constraints placed on any response. **[Jalālayn]**

## 2:192

192192
*“Then if they desist, truly God is Forgiving, Merciful.”*

**Meaning.** The conditional phrase “if they desist” continues the discussion of aggression and persecution in 2:190–191. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The immediate sense is that when the opponents stop fighting or cease the persecution that prompted the conflict, hostilities are not to continue simply because they once began. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** In Maʿārif’s explanation of the Ḥudaybiyyah context, the verse responds to the believers’ fear that an opponent might violate a truce: if the anticipated aggression does not occur or is brought to an end, the exception for defense does not become an excuse to pursue conflict. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The short verse therefore functions as a hinge between the permission to resist attack and the limit that requires stopping when the cause has ceased. **[Saʿdī]**

The verb “desist” is explained in the commentaries with attention to what must stop. **[Ṭabarī]** Some reports gloss it as ceasing to fight; others include ending persecution, obstruction, or the acts of disbelief that earlier commentators identify with *fitna*. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** A number of classical exegetes also connect cessation with entering Islam or joining the community of believers, while other readings focus on the end of hostilities rather than making conversion the sole measure. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The Study Quran cautions that the sequence should not be made to teach forced conversion: the surrounding Qur’anic guidance includes protection for people seeking safety, as in 9:6. **[Study Quran]** The range of interpretation should be preserved, since the phrase’s application is precisely where different commentators place emphasis. **[Maʿārif]**

The verse’s relation to 2:191 is especially important. That verse allows a defensive response if fighting is initiated at the Sacred Mosque, while 2:192 states that the response must end when the other side desists. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Read together, the clauses prevent the exception from turning into an unlimited pursuit: defense is linked to actual aggression, and cessation removes the stated occasion for continuing it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Some commentators place the verse within the continuing debate about whether particular restrictions were later abrogated, but even where they differ about legal scope, the wording here explicitly commends stopping when the opposing party stops. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

“God is Forgiving, Merciful” gives theological weight to that stopping point. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** The commentaries explain the divine forgiveness in relation to the past: once people desist, God may forgive their earlier hostility or disbelief if they repent and turn toward Him. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The wording also keeps the door of mercy open to people who change course, rather than treating a previous wrong as an identity from which there is no return. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** This is not an assertion that every injury between human beings is automatically erased; it is a statement about God’s forgiveness and the end of the conflict described here. **[Study Quran]**

The verse also clarifies why mercy follows a passage about fighting. **[Maʿārif]** The goal is not to keep hostility alive after the cause named in the text has ended; the transition from fighting to cessation is accompanied by divine forgiveness and mercy. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī’s material includes explanations in which an opponent’s cessation of fighting, together with acceptance of the faith, ends the immediate conflict. **[Ṭabarī]** Other expositors stress that the cessation of persecution is itself central to the command’s operation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Keeping both emphases visible prevents the verse from being paraphrased either as an unconditional rule to stop in every possible circumstance regardless of other duties or as a demand that the adversary must convert before any restraint is possible. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

The phrase “then, if they desist” also links this verse to the next one, which restates the objective as the end of *fitna* and says that if the opponents desist, there is no hostility except against wrongdoers. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The repetition is purposeful: 2:192 stresses forgiveness and mercy, while 2:193 expands on the aim and boundary of the conflict. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The commentators use the repetition to discuss what counts as cessation, whether it means stopping armed resistance, ending religious persecution, or a broader turn from disbelief. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The text’s own sequence makes clear that cessation is a condition that matters, not a detail to be ignored. **[Saʿdī]**

Nothing in the verse asks the reader to celebrate conflict or to confuse divine forgiveness with human permission to retaliate indefinitely. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** It addresses a particular sequence: aggression or persecution, a conditional response, then cessation and mercy. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The historical reports surrounding Ḥudaybiyyah help explain why the believers were concerned about being attacked in sacred territory, but the reports are contextual explanations, not a replacement for the verse’s stated condition. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** An interpreter should therefore distinguish a report about the occasion from the rule communicated by the wording. **[Jalālayn]**

**Interpretive note.** The phrase “if they desist” is not glossed identically across the tafsīrs. **[Ṭabarī]** Some authorities take it as stopping armed conflict; others relate it to ceasing *fitna*, with many early glosses of that term as shirk or disbelief. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Some classical readings connect cessation with accepting Islam, while the Study Quran cautions against treating conversion as the only possible endpoint, drawing attention to the protection of those who seek safety in 9:6. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** That distinction should be stated rather than blurred, especially because the surrounding verses also address persecution and aggression. **[Jalālayn]**

The divine names at the end are not decorative. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** They ground the transition away from hostilities in the possibility of forgiveness and renewed relationship with God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** Ibn Kathīr relates the forgiveness to the cessation of the opponents’ prior wrongs when they turn away from them, while al-Qurṭubī likewise discusses mercy for those who repent. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran’s reading stresses that the passage cannot be reduced to a demand for uniform belief when the broader revelation provides safety to people who seek protection. **[Study Quran]** Thus divine mercy supports the cessation condition without making the historical dispute disappear. **[Ṭabarī]**

**Reflection.** This verse makes the end of hostility as significant as its beginning. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Where the cause named in the passage ceases, the response should not become an end in itself; mercy, forgiveness, and restraint return to the foreground. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** The exegetes differ on the full meaning of “desist,” and that disagreement should remain visible. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** Yet the sequence clearly refuses to treat conflict as open-ended: the text explicitly marks cessation and divine mercy as the next possibility. **[Maʿārif]**

## 2:193

193193
*“Fight them until there is no persecution and religion is for God. But if they desist, then there is no hostility save against the wrongdoers.”*

**Meaning.** This verse completes the sequence begun in 2:190 by stating the aim of the struggle and repeating the condition that hostilities stop when the opponents desist. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** A frequent early interpretation takes *fitna* here as shirk or idolatry, so that worship is directed to God alone; other commentators explain it as persecution, coercion, or the obstruction of believers’ worship. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** These glosses overlap in the historical setting, where religious allegiance and coercive pressure were intertwined, but they lead to different emphases and should not be collapsed into a single translation without qualification. **[Study Quran]** **[Jalālayn]**

Al-Ṭabarī transmits explanations in which the verse calls for the removal of shirk and the establishment of worship devoted to God, while Ibn Kathīr likewise reports *fitna* as shirk and relates the verse to ending polytheist opposition. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī records a range of early definitions, including shirk, persecution, and the conditions that keep believers from their religious duties. **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif links the term to both disbelief and the prevention of worship, emphasizing the reported Meccan context. **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran gives particular attention to the alternative sense of persecution and warns against reading the verse as a simple mandate to compel everyone to convert. **[Study Quran]** The difference is interpretively important: a prohibition on persecuting worshippers is not identical in meaning to an instruction that every person must adopt one belief. **[Saʿdī]**

The words “religion is for God” are also explained with different shades of meaning. **[Ṭabarī]** They may mean that worship and obedience belong to God alone, or that no one should be forced from the worship they practice by violent persecution; some exegetes combine those senses in describing the end of the conflict. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** In the early setting, the verse addresses a community that had faced expulsion, pressure, and obstruction of pilgrimage, so “until” marks the point at which the source of hostilities is removed. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī describes the aim in terms of ending shirk and making worship sincere for God, while the broader set of readings needs to remain visible. **[Saʿdī]**

The final clause is essential: “if they desist, then there is no hostility save against the wrongdoers.” **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** It echoes 2:192 and makes cessation a condition, rather than allowing the first command to be read as perpetual conflict. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Commentators explain *ʿudwān* (hostility or aggression) as applying to those who continue wrongdoing; when the acts prompting the response end, the cause for hostility ends as well. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse therefore links the objective of ending *fitna* to a prohibition on continuing aggression against those who desist. **[Study Quran]**

Exegetes discuss whether the phrase “religion is for God” signifies the disappearance of all unbelief or the freedom to worship without coercion. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Some classical interpretations understand the phrase as a call to exclusive monotheism and connect the cessation of fighting with acceptance of Islam; others focus on the cessation of persecution and hostilities. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran cautions against isolating one clause from the rest of the Qur’anic discourse, noting the explicit protection afforded to those who seek asylum in 9:6. **[Study Quran]** The text’s own closing condition, along with 2:190’s prohibition on transgression and 2:192’s call to stop when opponents desist, matters to the interpretation. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]**

The relationship with the preceding verses makes it difficult to read 2:193 as an unlimited command. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Verse 190 first restricts the fighting to those who fight the believers and forbids transgression; verse 191 discusses expulsion and the special status of the Sacred Mosque; verse 192 says to stop when the opponents desist. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Verse 193 then identifies an aim and repeats that the end of hostility changes what may be done. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** The sources do not all resolve the legal scope in the same way, but the adjacent limitations must be included in any careful summary. **[Maʿārif]**

The phrase “no hostility except against the wrongdoers” does not turn past wrongdoing into an inherited status for every member of a group. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Its grammar and context associate hostility with continuing *ẓulm*, not with a permanent license to target people after the relevant conduct has ceased. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** Ibn Kathīr reads the conclusion as allowing the response only toward those who persist in wrongdoing, while the verse’s conditional opening points toward cessation and forgiveness. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Interpretive note.** The main disagreement turns on *fitna*. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Many early authorities gloss it as shirk; other readings stress persecution, coercion, and the obstruction of worship. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran argues that the verse should not be presented as requiring conversion as the sole endpoint, and it notes 9:6 as a passage granting protection to those seeking safety. **[Study Quran]** The interpretations differ in emphasis, and the verse should be read with the preceding restrictions on aggression and the following condition that hostilities cease when the opponents desist. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]**

The wording “until” connects the command to an objective rather than making conflict self-justifying. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** Classical commentators variously define that objective as the end of idolatry, the establishment of worship for God, or the removal of persecution against believers. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Whether an exegete treats the goal as religious or political, the clause “if they desist” still qualifies the action and forbids hostility against those who have stopped. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

The verse’s placement after 2:191 also matters: the discussion has just named expulsion from homes, the danger of persecution, and a special restriction at the Sacred Mosque. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The target of the response is thus not every outsider without distinction but the wrongdoing, coercion, and armed opposition described in the passage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The sources preserve wider medieval debate about the reach of the command, but they also preserve the conditional language and the moral boundary against transgression. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** Read with the preceding verses, this is a statement about the end of persecution and hostility, not a detached celebration of force. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]** The commentators differ over whether *fitna* chiefly means shirk, coercion, or both in the circumstances described; a responsible account should identify that difference. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran’s caution about forced conversion and its cross-reference to 9:6 help keep the verse’s restrictive context in view. **[Study Quran]** The closing condition that opponents who desist are not to be treated with hostility preserves the passage’s call to restraint and mercy. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

## 2:194

194194
*“The sacred month is for the sacred month, and sacred things are subject to retaliation. So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like measure as he transgressed against you. And reverence God, and know that God is with the reverent.”*

**Meaning.** “The sacred month is for the sacred month” is read against the background of the believers being turned back from the pilgrimage at Ḥudaybiyyah and returning the following year to perform the ʿumrah in Dhū al-Qaʿdah. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The month in which they had been prevented was answered by a sacred month in which they could perform the rite; the wording asserts a form of equivalence rather than treating sacred time as a license for revenge. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The commentators connect the occasion to the treaty and the Prophet’s return, though details of the reports are to be presented as transmitted context, not as if every narrative detail were equally certain. **[Jalālayn]**

The word *ḥurumāt* (“sacred things” or “inviolabilities”) is broader than the month alone in several commentaries. **[Ṭabarī]** It can include the sacred month, the Sacred Precinct, the state of *iḥrām*, and other things God has made inviolable. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The clause “sacred things are subject to retaliation” is understood as a rule of equivalence: if an opponent violates a protected time or place, the response is not to exceed the violation, and the believer must still observe the limits God has set. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse thus recognizes that sacredness can be violated by an aggressor without declaring that every restraint disappears for the one who has been harmed. **[Study Quran]**

The instruction “whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like measure” uses *iʿtidāʾ* (transgression) for the reciprocal response. **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators explain this wording as *qisāṣ* or proportionate retaliation, not an endorsement of exceeding the original harm. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The same verb describes both actions, but the second is qualified by “in like measure”; the qualification is decisive. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī records legal questions about how such equivalence is established and who may enforce it, while the verse itself provides the principle without becoming a complete procedural manual. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The connection with Ḥudaybiyyah helps explain why a “sacred month for a sacred month” is named first. **[Maʿārif]** The believers had been prevented from reaching the Sacred House during Dhū al-Qaʿdah; the treaty permitted them to return in the next year and complete the ʿumrah in the same month. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The passage treats that return as a restoration of a right, not as an excuse to punish people without limit. **[Ṭabarī]** Some reports mention the fear that the Meccans might attack again in the sacred precinct or month; Maʿārif explains the defensive exception as the answer to that concern. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The sources differ over the later status of fighting in sacred months. **[Qurṭubī]** Some classical jurists understood the general prohibition on initiating war in the four sacred months to have been abrogated by later revelation, while others described the sanctity as continuing with an exception when defense is necessary. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Maʿārif says the prohibition was later lifted by consensus in one legal framing, yet it also preserves a preference not to initiate fighting without need and compares the exception to that of the Sacred Precinct. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī records more than one view about whether this verse abrogates or confirms the earlier sacred-month rule. **[Qurṭubī]** The disagreement should be reported as a classical interpretive debate rather than settled here as current legal advice. **[Study Quran]**

The final command, “reverence God,” recalls that the right to respond is itself bounded. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The promise “God is with the reverent” encourages restraint at the very moment when retaliation might tempt someone to exceed what was suffered. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse therefore refuses two extremes: it does not require a community to accept a violation without any response, but it also does not allow a victim to turn a limited right into unmeasured vengeance. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Proportionality is not an afterthought; it is the explicit measure built into the command. **[Study Quran]**

The wording “the sacred month is for the sacred month” also indicates that sacred time does not become a tool for one side to harm another with impunity. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** A protected season can be violated, but the answer must be measured against the violation and governed by *taqwā*. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The clause about “sacred things” makes that principle wider than one event, while not erasing the distinct inviolability of the sanctuary and *iḥrām*. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]**

**Interpretive note.** The commentators do not reduce *al-ḥurumāt* to one referent. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Alongside the month, they discuss the sanctuary, the pilgrim’s *iḥrām*, and other sacred limits; the plural allows the verse to address a cluster of inviolabilities. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** The phrase “in like measure” then prevents the plurality of sacred interests from becoming a pretext for unlimited punishment. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]**

The legal discussion in the tafsīrs is extensive and not uniform. **[Qurṭubī]** Some authorities debate whether a violation of a sacred month changes the rule about initiating combat later, while others stress that defensive necessity is a separate case from initiating aggression. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran notes that the verse is rooted in an early treaty and pilgrimage dispute and should be read in that context rather than extracted as a universal license for private retaliation. **[Study Quran]** Its ethical principle is proportionate response under reverence for God. **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse acknowledges the harm of a violated sanctuary or sacred time but refuses to let retaliation reproduce the original excess. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The returning pilgrims’ claim to perform the ʿumrah in the agreed sacred month illustrates restoration rather than limitless vengeance. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** “In like measure” and “God is with the reverent” hold justice and self-restraint together. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The historical juristic disagreement over sacred-month rules remains part of the commentary record, but it does not cancel the verse’s explicit demand for equivalence and *taqwā*. **[Study Quran]**

## 2:195

195195
*“Spend in the way of God, and do not cast yourselves by your own hands into destruction. And do good; truly God loves the doers of good.”*

**Meaning.** The verse opens with a command to spend “in the way of God.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** In its immediate context, the exegetes commonly connect this spending with provision and support for the community’s efforts, including the needs of the pilgrimage and defense; they also draw a broader lesson about generosity and obedience. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran notes that the phrase is not limited to one narrow charitable transaction, even though many early explanations center on expenditure for the communal cause. **[Study Quran]** It is therefore more accurate to preserve both the immediate setting and the verse’s wider ethical application than to reduce it to a single modern slogan. **[Saʿdī]**

The warning “do not cast yourselves by your own hands into destruction” generated several interpretations in the early commentaries. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** A well-known report from Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī explains that some people wanted to abandon communal effort and remain occupied with their property after Islam had become established; he understood that withdrawal and refusal to spend as a cause of communal ruin. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** This report is about neglecting support, not an authorization for reckless individual violence. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī treats the wording as broad enough to include more than one form of self-inflicted harm, while regarding withholding needed expenditure as a prominent contextual reading. **[Ṭabarī]**

Other interpretations warn against a person deliberately entering a situation where he is sure to be destroyed, including the example of an isolated attack with no realistic capacity to act. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Some commentators also understand the warning as forbidding extravagance that leaves one’s dependants without their due, or as forbidding despair of God’s mercy after sin. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** These readings should not be flattened into one identical ruling: they arise from the general language of the verse and from reports about different circumstances. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Their common concern is that people must not knowingly create ruin through neglect, excess, or hopelessness. **[Saʿdī]**

The Abū Ayyūb report needs particular care. **[Maʿārif]** It presents “destruction” as abandoning a needed communal effort to tend one’s possessions, not as a proof that every person must enter a dangerous confrontation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Other early reports apply the phrase to reckless exposure to death, and al-Qurṭubī gathers both types of interpretation. **[Qurṭubī]** The sources thus give reasons to reject a simplistic reading that either turns the verse into blanket military guidance or uses it to condemn every risk. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The concern is self-destruction, while the surrounding command to spend frames the primary communal issue as refusing needed support. **[Maʿārif]**

Al-Ṭabarī reports that early interpreters connected the phrase with neglecting expenditure, exceeding proper limits in spending, or abandoning hope in forgiveness; he brings these meanings together under the broad wording. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran likewise records that the verse was applied to withholding resources, choosing wealth over communal obligation, and exposing oneself recklessly. **[Study Quran]** Maʿārif quotes al-Jaṣṣāṣ’s synthesis that multiple rules may be inferred from the verse, while emphasizing that the early context made spending the central concern. **[Maʿārif]** These interpretations are best presented as a family of readings, not as interchangeable proof-texts for every later dispute. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The verse closes, “And do good; truly God loves the doers of good.” **[Jalālayn]** The term *iḥsān* broadens the instruction beyond a minimum payment: it includes doing the act well, obeying God, and treating people with excellence. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Maʿārif connects *iḥsān* in worship with the well-known prophetic teaching to worship God as though one sees Him, and in social dealings with wishing for others what one wishes for oneself. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse thus joins material support, prudence, and excellence of conduct; spending is not separated from the moral quality with which it is done. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The transition from “spend” to “do not cast yourselves into destruction” is significant. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Expenditure can be withheld to the point that the community’s needs go unmet, but generosity can also be distorted into waste or neglect of dependants; the commentaries discuss both dangers. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse does not praise either hoarding or self-destructive excess. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Its final command to do good gives the measure: support what is right, avoid actions that knowingly produce ruin, and act with excellence. **[Jalālayn]**

**Interpretive note.** The reports about Abū Ayyūb and the abandonment of expenditure are prominent, but they are not the only explanations transmitted. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī’s discussion includes withholding resources, overextending one’s spending, reckless exposure to danger, and despair of forgiveness; al-Qurṭubī also gathers several applications. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran warns against turning one strand into simplistic military guidance, and the accounts should be read as interpretations of a broad expression rather than as instructions for private violence. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]**

The verse’s immediate call to spend gives the warning a material dimension as well as a personal one. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** People may bring harm upon themselves by refusing necessary support and letting a collective obligation collapse, but they can also harm themselves through excess that neglects those who depend on them. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The sources do not treat prudent provision for family as opposed to generosity; rather, they distinguish appropriate spending from withholding or waste. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]**

The command to *iḥsān* further prevents the verse from being reduced to a single legal transaction. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī connects it with obedience and good conduct, while Maʿārif draws on the prophetic explanation of *iḥsān* in worship and social relations. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The ideal is not merely to avoid the most obvious form of ruin, but to respond to God’s command with careful generosity, restraint, and concern for others. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** This verse places generosity beside prudence: neither withholding needed support nor rushing into self-destruction embodies the good it commands. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The early interpretations differ in application, but their shared warning is against knowingly creating ruin through neglect, waste, or despair. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** The closing promise that God loves the *muḥsinūn* gives the passage its positive direction: spend for what is good, preserve legitimate responsibilities, and pursue excellence in worship and dealings. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:196

196196
*“Complete the pilgrimage and the ʿumrah for God. If you are hindered, then offer what is easy of the offering. Do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place. Whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head may ransom himself by fasting, charity, or sacrifice. When you are secure, whoever enjoys the ʿumrah until the pilgrimage must offer what is easy of the offering; whoever finds none must fast three days during the pilgrimage and seven when you return—that is ten complete. This is for those whose families are not present at the Sacred Mosque. And reverence God, and know that God is severe in punishment.”*

**Meaning.** The command to complete the pilgrimage and the ʿumrah “for God” is explained as performing their rites with sincerity and carrying a rite through once one has entered it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The commentaries do not agree that the verse by itself settles whether initiating ʿumrah is obligatory: al-Ṭabarī argues that it commands completion after entry but does not establish an original obligation, whereas other scholars infer an obligation from the wording. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī likewise describes completion as binding once the pilgrim begins, while noting the legal reasoning that connects the command with the duty to perform both rites. **[Saʿdī]** The shared point is that the acts are to be performed according to their prescribed bounds and for God, not diverted into worldly display. **[Jalālayn]**

The next clause, “if you are hindered,” recalls the believers who were stopped at Ḥudaybiyyah while in consecration. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The term *iḥṣār* is understood broadly by some authorities to include illness, injury, fear, or another obstruction that prevents completion; others distinguish an enemy’s blockade from bodily illness. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī weighs these positions and treats both fear and illness as possible impediments, while reporting the lexical and legal arguments behind narrower readings. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** If a pilgrim is genuinely prevented, the verse directs an offering of what is accessible, but the sources differ over where it must be sacrificed, when the person may leave *iḥrām*, and whether the interrupted rite must be made up later. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The instruction not to shave until the offering reaches its place also has a scope discussed by the commentators. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī connects it closely with the situation of being prevented and understands the place of sacrifice in light of the Prophet’s practice at Ḥudaybiyyah; Ibn Kathīr argues that the clause also governs the ordinary pilgrim who can safely reach the sanctuary, not only the one who is blocked. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Their difference should remain explicit. The narrative of the Ḥudaybiyyah sacrifice is important to the discussion, but the jurists draw different conclusions from where the animals were slaughtered and what “its place” means. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The verse then allows a ransom for someone whose illness or head ailment makes shaving necessary before the ordinary time. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The report of Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah is the principal explanation cited: lice caused him severe discomfort while he was in *iḥrām*, and he was told to shave and make a choice among fasting, feeding poor people, or offering a sacrifice. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī give the ransom as three days of fasting, feeding six needy people, or sacrificing an animal; commentaries discuss the amount of food and the order of the options. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse’s principle is relief in a genuine need accompanied by a specified ransom, not an instruction to endure injury at all costs. **[Saʿdī]**

“When you are secure” turns to *tamattuʿ*, the arrangement in which the ʿumrah is performed before the pilgrimage and the pilgrim leaves *iḥrām* between the two rites. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The commentators also discuss *qirān*, joining the rites in one consecration, and *ifrād*, performing the pilgrimage alone; they differ over which arrangement is most meritorious. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** A person who enjoys the interval outside *iḥrām* owes an offering when able. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The alternative for one who cannot provide it is ten days of fasting: three during the pilgrimage and seven after returning. **[Saʿdī]**

The sources differ on the timing of the three fasts and the meaning of “when you return.” **[Qurṭubī]** Some authorities place the three before the Day of ʿArafah, while others allow them during the pilgrimage days; the seven are understood by many as after returning home, though some interpret “return” more broadly. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** “That is ten complete” removes any impression that the seven replace the three or that the total is optional. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The offering or fast is specified for those whose families are not resident near the Sacred Mosque, but the schools differ over the geographical reach of “present” there and the legal scope of the exemption. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The verse ends by calling for reverence and warning of punishment. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]** That ending frames the detailed rites as acts of obedience, not as a puzzle to be resolved by personal invention. The commentaries preserve substantial legal disagreement about obstruction, sacrifice, shaving, fasting, and residence, so this verse is not a stand-alone guide to contemporary pilgrimage procedure. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** Its central movement is nevertheless clear: complete the rites sincerely, accept lawful relief when hindered or ill, fulfil the offering or its alternative where required, and remain mindful of God’s limits. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Interpretive note.** The word *tamattuʿ* is not used with one narrow technical meaning in every report. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some sources use it for performing the ʿumrah, leaving *iḥrām*, and entering it again for Hajj; others include *qirān* because the pilgrim gains the benefit of combining the two rites in one journey. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran explains the three broad arrangements and notes disagreement among the legal schools about their relative merit. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** The contribution required of a pilgrim who combines the rites is presented as gratitude for the concession and benefit, not as evidence that the permitted rite is blameworthy. **[Jalālayn]**

The verse also distinguishes obstruction from the head ailment that requires a ransom. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** In the first case, the pilgrim is prevented from completing the rite; in the second, the pilgrim can face an urgent need to remove hair while otherwise remaining in *iḥrām*. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The Kaʿb report explains why the concession is merciful: a real physical hardship is acknowledged, and the ransom gives a defined form to the adjustment. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** These passages should not be merged into one rule or expanded beyond what their distinct circumstances support. **[Jalālayn]**

**Reflection.** The verse combines commitment and accommodation. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The pilgrim is asked to complete worship carefully, but the text recognizes obstruction and illness and assigns alternatives rather than demanding avoidable harm. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The many juristic differences about the details underline the need to distinguish the verse’s broad principles from the legal procedures developed by the schools. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:197

197197
*“The pilgrimage takes place in months well known. Whoever undertakes the pilgrimage during them, there is no sexual intimacy, iniquity, or disputation in the pilgrimage. Whatever good you do, God knows it. And take provision, for the best provision is reverence. And reverence Me, O possessors of intellect.”*

**Meaning.** “The pilgrimage takes place in months well known” identifies a fixed season for Hajj. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The majority of early authorities name Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿdah, and the first ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah; other reports count the whole of Dhū al-Ḥijjah among the months. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī prefers the first ten days, reasoning that the rites themselves do not extend through the entire month, while Qurṭubī records both definitions and notes their legal implications. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse also frames a disagreement about entering *iḥrām* before those months: some jurists reject or discourage it, while others consider it valid. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

“Whoever undertakes the pilgrimage during them” is generally explained as entering into *iḥrām* and obligating the pilgrimage upon oneself. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī reports differences over whether the decisive act is intention, *iḥrām*, or the audible *talbiyah*, but he treats the verse as describing the commitment to the rite. **[Ṭabarī]** The important consequence is that the pilgrim must respect the special limits of the consecrated state. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

The first prohibition, *rafath*, is often explained as sexual intercourse, but it can include its preliminaries, erotic speech, or obscene talk about intimacy. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī records the range and notes the particular seriousness of intercourse before the standing at ʿArafah in the legal discussion. **[Qurṭubī]** The prohibition directs pilgrims to safeguard the consecration in conduct as well as in formal rites. **[Jalālayn]**

*Fusūq* is interpreted broadly by some as disobedience or sin generally; others specify violations attached to *iḥrām*, such as hunting or removing hair, while reports also gloss it as insult, abusive speech, or other misconduct. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī reasons that because ordinary sins are forbidden in every state, this verse may particularly emphasize the acts made unlawful by consecration, though he preserves the broader early definitions. **[Ṭabarī]** The difference is one of emphasis: the pilgrimage intensifies the call to avoid sin, whether the commentator stresses all disobedience or the specific restrictions of *iḥrām*. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]**

The meaning of *jidāl* (disputation) also varies. **[Ṭabarī]** Many interpreters understand it as quarrelling with fellow pilgrims until anger and insult arise; others relate it to the pre-Islamic disputes about the correct time of Hajj, the station at which to stand, or whose pilgrimage was superior. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī favors an interpretation connected with the settlement of the pilgrimage’s time and rites, including the older calendar disagreements; al-Qurṭubī considers the historical disputes about the place and season among the strongest readings. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse should not be taken as forbidding every calm exchange of knowledge, but as excluding destructive quarrels and, in the historical reading, disputes that contested the revealed order of the rites. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

“Whatever good you do, God knows it” turns the pilgrim from mere avoidance of wrong toward affirmative acts of worship and service. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī includes prayer, charity, remembrance, and good speech among the works fitting for the sacred season. **[Saʿdī]** The verse assures that even an unobserved good deed is known to God. **[Jalālayn]** It then commands physical provision for the journey: commentators report that some people travelled to Hajj without food and relied upon others, claiming trust in God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The injunction corrects neglect of practical preparation; taking supplies does not contradict *tawakkul*. **[Maʿārif]**

“Take provision, for the best provision is reverence” joins material preparation with spiritual readiness. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** The journey requires food and resources, while *taqwā* prepares a person for the journey beyond this life; the physical and spiritual senses complement one another rather than compete. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī stresses that abandoning provision and making oneself dependent on others is not automatically a sign of trust in God. **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif similarly distinguishes genuine reliance from neglect of the means God has made available. **[Maʿārif]** The address “O possessors of intellect” calls thoughtful believers to observe both practical responsibility and reverence. **[Jalālayn]**

**Interpretive note.** The verse’s three prohibitions have overlapping but not identical scopes. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** *Rafath* focuses on sexual conduct and indecent speech; *fusūq* includes sin broadly, though Tabari emphasizes the acts specifically forbidden in *iḥrām*; *jidāl* may mean quarrelling or the historical arguments about the pilgrimage’s time and station. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** These interpretations show how the verse protects both the pilgrim’s ritual state and the unity of the pilgrimage. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

The prohibition on disputation is not necessarily a ban on reasoned learning or clarification. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some interpreters distinguish useful discussion from quarrels that lead to anger, insult, boasting, or factional division. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** In al-Ṭabarī’s preferred historical reading, the verse also rejects disagreement about when and where the pilgrimage rites should be performed after revelation has clarified them. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** The range of glosses should be retained rather than reduced to “no discussion of any kind.” **[Jalālayn]**

The provision instruction also challenges a mistaken display of asceticism. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Reports describe people setting out without food, sometimes saying that they relied upon God, then becoming dependent on others. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The commentators distinguish this from real reliance: preparing what is needed for a journey does not diminish trust in God, while making others carry one’s avoidable burden is not itself a virtue. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse calls the pilgrim to prepare in two senses: bring what sustains the body, and cultivate the reverence that sustains the heart. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The special season does not suspend ordinary responsibilities; it intensifies the need to avoid sexual misconduct, sin, and needless conflict. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Its command to take provision rejects the idea that faith requires careless dependence, while its final reminder makes *taqwā* the provision with the lasting reach. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:198

198198
*“There is no blame upon you in seeking bounty from your Lord. Then when you pour forth from ʿArafāt, remember God at the Sacred Monument, and remember Him as He has guided you, though before that you were surely among those astray.”*

**Meaning.** The first clause makes clear that seeking “bounty from your Lord” during pilgrimage is not sinful. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The commentators commonly understand this bounty as trade, wages, or other lawful means of earning during the Hajj season. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** Reports explain that some Muslims hesitated to trade because the pre-Islamic pilgrimage fairs had mixed commerce with customs they rejected; the verse reassures them that lawful earning does not invalidate the pilgrimage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Qurṭubī says that trade alongside the rites is permissible, while also noting that a pilgrim may better devote himself entirely to worship when able. **[Qurṭubī]**

The permission is not a command to make commerce the purpose of the journey. **[Maʿārif]** Maʿārif emphasizes intention: pilgrimage remains the primary purpose, and incidental earning to meet genuine needs does not erase sincerity; allowing trade does not turn the sacred season into an unrestricted commercial fair. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran likewise notes that commerce does not nullify Hajj, while al-Saʿdī stresses that seeking provision is acceptable so long as it does not distract from the worship. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse’s wording “no blame” clears an unwarranted prohibition; it does not praise distraction or exploitation. **[Jalālayn]**

The verse then describes the movement from ʿArafāt and the remembrance of God at *al-Mashʿar al-ḥarām*, commonly identified with Muzdalifah. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Exegetes discuss whether the “Sacred Monument” means the specific place or mountain at Quzah, its surrounding area, or Muzdalifah more broadly. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī records reports that all of Muzdalifah is a place of remembrance, while also noting a preferred station around Quzah; the difference concerns the precise geography, not the instruction to remember God after leaving ʿArafāt. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

“Remember Him as He has guided you” makes the rites a response to divine guidance rather than an occasion for self-congratulation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The commentators explain remembrance at the Sacred Monument through prayer, supplication, praise, and other forms of *dhikr*. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** They also connect “as He has guided you” with gratitude: believers had not known the revealed form of worship until God showed them the way. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The final reminder of their former misguidance is therefore meant to increase appreciation for guidance, not to demean people who had not yet received it. **[Study Quran]**

The sequence of ʿArafāt and Muzdalifah links this verse to the next one. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The pilgrims depart from ʿArafāt, remember God at the Sacred Monument, and then move with the wider body of pilgrims through the remaining rites. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The sources differ over the exact point denoted by the following command to “pour forth,” but they agree that the verse situates pilgrimage within shared movement and remembrance. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The permission to seek bounty also answers a moral anxiety about combining worldly needs with worship. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** A person who works or trades during the season can still be a pilgrim, provided that the lawful earning does not displace the required rites or become the controlling intention. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran notes that refraining from trade to devote oneself to worship may be spiritually preferable, but that preference should not be turned into a false claim that commerce itself is forbidden. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The commentaries also draw practical inferences from the order of the rites. **[Saʿdī]** The departure from ʿArafāt follows the standing there, and the remembrance at al-Mashʿar follows the departure; as-Saʿdī treats both places as recognized pilgrimage stations, with ʿArafāt outside the sanctuary and Muzdalifah within it. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The verse does not itself spell out a single formula for remembrance. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Jalālayn gives examples including the *talbiyah*, the declaration of divine oneness, and supplication; it also cites the Prophet’s extended remembrance and supplication at Quzah. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** These are explanatory examples of *dhikr*, not an exhaustive list that limits the command. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

As-Saʿdī reads “as He has guided you” as a call to remember God for having granted guidance after misguidance and taught people what they did not know. **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr reports that “before it” may refer to guidance, the Qur’an, or the Messenger; the commentaries preserve these related possibilities rather than insisting on a single antecedent. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** In each case the contrast is between prior lack of knowledge and the gift of revealed direction. **[Maʿārif]** The rites are therefore not self-invented achievements: their correct form and the knowledge to perform them are themselves reasons for gratitude. **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The phrase “there is no blame” is a removal of scruple, not an assertion that every kind of trade or motive is automatically sound. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The sources distinguish lawful earning during Hajj from letting business overwhelm the purpose of pilgrimage; Maʿārif particularly emphasizes the pilgrim’s primary intention. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī’s reports of markets at ʿUkāẓ and other places explain why the believers questioned the practice, but the verse resolves their uncertainty without reinstating the pre-Islamic customs. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The geographical phrase “the Sacred Monument” is also treated with some range. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some commentators identify a specific hill or station in Muzdalifah, while others understand the sacred area as the whole plain or its broader setting. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The remembrance commanded there includes prayer and supplication, and is not limited by the verse to a single formula. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse permits worshippers to attend to lawful needs while retaining the purpose of pilgrimage. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** Its movement from earning to remembrance reminds the pilgrim that worldly activity may accompany devotion but should not displace it. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The rites themselves are received as guidance and answered with gratitude, humility, and praise. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]**

## 2:199

199199
*“Then pour forth from where the people pour forth, and seek forgiveness from God. Truly God is Forgiving, Merciful.”*

**Meaning.** Many commentators explain the command as a correction to the Quraysh and their allies, known as the *ḥums*, who regarded themselves as custodians of the Sacred House and used to remain at Muzdalifah rather than stand with the other pilgrims at ʿArafāt. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** They claimed that they should not leave the sanctuary, while the wider body of pilgrims went to ʿArafāt and then departed from there. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse commands the *ḥums* to join the people rather than create a privileged pilgrimage practice for themselves. **[Study Quran]** **[Jalālayn]**

The historical explanation is supported in the commentaries by a report from ʿĀʾishah describing Quraysh and those sharing their custom as standing at Muzdalifah while other Arabs stood at ʿArafāt. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī cites the report and treats the command to depart “from where the people depart” as a direct correction of the *ḥums* practice. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Maʿārif adds that the custom expressed a claim to special status: Quraysh treated remaining within the Haram as proof of their distinction. **[Maʿārif]** The verse counters that display by placing them in the same pilgrimage pattern as everyone else. **[Saʿdī]**

The most common interpretation therefore takes “the people” as the pilgrims who stood at ʿArafāt and understands the verse to require the *ḥums* to join them there and depart with them. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī ultimately favors this reading on the basis of the transmitted explanations, even though he notes a difficulty in the verse’s sequence: 2:198 has already mentioned the departure from ʿArafāt to Muzdalifah. **[Ṭabarī]** He records another interpretation in which “the people” refers to Abraham and the command is to depart from Muzdalifah toward Mina, a reading that fits the sequence more literally. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The sources preserve this distinction rather than silently smoothing it away. **[Study Quran]** The Study Quran explains that the command to depart from where the people departed can be read in connection with the *ḥums*’ earlier refusal to join the people at ʿArafāt, and notes that “then” need not function as a strict chronological connector. **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī describes a departure from Muzdalifah with the pilgrims toward Mina, while also explaining that the verse’s concern is to join the common pilgrimage movement rather than claim a separate station. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The shared focus is conformity to the revealed rites and rejection of self-exemption, even where the exact point of departure is understood differently. **[Maʿārif]**

“Seek forgiveness from God” follows the command to participate in the common rite. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The commentators explain this as seeking pardon for shortcomings and for the pride or custom that separated some pilgrims from the rest. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** As-Saʿdī treats the request for forgiveness after worship as an acknowledgment that a servant’s performance is never entirely free of deficiency, while remembrance and gratitude acknowledge the blessing of having been enabled to worship. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The final names, “Forgiving, Merciful,” assure the worshipper that sincere return to God is met with mercy. **[Study Quran]**

The verse thus addresses both ritual practice and social pride. **[Maʿārif]** The common clothing, movement, and purpose of pilgrimage make it difficult to justify a special status based only on lineage or proximity to the Kaʿbah. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The *ḥums*’ practice, as described in the commentaries, set them apart from ordinary pilgrims and treated sacred geography as a reason not to share the same station. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The command restores participation with the people and displaces the presumption that inherited prestige can alter the rites. **[Saʿdī]**

As-Saʿdī’s explanation of the later departure from Muzdalifah makes the alternate sequence more concrete: he connects the movement with the rites that follow, including casting the pebbles, sacrifice, circumambulation, *saʿy*, and the stay at Mina during the days of *tashrīq*. **[Saʿdī]** He then explains the command to seek forgiveness as recognition of shortcomings in worship, and remembrance as gratitude for having been enabled to perform it. **[Saʿdī]** This reading differs in its immediate ritual sequence from the historical explanation focused on the *ḥums*’ exclusion from ʿArafāt, but both place the pilgrim within a shared, inherited rite and end in humble return to God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** There are two main readings of “from where the people pour forth.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The first, favored by al-Qurṭubī and supported by the report from ʿĀʾishah, addresses the *ḥums* and directs them to join the pilgrims at ʿArafāt. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The second takes “the people” as Abraham and understands the verse as a command to depart from Muzdalifah in the customary rite. **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī’s explanation also attends to the later departure from Muzdalifah; the exegetical sequence is not identical in every source. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The verb *afāḍa* conveys a collective surge or flow of pilgrims, and the image suits a rite in which people move together rather than claim separate privilege. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that “then” can connect an independent sentence rather than enforce a simple chronological sequence, which helps explain the common *ḥums* reading after the preceding mention of Muzdalifah. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī acknowledges that the sequence can support another reading but gives priority to the transmitted explanation about Quraysh’s practice. **[Ṭabarī]**

The command to seek forgiveness adds humility to the correction. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse does not merely replace one geographical custom with another; it calls the pilgrims to recognize that they may have erred and to ask God for pardon. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]** The reports about the *ḥums* are historical explanations of the ritual difference, while the ethical criticism of pride and separation is drawn from the commentators’ reading of that practice. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The verse places shared worship above inherited claims to special status. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Pilgrims move together, and the one who recognizes a prior mistake asks for forgiveness rather than defending it as a badge of distinction. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The interpreters differ over whether the verse’s immediate departure is from ʿArafāt or Muzdalifah, but they connect it with joining the common rites and turning to God in humility. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:200

200200
*“When you have completed your rites, remember God as you remember your fathers, or with yet stronger remembrance. Among the people are those who say, ‘Our Lord, give us in this world,’ and they have no share in the Hereafter.”*

**Meaning.** “When you have completed your rites” is understood by some commentators specifically as completing the sacrifices, while others take *manāsik* broadly to mean the rites of pilgrimage as a whole. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The broader reading includes the acts through which Hajj is completed and makes remembrance the response to worship; the narrower reading emphasizes the offerings made at the close of particular rites. **[Study Quran]** **[Jalālayn]** In either case, the verse directs the pilgrim from completion of ritual toward continued remembrance, rather than treating the finished rite as an occasion for self-congratulation. **[Saʿdī]**

Many commentators relate “remember God as you remember your fathers” to a pre-Islamic custom after the pilgrimage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** People would gather and boast of their ancestors’ generosity, courage, or achievements; some reports describe a person asking God to grant him wealth or status like that of his father. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse redirects this energy toward the remembrance and praise of God, whose gifts sustain both the worshipper and the ancestors whose deeds people once celebrated. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The point is not that family memory is forbidden, but that ritual devotion should not be displaced by tribal boasting and rivalry. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

A second interpretation compares remembrance of God to the way a young child repeatedly calls upon and depends on a parent. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and other early authorities explain the image as constant recourse, trust, and need, with the believer’s dependence on God exceeding a child’s dependence on parents. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī does not force a choice between the two pictures; he allows the verse to call for abundant remembrance marked by humility and need, whether by contrast with tribal boasting or by analogy with a child’s reliance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

The phrase “or with yet stronger remembrance” intensifies the command. **[Jalālayn]** It does not mean that God is uncertain which measure of remembrance is appropriate; the “or” urges believers to remember Him at least as much as, and even more than, the people once remembered their forebears. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī connects the command with the takbīr and other forms of remembrance associated with the days after the rites, while also emphasizing obedience, praise, and supplication. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The verse then contrasts two kinds of supplication. **[Ṭabarī]** Some people ask only for “give us in this world,” seeking immediate provision, livestock, victory, or other worldly benefits, while the verse says they have no share in the Hereafter. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The criticism is directed at a life and prayer narrowed to this world with no concern for the Hereafter, not at every request for health, livelihood, family, or other good in worldly life. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The next verse, 2:201, provides the contrast of a prayer that asks for good in both worlds and protection from the Fire. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The ordering matters: remembrance comes first, then the petition. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The worshipper is taught not only what to ask for but how to situate personal needs within gratitude, devotion, and concern for the life to come. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Saʿdī notes that human beings in both groups ask God for their needs, but their aims differ; the verse critiques the person whose horizon ends with worldly gain. **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif likewise explains that the passage corrects a pilgrimage prayer focused exclusively on material prosperity or social prestige. **[Maʿārif]**

As-Saʿdī adds that the difference between the two groups is their purpose and horizon, not that one makes supplication and the other does not: people ask God for needs, but their aims diverge, and each is recompensed according to deeds and intentions. **[Saʿdī]** He cautions that obtaining a worldly request is not, by itself, proof that its recipient is specially loved or close to God; the lasting measure is the person’s orientation toward faith and the Hereafter. **[Saʿdī]** This reinforces the verse’s criticism of a prayer confined to worldly aims without turning lawful worldly requests into something blameworthy. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The two explanations of remembering fathers are complementary in the commentaries: the verse replaces public boasting with praise of God, and it also portrays the worshipper’s dependence as more profound than a child’s dependence on parents. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran records both readings, while Maʿārif describes how the old gatherings of ancestral praise were redirected toward *dhikr*. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The imperative to remember “more strongly” intensifies devotion rather than creating uncertainty about whether remembrance is required. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]**

The contrast between worldly and otherworldly petitions should not be misread as forbidding supplication for worldly good. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse criticizes those who ask only for this life and have no share in the Hereafter; the following verse commends a prayer that includes good in both. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī includes lawful provision, a good family life, beneficial knowledge, and righteous work among worldly goods that may rightly be sought, provided the petitioner does not abandon the Hereafter. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The sources also preserve differing explanations of *manāsik*. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Mujāhid explains it as the sacrificial offerings, while other authorities take it as the full set of Hajj rites; the command to remember God follows either completion of offerings or the wider pilgrimage service. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The broader reading best explains why the verse moves directly from finishing the rites to a continued pattern of remembrance and supplication. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse redirects the attention gathered at pilgrimage: from boasting about ancestors to remembering God, and from requests confined to material gain to prayers mindful of the Hereafter. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** Its critique is not of remembering one’s family or seeking lawful provision, but of letting lineage, rivalry, or worldly ambition become the entire content of worship. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The next verse’s balanced supplication shows how concern for this world can remain within a larger hope for salvation and divine mercy. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** **[Jalālayn]**
## 2:201

201201
*“And among them are those who say, ‘Our Lord, grant us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.’”*

**Meaning.** The verse offers the balanced supplication that contrasts with the worldly-only request in 2:200. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** Its opening “among them” continues the account of people’s different aims at pilgrimage: some narrow their petitions to immediate worldly gain, while others ask God for good in both lives and for deliverance from punishment. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The wording does not condemn asking for this-worldly needs. It teaches the worshipper to ask for what is genuinely good, to include the Hereafter in the horizon of prayer, and to seek protection from the Fire. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The word *ḥasanah*, “good,” is deliberately broad. **[Ṭabarī]** Early explanations identify good in this life with health, sound livelihood, knowledge, worship, or lawful wealth, and good in the next with Paradise. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī declines to restrict the word to one of these examples: since the verse gives no limiting qualification, he understands it to include the many forms of well-being God grants in this life, including bodily safety, provision, learning, and obedience. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī likewise says that the phrase encompasses the blessings of both worlds, and notes that “good” in the Hereafter means Paradise. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]**
