The breadth is not an invitation to treat every desire as good simply because someone wants it. **[Maʿārif]** Its surrounding contrast is with the person who asks for unqualified worldly acquisition, without concern for whether it is lawful or beneficial and without regard to the next life. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** The adjective *ḥasanah* places the request under a moral measure: provision should be wholesome, knowledge beneficial, and family life a source of goodness rather than merely possession or status. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī lists examples such as lawful ample provision, a righteous spouse and family, beneficial knowledge, righteous work, and rest; these examples illustrate the scope, not an exhaustive checklist. **[Saʿdī]**

The phrase “good in the Hereafter” includes Paradise and its lasting blessings, but the commentators also connect it with safety on the Day of Resurrection, forgiveness, and God’s pleasure. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** The supplication thus reaches beyond comfort to the final state of the servant. **[Qurṭubī]** The concluding request, “protect us from the punishment of the Fire,” makes that concern explicit. **[Ṭabarī]** It asks God to avert the punishment itself; it is not a metaphor for an unpleasant worldly circumstance. **[Qurṭubī]** Some explanations also note that seeking protection includes asking for guidance away from sins and prohibited actions that lead toward punishment. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

The Prophet’s regular use of this prayer gives the verse a practical place in Muslim devotion. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Anas reports that it was among the supplications the Prophet repeated most often; al-Qurṭubī cites the report from the sound collections, and Ibn Kathīr relates it alongside other narrations about the prayer. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Maʿārif notes its established use during circumambulation of the Kaʿbah, while the Study Quran observes that it has become one of the most frequently recited prayers in individual worship. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** Its memorability is joined to its comprehensiveness: a short formula gathers worldly good, otherworldly good, and protection from loss. **[Saʿdī]**

The commentaries also report the Prophet redirecting a sick man who had asked God to bring his future punishment upon him in this life. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Prophet told him that no person could bear such a request and taught him instead to ask for good in both worlds and protection from the Fire. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** The episode clarifies the prayer’s balance: devotion is not proved by asking for needless suffering, and hope in the Hereafter does not require rejecting lawful ease in this life. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

Al-Qurṭubī mentions an interpretation attributed to ʿAlī that assigns specific spouses to the two “goods” and treats the Fire as a bad spouse, but he rejects it as far-fetched and says it is not soundly established from ʿAlī. **[Qurṭubī]** The more straightforward reading, supported by the broader lexical form and the other commentaries, understands *ḥasanah* comprehensively. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The interpretive caution matters: a vivid isolated report should not displace the verse’s open wording or its well-attested use as a general prayer. **[Qurṭubī]**

**Reflection.** The prayer refuses a false choice between spiritual aspiration and ordinary human need. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** It permits the believer to ask for the good of family, health, knowledge, work, and livelihood, while teaching that none of these is the whole of life. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** A prayer becomes comprehensive when it asks that worldly gifts be good, that the Hereafter be good, and that the servant be protected from the Fire. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The sources also reject a false opposition between asking for the Hereafter and asking for ordinary lawful needs. **[Maʿārif]** Maʿārif argues that bodily well-being, livelihood, family, and other beneficial worldly goods can support a person’s worship; the prophetic model is to ask God for good in both lives rather than pretend that worldly needs do not exist. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** As-Saʿdī likewise includes lawful provision, beneficial knowledge, righteous work, and a good family among the goods that may be sought. **[Saʿdī]** The correction is directed at making material gain the whole purpose of prayer, not at mentioning it. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

As-Saʿdī adds that a response to a worldly prayer is not, by itself, proof that its recipient is specially loved by God; the believer’s lasting success is measured by faith, righteous intention, and the Hereafter. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** That caution complements the breadth of *ḥasanah*: the supplicant asks for good rather than insisting on a particular possession whose consequences may be unknown. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** The command to seek protection from the Fire also places every worldly request within an ethical frame: one asks for provision and success that do not lead away from God. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The prayer’s frequent recitation is therefore not a charm guaranteeing that every desired outcome will occur, but a concise expression of trust, need, and hope. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

## 2:202

202202
*“Those will have a share of what they have earned, and God is swift in reckoning.”*

**Meaning.** “Those” most directly refers to the people in 2:201 who ask for good in both worlds and for protection from the Fire. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that they receive a share and reward for the pilgrimage, supplication, and worship they undertook with hope in what God has promised. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī gives this as the primary connection too, identifying the recompense with the reward of Hajj or of supplication, which is itself an act of worship. **[Qurṭubī]**

The commentators also preserve a broader grammatical and exegetical possibility: “those” may include both groups described in 2:200–201. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** On this reading, each receives the consequence fitting the direction of their actions: the one whose purpose is confined to worldly gain receives no share in the Hereafter, while the one who asks for both worlds seeks a share in both. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The difference is worth retaining, because the verse’s plural reference can summarize the contrasting petitioners even though its most immediate praise falls on those who ask for both kinds of good. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

The phrase “what they have earned” connects prayer with conduct rather than treating supplication as a substitute for it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** In the immediate passage, the “earning” includes the effort of pilgrimage, its rites, and sincere petitions; the worshipper’s actions and aims belong together. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** As-Saʿdī explains that the two groups’ aims and deeds differ, and that each is recompensed according to actions, intentions, and the purpose that shaped them. **[Saʿdī]** The verse does not promise that every request will be granted exactly as imagined, nor does it say that worldly prosperity alone is proof of divine favor. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

A report discussed by al-Qurṭubī applies the “share” to someone who performs Hajj on behalf of another person and asks whether he too receives reward. **[Qurṭubī]** He records an account attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās in which the worker receives a share for the pilgrimage, while the person represented also benefits; the legal discussion that follows distinguishes the reward for bodily worship from the one who provided the funds. **[Qurṭubī]** This is a particular juristic application, not the sole meaning of the verse, and it should not obscure al-Ṭabarī’s broader reading of reward for those who pray and act with the Hereafter in view. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

“God is swift in reckoning” means that no act or intention escapes divine knowledge and accounting. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Unlike human accountants, God does not need to count on fingers, consult records to discover what happened, or deliberate because information is missing. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī explains that the purpose of reckoning is to make the measure of recompense known to people and to remind them of what they may have forgotten; he also records explanations that “swift” refers to the speed of recompense or to the nearness of the Day of Reckoning. **[Qurṭubī]** These explanations converge on certainty rather than delay or oversight. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]**

The phrase therefore places both kinds of petitioners under the same comprehensive judgment. **[Study Quran]** God knows which person asked only for immediate gain and which asked for lasting good; He also knows the actions and motives that accompany each prayer. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The warning is not that God needs time to sort out the details, but that the consequences of one’s chosen horizon are certain even when they are not immediately visible. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

Read with 2:201, this verse gives prayer both breadth and accountability. **[Qurṭubī]** The believer asks for comprehensive good, undertakes the rites and other good deeds, and entrusts the full measure of reward to God. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** A “share” is not measured merely by how much worldly success appears in a person’s life; the verse points to what is earned in God’s knowledge and reckoning. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]**

**Reflection.** Supplication and striving are not rivals: the one who asks God for good also acts in ways that seek it. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse encourages hope in reward while removing any illusion that hidden motives are beyond account. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Its closing assurance that God is swift in reckoning calls the pilgrim and every reader to carry the balanced prayer of 2:201 into choices made after the pilgrimage has ended. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The contrast with the first group in 2:200 clarifies why intention matters. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī reports that the worldly-only petitioner may perform the tiring journey and rites while seeking only immediate gain, whereas the one asking for both worlds directs the effort toward God’s reward as well. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif similarly warns against turning even a sacred occasion into a vehicle for material ambition while leaving the Hereafter out of one’s concern. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The verse does not deny that different people may receive worldly portions; it directs attention to the lasting share and the purpose for which acts are performed. **[Qurṭubī]**

Al-Qurṭubī’s explanations of “those” preserve a useful distinction: the pronoun may refer directly to the people of the balanced prayer, or summarize both groups and the consequences of each one’s conduct. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The broad reading does not cancel the warning that the worldly-only group has no share in the Hereafter; rather, it places both groups under one judgment in which each is treated according to deeds and aims. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The closing phrase assures the reader that God’s knowledge is complete even when human beings cannot see the inward measure of another person’s worship. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The noun *naṣīb*, “share,” suggests a portion allotted in justice, not a claim that people can compel God to reward them on their own terms. **[Ṭabarī]** The servant’s work includes the rites and petitions, while the final measure of reward belongs to God’s knowledge and generosity. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** This distinction keeps the verse from turning worship into a transaction in which an outward act guarantees a preferred worldly result. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The balanced prayer of 2:201 expresses hope; this verse reminds the worshipper that God knows how the prayer was joined to intention and conduct. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]**

## 2:203

203203
*“Remember God during days numbered. Whoever hastens to leave after two days, there is no blame upon him; and whoever stays longer, there is no blame upon him—for one who is reverent. And reverence God, and know that you will be gathered unto Him.”*

**Meaning.** “Days numbered” is most commonly explained as the days of Minā after the Day of Sacrifice, the three days of *tashrīq*, the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī reports agreement among the jurists that the phrase refers to the days of Minā and the stoning of the pillars, while Ibn Kathīr also records an early view that counts the Day of Sacrifice with the following three days. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The common interpretation identifies the three days after the sacrifice as the period in which pilgrims remain at Minā and perform the rites described here. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The command to remember God includes the prescribed *takbīr*—magnifying God—as pilgrims stone the *jamārāt*, as well as remembrance after the obligatory prayers and at the sacrifice. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Saʿdī cites the prophetic description of the days of *tashrīq* as days of eating, drinking, and remembering God; the report explains why the rites and the celebration are joined. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** These are not days of fasting for most pilgrims: the transmitted reports describe them as days of food and remembrance, while legal discussion preserves an exception for a pilgrim who lacks the required offering in the relevant expiation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The verse then grants two options for leaving Minā. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** A pilgrim may depart after completing the rites of two days, conventionally by leaving on the twelfth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, or may remain for the third day and depart on the thirteenth. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Both courses are described as free of blame, correcting competing customs that condemned either the early departure or the longer stay. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The permission does not mean the rites themselves may be omitted: the pilgrim completes the stoning required for the chosen schedule and follows the order of departure. **[Qurṭubī]**

The detailed timing of departure and stoning belongs to a juristic discussion, and the sources report differences on matters such as the precise point on the twelfth day after which a pilgrim who remains must complete the later stoning. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Maʿārif summarizes the common distinction that leaving before sunset on the second day permits early departure, whereas one who remains until sunset stays for the next day’s rite. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī records differences over stoning times, missed pebbles, and whether residents of Mecca share the same option as other pilgrims. **[Qurṭubī]** These are legal details, not reasons to portray either of the two departures explicitly allowed by the verse as sinful. **[Study Quran]**

The qualification “for one who is reverent” has several explanations. **[Ṭabarī]** Some authorities connect it to the person who observes God’s limits during the pilgrimage, while others understand it as a condition for the forgiveness and removal of sin that accompany a properly observed Hajj. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī prefers a reading in which either pilgrim is free of sin and receives forgiveness if the rites are performed within their prescribed bounds and the pilgrim avoids what God prohibited. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Saʿdī emphasizes that the permission covers the two stated departure choices and that *taqwā* remains required in every part of the pilgrimage. **[Saʿdī]**

The clause should not be misread as saying that a pilgrim who has ordinary shortcomings forfeits the legal permission to depart after two days. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** Rather, the commentators connect reverence with the quality of the whole rite and with the promised spiritual benefit; Maʿārif distinguishes formal discharge of the obligation from the deeper question of accepted worship. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī similarly reads the final words as a reminder that the pilgrim’s freedom from blame and hope of forgiveness belong with obedience, not with treating the rites casually. **[Ṭabarī]**

The ending, “reverence God, and know that you will be gathered unto Him,” moves from the practical calendar of Minā to the ultimate gathering. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** Pilgrims who disperse after worship will return to God, who knows their deeds and repays them with justice. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī says knowledge of this final recompense is among the strongest reasons to maintain *taqwā*: the person who remembers the gathering will not treat the end of Hajj as the end of responsibility. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Interpretive note.** The main exegetical difference is whether the “numbered days” are only the three days after the sacrifice or include the sacrifice day as well; the prevailing explanation in al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī is the three days of *tashrīq*. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The permission to leave early or remain is shared, while jurists differ in detailed timing and in the scope of application. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

The remembrance is not limited to pilgrims as isolated individuals. **[Study Quran]** The Study Quran notes that the takbīr associated with the days of sacrifice and *tashrīq* is recited by Muslims more broadly, including after prayers, while the pilgrim also remembers God at the stoning and other rites. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī records disagreement over the beginning and ending of the post-prayer takbīr, and over its wording; those differences belong to ritual law, while the verse’s central command is remembrance. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The prophetic description of these days as days of eating, drinking, and remembrance keeps celebration from becoming heedlessness. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

The two departure choices also answer a social problem: pilgrims should not condemn one another merely for taking one of the alternatives God has allowed. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** The sources report that people had treated either haste or delay as blameworthy, and the verse removes the reproach from both. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** As-Saʿdī observes that staying longer may be preferable because it includes additional worship, but he presents early departure as a genuine allowance rather than a sin. **[Saʿdī]** This balances preference with permission: more time in devotion can be virtuous without making the shorter lawful course defective. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The final command to remember the gathering with God prevents the departure from Minā from becoming the end of religious responsibility. **[Maʿārif]** A pilgrimage may conclude formally, yet the worshipper’s later conduct remains part of the account. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

## 2:204

204204
*“Among people is one whose speech about the life of this world impresses you, and who calls God to witness what is in his heart, while he is the fiercest of adversaries.”*

**Meaning.** The verse introduces the opposite of the sincere people just described: a person whose polished speech appears pleasing but whose inward state and conduct do not match it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The opening does not condemn eloquence itself; it warns that convincing language and solemn appeals to God cannot, by themselves, establish sincerity. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The next verses test the claim against what the person does when outside the audience’s view. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]**

The phrase “about the life of this world” can describe speech that is attractive in worldly dealings and persuasive to listeners. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The speaker may know how to sound reasonable, friendly, or religious, and may even invoke God as witness to an asserted inner faith. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Yet God already knows the heart; an oath does not make a false claim true or compel others to accept a person’s private account as divine testimony. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Saʿdī stresses the contrast between speech and deed: where a person’s actions contradict the claim, the speech has not proved the sincerity it advertises. **[Saʿdī]**

The commentators relate different occasions to the description. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** One report associates it with al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, who is said to have presented himself as a well-wisher and then harmed Muslim property; another connects the passage with hypocrites who criticized the Companions killed at al-Rajīʿ. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī notes a historical objection to the first account, reporting Ibn ʿAṭiyyah’s observation that al-Akhnas’s conversion is not established. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran accordingly emphasizes that many exegetes treat the verses as a general description of hypocrisy rather than limiting them to one incident. **[Study Quran]**

“Fiercest of adversaries” translates *aladd al-khiṣām*. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains *al-add* as intensely disputatious and also records the sense of crooked or unfair argument; he considers these meanings close, since obstinate disputation can twist the issue rather than seek truth. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr connects the description with a report that a hypocrite lies in speech, breaks promises, and becomes vicious in dispute. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The concern is not firm disagreement conducted honestly; it is argument used to deceive, evade evidence, or wound an opponent. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The sources preserve a grammatical and recitational difference in “he calls God to witness what is in his heart.” **[Ṭabarī]** The widespread reading has the person invoking God as witness to his claim; al-Ṭabarī prefers that reading because it is the reading of the recognized reciters. **[Ṭabarī]** Another transmitted reading makes God the subject—“God bears witness to what is in his heart”—and al-Qurṭubī also mentions a reading that explicitly says the person “seeks God’s witness.” **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The alternate form sharpens the irony: the hidden interior that the speaker claims to certify is in fact fully known to God. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The account of al-Rajīʿ links the verse’s denunciation to the following verse’s description of self-sacrifice. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** In that report, some hypocrites disparaged the slain Companions for leaving home on a mission, and the passage contrasts their criticism with the believers who gave themselves in God’s cause. **[Qurṭubī]** This remains one reported setting among competing explanations; the general moral does not depend on deciding that every detail belongs to a single historical occasion. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The legal and social caution is equally important. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī discusses the need to investigate evidence in matters such as testimony and judgment, but he also reports ʿUmar’s principle that people are dealt with according to what appears outwardly, while God alone judges their hidden states. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse therefore warns against being deceived by performance without licensing suspicion toward every articulate person or a claim to read another’s heart. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** Its signs are the conjunction of false claims, persistent adversarial conduct, and the destructive behavior described in the continuation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Reflection.** Speech matters, but it is not a substitute for truthful conduct. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse asks listeners to consider whether words and actions cohere, while leaving ultimate knowledge of the heart to God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Its warning is especially sharp when religious language is used to claim a virtue that one’s treatment of others contradicts. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The expression *aladd* has a linguistic force beyond simply “someone who argues a lot.” **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī relates it to a person who can turn to either side in a dispute and press an argument stubbornly; the defect is crookedness and refusal to yield to truth, not merely confidence or forceful speech. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** As-Saʿdī contrasts such conduct with the believer’s willingness to submit to truth and to deal gently, even when disagreement is difficult. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The verse thus judges the direction and honesty of argument, not a speaker’s rhetorical skill alone. **[Maʿārif]**

Al-Qurṭubī draws a caution for judges and witnesses from the gap between outward presentation and inward reality, but he does not claim that ordinary people can inspect hearts. **[Qurṭubī]** He also quotes ʿUmar’s statement that people are treated according to what appears in their actions, while their hidden intentions remain for God to judge. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** This distinction guards against two opposite errors: credulously accepting an oath as proof of sincerity, and unjustly accusing someone whose heart is unknown. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verses that follow supply observable conduct in this reported portrait—corruption, rejection of counsel, and the contrasting sincerity of 2:207. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The alternate reading that makes God the grammatical subject—“God bears witness to what is in his heart”—draws attention to the limit of human testimony. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The dominant reading instead portrays the person himself invoking God to strengthen a claim that may not be true. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Both readings warn that divine witness cannot be manipulated: God knows the inward truth whether or not a speaker uses His name to persuade an audience. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The passage’s later contrast with the sincere person in 2:207 also prevents the reader from equating every act of self-sacrifice with hypocrisy or every eloquent speech with falsehood; the judgement rests on the whole pattern, not one isolated sentence. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

## 2:205

205205
*“When he turns away, he strives throughout the land to spread corruption there and to destroy crops and offspring; and God loves not corruption.”*

**Meaning.** This verse continues the portrait of the person whose speech sounds admirable but whose actions reveal another character. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The phrase “when he turns away” can refer to leaving the Prophet’s presence, as several commentators explain, or to turning aside inwardly and acting from anger and opposition. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Either reading contrasts public speech with what the person pursues when no longer speaking face-to-face. **[Maʿārif]**

The verb *saʿā* can mean to strive or exert oneself, not merely to walk quickly. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī records an interpretation in which the person’s schemes and intention are bent on harming Islam and its people, and another in which he physically goes through the land causing damage. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The common point is deliberate effort toward *fasād*, corruption, rather than an accidental loss or an isolated mistake. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

“Crops and offspring” names visible forms of the harm. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The primary explanations refer to cultivated land and livestock: fields are burned, animals killed, and the means of livelihood damaged. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** Reports linked to al-Akhnas describe a field belonging to Muslims being burned and donkeys being killed, though the verse is not restricted to that reported episode. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr also records an explanation in which “offspring” includes the young of animals and the people who depend on them. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The commentaries preserve other, broader readings. **[Qurṭubī]** Some explain the “crops” figuratively as women and “offspring” as children, emphasizing that discord and violence can destroy families and human life; others understand the words in their direct agricultural and animal sense. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Qurṭubī treats the verse’s general wording as covering corruption in land, property, and religion, and notes an interpretation in which wrongdoing brings wider harm to crops and herds. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** These readings expand the ethical scope without erasing the concrete injuries named by the verse. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

The Study Quran notes that some Muslim interpreters also apply the verse to social injustice and destruction of the natural environment. **[Study Quran]** Such applications are contemporary extensions of the broader category of *fasād*, not a claim that every classical commentator was writing about modern environmental policy. **[Study Quran]** The text itself condemns a pattern in which a person’s pursuit of power, deceit, or wrongdoing damages the conditions that sustain life. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

Al-Saʿdī explains that actions contrary to God’s commands can diminish the yield and blessing of crops, fruit, and livestock, and that good words do not excuse destructive deeds. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The point should not be turned into the simplistic claim that every drought, poor harvest, or animal loss proves a particular person’s sin; rather, the commentators identify the moral connection between persistent wrongdoing and harm to the shared order of life. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]**

“God loves not corruption” states the divine judgment on the conduct described. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** It is not merely a statement that destruction is aesthetically unpleasant: *fasād* violates the order and trust on which human, animal, and agricultural life depend. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī explicitly extends the phrase to corruption in religion, property, and the land, while al-Saʿdī contrasts the hypocrite’s deeds with the gentle conduct of believers. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The divine disapproval exposes the gap between a pleasing public persona and the damage done in private. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The transition from 2:204 to 2:205 is a test of credibility: what looked persuasive in conversation is followed by conduct that harms other people and their means of life. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse does not teach that every departure from a conversation proves corruption; it describes the person in the preceding portrait, whose actions reveal a settled intention to do harm. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** The verse measures public claims by their fruits. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]** Words of faith and reconciliation lose credibility when followed by the destruction of land, livelihood, or the lives that depend on them. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Its condemnation of corruption is broad enough to address abuse of property and social order, yet careful readers should avoid turning calamity into a verdict on its victims. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The vocabulary reinforces that the damage is active. **[Qurṭubī]** *Al-ḥarth* denotes cultivation or tillage, while *al-nasl* is what is born and grows; together the terms evoke the productive sources on which communities depend. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Jalālayn summarizes them as tillage and livestock, and Ibn Kathīr notes that commentators include both crops and the young of animals. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The figurative interpretation of women and children widens the image to human families, but it should be presented as an exegetical alternative rather than as the only meaning. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The report of burning fields and killing animals gives one concrete example of the corruption described, while al-Qurṭubī says the wording extends to anyone who repeats such conduct. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse is not a technical ruling about one kind of property damage; it identifies a broader moral pattern in which apparent religious or social respectability coexists with deliberate injury. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī explicitly includes harm to land, wealth, and religion within *fasād*, and the Study Quran records later applications to social injustice and environmental destruction. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Those applications are strongest when they preserve the verse’s central concern with harm, rather than turning it into a claim that every natural misfortune proves moral guilt. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

The direct agricultural sense also makes a positive point about human life. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī says the verse indicates the value of cultivating land, planting trees, and seeking offspring, since these sustain human society; it therefore answers those who would abandon ordinary means under the guise of devotion. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The condemnation is of destruction, not of livelihood or productive work. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** That distinction matters because the verse names the goods being harmed—crops, herds, and dependants—as part of the shared provision by which people live. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** It invites stewardship and restraint without claiming that every economic or agricultural change is automatically *fasād*. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:206

206206
*“When he is told, ‘Reverence God,’ pride seizes him through sin. Hell will suffice him—and what an evil resting place.”*

**Meaning.** The sentence completes the description begun in 2:204: the person who appears persuasive in speech damages the land and then rejects correction. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** “When he is told, ‘Reverence God’” is a call to stop wrongdoing and to fear the One who knows both public conduct and hidden intention. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** The person’s response exposes the danger of a conscience governed by pride: instead of considering whether the advice is true, he treats correction as an affront to his status. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The expression *akhadhat-hu al-ʿizzatu bi-l-ithm* carries several shades of meaning. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that the man grows arrogant and persists in the sins already named, including corruption and harm to crops and animals. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī records *ʿizzah* as power, pride, heated partisanship, or a sense of self-protection that hardens into defiance. **[Qurṭubī]** The preposition *bi* can be understood as “through,” “with,” or “because of” sin; across these readings, wrongdoing and pride reinforce one another rather than allowing the person to accept admonition. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

Al-Saʿdī describes the reaction as combining disobedience with arrogance toward those who advise him. **[Saʿdī]** The verse is not condemning every strong emotion or every disagreement with a particular adviser. **[Maʿārif]** Its subject is the person already characterized by false claims and destructive conduct, who responds to the call to fear God by persisting in sin. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The distinction matters: sound counsel should be considered on its merits, while the described vice is to reject correction merely to defend a sinful course or the pride invested in it. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The sources connect the description with al-Akhnas in some reports and with hypocrites or wrongdoers more generally in others. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī transmits a report in which ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās understand the passage as a confrontation between a corrupt person and someone who calls him to reverence; al-Qurṭubī likewise cites explanations that generalize the traits to anyone whose inward state contradicts the outward claim. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** These accounts show how the passage can apply beyond a single reported individual, but they do not justify assigning the label “hypocrite” to someone merely because he resists one piece of advice. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

“Hell will suffice him” uses the idea of sufficiency in a severe sense: Hell is enough as requital for the wrong described. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Qurṭubī explains *ḥasbuhu* as “it is sufficient for him,” and reads *al-mihād* as a prepared resting place or bed; the bitter contrast is that a place associated with comfort becomes a place of punishment. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The phrase is not praise of sufficiency but a warning that no worldly status or eloquence can protect the person from divine judgment. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

As-Saʿdī dwells on the permanence of the punishment as it is described in the afterlife: a resting place from which the wrongdoer cannot simply depart, and a consequence that answers a life of persistent arrogance and corruption. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** His reflection is an admonition about the gravity of refusing truth, not a warrant for human beings to pronounce the final fate of particular individuals. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse’s warning belongs to God’s judgment, whose knowledge encompasses what people cannot see. **[Ṭabarī]**

The sequence also prepares the contrast in 2:207. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The person of 2:206 protects his pride even at the cost of wrongdoing; the person in the next verse is described as giving himself in pursuit of God’s pleasure. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The juxtaposition contrasts self-protection that serves sin with self-giving that seeks the good, and it returns the passage from the danger of hypocrisy to the possibility of sincere action. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** A genuine call to reverence asks a person to become answerable to God rather than to the fragile demands of pride. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse warns that refusing all correction to preserve one’s self-image can make sin self-reinforcing: the wrong is committed, defended, and repeated. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** Its warning should prompt self-examination before accusation of others, since outward conduct can be observed but the ultimate state of a heart belongs to God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The phrase also exposes a counterfeit form of dignity. **[Qurṭubī]** *ʿIzzah* can mean strength or honor, but in this verse the commentaries understand it as arrogance, heated pride, or partisanship that prevents the person from receiving admonition. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The preposition in “through sin” can indicate that the pride drives him further into wrongdoing, or that the pride is bound up with the sin he refuses to abandon. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** These readings converge on a reversal: what the person treats as self-respect becomes an instrument of moral collapse. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The brief phrase “Hell will suffice him” is complete as a warning without requiring an anecdote about a particular ruler or opponent. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** It answers the arrogance of someone who imagines that no one may correct him: the final judgment is not subject to his status or eloquence. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Saʿdī reflects on the enduring nature of the punishment, while the lexical image of *mihād* as a prepared bed or resting place makes the contrast deliberately severe. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse’s force belongs to the warning revealed about persistent wrongdoing; it does not authorize people to decide that a living adversary is certainly destined for Hell. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The relation between admonition and pride is the verse’s central psychological observation. **[Saʿdī]** A person who has already tied identity to a harmful course may experience correction as humiliation and intensify the very conduct that prompted the warning. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The Arabic phrase admits several grammatical nuances for the preposition *bi*, but in each the connection between arrogance and sin remains: pride accompanies, causes, or clings to wrongdoing rather than leading the person to repentance. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse therefore asks readers to notice their own response when corrected, before they turn disagreement into a shield for continuing harm. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

## 2:207

207207
*“Among people is one who gives himself, seeking God’s good pleasure; and God is Kind to His servants.”*

**Meaning.** After describing a person whose impressive speech conceals harm, the verse presents a contrasting kind of person: one who spends or gives himself in pursuit of God’s pleasure. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The verb *yashrī* carries the sense of selling or exchanging, so the image presents the person’s self as something surrendered in a deliberate bargain. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī links this language with God’s promise to those who give themselves in obedience and cites the parallel in 9:111, where the believers’ lives and property are exchanged for Paradise. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

One widely reported occasion connects the verse with Suhayb al-Rūmī’s migration from Mecca to Medina. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** When Quraysh reportedly tried to prevent Suhayb from leaving with his wealth, he offered to surrender his property in exchange for being allowed to continue; the Prophet is reported to have welcomed him with the words that his bargain had prospered. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The accounts differ in their details, but their shared point is that Suhayb accepted material loss rather than abandon the faith and migration he valued. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The verse is not confined to this one person. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī reports other explanations, including the emigrants and Helpers, the believers killed at al-Rajīʿ, and those who spend themselves in obedience, struggle, or enjoining right and forbidding wrong. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** He ultimately prefers a general interpretation: whoever gives himself in obedience to God, whether in struggle or in standing against wrongdoing, can fall under the description. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran likewise notes the universal ethical sense of surrendering selfish desire or even one’s life for God, alongside reports about particular Companions. **[Study Quran]**

Some reports connect the verse with a person who risks death while confronting wrongdoing, and commentators discuss whether it refers to the slain at al-Rajīʿ or to a fighter who entered the enemy line. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** These accounts should be handled as interpretations of particular circumstances, not as a general license for reckless self-destruction or private violence. **[Study Quran]** The verse praises devotion that seeks God’s approval; its wording does not remove the need to judge an action by the actual teachings and limits of the religion. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The phrase “seeking God’s good pleasure” identifies motive as essential. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The contrast with 2:204–206 is therefore not simply between two personalities, but between two orientations: one uses religion and persuasive speech for advantage, while the other accepts loss for the sake of what God loves. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse connects this self-giving with *ikhlāṣ*, sincerity, and with acts that uphold what is right, but the sources do not make every dramatic act automatically sincere or praiseworthy. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

“God is Kind to His servants” gives the promise a tender close. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** The divine kindness appears in guidance to what pleases Him and in the reward promised to those who act sincerely. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Saʿdī emphasizes that God’s compassion enables the servant to make this choice and then fulfills the reward for which the servant hoped. **[Saʿdī]** The believer’s self-giving is not a bargain with an uncertain party: the verse places it in relation to the Lord who is kind and faithful to His promise. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The image of selling oneself should not be mistaken for self-hatred. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** It describes a willing reordering of priorities: the person no longer treats comfort, wealth, or reputation as the highest good when these conflict with obedience to God. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The parallel language of “trade” in the Suhayb report makes the sacrifice intelligible as a choice of lasting value over immediate property. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks what a person is willing to give up for what he or she believes to be true and pleasing to God. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** Its answer is not measured by public display or by the scale of apparent loss alone, but by sincere intention and obedience. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The contrast with the preceding verses warns against eloquence without integrity and commends service whose inward aim is matched by conduct. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The verb *yashrī* is important to the reported Suhayb story. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī takes it as “sell,” the person giving himself in obedience for the reward God promises; al-Qurṭubī notes that the root can also be used in the sense of buying or exchanging, which helps explain why Suhayb’s surrender of wealth to secure his migration is described as a successful bargain. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The reports do not have to be collapsed into one literal transaction: the Qur’anic image is an exchange of what is temporary for God’s pleasure and reward. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]**

The reported applications to migration, the martyrs at al-Rajīʿ, and enjoining right show the breadth of the verse, but they are not identical occasions. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī’s preferred synthesis includes anyone who gives himself in sincere obedience, whether in struggle or in calling another away from wrongdoing. **[Ṭabarī]** The Study Quran notes the wider ethical principle of enjoining right and forbidding wrong and records ʿUmar’s reported application to a person killed while carrying it out. **[Study Quran]** These reports underline moral courage while leaving the circumstances and limits of each action to the sources’ broader legal and ethical teaching. **[Maʿārif]**

The closing name *raʾūf*, “Kind” or “Most Tender,” keeps sacrifice from being presented as futile loss. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Divine kindness is shown in guiding servants toward what pleases Him and in rewarding sincere effort. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse’s “bargain” is therefore not a human claim to force reward from God, but a metaphor for trust in the promise of the One whose mercy exceeds the servant’s offering. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The companion verse also explains why the phrase “sell himself” is not a command to seek harm for its own sake. **[Qurṭubī]** The person acts “seeking God’s pleasure,” and the commentators connect the expression with obedience, migration, defending the vulnerable, or other actions whose purpose is God’s approval. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** Ibn Kathīr relates the phrase to the wider promise in 9:111, where self-giving is framed by a covenant and an assured reward, not by a desire for death as an end in itself. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The ethical test is therefore the revealed purpose and the circumstances of the act, not how dramatic the sacrifice looks to observers. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]**

## 2:208

208208
*“O you who believe, enter into submission completely, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Truly he is a manifest enemy to you.”*

**Meaning.** The address calls believers to enter *al-silm* *kāffatan*, a phrase interpreted in more than one way. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Many early authorities understand *silm* here as Islam or submission to God, and al-Ṭabarī prefers that meaning; other explanations hear the word’s sense of peace or reconciliation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Jalālayn likewise glosses the word as Islam and explains *kāffatan* as observing all of its precepts. **[Jalālayn]**

The grammar allows two closely related emphases for *kāffatan*. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** It can describe believers entering the way together, or it can describe entering the whole of the way rather than accepting only selected parts. **[Study Quran]** The first reading stresses collective unity; the second stresses completeness of commitment. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** As-Saʿdī explains the command as accepting all the religion’s teachings and not treating personal preference as the test of which obligations to follow. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The emphases can reinforce one another without pretending that the Arabic permits only one syntactic reading. **[Qurṭubī]**

A reported context associates the verse with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and other Jewish converts who wished to retain particular observances from their earlier religious law, including reverence for the Sabbath or avoiding camel meat. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Maʿārif develops this account to explain the instruction to accept the revealed religion as a whole rather than treating earlier customs as additional Islamic rites. **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran presents it as one reported setting, while also recording interpretations addressed more generally to Muslims or to communities who had received earlier revelation. **[Study Quran]** The report should be identified as a context offered by commentators, not treated as the only possible meaning of the verse. **[Qurṭubī]**

On the reading “enter Islam completely,” the verse rejects selective obedience in which a person accepts only commands that happen to fit personal desire. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif stresses that the religion embraces beliefs, worship, social dealings, and personal conduct, rather than being confined to the mosque or to devotional acts alone. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** This does not mean every believer performs every duty identically or is free of weakness; it means that no person should deliberately make private preference the authority that decides which revealed obligations count. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]**

If *silm* is heard as peace, the verse also has a communal dimension: believers are to enter peace together rather than let factionalism or hostility divide them. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran notes that this reading emphasizes collective reconciliation, while the more common exegetical reading takes the word as Islam or submission. **[Study Quran]** The two possibilities should not be collapsed into an assertion that the verse has no religious content or that every use of “peace” means the same thing as *islām*. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

“Do not follow the footsteps of Satan” explains why complete obedience and unity require vigilance. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The image of footsteps suggests following a path incrementally: small temptations, divisive insinuations, and disobedient choices can lead toward more serious error. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The phrase also appears in 2:168, where it warns against Satan’s prompting toward evil and false claims about God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Naming Satan as a manifest enemy calls believers not to mistake an attractive suggestion for a sound guide. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Interpretive note.** The commentators differ over whether *silm* means Islam, submission, peace, or obedience, and over whether *kāffatan* primarily qualifies the people entering or the completeness of what they enter. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The report about Jewish converts who wished to retain certain practices supplies a possible occasion but does not exhaust the verse’s application. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The shared direction is to avoid selective or divisive departures from the path God has made clear. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks for an integrated faith: public belief, inward conviction, and conduct should not be split into unrelated compartments. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** It also warns that division and misguidance can develop step by step, making vigilance and shared submission essential. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The report about Jewish converts is especially useful for distinguishing faith from the addition of a new religious obligation. **[Maʿārif]** In the account, the converts wished to retain certain earlier practices as a way of honoring revelation, but the verse directs them to receive the new dispensation as a complete way rather than treating inherited observances as required components of it. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The example does not mean that an individual may never keep a harmless custom or personal preference; the issue is whether a practice is made into a binding religious requirement or used to resist a command. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The wording “all together” also has a communal resonance. **[Study Quran]** If *kāffatan* qualifies the believers, the call is to enter peace without leaving one another behind; if it qualifies the submission, the call is to embrace the whole of it. **[Qurṭubī]** These readings address different dimensions—community and completeness—and can be heard together as an invitation to shared commitment without claiming that the grammar erases its interpretive alternatives. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]** As-Saʿdī makes the practical consequence explicit: a believer should not make desire the rule by which revealed commands are accepted or abandoned. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

Satan’s “steps” are a warning that deviation may proceed gradually. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The same expression appears in 2:168 and in other Qur’anic warnings against following Satan; it presents temptation as a path of linked choices rather than a single obvious invitation to evil. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse therefore asks for attentiveness before a small accommodation hardens into division or disobedience. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The verse’s collective reading also tempers the danger of treating comprehensive commitment as a reason for division. **[Study Quran]** If *kāffatan* is taken with the people, believers are called to enter peace together; if it is taken with the religion, they are called to embrace its whole teaching. **[Qurṭubī]** Neither construction licenses following Satan’s invitations to factionalism or to inventing religious obligations that revelation has not made binding. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī’s preferred gloss of *silm* as Islam gives the instruction its specifically religious force, while the peace reading remains an interpretive possibility worth acknowledging. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

## 2:209

209209
*“But if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that God is Mighty, Wise.”*

**Meaning.** The conditional sentence follows the command to enter the way of submission completely. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** “If you slip” uses an image of a foot losing its firm place; the commentators apply it to turning aside from the straight path, deviating from the truth, or failing to implement what has been made clear. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Ibn Kathīr explains it as turning from the truth after proofs have been established. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The metaphor describes deviation, not every unintentional mistake or moment of human weakness as an equivalent rejection of faith. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The “clear proofs” are explained in several related ways. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī says they include God’s arguments and guidance, and he specifically notes that Muhammad and the Qur’an are among the proofs for those addressed. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Other commentators refer to the signs of the Qur’an, the Prophet, Islam, or the proofs previously given to the People of the Book about the coming of Muhammad. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī’s wording is deliberately broad, since the argument may be made through more than one form of evidence. **[Ṭabarī]**

The warning is sharpened by the phrase “after the clear proofs have come to you.” **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** Knowledge increases responsibility: the person who has understood a matter cannot pretend that deliberate departure is the same as never having received guidance. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī draws from this a distinction between one who knows a prohibition and one who has not received the message, cautioning that a person who has not been reached by the Islamic call is not made culpable in the same way for failing to follow its laws. **[Qurṭubī]** This is a juristic and theological reflection, not a warrant for human beings to claim exhaustive knowledge of another person’s access to evidence. **[Study Quran]**

“God is Mighty, Wise” combines the power to hold people accountable with the wisdom by which judgment is made. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī explains *ʿazīz* as One whom no force can prevent from carrying out judgment, and *ḥakīm* as One who acts with wisdom, including in the punishment of those who knowingly disobey. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī similarly glosses the Mighty as One whom nothing overcomes and the Wise as One whose actions are not arbitrary. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The names therefore do not portray God’s response as impulsive anger. **[Saʿdī]** The warning is that divine power is real and that divine wisdom is not weakness or indifference. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** A delay in visible punishment does not mean that evidence has been lost or that actions will never be judged. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Saʿdī connects the warning with the possibility of punishment after deliberate disobedience, while the verse’s own wording leaves the ultimate judgment to God. **[Saʿdī]**

Read with 2:208, the verse warns against making selective obedience a settled practice after guidance is clear. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Satan’s steps may begin with an apparently small departure, but the believer is urged to recognize the direction of travel and return to the clear path. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The following verse then asks whether those who refuse submission are waiting for the final decisive signs of judgment. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources differ slightly in naming the “clear proofs”: Muhammad, the Qur’an, Islam, signs in earlier scripture, or all of these together. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** They agree that the warning concerns slipping away after guidance has been established, and that God’s might and wisdom make accountability certain. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** Clear guidance is a responsibility as well as a gift. **[Maʿārif]** The verse calls the reader to respond to understood truth before a refusal becomes a pattern that one defends out of pride or habit. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Its warning is joined to hope: the call to return remains meaningful while life continues, but the final judgment cannot be managed by human delay or denial. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]**

Al-Qurṭubī also records a variant pronunciation, *zaliltum*, alongside the more familiar *zalaltum*; both carry the image of slipping and do not overturn the verse’s basic warning. **[Qurṭubī]** The metaphor moves from a foot losing its place to a person or community leaving the path of truth. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī explains the “slip” as opposing Islam and its teachings after God’s proofs have removed the excuse of ignorance; he includes the Prophet and Qur’an among those proofs while allowing other evidence addressed to earlier communities. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The names *ʿAzīz* and *Ḥakīm* must be read together. **[Ṭabarī]** Might without wisdom would suggest arbitrary force, while wisdom without might could be misunderstood as inability to enforce judgment; the verse affirms both divine sovereignty and purposeful judgment. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The sources use the warning to emphasize the seriousness of knowingly departing from guidance, not to declare that sincere questions or ordinary uncertainty are rebellion. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The conditional structure addresses a course of deviation after clarity, and the response it calls for is renewed reverence rather than despair. **[Maʿārif]**

Its placement before the image of 2:210 underscores the urgency of responding now. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** If people wait until the final decree is visible, they will have waited too long to choose the path their earlier evidence already made clear. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The warning also distinguishes certainty of accountability from the limits of human judgement. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī says punishment for knowingly committing a wrong is graver than punishment for ignorance, but he also notes that one who has not received the call cannot be judged as though clear proofs had reached him. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The verse’s address is not a tool for declaring that a particular person has knowingly rejected evidence; that knowledge belongs to God. **[Maʿārif]** Its purpose is to make the addressed hearers take seriously the guidance that has come to them. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The next verse intensifies the warning by asking whether they will wait for the final decree, when choices can no longer be revised. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

## 2:210

210210
*“Do they wait for anything other than that God should come to them in canopies of cloud, with the angels, and the matter be decided? Unto God all matters are returned.”*

**Meaning.** The verse continues the warning to those who have turned away from entering the way of submission described in 2:208. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** “Do they wait?” is a rhetorical question: are they postponing response until the decisive signs of judgment arrive, when there will be no opportunity to undo a life of refusal? **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī explains the opening as “what are they waiting for?” and identifies the people in question as those who leave the call to submission. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse places the warning of 2:209 in an eschatological frame: clear proofs have already come, and the final scene will make the outcome unmistakable. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The imagery is of the Day of Resurrection, when the clouds, angels, and decree of judgment appear. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Saʿdī describes the heavens and earth transformed, the angels gathered, records opened, and people distinguished by their deeds as judgment is made. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran connects the cloud and angel imagery with 25:25 and notes that some commentaries also associate the coming of angels with the moment of death; the Resurrection is the more evident context in this passage. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The phrase “God should come to them in canopies of cloud, with the angels” has been read in different ways. **[Ṭabarī]** Some exegetes understand the wording as affirming the divine coming described in revelation, without specifying how it occurs; others interpret it as the coming of God’s command, judgment, reward, or punishment. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Jalālayn glosses it as the coming of God’s command, while al-Qurṭubī records both that reading and explanations that refer to the divine judgment or recompense. **[Jalālayn]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran cautions that the language cannot mean movement from one place to another or containment in a location, since that would impose bodily limitation on God. **[Study Quran]**

The theological approaches should be distinguished rather than forced into one formula. **[Maʿārif]** Maʿārif treats the description as belonging to the verses whose full modality is beyond human knowledge: one affirms what revelation states without speculating about the “how.” **[Maʿārif]** Ibn Kathīr and al-Saʿdī affirm the event of divine coming as befits God, while denying resemblance to created beings; al-Saʿdī polemically argues against those who deny the attributes, but that polemic is his doctrinal stance rather than a neutral consensus among all the commentators. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī records several interpretive positions, including the reading that the verse refers to God’s command or recompense. **[Ṭabarī]**

There is also a recitational and grammatical difference in the phrase about the angels. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The majority reading places *al-malāʾikatu* in the nominative, which al-Ṭabarī understands as coordinating the angels with the coming described in the verse; other readings place it in the genitive, connecting the angels with the clouds. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī notes both constructions and reports an alternate reading that makes the relation explicit: God and the angels come in canopies of cloud. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran similarly explains that an alternate grammatical reading can attach “in the clouds” to the angels rather than to God. **[Study Quran]**

“Then the matter is decided” points to the finality of judgment. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The deeds have been completed, the reckoning takes place, and no person can add to or erase what has already been done. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī explains the decision as judgment between creatures, including the restoration of rights between wrongdoers and those wronged; he notes that justice is carried out without the limitations that affect human courts in this world. **[Ṭabarī]** The verse’s warning is therefore not merely that a dramatic scene will occur, but that God’s judgment will bring every unresolved matter to account. **[Qurṭubī]**

The last clause, “unto God all matters are returned,” states the ultimate destination of every affair. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** All disputes, acts of obedience, and acts of wrongdoing return to God for judgment, even when people in this life appear to escape accountability or to misuse power. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī notes variant readings with active and passive forms—“the matters return” and “the matters are returned”—and treats both as expressing the same ultimate dependence on God. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** The Study Quran also reads the phrase as the return of all affairs to God in the Hereafter. **[Study Quran]**

The exegetes preserve a lengthy report about the final gathering in al-Ṭabarī, but his editor identifies it as weak and containing objectionable material; it should not be repeated as established teaching. **[Ṭabarī]** *(weak)* The verse itself is sufficient for the central point: judgment belongs to God, and the return of all matters is certain. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Interpretive note.** The commentaries differ over whether the “coming” means the divine attribute as affirmed without modality, God’s command, or the arrival of judgment and recompense; they also record grammatical differences in how “and the angels” attaches to the sentence. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The scene is placed in the final judgment, when the decree is carried out and all affairs return to God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse warns against postponing a response to guidance until the reality of judgment can no longer be denied. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Worldly influence cannot permanently shield wrongdoing, and the final return to God levels the distinctions people use to avoid accountability. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The proper response to descriptions of the unseen is to preserve the sources’ distinctions, avoid imagining God in created terms, and take seriously the certainty of the reckoning. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The cloud imagery should not be turned into a picture of God moving through space like a created body. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī explicitly rejects interpreting such language as transition, motion, or departure from one place to another; he explains divine acts without an instrument or bodily cause. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran makes the related point that locating God in space or imagining change in the divine nature would impose created limitations. **[Study Quran]** Maʿārif’s approach is to affirm the revealed wording while refraining from speculation about its modality. **[Maʿārif]** These cautions preserve reverence while still reporting that Ibn Kathīr and al-Saʿdī affirm the divine coming as an attribute befit for God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī also discuss alternate case readings of “the angels” and different forms of the word for clouds or shade. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The syntactic difference affects whether the angels are coordinated with God’s coming or are described as arriving in the cloud canopies; it does not alter the scene’s placement at the decisive judgment. **[Study Quran]** A separate reading of “the matters return” makes the affairs the grammatical subject, while the passive form says they are returned to God; both express the same final dependence. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]**

Al-Ṭabarī transmits an elaborate report about the gathering, but its editor identifies serious weakness and objectionable material in its chain and content. **[Ṭabarī]** *(weak)* It should not be used to establish details beyond what the verse and stronger explanations support. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The secure exegetical emphasis is the certainty of judgment, the presence of the angels, and the return of every affair to God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

## 2:211

211211
*“Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them. Whoever changes God’s blessing after it has come to him—truly God is severe in punishment.”*

**Meaning.** The question “how many” is not a request for a tally. It is a rebuke that makes the hearers recall the abundance of evidence entrusted to Israel and the responsibility that followed from receiving it. Al-Ṭabarī reads the address to the Prophet as a reminder of the many proofs delivered to Israel through earlier messengers, and as comfort that rejection after evidence is not a new challenge in the history of prophecy. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī likewise calls the question reproachful, and treats the signs as demonstrations of truth. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse looks back from the immediately preceding warning about slipping after clear proofs: when guidance has been made manifest, turning away is more serious than mere ignorance. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]**

Commentators give examples of the clear signs, while the verse itself leaves the list open. **[Qurṭubī]** The staff and the luminous hand of Moses, the sea parted for Israel, the drowning of Pharaoh’s forces, shade from clouds, and the provision of manna and quails are among the signs mentioned by the exegetes. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran also names Moses’ staff, hand, and the passage through the waters. **[Study Quran]** These signs addressed different dimensions of life: prophetic proof, rescue from oppression, and sustenance in the wilderness. Their variety underscores that the charge is not based on one obscure event but on a long history of divine favor and guidance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

“God’s blessing” (*niʿmat Allāh*) is interpreted in a closely related range of ways. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī identifies it particularly with Islam and the obligations of God’s religion; changing it means abandoning the covenant and turning from belief to disbelief. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī also connects the phrase to the covenant and to recognition of Muhammad, but stresses that the wording is general: anyone who replaces a blessing with ingratitude falls under its warning. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran reports interpretations in which the blessing is the trust and covenant given to Israel, and notes that some commentators associate “altering” with the charge of scriptural distortion (*taḥrīf*). **[Study Quran]** That association should not erase the verse’s broader point: its grammar speaks of changing God’s favor after it has reached a person, not only of one historical dispute over a text. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

Al-Maʿārif elaborates the pattern through episodes from Israel’s history: a revelation was met with resistance, deliverance from Pharaoh was followed by worship of the calf, provision in the wilderness by complaint, and the mission of prophets by rejection and, in some cases, violence against them. **[Maʿārif]** Ibn Kathīr likewise lists the signs associated with Moses and describes the response of some Israelites as preferring disbelief to faith. **[Ibn Kathīr]** These are examples of the moral sequence the verse condemns: a gift supplies knowledge and opportunity, but gratitude requires a response in belief and conduct. **[Saʿdī]** To “change” the blessing is not simply to fail to feel grateful; it is to exchange its intended guidance for a contrary allegiance or practice. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The phrase “after it has come to him” makes the timing ethically important. **[Qurṭubī]** A person cannot treat clear guidance as though it never arrived once its claims have become known. **[Maʿārif]** Saʿdī describes divine favor as religious or worldly: when a person does not give thanks or fulfill its due, the blessing may be withdrawn or replaced by disobedience and denial; gratitude, by contrast, preserves favor and is a cause for increase. **[Saʿdī]** The verse does not say that every worldly loss proves a person’s ingratitude. Rather, it warns against a deliberate moral reversal—using received guidance, capacity, or evidence as an occasion for rejecting the Giver. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

Al-Qurṭubī emphasizes that the verse begins with Israel but is not confined to one community: its general wording also includes the Quraysh, to whom the sending of Muhammad was itself a favor, and anyone who rejects a blessing after recognizing it. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr draws a parallel with the Qur’anic description of those who “changed God’s blessing into disbelief” and brought their people to ruin (14:28–29). **[Ibn Kathīr]** The connection is not an ethnic accusation against later generations; it is a warning about a recurring human choice. **[Study Quran]** A community may inherit revelation, institutions, or material security and still lose their purpose if it treats them as possessions rather than trusts. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

The words “God is severe in punishment” give the warning its consequence without specifying a timetable or naming every form of punishment. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī explains the phrase as a threat, and notes that the Arabic word for requital evokes the consequence that follows an act. **[Qurṭubī]** The emphasis is that rejection after evidence carries accountability; it is not permission for people to pronounce divine judgment on others. **[Study Quran]** The passage leaves the judgment to God, who knows what signs reached each person and how they responded. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Interpretive note.** Exegetes identify the signs with particular miracles of Moses, with the wider history of Israel’s prophets, and—by extension—with the guidance concerning Muhammad. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The central wording remains deliberately broader than any one inventory: it condemns changing a divine favor after receiving it. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]**

**Reflection.** Gratitude is more than remembering what one has received; it is allowing a gift to lead toward its rightful purpose. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse invites readers to ask whether knowledge, opportunity, or security has made them more faithful and just, or has instead been turned into a pretext for neglect. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:212

212212
*“The life of this world is made fair to those who disbelieve, and they mock those who believe. But the reverent will be above them on the Day of Resurrection. God provides for whom He wills without measure.”*

**Meaning.** This verse explains why a person might exchange guidance for disbelief: the present life can appear so attractive that its immediate wealth, status, and pleasures seem to be the whole measure of success. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The passive wording “is made fair” describes a perception that can become dominant, not a claim that worldly beauty is intrinsically evil. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the earth’s adornments are part of a test: those who remain within God’s guidance are not mastered by them, whereas those who make this life their only horizon become captive to it. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The verse then describes the social expression of that outlook: the disbelievers deride the believers. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Some reports identify the mockery with Quraysh leaders who looked down on early Muslims because they were poor, socially vulnerable, or formerly enslaved. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The exegetes name Bilāl, ʿAmmār, Suhayb, and Ibn Masʿūd among the believers whose low worldly standing was used against them. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** Their example exposes the error of treating money or tribal rank as proof that God favors its possessor. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

Al-Ṭabarī explains that the mockers pursued accumulation, rivalry, and leadership while belittling those who sought the afterlife and spent for God’s sake. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr similarly contrasts those satisfied with worldly acquisition and reluctant to spend in obedience with believers who direct their resources toward God’s pleasure. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The contrast is not between every wealthy person and every poor person; wealth itself is not the measure of faith. It is between making possessions an ultimate end and using one’s circumstances in a way consistent with reverence and accountability. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The phrase “those who are reverent will be above them on the Day of Resurrection” reverses the mockers’ ranking. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī understands “above” as the believers’ superior place in the Garden while the disbelievers are in the Fire. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records readings of superiority in rank and of location, and also notes that the verse answers those who assumed that, even if there were a resurrection, their worldly advantage would continue there. **[Qurṭubī]** The decisive comparison is thus deferred to the Day when the visible conditions of this life no longer obscure moral reality. **[Study Quran]**

The promise does not require the believer to be materially prosperous in this life or to answer every act of mockery with a visible worldly victory. **[Saʿdī]** The verse names the Day of Resurrection as the point at which the full ranking is disclosed. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** This qualification matters: poverty is not itself a guarantee of righteousness, nor is wealth proof of divine approval. The criterion is reverence and faithful action, not the social status that others assign. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]**
