“God provides for whom He wills without measure” completes the correction of worldly boasting. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī understands the phrase as the generosity of God, whose provision is not constrained by fear that His stores will be exhausted or require human accounting. **[Ṭabarī]** He applies it especially to the honor and gifts granted to the reverent in the Hereafter. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr reads the provision as potentially encompassing this life and the next, while the Study Quran records several interpretations: God is not answerable for His giving, His gifts are not diminished by being given, and His mercy and reward exceed calculation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The clause can also be read beside the preceding reversal: those mocked for having little in this world are not thereby cut off from God’s limitless bounty. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Saʿdī distinguishes material provision, which reaches believers and disbelievers alike, from the provision of hearts—knowledge, faith, love, awe, and hope—which God grants to whom He wills. **[Saʿdī]** This prevents “without measure” from being reduced to a promise that every faithful person will become rich. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The Study Quran relates a report in which the Prophet asks Abū Dharr to compare a finely dressed, socially exalted man with a weak man in worn clothes, then says that the latter is better in God’s sight than a world full of the former’s kind. **[Study Quran]** The report illustrates the verse’s reversal of status, but the argument does not depend on judging people by their appearance: only God knows the reality of their faith and deeds. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr connects the warning against converting blessing into disbelief with the Qur’anic account of those who changed God’s favor into rejection (14:28–29). **[Ibn Kathīr]**

Read alongside 2:211, the verse contrasts two responses to received guidance: the earlier verse recalls clear signs, while this one shows how apparent worldly success can encourage people to dismiss those signs and ridicule their bearers. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The mockery is therefore part of a distorted scale of value, not proof that the mockers have correctly judged the believers. **[Study Quran]** Reports identify the mockers with Makkan idolaters, Madinan hypocrites, or Jewish leaders in Madinah, so the verse is not confined to one reported setting. **[Study Quran]** The community’s lower status in the present moment does not settle its standing before God, and its eventual elevation does not mean that every faithful person must win a social contest now. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Interpretive note.** The commentators differ on the precise sense of “without reckoning”—unmeasured abundance, provision without depletion, gifts in the Hereafter, or gifts granted without the recipient being called to account; the Study Quran also notes an interpretation referring to those admitted to Paradise without reckoning. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** They agree that worldly wealth is not a reliable measure of a person’s standing with God. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks its readers to notice how easily social contempt borrows the language of worldly success. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ṭabarī]** A believer’s dignity does not rest on whether others applaud their possessions, and a person’s wealth does not entitle them to humiliate someone with less. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The final judgment belongs to God, whose generosity is not bounded by the scales people use in this world. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

## 2:213

213213
*“Mankind was one community; then God sent the prophets as bearers of glad tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth, to judge among people concerning that over which they differed. None differed concerning it except those who were given it, after clear proofs came to them, out of envy among themselves. Then God guided those who believe to the truth of that over which they differed, by His leave. God guides whom He wills to a straight path.”*

**Meaning.** The verse opens with a compressed account of humanity’s religious history. The commentators offer more than one account of the “one community”: al-Ṭabarī prefers that people were once united in the religion of truth, before disagreement arose; he reports the view that this unity lasted between Adam and Noah, but says the Qur’an does not require certainty about its exact duration. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī records other early interpretations: the people may mean Adam, Adam and Eve, the generations before Noah, Noah and those in the Ark, or—according to some reports—a community united in disbelief at a later time. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran also mentions an allusion to the pretemporal covenant and the possibility that “community” can refer to one person, as in Abraham being called an *ummah* in 16:120. **[Study Quran]**

The wording does not explicitly state “then they differed” between the first clause and “God sent the prophets.” **[Qurṭubī]** Many commentators supply that phrase in the meaning: people were one community, then disagreement arose, and God sent messengers to guide them. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** This implied transition explains why prophets and revealed books are described as judging among people in matters of dispute. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Maʿārif likewise reads the passage as moving from an early unity in true belief to later divisions in belief and practice. **[Maʿārif]** The compressed style does not imply that revelation caused the first division; it sets out the divine response to division once it had arisen. **[Study Quran]**

The disagreement about the first community should be kept visible. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī argues from 10:19 that the initial unity was on faith and that the blame falls on the later divergence, not on being one community. **[Ṭabarī]** Other commentators consider a state of shared error before prophetic guidance, or describe a more limited period in which humanity had not yet divided over revealed commands. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Saʿdī preserves more than one construction, including the reading that people were first on guidance and later divided, and the alternative that messengers were sent to a people already in misguidance. **[Saʿdī]** These are exegetical alternatives, not a license to present uncertain early chronology as established fact. **[Study Quran]**

The prophets are sent as “bearers of glad tidings and warners.” **[Ṭabarī]** They announce the reward promised to those who obey and the consequence awaiting those who reject, making the moral stakes of revelation clear. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The Book is described as sent “in truth”; al-Qurṭubī understands *al-kitāb* either generically, for the revealed books, or—if the passage is focused on the People of the Book—as the Torah. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī likewise identifies it with the Torah in his preferred contextual reading, while acknowledging the broader language of scripture. **[Ṭabarī]** The Study Quran records both the general reading and the more specific one. **[Study Quran]**

The Book “judges among people” because it supplies the revealed standard by which disputes are resolved; al-Ṭabarī explains that prophets judge by what the Book teaches, so the judgment is attributed to the scripture itself. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse does not say that every disagreement among human beings is settled by force. Its focus is the guidance and criterion God has revealed, which should be returned to when disputes concern truth and religious practice. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Saʿdī draws a practical principle: when disagreement arises, people are to refer it to God and His Messenger, because scripture and prophetic teaching provide the means of distinguishing truth from error. **[Saʿdī]**

The verse’s sharpest rebuke falls on those who differed after receiving clear proofs. **[Maʿārif]** Their divergence was not simply an innocent failure to encounter evidence; *baghyan baynahum* points to envy, aggression, rivalry, or a desire for worldly authority. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī describes people seeking leadership and worldly display, while al-Qurṭubī calls the motive injustice and pursuit of rank. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Maʿārif stresses that self-interest can turn knowledge into an instrument of opposition. **[Maʿārif]** The verse therefore distinguishes honest inquiry from division maintained for advantage. **[Study Quran]**

“Then God guided those who believe to the truth of that over which they differed, by His leave” describes both the gift of guidance and its content. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī interprets the believers as the followers of Muhammad and says that God enabled them to recognize the truth where earlier communities had differed. **[Ṭabarī]** Ibn Kathīr reports examples: the day of congregation, the direction of prayer, fasting, Abraham’s religion, and the status of Jesus. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī also mentions disputes about Friday, the qiblah, and the identity of Abraham and Jesus. **[Qurṭubī]** The examples show that guidance is not limited to abstract doctrine; it shapes worship, community life, and the way earlier prophets are understood. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

An early report, transmitted by al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr from Abū Hurayrah, links the verse to Friday: the Prophet describes the Muslim community as coming later but being brought first to the truth of the day over which previous communities differed. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** It is one example of guidance, not an exhaustive summary of everything the verse means. **[Qurṭubī]** The Prophet’s reported night prayer asks God to guide him to the truth in disputed matters, an invocation that Ibn Kathīr cites from the report of ʿĀʾishah. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse thus supports humility: believers should ask for guidance rather than assuming that possession of evidence makes them immune to error. **[Saʿdī]**

“By His leave” is explained as God’s will, command, knowledge, or enabling grace. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Saʿdī emphasizes that the call to the straight path establishes responsibility for all, while God’s particular enabling and mercy guide whom He wills. **[Saʿdī]** This sentence does not excuse those who use evidence for selfish ends; the verse has just criticized such conduct. **[Maʿārif]** Rather, it teaches that correct guidance is not a possession secured independently of God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The commentators differ over who comprised the first “one community,” how long that unity lasted, whether *the Book* means all scriptures or the Torah in particular, and the precise referent of what people disputed. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The verse’s stable emphasis is that God sends revelation to guide people, that rivalry can corrupt those who have received it, and that true guidance comes by God’s leave. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** Revelation is a mercy because it gives a shared criterion where human interests and judgments diverge. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** Yet receiving guidance does not make a person or community incapable of envy; knowledge must be joined to humility and fairness. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The prayer for guidance in disputed matters is therefore not a sign of weakness but a fitting response to the verse’s account of human disagreement. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:214

214214
*“Or do you think that you will enter Paradise before there comes to you the like of what befell those who passed away before you? Poverty and affliction touched them, and they were shaken, until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, ‘When will God’s help come?’ Surely God’s help is near.”*

**Meaning.** The opening question challenges the assumption that faith exempts a community from hardship. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** It does not say that suffering purchases Paradise as though it were a price; rather, the verse recalls that commitment to God has historically been tested, and calls believers to patience as earlier believers endured difficulty. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The shared theme with 3:142 and 29:2–3 is that a claim of faith is exposed and strengthened through trials, not merely by words. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The two forms of distress are described as *baʾsāʾ* and *ḍarrāʾ*. Al-Ṭabarī glosses the first as severe need and poverty and the second as illness and bodily affliction. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The exegetes also include the wider hardships that accompany persecution: fear, loss, injury, separation from home, and pressure from enemies. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The verbs do not reduce the trial to one kind of pain; they name both deprivation and harm, followed by the image of being shaken by danger. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

Several commentators connect the verse with the Battle of the Confederates, when the Muslims in Madinah faced a siege, cold, scarcity, and fear from the allied forces. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr relates that the believers’ ordeal at al-Aḥzāb is described in 33:10–12 as a severe shaking. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Other reports connect the passage with Uḥud or with the hardship of the emigrants who left their homes and property in Makkah. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The reports preserve more than one setting for the warning; the verse’s language is broad enough to address the continuing trials of believers without being confined to a single campaign. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The word *zulzilū*—“they were shaken”—is explained as intense fear and distress, not simply a physical earthquake. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The image captures how external danger can unsettle even people of firm faith. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse does not condemn a person for feeling fear or weariness; it acknowledges how prolonged pressure can bring a community to the edge of its endurance. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The example of earlier messengers and their followers prevents later believers from interpreting hardship as proof that God has abandoned them. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī discuss the reading and syntax of “until the Messenger and those who believed with him said.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The phrase marks the extremity of the trial, when even the messenger and believers asked, “When will God’s help come?” **[Jalālayn]** That question is not necessarily doubt in the promise. Maʿārif explains it as a plea for the promised help to arrive sooner, not a denial that God would help; al-Qurṭubī likewise says the appeal expresses urgent longing under strain. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** It is a human cry from within faith, not a theological accusation against God. **[Saʿdī]**

Ibn Kathīr cites the report of Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt, who recalls asking why the Prophet did not pray for immediate support. The Prophet answered by describing the severe torture endured by believers before them—some were sawn apart or combed with iron, yet did not abandon their religion—and said that the matter would spread, while warning his companions against haste. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The report reinforces the verse’s comparison with earlier communities; its point is not to romanticize torture, but to show that perseverance under oppression has been part of prophetic history. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

The reply, “Surely God’s help is near,” interrupts the question with certainty. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The promise counters despair, but the verse does not give a calendar by which human beings can demand relief or guarantee that every difficulty will end in the precise form they desire. **[Study Quran]** The nearness is grounded in God’s power and faithfulness, not in the sufferer’s ability to control its timing. **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr links the assurance with 94:5–6, where hardship is accompanied by relief. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī notes that the promise is fulfilled by God’s raising the believers over their enemy. **[Ṭabarī]**

As-Saʿdī draws a general lesson: when people hold to truth, trials may increase before relief, and perseverance can turn hardship into a means of spiritual growth and eventual victory. **[Saʿdī]** This is not a claim that every faithful person receives an immediate political triumph; the verse addresses a community under divine care and leaves the form of help to God’s wisdom. **[Study Quran]** The text gives believers permission to name the strain honestly while directing them toward patience and hope. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The comparison with earlier communities is one of likeness, not a requirement that every believer undergo an identical sequence or degree of hardship. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Saʿdī presents the enduring pattern as a trial of those who claim faith, while the particular forms of poverty, illness, fear, and persecution vary with time and circumstance. **[Saʿdī]** The fact that the Messenger and believers voiced their longing for help also shows that turning to God with a question is compatible with faith; the verse does not demand silence about pain. **[Maʿārif]** The answer that follows redirects that longing toward hope without denying the reality of the trial. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Interpretive note.** The exegetes differ on the particular historical setting—al-Aḥzāb, Uḥud, or the emigrants’ hardship—but agree that the verse places present trials within the longer history of prophetic communities. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The Messenger’s question is understood as a plea for hastened aid under intense pressure, not as unbelief. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** Faith does not require pretending that distress is easy. The verse records the question “When will help come?” and pairs it with an answer that sustains hope. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** Remembering earlier believers can steady a person without making another’s suffering a reason to ignore present needs. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The promised nearness asks for endurance, compassionate support, and trust in God’s timing. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]**

## 2:215

215215
*“They ask you what they should spend. Say, ‘Whatever good you spend is for parents, near relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler. Whatever good you do, God knows it.’”*

**Meaning.** The question concerns both the object of spending and its destination. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that the Companions asked what they should give from their wealth and on whom it should be spent; the answer names the recipients, then closes by affirming that every good deed is known to God. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Maʿārif notes that the first half of the question—where the money should go—is answered directly, while the question of how much to give returns in 2:219 with the instruction to give *al-ʿafw*, the surplus. **[Maʿārif]** The two verses therefore complement rather than duplicate one another. **[Study Quran]**

Al-Qurṭubī and al-Jalālayn connect the question with ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ, a wealthy older Companion who asked what to spend and whom to support. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī also transmits reports that the question came from believers more generally, and does not make the verse depend on a single questioner. **[Ṭabarī]** This difference in reported occasion does not affect the general answer: spending should meet real human needs, beginning with those whose claims are closest and most pressing. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

The ordered list begins with parents, then near relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler. **[Jalālayn]** The order makes visible a progression of relationship and need. **[Saʿdī]** Parents have a profound claim through their care and the duty of filial kindness; as-Saʿdī notes that financial support for parents in need is among the forms of honoring them that can become obligatory for a child who has the means. **[Saʿdī]** Relatives combine charity with maintaining kinship, and the nearer and more needy generally have priority. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

Orphans are named because, lacking a mature provider of their own, they are especially vulnerable to neglect. **[Saʿdī]** The needy are those pressed by want and necessity, while the “son of the road” is a traveler cut off from resources away from home, who needs enough aid to reach a safe destination. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The list is not a ranking of human worth; it identifies groups for whom a person’s wealth can answer a concrete need. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The phrase “whatever good you spend” uses *khayr* for wealth given in charity. **[Ṭabarī]** It also broadens the conclusion: God knows not only the amount but the intention, the need met, and the benefit produced. **[Saʿdī]** The verse does not suggest that an act becomes good merely because the giver calls it charity; the earlier word “good” and the named recipients frame giving as an act directed toward real welfare. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** As-Saʿdī adds that reward corresponds to sincerity, the giver’s capacity, and the extent to which the expenditure meets an important need. **[Saʿdī]**

The legal status of the spending is discussed by the commentators. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Some early reports describe this as an instruction given before the fixed alms-tax and then superseded by zakāh; al-Ṭabarī records that view but says the verse itself does not establish that it was a compulsory levy later canceled. **[Ṭabarī]** He prefers to read it as guidance about voluntary beneficence, which remains in force alongside prescribed zakāh. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī likewise reports that many jurists regard it as recommended spending, while noting that separate duties of maintenance may apply to poor parents. **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif also distinguishes this general charity from zakāh, whose thresholds and recipients are governed by separate rules. **[Maʿārif]**

That distinction avoids two confusions. A person should not assume that voluntary gifts to parents replace zakāh obligations, nor assume that the verse’s list means zakāh may be assigned to every named relative in every circumstance. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse encourages generosity toward close dependents and vulnerable people; the detailed rules governing obligatory support and alms-tax are treated elsewhere. **[Qurṭubī]** The present passage keeps the ethical emphasis in view: wealth is to circulate toward those with claims upon the giver, not be hoarded while pressing needs are ignored. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The wording “whatever good you do, God knows it” extends beyond financial transfer. **[Saʿdī]** The verse begins with spending, but its closing reassurance can encompass other acts of kindness and obedience; nothing good is lost merely because people do not see or praise it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that God records the act and repays it fully, so the giver is not dependent on public recognition or immediate return. **[Ṭabarī]** The knowledge of God also makes the line a warning against giving in a way that humiliates recipients or disguises self-interest as care. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

The list gives priorities, not a fixed percentage or equal allotment for every recipient. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** A person’s family responsibilities, the severity of another’s need, and the resources available can all affect what a just act of spending looks like. **[Saʿdī]** The verse does not require a giver to ignore dependent children in order to aid a stranger, nor does it let a wealthy giver overlook a needy relative simply because another form of charity is more visible. **[Maʿārif]** Its closing assurance that God knows every good deed shifts the measure away from public display and toward sincere, fitting care. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Interpretive note.** The exegetes differ over whether the initial question came from ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ or from the believers collectively, and whether this passage was ever superseded by zakāh. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī’s preferred view and the reading in Maʿārif treat the verse as continuing guidance for voluntary spending, while recognizing separate obligations of zakāh and family maintenance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** The verse redirects charity from abstraction to relationship: begin by noticing who depends on you, who is vulnerable, and who has become stranded. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** It also frees the giver from the need to advertise generosity; the One who knows every act is the One who rewards it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

## 2:216

216216
*“Fighting is prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you. Perhaps you dislike a thing that is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing that is bad for you. God knows, and you do not know.”*

**Meaning.** The verse turns from the charity and care discussed above to the burden of armed conflict, which the first audience found difficult. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The word *kutiba* means “was prescribed” or “was written,” and the exegetes take it as establishing an obligation rather than merely praising a voluntary act. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** But the scope of that obligation is explained in the legal commentaries, not settled by the single word alone. **[Study Quran]**

The dislike described here is not necessarily rebellion against God’s command. **[Qurṭubī]** Fighting naturally involves danger, loss of life, separation from family, financial cost, and the fear of injury, so aversion is understandable even for a believer who accepts the duty when it applies. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī distinguishes this human reluctance from rejecting the divine ruling itself. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Maʿārif similarly notes that people can dislike the hardships associated with an obligation while remaining committed to obeying God. **[Maʿārif]** The verse acknowledges that emotional tension rather than pretending that duty is always easy. **[Saʿdī]**

Classical jurists commonly describe fighting as a communal obligation: if a sufficient group undertakes the duty, the rest are not all required to go. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī reports this as the predominant position, while preserving other opinions about the obligation’s breadth. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī likewise records a communal-duty reading, alongside rulings that can make the obligation individual in particular circumstances—for example, when a community is directly attacked, when a person is specifically summoned, or when the defenders need support. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran also notes the distinction between a general communal duty and defense when an enemy enters a Muslim land. **[Study Quran]** These are juristic interpretations tied to organized public responsibility; the verse should not be detached from that legal discussion and treated as a license for private violence. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]**

Al-Qurṭubī describes disagreement over whether fighting was initially made obligatory on every believer and later became a communal duty, or whether it was communal from the outset. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī also records a view that fighting remains obligatory until the Hour, but explicitly prefers the position that it is a communal obligation fulfilled when a sufficient group undertakes it. **[Ṭabarī]** Saʿdī frames the verse as an obligation whose application depends on circumstances and the capacity of the community. **[Saʿdī]** The commentators’ differences warn against reading this single verse as a complete account of the rules, authorities, aims, and limits governing warfare. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The wording translated “hateful” can be read with different vocalizations of *kurh* and *karh*. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī reports a distinction between something disliked by nature and something undertaken under compulsion, while also observing that the readings converge on the difficulty of fighting. **[Ṭabarī]** The point is not that every person must feel the same emotion; the verse names the common human reluctance associated with an arduous duty. **[Qurṭubī]**

The paired clauses, “perhaps you dislike a thing that is good for you” and “perhaps you love a thing that is bad for you,” correct confidence in one’s limited perspective. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** In this immediate setting, fighting may bring protection, the removal of oppression, or a good outcome that the believers cannot yet see. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Conversely, avoiding conflict may feel safer but could leave the community exposed to injury or coercion. **[Maʿārif]** The verse does not praise violence for its own sake; it asks believers to recognize that initial preference is not always a reliable measure of what is ultimately beneficial. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]**

As-Saʿdī extends the lesson to choices beyond warfare: people often desire what brings harm and dislike what contains benefit, so they should measure decisions by revelation and sound reflection rather than immediate appetite. **[Saʿdī]** That general lesson must remain a principle of humility, not a claim that every disliked event is secretly good in a way humans can identify. **[Study Quran]** The verse itself ends by locating complete knowledge with God: “God knows, and you do not know.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]**

Al-Ṭabarī transmits an attributed statement from Ibn ʿAbbās about accepting God’s decree in all circumstances; the editor of the source marks its chain obscure and its text objectionable (*munkar*). **[Ṭabarī]** *(weak)* It should not be used as a sound Prophetic report or as a substitute for the verse’s actual argument. The secure point is the contrast between God’s encompassing knowledge and human beings’ incomplete grasp of consequences. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]**

The transition to the following verse is important: 2:217 acknowledges that fighting in a sacred month is grave, even as it weighs that act against the wider persecution described there. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** This makes clear that 2:216 is not a general slogan detached from legal limits or an instruction for each person to initiate violence according to private judgment. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The juristic discussions in the commentaries concern when a public duty falls on a community or becomes immediate in a particular defense, not the emotional preference of an individual acting alone. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Interpretive note.** The commentators differ on whether the duty was originally individual or communal and on the conditions that can make it individual; they also discuss whether *kurh* emphasizes natural aversion or coercive burden. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Their shared explanation is that an unpleasant duty may serve a good whose consequences are not immediately visible, while the legal application must be read with the wider rules of the tradition. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** The verse does not tell a person to silence every fear. It recognizes the weight of a difficult responsibility while asking that fear not become the sole measure of right and wrong. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** Humility before what one cannot yet know can make obedience more thoughtful, not less humane. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:217

217217
*“They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say, ‘Fighting in it is grave, but barring people from God’s way, disbelieving in Him, barring access to the Sacred Mosque and expelling its people from it is graver in God’s sight. Strife is graver than killing.’ They will not cease fighting you until they turn you from your religion, if they are able. Whoever among you turns from his religion and dies a disbeliever—their deeds have come to nothing in this world and the Hereafter; they are the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein.”*

**Meaning.** The question arose in the context of an armed expedition led by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaḥsh near Nakhlah, in which a Quraysh man was killed and captives and goods were taken around the transition into the sacred month of Rajab. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The reports differ over the date, the party’s exact orders, and how the calendar was determined. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran recounts the expedition and notes that the Prophet did not immediately accept the captives or spoils while the question of fighting during the sacred month remained unresolved. **[Study Quran]** The historical setting explains the accusation directed at the Muslims, but the verse’s argument is larger than one disputed incident. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

The answer does not deny the seriousness of fighting in a sacred month. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** It says that the obstruction of God’s way, disbelief, exclusion from the Sacred Mosque, and expulsion of its people are graver in God’s sight. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The comparison exposes the selective moral outrage of opponents who condemned one act while ignoring a sustained pattern of persecution and displacement. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** It does not imply that a serious wrong becomes acceptable merely because someone else has committed a worse one; rather, it sets the contested action within a wider account of responsibility. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

“Strife” (*fitnah*) is given more than one closely connected gloss. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some early authorities explain it as associating partners with God, or disbelief that draws people away from worship of Him. **[Ṭabarī]** Other commentators emphasize persecution that attempts to force believers away from their religion, including torture, expulsion, and obstruction of worship. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Ibn Kathīr includes both meanings in the wider description of Quraysh’s campaign against the believers. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The phrase thus refers not to ordinary difference of opinion, but to a coercive assault on faith and religious life. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

The next clause says that opponents will continue fighting until they can turn believers from their religion. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that their aim is to bring the believers back to disbelief, and al-Qurṭubī interprets the condition “if they are able” as describing their intention and effort, not a prediction that they will succeed. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The warning is directed to a community facing pressure to abandon its faith; it should not be turned into a claim that every non-Muslim seeks to persecute believers. **[Study Quran]** The verse speaks about those who wage hostility and try to compel apostasy, as the surrounding account makes clear. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The final statement concerns a person who turns away from the religion and “dies a disbeliever.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The wording specifies the end condition: it speaks of apostasy followed by death in disbelief, and links that outcome with the loss of deeds in this life and the Hereafter and abiding in the Fire. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī records juristic disagreement about when deeds are nullified and whether a person who returns to faith regains the reward of earlier acts. **[Qurṭubī]** That legal debate is distinct from the verse’s explicit warning about dying in disbelief. **[Study Quran]** Here the passage describes an eschatological consequence; it does not itself set out a worldly penalty or a procedure for judging another person’s faith. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ṭabarī]**

Commentators also disagree about the later legal status of fighting in sacred months. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī and the majority position reported by al-Qurṭubī treat the prohibition as abrogated by later permission to fight, while al-Qurṭubī records ʿAṭāʾ’s view that the restriction remains. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Saʿdī says that many scholars considered the ruling abrogated, whereas Maʿārif preserves the view that initiating hostilities in those months remains prohibited while defense against attack is permitted. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** These are later legal readings of the sacred-month rule, not disagreements over the verse’s acknowledgement that the act under discussion was grave. **[Study Quran]**

The verse also refuses to let a legal question obscure the injustice of barring people from the Sanctuary and expelling its inhabitants. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Sacred Mosque was a place of worship, but access to it had been used as an instrument of political and religious exclusion. **[Study Quran]** The text names both the obstruction of the road to God and the forced removal of the people who worshipped there, making the harm public and concrete rather than merely theoretical. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The reply’s balance is deliberate: “fighting in it is grave” preserves the seriousness of the sacred-month question, while the list of obstruction, disbelief, exclusion, and expulsion prevents the debate from being used to hide the larger injustice. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The historical reports explain why the expedition was controversial, but their disagreement over date and orders cautions against building a detailed legal rule on one narrative alone. **[Study Quran]** The next verse’s reassurance that the believers may hope for mercy connects the legal dispute to spiritual accountability and hope, without declaring every detail of the episode beyond question. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Interpretive note.** Reports about Nakhlah differ on dates and details, and the commentators also differ over whether the sacred-month prohibition was later abrogated or remains in some form. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse itself acknowledges the gravity of fighting in the month while condemning disbelief, obstruction, exclusion, expulsion, and persecution as graver. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The passage challenges selective condemnation: a society cannot credibly claim to defend sacred limits while ignoring coercion, exclusion from worship, and the expulsion of a community. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** Its warning about dying in disbelief also directs the reader toward accountability before God, not toward hasty judgments about individuals. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

## 2:218

218218
*“Truly, those who believe, those who emigrate, and strive in God’s way—it is they who hope for God’s mercy. God is Forgiving, Merciful.”*

**Meaning.** This verse follows the account of the expedition at Nakhlah and addresses the believers associated with it, who feared that they might lose the reward of their actions because of the dispute over fighting in a sacred month. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī reports that they wondered whether they would receive a reward for the migration and effort they had already undertaken; the verse reassures them that those who believe, emigrate, and strive may hope for God’s mercy. **[Ṭabarī]** The immediate reassurance gives the verse historical force, while the three descriptions also make it relevant to believers beyond that party. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The sequence begins with faith, the root orientation that gives the other actions their religious purpose. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Migration means leaving a place, security, or property for God’s sake when remaining would obstruct obedience; in the first community it included leaving Makkah for Madinah and bearing separation from familiar people and homes. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī treats migration more generally as moving away from what prevents religious practice, so the word’s lesson is not confined to one historical route. **[Qurṭubī]**

“Strive in God’s way” completes the list with committed effort directed toward God’s cause. **[Ṭabarī]** In this setting it includes the struggle of the early Muslim community, including the expedition just discussed, but the phrase is not reducible to one military event. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The commentators explain striving as exertion in obedience and support of the religion; al-Saʿdī emphasizes that it entails doing what is within one’s ability for God’s sake. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse names belief, migration, and striving together, showing that faith is lived through choices and sacrifices, not merely claimed. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]**

The repeated “those who” gives the three qualities weight and distinguishes the group whose hope is being affirmed. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The verse does not say that the people named have earned mercy as a debt. It says that they “hope” for it. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Qurṭubī explains that believers combine hope with fear and do not presume that their deeds compel God to accept them. **[Qurṭubī]** As-Saʿdī makes a related distinction: these acts are means and causes for hoping in mercy, but a person must neither abandon action in the name of hope nor imagine that action alone makes God’s generosity unnecessary. **[Saʿdī]**

That balance matters because the verse could otherwise be misread in opposite directions. **[Saʿdī]** One error would be to treat God’s mercy as automatic and conclude that no effort is needed; another would be to treat migration and striving as a price that places God under an obligation to reward. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The wording rejects both presumption and despair: the faithful act, then look to God’s mercy. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī reads the clause as hope for God’s reward and forgiveness, not as certainty claimed independently of divine grace. **[Ṭabarī]**

The ending names God as *Ghafūr* and *Raḥīm*, “Forgiving, Merciful.” **[Jalālayn]** The names meet the situation of believers who may fear that an error or disputed action has erased every good deed. **[Ṭabarī]** God’s forgiveness can cover faults, while His mercy includes reward, support, and compassion beyond what a servant can claim. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif stresses that the divine attributes answer the preceding call to hope: people are not directed to rely on their own perfection, but to turn toward the One whose forgiveness and mercy are vast. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The commentators relate the verse closely to 2:217: it consoles those anxious after the Nakhlah incident and assures them that their belief, emigration, and prior striving have not become meaningless. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī likewise presents it as an answer to their concern about reward. **[Ṭabarī]** The historical setting should not be used to decide details that the sources themselves report differently; the point of the reassurance is clear even where the narrative chronology varies. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The wording also prevents the verse from being read as an endorsement of every action done in the name of striving. **[Saʿdī]** Its three descriptions begin with belief and culminate in striving “in God’s way”; the direction and moral character of the effort matter. **[Qurṭubī]** The clause therefore cannot be separated from the revealed guidance that defines the path, from the ethical obligations of faith, or from the accountability described in the preceding verse. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The three descriptions also prevent a purely inward reading of the reassurance. **[Ṭabarī]** Faith is named first, while migration and striving show the practical cost that commitment could entail in the first Muslim community. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** At the same time, the verse describes a group whose circumstances included leaving home and undertaking struggle; it is not a formula for measuring every believer by whether they have personally experienced the same historical events. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Its continuing invitation is to make faith active in the circumstances one actually faces, and to place the hoped-for outcome in God’s mercy rather than in a comparison of sacrifices. **[Saʿdī]**

**Interpretive note.** The verse’s immediate referent is commonly connected with the group involved in the Nakhlah episode, but its description of believers, emigrants, and those who strive gives the reassurance a broader application. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** “Hope” is not a guarantee that deeds create entitlement; the commentators frame it as a faithful expectation joined to humility and continued effort. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** Faith becomes visible in what a person is willing to leave, bear, and do for God, but even costly service is held within the larger reality of divine mercy. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse invites neither self-congratulation nor despair: act sincerely, seek God’s forgiveness, and hope in the compassion named at its close. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

## 2:219

219219
*“They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, ‘In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.’ They ask you what they should spend. Say, ‘The surplus.’ Thus God makes clear His signs to you, that you may reflect on this world and the Hereafter.”*

**Meaning.** This verse answers two questions, first about wine and *maysir*, then about the amount to spend in charity. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Maʿārif notes the change in subject: the first question asks about intoxicants and gambling, while the next concerns giving. **[Maʿārif]** The two answers share a moral concern with how people use their resources, judgment, and attention in the present life. **[Study Quran]**

Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī explain *khamr* through its covering or overpowering the mind. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The word is associated in early usage with fermented grape drink, but the commentators also discuss the wider rule for intoxicating drinks. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Saʿdī gives a functional description: anything that veils or impairs reason falls within the concern of the verse. **[Saʿdī]** The discussion is therefore about the loss of judgment caused by intoxication, not simply the name or source of one beverage. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]**

*Maysir* is commonly explained as gambling, with its name associated with acquiring a share or gain with little effort. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The historical form often described involved dividing a camel into shares by lots: winners received portions, and those who drew losing shares bore the cost. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Wealth might also be distributed to the poor, giving the practice an appearance of generosity, but this did not remove the wager or the transfer of property by chance. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators extend the central concern beyond that particular camel custom to games and arrangements involving stakes. **[Saʿdī]**

The precise boundary of *maysir* is discussed in different ways. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī records a broad category of gambling and also opinions that include games such as dice or chess, even where money is not staked. **[Qurṭubī]** Saʿdī focuses on contests in which participants wager against one another, while the Study Quran distinguishes gambling with stakes from idle games that many jurists disapprove of without classifying them as technically forbidden in the same way. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** These differences matter: the verse directly condemns the great sin in wine and gambling, but the commentators do not all treat every pastime without a stake as identical to a wager. **[Maʿārif]**

The verse openly acknowledges “benefits for people” before judging that the sin is greater. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators mention commercial profit, pleasure, appetite, physical warmth, winnings, and the distribution of meat or money among people. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī gives special weight to the price or gain obtained from wine and to the enjoyment people found in it. **[Ṭabarī]** The list describes perceived or material advantages; it does not endorse the medical claims sometimes repeated about alcohol or turn the practice into a net social good. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The harms outweigh those benefits because intoxication impairs reason, distracts from remembrance and worship, and can bring hostility, quarrels, injury, and financial loss. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Gambling likewise transfers wealth through chance and rivalry, can foster resentment between winner and loser, and keeps people preoccupied with the hope of gain. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Maʿārif stresses that a small or immediate advantage should not conceal wider harms to individuals, households, and society. **[Maʿārif]** The verse’s comparative form takes the attractions seriously but refuses to let them settle the moral question. **[Study Quran]**

The commentators commonly place 2:219 within the gradual clarification of the ruling on wine. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** It identifies great sin and says the harms exceed the benefits; 4:43 then restricts approaching prayer while intoxicated; 5:90–91 gives the explicit command to avoid intoxicants and gambling. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī distinguishes the present verse’s initial censure from the later, explicit prohibition. **[Ṭabarī]** The reports about the exact sequence and occasions vary, so the staged legal development is more secure than any single detailed anecdote. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The second question, “what should they spend?”, receives the word *al-ʿafw*. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī reviews interpretations including the surplus beyond basic needs, an easy amount, the best of one’s wealth, or an obligatory due; he prefers the surplus as guidance for voluntary spending, not a fixed zakāh rate. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī and the Study Quran record disagreement over whether the directive is obligatory, recommended, or later superseded by the rules of almsgiving. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Maʿārif reads it as giving from what remains after a person’s and family’s needs, without making the charity a source of preventable hardship. **[Maʿārif]**

The connection with 2:215 is instructive: the earlier verse names whom to support, and this verse addresses the amount. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** “Surplus” is not a single mathematical amount that applies to every household. **[Ṭabarī]** The sources stress provision for oneself and dependents, personal means, and the voluntary character of the guidance; Saʿdī also notes that the broader ethic of generosity can include modest acts of kindness. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** This is not a license to neglect obligations or to treat a private interpretation of surplus as a substitute for legally prescribed zakāh. **[Maʿārif]**

The verse closes by inviting reflection on “this world and the Hereafter.” **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** Wine and gambling can promise quick pleasure or gain in the present, while charity gives up part of one’s resources for the good of others and for lasting reward. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī reads the ending as an invitation to compare the transient world with the abiding life to come. **[Ṭabarī]** The question is not whether the world contains any benefit, but whether short-lived returns should outweigh harms and obligations whose consequences extend beyond the moment. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources agree on the verse’s moral comparison but differ over the range of games included in *maysir*, the force of the initial wording on wine, and whether *al-ʿafw* was voluntary or later displaced by zakāh. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The common reading treats the verse as an early stage in the prohibition of intoxicants and as continuing ethical guidance on voluntary giving. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** The verse trains the reader to compare benefits with costs rather than letting immediate pleasure, profit, or social habit decide what is good. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** It also connects restraint with generosity: what one refuses to consume or gamble away can remain available to meet the needs of relatives and vulnerable people. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ṭabarī]**

## 2:220

220220
*“They ask you about orphans. Say, ‘Setting their affairs aright is best. If you mingle with them, they are your brothers.’ God knows the one who corrupts from the one who sets things right. Had God willed, He would have made matters difficult for you. Truly God is Mighty, Wise.”*

**Meaning.** The verse’s question about orphans follows the warning against consuming their property unjustly, especially the warning in 4:10. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās describe guardians who became so cautious that they separated an orphan’s food, drink, and utensils from their own. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Leftover food might spoil, and the separation could make everyday care difficult for both the child and the guardian. **[Maʿārif]** Other reports say that avoiding orphans at meals was already a custom among Arabs because people feared the danger of mishandling an orphan’s property. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

“Setting their affairs aright is best” establishes the purpose that governs a guardian’s conduct. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** *Iṣlāḥ* includes protecting the orphan’s property, managing it prudently, and attending to the child’s welfare rather than allowing assets to decay through fearful neglect. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Saʿdī explains that guardians may trade with the property or take practical steps to preserve it, provided the aim and result are beneficial to the orphan. **[Saʿdī]** The verse does not replace the earlier prohibition against consuming orphan wealth; it identifies care and repair—not withdrawal or appropriation—as the governing standard. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The permission to “mingle with them” addresses shared life and shared expenses. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī includes mixing food, drink, housing, service, and other daily arrangements; al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr also discuss a guardian’s mixing the orphan’s food with the household’s. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The point is not that the orphan’s property becomes the guardian’s, but that the child need not be excluded from ordinary care merely because exact separation is difficult. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

“They are your brothers” places that permission within kinship and ethical solidarity. **[Jalālayn]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that orphans remain the believers’ brothers whether or not their funds are mingled; the phrase gives a reason for fair, close treatment rather than making the relationship conditional on sharing property. **[Ṭabarī]** The image of brotherhood counters both exploitation and cold isolation. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** It also clarifies that the objective is not to maintain a rigid barrier between a child and the household responsible for care, but to sustain the child as a member of the community. **[Saʿdī]**

The permission is bounded by the next clause: “God knows the one who corrupts from the one who sets things right.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** A guardian may share expenses in good faith, but cannot use the allowance as cover for taking what belongs to the orphan. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Saʿdī explains that a person who intends the orphan’s benefit is not blamed for a small incidental imbalance that arises in normal shared use, whereas a person who deliberately mixes funds in order to consume the orphan’s share is culpable. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The contrast makes intention central without treating intention as a substitute for responsible accounting or fair dealing. **[Study Quran]**

Al-Qurṭubī develops the legal implications at length: guardians may undertake transactions and investments when they serve the orphan’s interest, but jurists differ over dealings in which the guardian has a personal stake, such as buying the orphan’s property for himself. **[Qurṭubī]** *(digression)* His discussion is a record of legal disagreement, not a single rule stated in this verse. It illustrates why a fiduciary should avoid conflicts of interest or use transparent procedures where they can arise. **[Qurṭubī]** The broad principle is to favor the orphan’s welfare and guard against suspicion and abuse. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

“Had God willed, He would have made matters difficult for you” explains the mercy in the permission. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** A strict demand that every meal and expense remain entirely separate could impose hardship and, paradoxically, harm the child by preventing ordinary companionship and care. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī glosses *aʿnatakum* as imposing an exhausting burden through a prohibition on mixing; al-Qurṭubī gives related senses of hardship, constriction, or difficulty. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The dispensation does not lower the ethical standard; it replaces an impractical form of caution with a more demanding standard of honest stewardship. **[Saʿdī]**

The closing names, “Mighty, Wise,” hold power and wisdom together. **[Jalālayn]** God could impose strict rules and hold people accountable for failure, but in wisdom He permits a workable form of shared care while warning that He knows the difference between corruption and reform. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī emphasizes that divine power is not restricted, while al-Saʿdī notes that the ease of the law is itself an expression of wisdom and mercy. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

In a shared household, food and service do not always divide into perfectly measurable portions, and a rigid demand for exact separation can harm the child it is meant to protect. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** The permission therefore supports practical care—sharing meals, shelter, or ordinary household arrangements—while leaving the guardian responsible for a fair estimate of what the orphan’s property contributes. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Convenience cannot be used to conceal a pattern of taking more than the child’s benefit requires. **[Saʿdī]** The verse’s appeal to God’s knowledge gives the guardian both reassurance when honest judgment is imperfect and a warning against treating uncertainty as an excuse for exploitation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]**

**Interpretive note.** The historical reports differ on whether the immediate problem arose from excessive separation after warnings about orphan property or from a prior custom of avoiding orphans. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The jurists also debate particular transactions, but the verse’s standard remains the same: preserve the orphan’s welfare, allow reasonable shared care, and distinguish honest management from self-serving appropriation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** Ethical caution should protect vulnerable people without turning care into neglect or exclusion. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The guardian is trusted with practical judgment, but that trust is answerable to God, whose knowledge reaches both the outward transaction and its purpose. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse joins compassion and accountability: the orphan is a brother to be welcomed into ordinary life, and the orphan’s property remains a trust to be handled justly. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]**
## 2:221

221221
*“Do not marry idolatrous women until they believe. A believing enslaved woman is better than an idolatrous woman, even though she pleases you. And do not give believing women in marriage to idolatrous men until they believe. A believing enslaved man is better than an idolatrous man, even though he pleases you. They invite to the Fire, while God invites to the Garden and forgiveness by His leave. He makes His signs clear to people, that they may remember.”*

**Meaning.** The verse addresses both sides of marriage: Muslim men are not to marry women who remain in idolatry, and Muslim guardians are not to marry believing women to idolatrous men. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The second prohibition is stated as an instruction not to “marry off” believing women, and al-Qurṭubī reads it as a prohibition on a Muslim woman’s marriage to a polytheist man, a point he says the community accepted. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse thus places faith, not merely attraction or family preference, at the center of a marriage whose intimacy will shape a shared home. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

Its striking comparison is that a believing bondwoman is better than an idolatrous free woman, and a believing enslaved man better than an impressive polytheist. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The wording confronts the pull of outward rank: people might be attracted to beauty, wealth, lineage, or social standing, yet none of these can outweigh the religious commitment that the verse names as decisive. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Saʿdī makes the comparison vivid by saying that a believing woman remains better even if her appearance is modest, while a polytheist’s beauty does not make her the better choice. **[Saʿdī]** The same principle applies to a man whose wealth or good looks might otherwise impress a prospective family. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The contrast is not a praise of enslavement; it overturns a social ranking that would put status above faith. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The word *mushrikāt* is discussed in relation to women of the People of the Book. **[Ṭabarī]** Many commentators understand the permission in 5:5 for Muslim men to marry chaste Jewish or Christian women as specifying that they are not included in the prohibition here; others describe it as an exception or partial abrogation of a general rule. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The difference concerns how the two verses relate, not the commonly stated legal outcome: the Qur’an’s permission in 5:5 remains part of the discussion, and the present verse forbids marriage to women who fall under its prohibition. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī treats the prohibited women as polytheists other than the People of the Book, while al-Qurṭubī records both the “distinct categories” reading and the reading that 5:5 specifies a general prohibition. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif likewise discusses the scope of *mushrik* and the People of the Book, though its lengthy contemporary political digression is not needed to explain the verse. **[Maʿārif]**

The permission for a Muslim man to marry a chaste woman of the Book does not reverse the prohibition on a Muslim woman marrying a non-Muslim man. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī cites the related ruling in 60:10 and treats the verse’s second half as addressing Muslim women’s marriage to polytheists. **[Qurṭubī]** These clauses therefore do not establish an unrestricted permission for interfaith marriage; the commentators distinguish the direction and category of each ruling. **[Ṭabarī]** Some jurists also discouraged or restricted a Muslim man’s marriage to a woman of the Book in practice, despite recognizing the scriptural permission. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī reports that ʿUmar asked Ḥudhayfah to release his Jewish wife, not because he declared such a marriage unlawful, but because he feared that men would imitate it indiscriminately and neglect Muslim women. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The report preserves a distinction between the legal category and a leader’s prudential counsel about its consequences. **[Maʿārif]**

The reason given—“they invite to the Fire”—explains the seriousness of marriage across the prohibited boundary. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators understand “inviting” as more than a formal argument: a spouse’s words, habits, worship, and example can influence the religious life of the household and the formation of children. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr describes the danger as attachment to this life and preference for it over the Hereafter; Saʿdī says that close association can place faith at risk. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Read in context, this is a theological account of the direction of the beliefs at issue, not a claim that every individual of another faith deliberately seeks to harm a Muslim. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse’s concern is the formative closeness of marriage, not casual contact or hostility toward neighbors. **[Qurṭubī]**

By contrast, “God invites to the Garden and forgiveness by His leave.” **[Jalālayn]** The invitation comes through revelation: God makes clear what leads toward forgiveness and the Garden, and the prophets communicate that guidance. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** The phrase “by His leave” is explained as God’s command or will; it also keeps the promised outcome grounded in divine grace rather than human entitlement. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The final clause says that God clarifies His signs so people may remember: the prohibition is not meant to obscure the path but to make its moral consequences intelligible. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

*(digression)* Al-Saʿdī and al-Qurṭubī also cite “do not marry off” as evidence that a marriage guardian (*walī*) has a role. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī records a substantial juristic disagreement: many authorities require a guardian for the contract, whereas Ḥanafī jurists allow an adult woman to contract her own marriage under specified conditions. **[Qurṭubī]** This is a legal inference developed from the wording and other reports, not the verse’s only or primary subject; it should not be confused with the prohibition against marrying a polytheist. **[Qurṭubī]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources differ on whether the People of the Book are outside the term *mushrikāt* from the outset or are excepted by 5:5, and they preserve disagreement over how strongly to discourage a marriage that the Qur’an permits. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** They converge on the verse’s core contrast: beauty, wealth, and status do not displace belief as the criterion named here, and a believing woman is not to be given in marriage to a polytheist man. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks readers to examine what they treat as impressive in a prospective spouse and in their own community. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Its comparisons challenge status-consciousness, while its closing promise directs attention to the guidance by which God calls people toward forgiveness and lasting good. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:222

222222
*“They ask you about menstruation. Say, ‘It is a hurt, so keep away from women during menstruation and do not approach them until they are purified. When they have purified themselves, then come to them as God has commanded you.’ Truly God loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves.”*

**Meaning.** The question is answered with a practical boundary: menstruation is described as *adha*, “hurt” or “harm,” and vaginal intercourse is forbidden while menstrual bleeding continues. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The commentators explain *adha* in several related ways—as the blood itself, the discomfort it may cause, or its impurity for ritual purposes. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The word does not make a menstruating woman morally blameworthy or socially untouchable; the restriction concerns a particular act during a bodily state. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

Reports about the question’s setting describe communities in which menstruating women were avoided at meals or in shared sleeping spaces. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** A report from Anas says that the Prophet’s Companions asked after seeing Jewish practice, and that the Prophet responded that ordinary contact could continue apart from intercourse. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran notes that local customs may have been influenced by Jewish or Zoroastrian prescriptions, but the verse itself does not establish the history of that influence. **[Study Quran]** What is clear in the commentaries is the contrast between a sweeping social separation and the narrower rule the Qur’an states. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

“Keep away from women during menstruation” is interpreted by al-Ṭabarī as keeping away from sexual intercourse, not abandoning a wife or excluding her from family life. **[Ṭabarī]** The Prophet is reported to have said, “Do everything except intercourse,” and reports describe him eating with his wives, resting beside them, and showing affection while they menstruated. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** These accounts show why the phrase cannot be read as a command to shun all touch or companionship. **[Study Quran]** The verse marks a limit on intercourse while preserving ordinary marital closeness. **[Maʿārif]**

The commentators differ over how cautious a couple should be about physical contact near the site of bleeding. **[Ṭabarī]** Some reports permit all affection outside the vaginal opening; other jurists recommend that the woman wear a waist-wrapper and avoid contact with the area between navel and knee, following reports of the Prophet’s practice. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr likewise transmits both the general allowance of affection and reports in which a covering was used. **[Ibn Kathīr]** These are differences in the scope of precaution, not disagreement over the prohibition of vaginal intercourse during menstruation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

The two phrases translated “until they are purified” and “when they have purified themselves” are read together. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī prefers the reading that signals washing after the blood stops, and al-Qurṭubī argues that the permission to resume intercourse follows both cessation of bleeding and ritual bathing. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr likewise says that bathing—or dry ablution when water cannot be used—is required before intercourse. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The juristic record is not entirely uniform: al-Qurṭubī describes differing readings of the verb and reports a Ḥanafī position that allows intercourse after the maximum menstrual period has ended even before bathing, while the Study Quran notes a related school difference. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** These legal details should be distinguished from the verse’s shared premise that intercourse is barred during active menstruation. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that the lighter and doubled forms of the Arabic verb foreground different stages—bleeding coming to an end and ritual washing—and explains how jurists draw on both readings. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī adds that “then come to them” lifts the earlier prohibition; it is permission to resume intercourse, not a command that a couple must do so. **[Ṭabarī]** The wording therefore sets a condition for what is lawful; it does not command anyone to resume intercourse.

“When they have purified themselves, come to them as God has commanded you” also restricts the place of intercourse. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī records interpretations that refer either to the proper site—the vagina—or to the proper state of purity, and he emphasizes that the latter clause does not license an act prohibited at all times. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr likewise understand it as directing intercourse to the lawful site, not the anus. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** This reading links 2:222 to the following verse’s image of a “tilth”: permission returns within the limits that the text sets, rather than becoming unrestricted. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The closing says that God loves those who repent and those who purify themselves. **[Jalālayn]** The first expression includes turning back after sin; the second includes ritual washing, while al-Saʿdī also draws out moral cleansing from blameworthy conduct and character. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī records interpretations of purification from bodily impurity, from sin, and from prohibited sexual conduct. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse therefore places bodily discipline within a wider ethic of repentance: an involuntary cycle is not a moral fault, but the faithful response to God’s boundaries is a matter of choice. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

*(digression)* The jurists also ask whether intercourse during menstruation, if it occurs, requires a payment in addition to repentance. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī reports that Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Abū Ḥanīfah require seeking God’s forgiveness but do not make a payment obligatory; other reports recommend giving a dinar or half a dinar in charity. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran similarly distinguishes the absence of a formal expiation from reports that mention charity, while Maʿārif emphasizes sincere repentance if the boundary is violated unknowingly or carelessly. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** This is a question about the consequence of a violation, not a reason to confuse menstrual status with moral fault. **[Qurṭubī]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources agree on the ban on vaginal intercourse during menstruation and on the allowance of other forms of companionship, while differing over the recommended zone of physical caution and the legal effect of bleeding’s cessation before ritual bathing. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Qur’anic term *adha* describes a condition and its effects; it should not be turned into a stigma against the person experiencing it. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse combines a clear boundary with a refusal to turn a bodily condition into social exclusion. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** Its closing joins repentance and purification, reminding readers that physical practice and moral return both belong to a life lived with attention to God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

## 2:223

223223
*“Your wives are a tilth for you, so come to your tilth as you will, and send forth for yourselves. Be mindful of God, and know that you will meet Him; and give good tidings to the believers.”*

**Meaning.** The verse continues the discussion of lawful intimacy by using the image of *ḥarth*, cultivated land or a field. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The commentators understand the metaphor as referring to the site from which children may be conceived; it explains the permissive image without erasing the boundary already set in 2:222. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif stresses that the image connects sexual relations with the possibility of progeny, while the Study Quran notes that commentators use it to explain the verse’s focus on where intercourse occurs. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The metaphor is therefore not an unlimited permission to use any bodily site: the “tilth” identifies the place to which the permission applies. **[Saʿdī]**

The phrase “come to your tilth as you will” allows variation in position and direction of approach, provided intercourse remains vaginal. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The exegetes explain that a couple may approach from the front or from behind, lying, sitting, or in another posture; “from behind” in this discussion means entering the vagina from behind, not anal intercourse. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** This distinction is central because reports about differing customs in Madinah could otherwise be misunderstood as expanding the verse beyond the site named by *ḥarth*. **[Study Quran]**

Several reports connect the revelation with disagreements between Emigrants and Helpers about customary positions. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** One well-known report from Jābir says that some Jews claimed that intercourse from behind, while still vaginal, would make a child cross-eyed; the verse answered that the manner of approach could vary. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The report preserves the claim as a belief attributed to others, not as a medical fact endorsed by the Qur’an. **[Ṭabarī]** The Study Quran notes that reports give different accounts of the social occasion, so the broader point does not depend on one reconstructed conversation. **[Study Quran]** The reports are historical explanations offered by exegetes; the ruling follows from the verse’s own language and its placement beside the restrictions in 2:222. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** That distinction lets the reader benefit from the context without treating every detail in a transmitted account as equally certain. **[Study Quran]**

The word *annā* is variously glossed as “how,” “from where,” or, in some reports, “when.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī surveys these readings and prefers the sense “from which direction,” arguing from Arabic usage and from the word *ḥarth* that the verse concerns the direction of approach to the place of conception. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī similarly understands the mainstream interpretation as allowing different approaches to the same lawful site. **[Qurṭubī]** Thus the phrase widens the range of position, not the range of locations; “as you will” cannot be isolated from “your tilth.” **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]**

*(digression)* Al-Ṭabarī preserves reports attributed to Ibn ʿUmar that appear to read the permission more broadly, alongside reports and explanations that reject that inference. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records that some early figures were named in permissive attributions, but notes that Nāfiʿ denied the claim about Ibn ʿUmar and that Mālik strongly rejected the attribution to himself. **[Qurṭubī]** Both commentators ultimately argue that “tilth” and the prophetic reports restrict the permission to vaginal intercourse; al-Qurṭubī describes that as the sound position. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The disagreement is worth recording because the sources discuss it, but it should not obscure their stated conclusion or turn a disputed report into the verse’s plain meaning. **[Study Quran]**

“Send forth for yourselves” is explained first as preparing good deeds for the Hereafter. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī prefers this broad sense because the phrase is followed by the command to fear God and remember the coming meeting with Him. **[Ṭabarī]** Other commentators also mention saying “In the name of God” before intercourse, hoping for righteous children, or seeking reward by fulfilling marital relations lawfully. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** These readings need not compete: lawful intimacy can be accompanied by remembrance, intention, and hope for a good family, while the verse’s broad wording still calls for righteous preparation in every part of life. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

“Be mindful of God, and know that you will meet Him” places the permission within accountability. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse does not present desire as exempt from moral limits; its instruction to remember God follows the permission and guards against treating that permission as a license to disregard the boundaries of the preceding verses. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The rule about menstruation in 2:222 and the word *ḥarth* here together frame the permission; neither can be detached from the other. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran cautions that the commentators’ debate here concerns the place and direction of intercourse; *annā* should not be made to answer every separate question about marital conduct or timing. **[Study Quran]** The command to fear God therefore keeps private conduct within the same moral accountability as public acts. **[Ṭabarī]**
