The final command, “give good tidings to the believers,” is read as reassurance for those who obey God and trust His promise. **[Jalālayn]** Al-Saʿdī takes the glad tidings broadly, encompassing good in this life and the next, while al-Ṭabarī describes believers as those whose faith is expressed in obedience and avoidance of what God forbids. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse thus moves from lawful enjoyment to moral preparation, accountability, and hope. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources give different background reports and discuss more than one possible gloss of *annā*, but they distinguish freedom of posture from permission to use any site. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The majority interpretation presented in these commentaries confines the sexual permission to the vagina and excludes intercourse during menstruation as explained in 2:222. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse refuses to set spiritual seriousness against married life: it permits lawful intimacy while placing it alongside remembrance, fear of God, and preparation for the Hereafter. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Its limits are as important as its permission, and its image of cultivation makes the hope for future life inseparable from responsibility in the present. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:224

224224
*“Do not make God, by your oaths, an obstacle to your being righteous, reverent, and making peace among people. God is Hearing, Knowing.”*

**Meaning.** The verse warns against turning an oath in God’s name into a barrier to doing what is right. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The expression translated “an obstacle” is understood as making God’s name or one’s oath a pretext for refusing an act of goodness: someone swears not to give charity, visit a relative, fulfill an obligation, or help settle a dispute, then treats the oath as if it excuses the refusal. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The rebuke is not that every oath is forbidden, but that invoking God must not be used to block a duty or a good action that God approves. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The three examples—righteousness, reverence, and peacemaking—span both personal devotion and social responsibility. **[Ṭabarī]** *Birr* includes good works and dutiful conduct; *taqwā* includes guarding oneself from sin; and *iṣlāḥ* includes reconciliation between people whose conflict has ruptured relationships. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The phrase is therefore not limited to one kind of dispute or one act of charity. **[Ibn Kathīr]** If a person’s vow would keep them from maintaining family ties, supporting someone in need, or helping two people reconcile, the vow should not become a permanent excuse to persist in the harm. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

Al-Ṭabarī reads the construction as a warning not to let oaths stand between people and obedience to God. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records several explanations of the word *ʿurḍatan*, including an obstacle or something put forward as an excuse, and notes more than one reported setting for the verse. **[Qurṭubī]** Reports associate it with oaths not to support a relative or to reconcile with someone after a painful disagreement, but they differ in their details. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The general command does not depend on establishing one particular occasion: whatever the immediate setting, a self-imposed oath cannot convert the abandonment of goodness into piety. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

The next verse distinguishes careless or unintended oath-language from what the heart deliberately intends, while this verse addresses a commitment that is being used to refuse good. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The distinction matters: not every utterance has the force of an intentional pledge, but neither should a person invoke a pledge to avoid a higher obligation. **[Study Quran]** A sincere oath does not make the wrong course right merely because the speaker used God’s name. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ṭabarī]**

Al-Saʿdī draws out how the response depends on what the oath blocks. **[Saʿdī]** If keeping it would mean abandoning an obligation, the obligation takes precedence; if it would prevent a recommended good, breaking it for that good is better. **[Saʿdī]** If the oath commits one to a forbidden act, it must not be fulfilled; where it concerns a disliked act, leaving it may be better; and where it concerns an otherwise neutral matter, keeping the oath may remain appropriate. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** This framework explains why the verse does not simply say “keep every oath” or “break every oath”: the ethical weight of the promised act matters. **[Study Quran]** It also prevents an oath from becoming a tool for coercing relatives, avoiding generosity, or prolonging enmity. **[Maʿārif]**

Breaking an oath in order to do what is better is not treated as a license to disregard commitments without consequence. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The commentators connect the expiation for a broken oath to 5:89, where the Qur’an specifies feeding or clothing the needy, freeing a slave, or fasting when unable to do the first options. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The practical lesson is to make the better choice, repair the effects of one’s oath, and not repeat the misuse of God’s name. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

“God is Hearing, Knowing” closes the warning by joining the spoken wording of an oath to the intention behind it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** God hears what is uttered and knows whether the speaker seeks obedience, avoidance of responsibility, or harm to another person. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** An oath is not a hidden loophole: even if people accept it as a reason for refusing help, its purpose and consequences are not hidden from God. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse calls believers to value reconciliation and goodness more than the prestige of appearing consistent with a rash pledge. **[Saʿdī]** Its correction protects both the person who swore and those who would suffer if the oath were used to sustain a needless rupture. **[Qurṭubī]**

Al-Qurṭubī also preserves a reading that cautions against making God the object of frequent oaths. **[Qurṭubī]** This can sit alongside the main explanation: careless oath-making makes sacred language cheap, while a deliberately invoked oath becomes especially troubling when used to block a good action. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse therefore addresses both the speaker’s habit and the oath’s effect, without reducing its command to a ban on swearing. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The instruction to seek reconciliation is especially significant because a dispute can tempt people to turn a moment of anger into a lasting rule. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** A person might vow never to speak to a relative, never to return to someone who caused offense, or never to help a neighbor again. **[Study Quran]** The verse directs the believer to ask what God regards as righteous now, rather than to let yesterday’s anger determine whether today’s repair is possible. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ṭabarī]** This does not require entering an unjust or harmful situation; it prevents the oath itself from being treated as proof that refusing every form of repair is virtuous. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks whether a promise is serving integrity or merely shielding a person from a good deed. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** When a vow stands in the way of charity, duty, or reconciliation, fidelity to God is not measured by stubbornly preserving the wording; it is shown by turning toward the better act and making amends. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:225

225225
*“God will not take you to task for thoughtless speech in your oaths, but He will take you to task for what your hearts have earned. God is Forgiving, Forbearing.”*

**Meaning.** This verse qualifies the warning about oaths by distinguishing *laghw al-aymān*, idle or unintended oath-speech, from what a person deliberately means and earns inwardly. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The commentators do not give a single narrow definition of *laghw*: it can refer to habitual phrases such as “By God” uttered without intending a binding oath, to an assertion a speaker honestly believes true but that proves mistaken, or to speech produced in joking or argument. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran records these differing explanations, while Maʿārif likewise distinguishes ordinary slips from deliberate commitments. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

These examples share an absence of deliberate intent to bind oneself or to lie. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]** A person who says “no, by God” or “yes, by God” as a conversational habit may not be making a considered pledge about future conduct. **[Ibn Kathīr]** An honest statement based on a mistaken belief is also different from knowingly swearing to a falsehood. **[Qurṭubī]** Some reports include an oath spoken in anger among the meanings of *laghw*, but that is not the only view and should not be presented as consensus. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The point is not that every heated oath is automatically excused; the sources ask whether the words were intentional, what was intended, and whether the speaker knowingly violated truth. **[Ṭabarī]**

“What your hearts have earned” points to deliberate intention and responsibility, not merely to the sound of the words. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** A knowingly false oath about something already past is especially grave: it is not made harmless by calling it casual speech, because the speaker knows that the claim is false. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The commentators distinguish such perjury from an honest mistake and from a future-directed oath that one later breaks. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** These categories should not be collapsed into one rule: the verse’s mercy toward an unintended slip does not erase the sin of deliberate falsehood. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]**

A second distinction concerns expiation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** A deliberate oath about a future action may require expiation if it is broken; 5:89 gives the prescribed form of expiation. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** A knowingly false oath about the past is treated by the commentators as a more serious moral offense, and they report disagreement over whether the expiation prescribed for a broken future oath applies to it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** Some authorities emphasize that no material expiation can make deliberate perjury trivial; repentance and restoring any person’s rights remain essential. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse is not a detailed manual of every legal consequence, so its central contrast should remain clear: careless words are not the same as purposeful wrongdoing. **[Saʿdī]**

Read beside 2:224, the two verses prevent opposite errors. **[Study Quran]** One must not cling to an oath in order to avoid righteousness or reconciliation; nor should one invoke the exemption for *laghw* to excuse a calculated lie or a conscious breach. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** When a person intentionally undertakes a valid commitment, its moral weight is real; when the commitment blocks a better obligation, the previous verse points toward doing good and expiating the broken oath. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The relevant questions are therefore whether the words were meant as an oath, whether they were truthful, and what action the oath now prevents. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

“God is Forgiving, Forbearing” gives reassurance without making carelessness inconsequential. **[Jalālayn]** God forgives what was not deliberately earned and does not rush to punish, giving time for the one who sinned to repent and correct the wrong. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The wording also cautions a believer not to treat divine forbearance as permission to take oaths lightly. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** A person can learn to speak more carefully, seek forgiveness for deliberate wrongdoing, and discharge the expiation required for a broken oath without confusing that remedy with the more serious question of deliberate perjury. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The commentators preserve several definitions of *laghw* and differ on some consequences, especially the treatment of a knowingly false past oath. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** They agree that an unintended slip is not equivalent to what the heart deliberately intends; an honest error, an intentional future pledge, and a knowingly false oath must therefore be distinguished. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

The contrast between a broken oath and perjury deserves care. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** If someone deliberately swears about a future action and later recognizes that another course is better, 2:224 directs them not to let the oath block goodness; the expiation mentioned in 5:89 addresses that broken commitment. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** By contrast, knowingly describing a past event falsely invokes God’s name to make a lie appear credible. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** Some jurists discuss expiation for that deliberate false oath, but the sources warn against treating a payment as a substitute for repentance or for restoring the rights of anyone deceived. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The verse’s language about what the heart “has earned” also guards against policing every involuntary phrase as if it were a carefully formed vow. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The moral inquiry is into intention, knowledge, and choice: did the speaker mean to bind themself, believe the statement true, or knowingly manipulate the listener? **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The exegetes’ varied examples of *laghw* show why the same wording can have different weight in different circumstances. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** This qualification is not an invitation to claim an innocent intention after the fact, but a recognition that accountability is tied to what a person knowingly chose. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]**

**Reflection.** The verse makes sincerity more important than ritualized speech. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** Careful speech protects trust, while repentance and repair remain open to those who have spoken wrongly. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]**

## 2:226

226226
*“For those who swear to abstain from their wives is a waiting period of four months. If they return, then God is Forgiving, Merciful.”*

**Meaning.** The verse addresses *īlāʾ*: a husband’s oath that he will refrain from marital intercourse with his wife. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** It gives a fixed limit to a vow that could otherwise leave a wife in an indefinite state, neither receiving marital life nor being released to make a new one. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The exegetes describe a pre-Islamic practice in which a man could swear off his wife for a very long time, using the oath to keep her suspended; the four-month period curbs that harm. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The phrase “those who swear to abstain from their wives” defines the particular oath in view, rather than every instance of temporary distance between spouses. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The commentators discuss how long the husband must have intended to abstain for the rule to apply, whether the vow must have been made in anger or with an intention to injure, and whether an oath taken for a practical reason—such as a temporary arrangement connected to nursing—falls within the same category. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī favors the general wording, while other authorities distinguish vows by their purpose or by the length of abstention promised. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** These are legal disagreements about the scope of *īlāʾ*, not disagreement that the wife’s rights must not be indefinitely denied. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

“Four months” is the period of waiting established by the verse. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** It is not a permission to prolong the oath indefinitely, nor does the text invite husbands to use the period as a routine way to avoid marital responsibilities. **[Ṭabarī]** The legal discussions treat the waiting as protection for the wife and as a time in which the husband must face the choice between resuming marital relations and ending the marriage. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif likewise explains the limit against the background of a woman being left without the ordinary rights of marriage or a clear separation. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The words “If they return” are explained as the husband’s return to marital relations and the fulfillment of the wife’s right. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The main legal question is what form of return suffices when intercourse is impossible because of illness, travel, imprisonment, or another impediment. **[Qurṭubī]** Some authorities require actual intercourse when it is possible; others discuss whether a declared intention to resume, accompanied by testimony, may count when an excuse prevents it. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** This dispute concerns how a court or couple establishes the return; it does not turn an oath of abstention into a license to ignore the wife’s claim. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]**

The commentators also differ over the legal consequence when the four months end without return. **[Qurṭubī]** One major position holds that divorce does not occur automatically: the wife may bring the matter to an authority, who requires the husband either to return or to divorce her. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** Another position treats expiration of the period as effecting divorce. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The next verse’s wording—“if they resolve upon divorce”—is central to how exegetes weigh these positions, so the disagreement should be attributed rather than flattened into one universal procedure. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

“God is Forgiving, Merciful” accompanies the return to marital life. **[Jalālayn]** The sources connect forgiveness with the husband’s breaking of the oath when he resumes relations; many jurists require the expiation for a broken oath, while some early opinions treated the return itself as sufficient. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The difference over expiation does not soften the verse’s protection against leaving a wife in limbo. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The ending also presents reconciliation as open to mercy: a husband can return from an oath that has caused harm and resume the relationship with responsibility. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

One purpose of the deadline is to prevent the wife from being held by a private oath that she did not choose and cannot end herself. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** In the procedural view, after the period the wife may seek intervention, and the husband is required to make a real decision instead of simply waiting while she bears the consequences. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Some reports phrase this as an authority giving the husband a choice between return and divorce; al-Saʿdī likewise emphasizes the wife’s protection from harm and the obligation to resolve the situation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse gives the wife a claim to resolution, not merely an expectation that the husband will eventually change his mind. **[Study Quran]**

The opinions about the motive behind the oath affect which cases jurists classify as *īlāʾ*, but they do not erase the broader ethic of the passage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** Some commentators emphasize vows made in anger or as a means of injury; others take the wording to include any qualifying oath that prevents intercourse beyond the stated period. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** A temporary, mutually understood arrangement is not automatically identical to an oath meant to suspend a wife, though the schools differ over precise limits and exceptions. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The exegetes thus distinguish the verse’s protective function from an attempt to turn every period of marital distance into a formal divorce proceeding. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources disagree about whether *īlāʾ* is limited to vows made in anger or extends to any qualifying oath of abstention, and about whether a divorce follows automatically after four months. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** They share the core purpose of ending indefinite suspension by requiring a real choice between return and separation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** A religious vow must not be used as a shield for withholding another person’s rights. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** The four-month limit gives practical form to a moral principle: when a relationship is placed in suspension, mercy requires a timely decision and a just path forward. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:227

227227
*“But if they resolve upon divorce, then God is Hearing, Knowing.”*

**Meaning.** This verse completes the rule about *īlāʾ* begun in 2:226. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** After the four-month period, the husband’s course is not to keep his wife suspended: he returns to marital life or resolves upon divorce and carries it out. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The phrase “if they resolve upon divorce” is read by some commentators as referring to an actual decision and pronouncement, while others connect it to the legal consequences that follow the waiting period. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse therefore cannot be detached from the disagreement about whether the waiting period itself effects a divorce or whether a husband must be directed to choose. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

Al-Ṭabarī surveys early positions in which the marriage ends at the four-month mark, with some reports describing the resulting separation as one irrevocable divorce and others as a revocable one. **[Ṭabarī]** He also records the view that expiration of the period gives the wife the right to seek a decision, after which an authority requires the husband either to resume marital relations or to divorce her. **[Ṭabarī]** He prefers the latter interpretation: the verse’s mention of God hearing the divorce fits an actual spoken act, whereas the passage of time alone is not something heard. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr likewise presents the position that four months do not automatically dissolve the marriage, and al-Qurṭubī discusses the majority view that the husband must be called to return or divorce. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]**

Maʿārif presents a different legal position, under which the marriage ends irrevocably when the four months expire without return. **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran notes that exegetes disagree about whether a divorce is imposed by a judge or follows automatically after the period. **[Study Quran]** These positions should remain attributed: the verse establishes a four-month limit, but the sources do not give one unanimous account of what legal mechanism follows it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** The commentators’ shared concern is the wife’s protection from indefinite abstention, not the validation of an oath as a means to deny her rights. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The word *fayʾ* in the preceding verse is commonly understood as a return to intercourse, since the husband has sworn to abstain from that act. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Yet the legal discussions consider what happens when physical return is impossible or harmful because of illness or another excuse. **[Qurṭubī]** Some jurists require intercourse if the husband is able; others discuss an expressed intention to resume or testimony as a way of establishing the return when an impediment prevents intercourse. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** This is a juristic question about evidence and capacity, not a denial that a wife is entitled to a genuine answer after the stated period. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]**

The phrase “God is Hearing, Knowing” emphasizes that neither the husband’s spoken words nor his inward purpose is hidden. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** God hears the divorce if it is pronounced and knows whether the oath was used to cause harm, whether the husband truly intends reconciliation, and how he has treated his wife. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The wording thus gives moral weight to a decision that affects another person’s future; the issue is not merely how a technical formula is counted. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

A majority of jurists require expiation when the husband breaks the oath by returning to marital relations, because resuming what was sworn off is a breach of an oath. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Some early reports regard the return itself as sufficient, so the sources preserve a disagreement on this point as well. **[Ṭabarī]** The expiation question is distinct from the question of whether divorce occurs automatically at the end of four months; one concerns a broken oath, the other the legal status of the marriage. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The early reports about expiration itself do not even describe the resulting divorce uniformly. **[Ṭabarī]** Some call it one irrevocable divorce, while others treat it as a revocable divorce; another group insists that there is no divorce until an actual choice is made. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** This difference matters for whether a new marriage contract is needed and whether the husband can return during the waiting period, so it should not be hidden by a loose statement that “the marriage ends” after four months. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Maʿārif’s account of an automatic irrevocable divorce is one position among these transmitted legal readings, not a wording on which all commentators agree. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The verse’s two divine attributes give the decision both an audible and an inward dimension. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** A divorce is a spoken declaration that can be heard by witnesses and judged in the community, but the motive behind it—whether the husband intends an honest separation or is prolonging harm—belongs to God’s knowledge. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The passage therefore joins legal process with moral accountability: procedural disagreement does not make the wife’s distress invisible to God. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources record two major views: under one, the husband must be made to choose return or divorce after the waiting period; under another, divorce follows automatically when the period expires. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Ibn Kathīr and the Study Quran report this disagreement rather than treating the automatic-divorce view as unanimous. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** “Hearing, Knowing” turns a private vow into an accountable choice. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** A marriage may end, but neither silence nor an oath can be used to hold another person indefinitely between separation and return. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

## 2:228

228228
*“Divorced women shall wait by themselves for three courses, and it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs, if they believe in God and the Last Day. Their husbands have the better right to take them back during that period, if they desire reconciliation. Women have rights similar to their obligations, according to what is recognized as good; but men have a degree over them. God is Mighty, Wise.”*

**Meaning.** The verse sets a waiting period for divorced women who have experienced marital intercourse and continue to menstruate; the commentators distinguish them from women whose waiting period is defined by pregnancy, age, or a marriage that was not consummated. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** The word *qurūʾ* is famously interpreted in two ways: some jurists understand it as menstrual periods, while others understand it as intervals of purity between them. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī examine the Arabic usage and early reports supporting both readings; the difference affects when the third course is considered complete and when the woman is free to remarry. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran notes further juristic discussion about whether the relevant boundary is the onset or end of bleeding, or the ritual bath that follows it. **[Study Quran]**

The waiting period gives time to establish whether a pregnancy exists and prevents confusion of lineage. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** It also leaves space for reconciliation after a revocable divorce, rather than making the separation final at the moment the husband pronounces it. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse therefore combines a practical rule about time with protections for the woman, the former husband, and any child who may be born. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

“It is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs” is explained as including pregnancy and menstrual information relevant to the waiting period. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The commentators differ over which of these is the primary referent: some emphasize menstruation, others pregnancy, and some include both. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** A woman might otherwise claim that her waiting period had ended when it had not, or conceal that it had ended in order to prolong the former husband’s obligations; concealing a pregnancy could also deprive a child of the correct lineage or frustrate a lawful return. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]** These are examples of why the verse treats truthful disclosure as a trust, not as a private tactic in a conflict. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]**

Because the relevant facts are ordinarily known most directly to the woman herself, the exegetes understand her as entrusted to report them truthfully. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī cites the principle that people are not to inspect women’s bodies to verify each claim; the rule instead forbids concealment and relies on honest testimony. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The appeal “if they believe in God and the Last Day” intensifies the moral warning: accountability before God should restrain a false claim even when no witness can readily disprove it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]**

“Their husbands have the better right to take them back during that period” refers to a revocable divorce and not to a third, final separation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** During the waiting period, the husband may restore the marriage without a new contract, but the verse qualifies that right with the aim “if they desire reconciliation.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The sources agree that taking a wife back merely to injure her or prolong her waiting is forbidden; they differ over whether such a harmful return is legally effective even though sinful. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī reports that it may count in a court while remaining a sin before God, whereas al-Saʿdī argues that without a sincere intention to make things right the husband has no rightful claim to use the provision. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

“Women have rights similar to their obligations, according to what is recognized as good” establishes reciprocal duties within marriage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The commentators include good companionship, maintenance, clothing, housing, and consideration of each spouse’s needs among the matters governed by *maʿrūf*—what is recognized as decent and just under the law and sound custom. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī connects the wording to mutual protection from harm, and Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that he beautified himself for his wife as he wished her to beautify herself for him. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran also notes that some interpreters understand the verse to affirm women’s claim to marital intimacy and mutual protection, not merely a list of duties owed to husbands. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The phrase “men have a degree over them” is interpreted in more than one way. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some commentators associate the degree with responsibilities and legal roles such as financial support, household care, or the husband’s authority in the marriage; others understand Ibn ʿAbbās’s explanation as urging men to show generosity, forbearance, and readiness to relinquish some of their own claims. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī prefers the latter emphasis in this context: after affirming mutual rights, the verse calls men to fulfill what is due to women and to exercise grace rather than insist on every advantage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** Maʿārif likewise distinguishes worldly responsibility from a claim that every man is spiritually superior to every woman; it locates ultimate merit in faith and conduct. **[Maʿārif]** The closing names God as Mighty and Wise, reminding readers that these duties and distinctions are subject to divine judgment rather than personal preference. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources disagree over whether *qurūʾ* means menstrual periods or intervals of purity, and they report differing views about the legal effect of a return made with an intention to harm. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** They nevertheless frame the waiting period as a protection against uncertainty and the return as a chance for reconciliation, not a device for trapping a woman in marriage. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse makes the waiting period a time for truthfulness and considered choice, not for manipulation. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Its reminder that women have rights as well as obligations calls each spouse to measure conduct by fairness and the good recognized in their circumstances. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:229

229229
*“Divorce is twice; then retain her honorably or release her with kindness. It is not lawful for you to take anything from what you have given them, unless both fear that they cannot maintain God’s limits. If you fear that they cannot maintain God’s limits, there is no blame on either of them in what she gives to ransom herself. These are God’s limits, so do not transgress them; whoever transgresses God’s limits, those are the wrongdoers.”*

**Meaning.** “Divorce is twice” limits the repeated use of revocable divorce that had allowed a husband to take his wife back again and again as her waiting period neared its end. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse gives two occasions on which a husband may restore a marriage during the waiting period; after each, he must either retain his wife honorably or let her go without injury. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The reports describe the limit as a protection against using return and divorce to keep a woman suspended, while also leaving room for a couple to reconsider separation. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The commentators discuss whether “release with kindness” refers to letting the waiting period end after the second divorce or to a third divorce that makes the separation final. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** They agree on the basic staged structure: after a first or second revocable divorce, reconciliation remains possible; after the final divorce described in 2:230, the former husband cannot simply take the woman back. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** Retaining “honorably” means more than using a formal right to return; it calls for good companionship and an honest effort to repair the marriage. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]** Releasing “with kindness” forbids retaliation, humiliation, or withholding rights merely because the marriage has ended. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The prohibition on taking back what was given to a wife protects her property when the husband initiates divorce. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The husband may not pressure or mistreat her until she agrees to return her bridal gift or other property as the price of escaping a marriage he has chosen to end. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The exception is *khulʿ*: if the couple fear that they cannot observe the duties and limits of marriage, the wife may offer compensation to obtain separation, and there is no blame in what she gives or he accepts under that condition. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse’s exception does not authorize extortion; it is a way out when continued marriage threatens the observance of the spouses’ rights. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The phrase “both fear” receives several readings. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some exegetes require a mutual fear that the spouses will fail to uphold their obligations; others emphasize the wife’s aversion and fear that she will be unable to fulfill her husband’s rights, while some understand the following plural “if you fear” as addressing judges, relatives, or the community asked to assess the situation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī favors a concern that both parties will fail in the duties owed to one another, while recognizing that the wife’s estrangement can create the danger. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī reports that the majority permit *khulʿ* even without a prior finding of physical abuse, whereas some authorities connect it more narrowly to discord or harm. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

Commentaries associate the verse with a wife of Thābit ibn Qays who sought separation and returned his garden or bridal gift. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The reports differ in the woman’s name and in the details of the encounter, so the story illustrates the kind of case addressed without establishing one uncontested account as the sole occasion of revelation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The example shows that a wife’s serious aversion can be relevant even when she does not accuse her husband of irreligion or bad character. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

Jurists also differ over the amount that may be accepted in *khulʿ*. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Many allow the spouses to agree on compensation that may be less than, equal to, or more than the bridal gift, while other authorities restrict it to no more than what the husband gave. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Even commentators who allow a larger amount warn that it is not a license to coerce or exploit a woman; al-Ṭabarī recommends that a husband who can see she seeks release to protect her faith should separate without taking payment, and at least not take all that he gave. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The different legal positions leave the verse’s ethical floor clear: compensation is not to be extracted through harm. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

“Those are God’s limits” gathers the rules on marriage, divorce, return, and compensation into a binding moral framework. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The limits do not merely regulate a contract; they protect people from using a formal right to commit injustice. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Reports connected with the verse also condemn treating divorce as a game or using repeated declarations to defeat the staged protections of the law. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The closing names transgression as wrongdoing, making clear that legal power does not excuse a person from the duties of fairness. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]**

*(digression)* The commentators further debate whether *khulʿ* is classified as a divorce or as a dissolution, and how that classification affects the number of remaining divorces and the waiting period. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** This is a technical consequence of the verse’s ruling, not a change to its prohibition on coercive recovery of a wife’s property. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources differ over what kind of fear permits *khulʿ*, whether external arbiters are required, and how much compensation may be accepted. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** They agree that the husband may not create harm to force his wife to return her property, and that the limits of marriage and divorce must not be manipulated. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse allows separation where continuing a marriage threatens the spouses’ ability to act justly, yet repeatedly guards against turning divorce into leverage. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** Honor in retaining, kindness in releasing, and fairness in compensation are not optional courtesies; they are part of the limits God has set. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:230

230230
*“If he divorces her, she is not lawful to him afterward until she marries another husband. If he then divorces her, there is no blame on either of them if they return to one another, provided they think that they can maintain God’s limits. These are God’s limits, which He makes clear to a people who know.”*

**Meaning.** “If he divorces her” refers to the third divorce after the two opportunities described in 2:229. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** After that final separation, the former husband cannot restore the marriage simply by taking his wife back during a waiting period or by making a new contract immediately. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse sets a further condition: she must enter a genuine marriage with another husband, and only if that marriage later ends may she and her first husband consider returning to one another. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The majority of exegetes understand “until she marries another husband” to require a valid marriage followed by marital intercourse, not a contract that is never consummated. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** They cite the Prophet’s explanation that the second husband and wife must experience the intimacy described as “tasting one another’s sweetness.” **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** A minority report attributed to Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib treats a valid marriage contract as sufficient if the second husband did not intend to make the woman lawful for the first; other reports discuss whether intercourse must result in ejaculation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The mainstream reading, followed by most jurists in these commentaries, requires consummation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

This condition refers to an actual marriage, not a staged device to evade the consequence of the third divorce. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The second husband must be a real spouse, and the relationship must be a lawful marriage rather than a contract arranged only to return the woman to her first husband. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** Reports cited by the commentators condemn the *muḥallil*—the person who marries for the purpose of making the woman lawful again—and the former husband who arranges or benefits from such a scheme. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The legal schools differ on the precise validity of a marriage in which this intention is stated or privately held, but the verse’s sequence is not permission to manufacture a temporary intermediary. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

When the second husband divorces her, the woman must complete the waiting period due from that marriage before a new union with the first husband can be contracted. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** “There is no blame on either of them if they return to one another” therefore means a fresh marriage by mutual agreement, not an automatic restoration of the former bond. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]** The provision recognizes that a later marriage may change circumstances and that the former couple may sincerely wish to rebuild a lawful household. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The qualification “provided they think that they can maintain God’s limits” makes the possibility of return conditional on an honest assessment. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains *ẓann* here as hope or expectation rather than certainty, since no human being can know the future with certainty. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The two should have reason to believe they can fulfill the obligations of marriage and treat one another well; desire alone is not enough if the same pattern of harm is likely to continue. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī stresses that neither party should deceive the other about an inability to provide, a serious impediment to married life, or another matter that affects the rights expected in the new marriage. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The commentators also discuss what happens to the count of earlier divorces if the couple remarry after an intervening marriage. **[Qurṭubī]** One major view is that the earlier declarations remain counted, while another reported view treats the later marriage as beginning a new count. **[Qurṭubī]** This is a further legal disagreement about the consequences of remarriage; it does not remove the verse’s requirement that the third divorce has first been followed by a genuine intervening marriage. **[Study Quran]**

The condition is not satisfied by intercourse outside a lawful marriage or by a second contract that remains unconsummated according to the majority reading. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The waiting period after the second marriage ends must also be observed before the first couple can enter a new marriage. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** These details underline that the rule concerns a real intervening marital life, not a brief physical act or a paper arrangement designed to evade the consequence of the third divorce. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The words “there is no blame on either of them” remove a barrier to remarriage; they do not order the woman to return or give her former husband a right to compel her. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** If both freely choose the union, they enter it through a new marriage contract and its attendant rights, rather than an automatic restoration of the earlier bond. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** The woman remains able to choose another lawful future, and the first husband cannot treat the intervening marriage as a temporary reservation on her behalf. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** This distinction between permission and compulsion is central to the verse’s protection against control. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

“These are God’s limits, which He makes clear to a people who know” returns to the purpose of the passage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The rules prevent a husband from repeatedly ending and restoring a marriage without limit, and they protect the woman’s ability to enter another marriage rather than being held by a succession of threats. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The requirement of a genuine second marriage makes the third divorce consequential, while the possibility of return remains open only after circumstances have changed and both parties can reasonably expect to observe their obligations. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources differ over whether the second marriage must be consummated, how a deliberately arranged *taḥlīl* contract is classified, and whether earlier divorce counts remain after remarriage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Most commentators require a valid, consummated marriage and distinguish it from a contrived arrangement intended only to make the woman lawful for her former husband. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The final limit is not an invitation to construct a loophole, but a safeguard against making marriage and divorce instruments of control. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The possibility of reunion is tied to changed circumstances, mutual consent, and a realistic hope that both spouses will uphold their responsibilities. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

## 2:231

231231
*“When you divorce women and they near the end of their waiting period, either retain them honorably or release them honorably. Do not retain them to cause harm and transgress; whoever does that wrongs himself. Do not take God’s signs in mockery. Remember God’s favor upon you and what He has sent down to you of the Book and Wisdom, admonishing you thereby. Be mindful of God, and know that God knows all things.”*

**Meaning.** The verse returns to revocable divorce and sets a moral condition on the husband’s choice. As the waiting period draws near its end, he may restore the marriage or allow the separation to take effect, but he may not use the power of return as a device for keeping a woman trapped. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī stresses that “they near their term” here means approaching its completion: once the period has actually ended, the former husband no longer has the same unilateral right to take her back. **[Qurṭubī]** The distinction explains the verse’s timing. It speaks to a moment when a decision is still possible, and it requires that the decision be made with fairness rather than resentment. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]**

“To retain honorably” means that reconciliation should be genuine: the husband intends to continue the marriage, fulfill the wife’s rights, and live with her in an accepted and decent manner. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr mentions making the return known with witnesses and resuming kind companionship, while al-Ṭabarī understands the clause as a lawful return within the revocable period, not as permission to exploit physical relations while leaving the legal status uncertain. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** The shared point is that a return should restore an honorable marital relationship, not merely postpone a final separation. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

“To release honorably” is the other lawful course: do not revoke the divorce, and let the waiting period finish without humiliation, obstruction, or a demand that the woman surrender what is rightfully hers. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī connects this with fulfilling the rights due to a wife rather than leaving her to struggle for what the marriage requires; Maʿārif likewise emphasizes that divorce should not become a quarrel over dower, maintenance, or other rights. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** A marriage may end without turning the ending into a second injury. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The explicit prohibition is against “retaining them to cause harm.” **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The exegetes describe a man who would wait until his wife’s period was nearly over, take her back, then divorce her again and repeat the cycle. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Such conduct prolongs the woman’s uncertainty and blocks her from freely entering another marriage; in some accounts the husband hoped that the pressure would make her seek release by giving back her dower. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** The wrong lies not in reconciliation itself, which the law permits, but in feigning reconciliation as a means of control. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The warning that the wrongdoer “wrongs himself” turns the reader’s attention from the immediate power imbalance to accountability before God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** A husband may imagine that the other party bears the cost, yet he is the one who incurs sin by exceeding the limits. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** This is why the verse does not describe harm as a clever use of a legal option: a lawful power does not become a license to violate the purpose for which it was given. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

“Do not take God’s signs in mockery” extends the warning beyond this one pattern. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Divorce, return, and marriage are serious acts with consequences; they are not words to toss out in anger and then dismiss as a joke. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The commentaries connect mockery both with repeatedly manipulating the rules and with treating a formal declaration as though it has no weight because the speaker claims to have been playing. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** *(digression)* The jurists discuss separately when declarations made in jest take legal effect; the present verse’s central warning is not to trivialize God’s boundaries or use them to injure a spouse. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The command to remember God’s favor and the Book and Wisdom places family law within the larger gift of revelation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī identifies the favor with Islam and the Qur’an, and explains Wisdom here as the Prophetic teaching that clarifies how the revealed limits are to be observed. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Maʿārif emphasizes that such reminders aim not only to state a rule but to make justice easier to practice by awakening conscience and a sense of answerability. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

“Be mindful of God” and “God knows all things” close the verse by including intentions as well as outward acts. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** The person who stages a return, hides a plan to prolong the waiting period, or invokes a technicality to take what is not due cannot make the injustice invisible to God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The same knowledge also sees an honest attempt to reconcile or a respectful decision to separate. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The surrounding rule in 2:229 helps explain why this choice is not open-ended: the passage treats the first and second revocable divorces as chances either to restore the marriage fairly or to release the woman without injury. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** That sequence does not authorize a husband to keep restarting the waiting period indefinitely; the limit is precisely what protects the wife from being held in a state of uncertainty. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The reports differ over particular examples of harmful revocation, but the sources converge on the operative rule: retain only for a sincere, fair marriage, or let the waiting period end without abuse. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** A right to reconcile is not a right to keep another person suspended. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The verse asks that both reunion and separation be measured by good conduct, so that the end of a marriage does not become an opportunity for retaliation. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

## 2:232

232232
*“When you divorce women and their waiting period has ended, do not prevent them from marrying their husbands when they have mutually agreed honorably. This is an admonition for whoever among you believes in God and the Last Day. That is more virtuous and purer for you. God knows, and you do not know.”*

**Meaning.** Here “their term has ended” means the waiting period is complete, not merely approaching its end as in the previous verse. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** Once the period has passed, a revocable divorce has become a separation; if the former couple wish to reunite, they need a new marriage by mutual agreement rather than a husband simply taking the woman back. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse therefore protects the woman’s choice at precisely the point when relatives or a former husband might try to substitute their anger for her consent. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The best-known occasion reported for the verse concerns Maʿqil ibn Yasār and his sister. After her husband divorced her and her waiting period ended, the former husband regretted the separation and sought to marry her again; she was willing, but Maʿqil, angry at the earlier divorce, refused. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** When the verse was recited to him, he accepted its instruction and arranged the marriage. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** The report illustrates that even understandable family hurt cannot justify overriding the woman’s lawful wishes. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

Al-Ṭabarī also records versions that associate the case with Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh and a cousin, alongside differing names and details in the Maʿqil reports. **[Ṭabarī]** The reliable core of the Maʿqil account is sufficient to explain the rule; the variations should not be turned into competing legal conditions or a claim that only one family could be addressed by the verse. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Its wording is general: guardians and relatives are not to prevent a woman from a lawful marriage she wants. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

The word *ʿaḍl* means to restrain, constrict, or obstruct. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The prohibition is thus broader than physical confinement: a guardian can wrong a woman by withholding consent out of pride, revenge, financial interest, or disapproval of a former husband, even when the woman and man agree to marry properly. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** A former husband may also abuse the power of revocation during an earlier waiting period in order to keep her from marrying someone else, a related harm noted by commentators. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]**

The condition “when they have mutually agreed honorably” is essential. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** It does not command a woman to return to a former husband, nor does it force relatives to approve a union that is unlawful. It describes a marriage freely wanted by both parties and conducted within the recognized rules, with a new contract and its proper rights. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** If consent is absent, if coercion is involved, or if the proposed arrangement violates a clear legal limit, the verse’s permission is not a license to proceed regardless. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The verse also became important in the juristic debate over the role of a guardian in marriage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī reasons that the command not to obstruct guardians presumes a role for them in arranging the marriage; Ibn Kathīr and al-Saʿdī likewise cite the verse as evidence that marriage is not simply a woman’s unilateral contract. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī records the counter-argument of Ḥanafī jurists, who note that the verse attributes the act of marrying to the women and interpret this as evidence that an adult woman may contract her own marriage. **[Qurṭubī]** *(digression)* Maʿārif further discusses compatibility and dower in the guardian’s assessment, while the schools differ over the precise limits of that authority. **[Maʿārif]** These legal inferences should be distinguished from the verse’s direct prohibition on unjustly blocking a mutually desired, lawful marriage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The reminder that this is counsel for believers in God and the Last Day makes the rule a test of faith, not merely a private family custom. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** “More virtuous and purer” describes the good of respecting the couple’s lawful agreement: it protects chastity, prevents resentment and suspicion, and avoids the harms that can follow when a capable woman is denied marriage without a valid reason. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The closing “God knows, and you do not know” challenges the guardian’s confidence that anger, honor, or hoped-for advantage gives him better judgment than revelation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** People may mistake wounded pride or control for a sound protective decision; God knows what is beneficial for the parties and the consequences they cannot see. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse therefore joins lawful procedure to a deeper ethic: the woman’s consent is real, family concern must not become oppression, and neither side may use marriage to evade God’s limits. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The word “mutually” matters as much as “honorably”: neither the former husband nor the family can turn the verse into a forced reunion. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Nor does this permission undo the separate limit in 2:230 on reunion after a third divorce; a lawful return must still respect the rules governing that case. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse opens a door where both former spouses choose it, not a means for one to reclaim authority over the other. **[Qurṭubī]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources differ on the exact guardian’s role in concluding a marriage, but they agree that guardians may not withhold a lawful union merely to punish a woman or her former husband. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** Respect for a person’s choice is not indifference to law; the verse asks families to honor both consent and the boundaries that make a marriage legitimate. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Its warning is especially pointed when an elder’s authority is used to settle an old grievance at the expense of someone else’s future. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]**

## 2:233

233233
*“Mothers shall nurse their children for two complete years, for those who wish to complete the nursing. The father must provide their food and clothing honorably. No soul is charged beyond its capacity. No mother shall be harmed through her child, nor father through his child. The heir has a like duty. If the two parents wish to wean by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame on them. If you wish to have your children wet-nursed, there is no blame on you, provided you pay what you give honorably. Be mindful of God, and know that God sees what you do.”*

**Meaning.** The passage turns from divorce to the child who may remain between separated parents. Its concern is not only how long a child may nurse, but how parents can meet the child’s needs without turning feeding, custody, or money into weapons against one another. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The mother is named first because of her direct care and the tenderness she ordinarily provides; al-Ṭabarī understands the verse to recognize her priority in nursing rather than to compel every mother in every circumstance to nurse regardless of capacity or arrangement. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

“Two complete years” sets out the full nursing period for parents who wish to complete it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The word “complete” prevents a partial year and a few months from being mistaken for two full years, while “for those who wish” shows that the full term is not imposed when both parents have a sound reason to wean earlier. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse thus establishes a clear reference point but also provides a lawful route for a shorter period when the child’s interests are served and the parents agree. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The commentators distinguish the child’s interest in nursing from the question of whether the mother can be compelled to provide it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī reads the wording as giving the mother first claim to nurse and marking the maximum ordinary period, not as an absolute duty where the father can arrange suitable nursing another way. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī surveys different circumstances, including the ongoing marriage, a revocable or irrevocable divorce, the mother’s ability, and whether the child will accept another nurse. **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif presents nursing as the mother’s duty within marriage but recognizes that a divorced mother may receive a fair wage after the relevant waiting period. **[Maʿārif]** These are juristic distinctions about obligation, right, and payment; they do not cancel the shared priority of the infant’s welfare. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

The father, described as the one “to whom the child is born,” bears the cost of the nursing mother’s food and clothing in a fair manner. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** This applies to the practical burden of caring for his child; it is not a reward that depends on whether the parents remain on good terms. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** “Honorably” calls for an amount in keeping with recognized need and the father’s means, neither extravagant nor miserly. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The next phrase, “no soul is charged beyond its capacity,” prevents the support rule from becoming an impossible demand on a poor father, while also preventing poverty from being used as an excuse to impose more on the mother than she can bear. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

“No mother shall be harmed through her child, nor father through his child” bars retaliatory behavior in both directions. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** A mother must not withhold nursing, access, or care simply to punish the father; the father must not use the child to coerce her, withhold her due support, or take the child from her merely to cause pain. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The sources give different examples of how such harm could occur, but the principle is reciprocal: the child is not an instrument for settling adult grievances. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The phrase “the heir has a like duty” carries a substantial juristic discussion. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some commentators understand the father’s heir to assume the provision due when the father dies; others limit the clause to a duty not to harm the mother or child, or identify the relevant heir differently. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Maʿārif explains it through the relatives who inherit from an orphaned child and share responsibility for the child’s maintenance, while other exegetes record narrower readings. **[Maʿārif]** *(digression)* The verse’s precise allocation of support among heirs is disputed; its unifying safeguard is that the father’s death must not become a pretext to abandon the child or injure the surviving parent. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

Parents may wean before the two years only if they both agree and consult one another. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Consultation requires more than a unilateral announcement: the parents should consider whether early weaning is genuinely in the child’s interest. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** A disagreement should not be settled by one parent using custody or nursing as leverage. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** If a wet nurse is chosen, the arrangement is permitted, but the agreed payment must be delivered fairly; the permission does not erase the worker’s right to her wage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The closing command to be mindful of God, who sees what people do, returns the discussion to private conduct. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** A family may keep a dispute hidden from neighbors, but God sees whether its decisions protect a child or disguise revenge. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse’s detailed allocation of care therefore serves a larger ethic: parents may separate, but their child remains a trust requiring cooperation, proportionate support, and restraint from harm. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

*(digression)* Many jurists also use the two-year term to define when nursing establishes foster kinship that affects marriage prohibitions; Ibn Kathīr and al-Saʿdī describe the two-year limit, while Maʿārif reports a Ḥanafī extension to thirty months in particular circumstances. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** That is a related legal consequence, not the verse’s main instruction to parents about completing or shortening a child’s nursing period. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources differ on when nursing is compulsory, who bears the cost if the father dies, and the precise duration relevant to foster kinship. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** They converge on fair provision, protection from retaliatory harm, and consultation centered on the child. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** Separation does not dissolve parental responsibility. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The verse refuses to let a child’s needs be held hostage to adult bitterness: care and fairness remain obligations even when the household has changed. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

## 2:234

234234
*“Those among you who die and leave wives behind, their wives shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days. When they have completed their term, there is no blame on you concerning what they do with themselves honorably. God is aware of what you do.”*

**Meaning.** This verse sets the waiting period for a widow at four months and ten days. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The commentators treat the command as applying whether or not the marriage was consummated, and they distinguish it from the waiting period after an ordinary divorce. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The period is a defined obligation, not an estimate that relatives may lengthen at their discretion or shorten because they believe the woman is ready to remarry. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

Pregnancy is a special case governed by the related verse that says pregnant women’s term ends when they give birth. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** The majority position reported by al-Qurṭubī and followed by Ibn Kathīr is that a pregnant widow’s waiting period ends at delivery, even if the birth occurs shortly after her husband’s death. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** They cite the report of Subayʿah al-Aslamiyyah, who gave birth soon after being widowed and was told by the Prophet that she could marry after delivery. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī also records an earlier view attributed to ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās that she should observe whichever is later, childbirth or the four months and ten days; the Subayʿah report is why the majority does not require both periods in every case. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

“Wait by themselves” means, at minimum, that the widow refrains from entering a new marriage until the appointed term is complete. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The sources also connect the period with mourning (*iḥdād*), such as abstaining from perfume and conspicuous adornment, through Prophetic reports. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verse itself does not list every mourning practice; the details are supplied by the Sunnah, including reports about a widow remaining in her home during the waiting period. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Some early authorities understood the phrase primarily as abstention from marriage, while other jurists require the additional restrictions of mourning and residence. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** These distinctions should not be blurred: the four months and ten days are explicit in the verse, while further conduct is derived from transmitted practice. **[Qurṭubī]**

The waiting period also marks a change from the harsher practices reported from pre-Islamic Arabia, when some widows were confined and mourned for a full year. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Reports describe women wearing poor clothing and refraining from adornment; the Qur’anic rule provides a determinate term rather than leaving a woman under indefinite family control. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The contrast should be stated carefully: the verse fixes the legal period, while the commentators’ reports about older customs supply background rather than additional Qur’anic requirements. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

“When they have completed their term” is the point at which the widow may make a lawful new choice. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The phrase “there is no blame on you” addresses guardians and others who might otherwise object to her taking up an honorable course, including accepting a proposal and entering a new marriage. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** “Honorably” keeps that freedom within lawful bounds; it does not authorize a marriage contract during the waiting period or an act contrary to the prescribed rules. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The wording speaks to the woman’s actions after the term, but it also assigns responsibility to those around her. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The widow is not to be treated as though she remains married after the period has ended, nor can her family convert the period into permanent guardianship over her choices. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The sources mention beautification and suitors as examples of what may again become lawful, but the governing limit is *maʿrūf*: recognized, decent conduct under the law. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]**

“God is aware of what you do” closes the ruling with a reminder that both women and guardians answer for their conduct. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** It reassures the widow whose rights are respected and warns anyone who secretly obstructs her or pressures her into a decision. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** God knows whether a family’s concern is protective or a pretext for control, just as He knows whether a proposal is honorable or exploitative. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

*(digression)* Some jurists discuss how the four months and ten days are counted when a lunar month begins partway through a month; Maʿārif gives a detailed calculation. **[Maʿārif]** This calendrical question should not obscure the verse’s basic rule or be presented as an agreed practical calculation without its juristic context. **[Qurṭubī]**

The waiting period should also be distinguished from a judgment that a widow is socially untouchable. **[Study Quran]** The additional mourning practices described by the exegetes—such as refraining from perfume or conspicuous adornment and, according to many jurists, remaining in the marital home—come through Prophetic reports and legal interpretation, not from a list of prohibitions spelled out in this verse itself. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Maʿārif gives examples of such restraint, while the Study Quran notes that early authorities differed over whether “wait by themselves” itself requires staying home or primarily means abstaining from marriage. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** This distinction preserves both the widow’s dignity during mourning and the limits of what the verse explicitly states. **[Ṭabarī]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources agree on the four-month-and-ten-day term for a nonpregnant widow and on the right to act honorably once it ends. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** They record a minority view on the pregnant widow’s term, while the majority follow the report of Subayʿah and end it at childbirth. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** Bereavement receives a definite period of respect, but it does not erase a woman’s future or authorize others to control it indefinitely. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse places the end of waiting under God’s knowledge and the woman’s honorable choice, not under the preferences of relatives. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:235

235235
*“There is no blame on you if you intimate a proposal to women or keep it within yourselves. God knows that you will remember them. But do not make secret promises with them; speak only an honorable word. Do not resolve the marriage bond until the prescribed term is complete. Know that God knows what is within you, so be mindful of Him; and know that God is Forgiving, Forbearing.”*

**Meaning.** The verse addresses a person who hopes to marry a woman still observing a waiting period, especially a widow. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** It distinguishes an indirect indication of interest from an explicit proposal or agreement. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** A man may speak in general, honorable terms—such as saying that he hopes to marry a righteous woman—without asking her to make a binding promise before she is free to decide. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** This permission acknowledges that grief does not erase the widow’s future or the possibility that another person may hope to marry her. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The commentators extend the rule to a woman whose divorce is irrevocable, while distinguishing her from a woman in a revocable waiting period, who remains a wife and may not be approached by another suitor. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī focuses his explanation on widows, the immediate context of the preceding verse; the broader application to irrevocably divorced women is stated explicitly by other commentators. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The rule is therefore not a blanket permission to court anyone in any kind of *ʿidda*. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]**

“Or keep it within yourselves” recognizes a private intention that has not become a coercive act or a secret contract. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The text does not condemn a person for anticipating a future marriage after the waiting period; it does warn that intention must remain within lawful limits. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The permission to hint is not a license to pressure a bereaved woman, test her vulnerability, or make her feel bound to accept a future proposal. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

“Do not make secret promises with them” is explained in more than one way. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Many commentators take it to prohibit a private pledge that the woman will marry a particular man or refuse other suitors after her waiting period. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Others include sexually suggestive speech or a covert agreement that crosses the boundary between hint and formal engagement. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The sources differ on the exact scope of “secretly,” but they agree that indirect, honorable words must not be turned into a concealed contract. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The exception, “speak only an honorable word,” confines the permitted hint to what the law recognizes as decent. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Examples include a general expression of interest, or a restrained inquiry through a guardian, rather than a demand for exclusivity. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** A person may acknowledge the possibility of a later proposal but must leave the woman free to consider it when her term is complete. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** This limitation protects her time to grieve, preserves the current waiting period, and prevents a suitor from using a hint to claim a right he does not yet have. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

“Do not resolve the marriage bond until the prescribed term is complete” makes the limit unmistakable: the marriage contract itself must wait. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The woman cannot enter a new marriage before her prior waiting period has ended, and the interested man cannot make the future contract effective by private agreement. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr reports agreement among the scholars that a marriage contract made during the waiting period is invalid. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse thus distinguishes lawful anticipation from premature action. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The warning that God knows what is within people’s souls applies both to sincere restraint and concealed plans. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The person who outwardly uses vague language but privately seeks to bind or exploit the woman is not beyond accountability. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** “Be mindful of Him” calls for truthful intention as well as careful speech. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The closing names, “Forgiving, Forbearing,” leave room for repentance and acknowledge that desire can be strong, while still requiring a person not to cross the legal boundary. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

*(digression)* The commentators discuss the consequences if a man contracts a marriage before the woman’s waiting period ends, including whether the couple may marry one another afterward. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Those technical rulings vary and are distinct from the clear rule here: no marriage bond is to be concluded until the waiting period is complete. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

Al-Qurṭubī describes two ordinary ways an indirect proposal may be conveyed: a man may speak to the woman’s guardian and ask to be informed before she is promised to someone else, or he may use a restrained, general expression to the woman herself. **[Qurṭubī]** He also reports that some authorities disliked wording such as “do not let anyone precede me,” because it can approach the forbidden form of a private promise. **[Qurṭubī]** This borderline example shows why the verse regulates not just vocabulary but the effect of speech: a hint must leave the woman free, not claim her future in advance. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**
