The phrase “until the prescribed term is complete” refers to the waiting period applicable to that woman, not to an open-ended postponement of her future. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** A hint does not shorten that term or create an engagement that binds her; when the period ends, she remains free to accept or refuse a proposal. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī also emphasizes that a woman in a revocable divorce is still legally a wife, so another suitor may not even hint at marriage to her during that period. **[Qurṭubī]** This contrast clarifies why the permission is limited to widows and, in the broader juristic application, women whose divorce is irrevocable. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Interpretive note.** The main distinction is stable across the sources: an honorable hint may be permissible in specified cases, but a direct or secret commitment and the marriage contract itself must wait. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The exact scope of indirect speech and the cases beyond widowhood are treated differently by the commentators. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** This permission respects future hope without letting desire overtake a woman’s period of grief or choice. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** Restraint, honest speech, and patience allow a lawful proposal to arrive at the proper time rather than becoming a private claim in advance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

## 2:236

236236
*“There is no blame on you if you divorce women before you have touched them or appointed a dowry for them. Provide for them, the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means: an honorable provision, a duty upon the virtuous.”*

**Meaning.** This verse treats a specific case: a marriage contract has been made, but the couple have not consummated the marriage and no dower has been specified. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** “Touched” is a modest expression for sexual intercourse, not ordinary contact. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The verse does not portray such a divorce as ideal or painless; it says that a husband may end a marriage in these circumstances without owing a specified dower that was never named. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

The phrase “no blame on you” removes the mistaken idea that the contract can never be ended merely because no dowry was fixed. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse also confirms the validity of a marriage concluded without naming the dower at the ceremony; al-Qurṭubī discusses this as *nikāḥ al-tafwīḍ*, in which a dower may be agreed later. **[Qurṭubī]** *(digression)* This technical point concerns the form of the marriage contract; the verse’s immediate direction is how a husband must act if he divorces before consummation and before a dower has been set. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

Although there is no specified dower in this case, the husband is told, “provide for them.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The gift, often called *mutʿa*, is a material provision intended to ease the hurt and disruption of a marriage that has ended before the woman received the settled dower or the companionship she expected. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** It is neither the fixed dower of the next verse nor a payment that buys the woman’s consent to divorce; it is a humane parting provision. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The scale is deliberately tied to means: “the wealthy according to his means, and the poor according to his means.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī argues that the measure should reflect the husband’s financial capacity rather than be mechanically set by the woman’s customary dower. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Saʿdī likewise says the amount varies with circumstances and accepted custom, while Maʿārif presents a reasonable gift as obligatory and notes that the Qur’an fixes no single amount. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

Early reports give examples such as clothing or a more substantial gift according to a husband’s resources. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some authorities describe a modest set of clothes as a minimum in ordinary circumstances, while others cite much larger gifts from men of means. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** These are examples of how the principle may be applied, not a universal price list or a single amount binding on every family. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** The key is that a man should not use the absence of a specified dower to leave the woman with nothing after he has initiated the separation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

“An honorable provision” links the amount with proper conduct. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** A payment meant to humiliate, to display wealth, or to buy silence would miss the verse’s purpose; the gift should be appropriate, decent, and delivered without renewed insult. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The next verse makes a different calculation when a dower was specified: in that case, half of the named amount is due before consummation unless one party remits it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Keeping these cases distinct prevents the discretionary-looking gift here from being confused with a clear half-dower entitlement there. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]**

The closing phrase calls the provision a “duty upon the virtuous.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The sources discuss whether the requirement is legally enforceable in every case or especially a moral obligation of beneficence; al-Saʿdī and Maʿārif stress that a husband must not withhold it, while al-Ṭabarī records differing views about its legal force. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Whatever the juristic classification, the verse presents generosity here not as an optional flourish that can be mocked, but as the honorable way to end a contract. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The surrounding verses map distinct financial outcomes rather than treating every divorce alike. **[Qurṭubī]** When no dower has been fixed and the marriage ends before consummation, this verse assigns a reasonable *mutʿa*; when a dower has been fixed but consummation has not occurred, the next verse gives the woman half of that named amount. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** If consummation has occurred, or if a dower was not named despite consummation, the sources discuss other rules for the full dower or its customary equivalent. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī also notes that the woman divorced before consummation has no waiting period under the related rule in 33:49. **[Qurṭubī]** These comparisons show why a gift here is not a substitute for every other financial right. **[Study Quran]**

The wording “provide for them” also prevents a technical distinction about the dower from becoming an excuse for total neglect. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Maʿārif cites a set of clothing as a low-end example, while early reports collected by al-Ṭabarī range from clothing to a more substantial gift for a husband who can afford it. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ṭabarī]** Their examples illustrate the scale; they do not replace the verse’s direction that each man give according to his own means. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** A wealthy husband cannot invoke a poor man’s limit to give an insulting token, and a poor husband is not burdened with an amount beyond his capacity. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources agree that the verse concerns divorce before consummation with no dower fixed, but they discuss the gift’s minimum and whether its payment is enforceable in every case. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The principle is proportionality: means determine the amount, while fairness determines the manner. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** A lawful separation can still be handled with generosity. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The gift recognizes that a person may be hurt even where no fixed dower was promised, and it asks the one ending the marriage not to treat the absence of a number as the absence of responsibility. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:237

237237
*“If you divorce them before you have touched them, after having appointed a dowry for them, then half of what you appointed is due—unless they forgive, or the one in whose hand is the marriage bond forgives. To forgive is nearer to reverence. Do not forget graciousness among yourselves. God sees what you do.”*

**Meaning.** This verse completes the previous ruling by treating the other case: the marriage was not consummated, but a dower was named. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The woman’s legal entitlement is half of the agreed amount, not an unspecified gift. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** This is the basic rule described by the commentators; it prevents the husband from treating the end of a marriage as permission to reclaim the whole dower after the contract has given the woman a claim to it. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The exception “unless they forgive” refers to the woman willingly relinquishing the half that is hers. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Because that share is her property, the waiver must be hers to make; al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī discuss the woman’s capacity to act for herself, and Maʿārif likewise treats forgiveness as voluntary. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** A relative cannot turn the verse into permission to surrender her right on her behalf merely because he is displeased with the divorce. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The phrase “or the one in whose hand is the marriage bond” is interpreted by most of the commentators as the husband, who may forgo the half he could otherwise recover and leave the woman with the full dower. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Ibn Kathīr cites a report identifying the husband as the person who holds the marriage tie; al-Saʿdī says this is the stronger view because the guardian does not own the woman’s financial right. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī and al-Jalālayn also record an alternative interpretation that the phrase refers to a guardian, particularly in the case of a woman who cannot act independently, while al-Ṭabarī transmits both readings. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]**

*(digression)* The identity of the person who can forgive is a legal disagreement, not a reason to blur ownership of the dower. **[Qurṭubī]** The wife’s right is not the guardian’s to dispose of without the conditions recognized by the relevant school, whereas a husband who waives his recoverable half gives more than the minimum the law requires. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The verse places forgiveness on either side as an act of generosity, not as a condition that the woman must surrender her lawful share. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

“To forgive is nearer to reverence” praises voluntary graciousness beyond the strict minimum. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** If the woman remits her half, the husband keeps what he received; if the husband remits his half, she keeps the entire amount agreed upon. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse does not make either waiver compulsory. Its moral invitation is to give freely where one can, rather than turn a painful separation into a contest over the last possible coin. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

“Do not forget graciousness among yourselves” widens the instruction beyond the calculation of a dower. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Even when a marriage ends, former spouses should remember the good that passed between them and avoid spiteful bargaining or public humiliation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The word *faḍl* points to a measure of kindness above bare justice: justice secures each person’s right, while graciousness lets one party voluntarily give more or demand less. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The sources also discuss whether seclusion without intercourse has the same legal consequence as consummation for the dower and waiting period. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Some jurists count a legally significant seclusion differently from others; that technical question should not be confused with the verse’s explicit case of divorce before sexual consummation. **[Qurṭubī]** *(digression)* The verse’s direct instruction remains clear: where a dower was fixed and the marriage ends before consummation, half is due unless a valid, voluntary waiver changes the result. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The final statement, “God sees what you do,” makes the private settlement morally visible. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** God sees both the formal payment and whether forgiveness was freely given or extracted under pressure. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse thus joins a precise financial entitlement to a higher ethic of dignified separation. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The majority reading understands the husband’s forgiveness as a voluntary decision not to reclaim the half he could otherwise recover; the alternative reading assigns a role to a guardian in a limited class of cases. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Whatever legal view one follows about the phrase, its moral direction is clear: the husband may leave the woman the full dower, while the woman may choose not to claim the half owed to her. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The two options do not make the wife’s entitlement less real; they make generosity possible on either side. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

The default half-payment is a settled right; forgiveness is a later choice, not a condition for receiving it. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** If the wife remits her half, the husband keeps the portion already paid; if the husband remits what he could reclaim, she retains the full dower. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī discusses the ownership of the dower and the woman’s ability to waive it when she is competent to manage her property, reinforcing that her share is not a family asset for relatives to bargain away. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** This is why the verse’s praise of generosity cannot be used to pressure the woman into surrendering her right. **[Saʿdī]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources agree on the half-dower rule but differ over who may remit the amount on the husband’s side and over the treatment of seclusion without consummation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The woman’s right remains hers; the invitation to generosity is not a command to waive it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks people to let a relationship end without allowing a dispute over money to erase every memory of care. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Its ideal is not forced sacrifice but mutual dignity: each party knows the right, and either may choose, freely, to act with greater generosity. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:238

238238
*“Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer, and stand before God devoutly.”*

**Meaning.** The passage on family law pauses to command the faithful to preserve the prayers. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The wording is comprehensive: guard the prescribed prayers by observing them at their times and fulfilling their required form, rather than allowing family responsibilities, work, or other concerns to make worship careless. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Ibn Kathīr connects the command with the Prophetic teaching that prayer performed at its appointed time is among the most beloved deeds. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse singles out *al-ṣalāt al-wusṭā*, “the middle prayer,” for particular attention, but that emphasis does not exempt the other prayers from the command to guard them. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]**

The commentators offer more than one identification of the middle prayer. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** The majority view in Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, and Maʿārif is that it is the afternoon prayer, ʿAṣr; they cite reports in which the Prophet and his Companions were kept from it during the Battle of the Confederates and called it “the middle prayer, the ʿAṣr prayer.” **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī gathers numerous reports for this identification, while their chains and details are not all of equal strength. **[Ṭabarī]** *(weak)* Some variant reports in the long collection have been judged weak or differ in the setting; they should not be treated as equivalent to the better-attested reports naming ʿAṣr. **[Ṭabarī]**

Al-Qurṭubī records a wide range of identifications, including Ẓuhr, Maghrib, ʿIshāʾ, Fajr, Friday prayer, and the five prayers taken collectively. **[Qurṭubī]** He notes that ʿAṣr is the majority position but ultimately cautions against claiming certainty where the transmitted interpretations conflict, urging preservation of all the prayers. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Jalālayn likewise records several views and explains that the middle prayer is singled out for its merit. **[Jalālayn]** The Study Quran also surveys alternatives, including a view identifying it with the ʿĪd prayer. **[Study Quran]** The disagreement concerns which prayer receives the title; it does not weaken the plain command to safeguard every obligatory prayer. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The word *wusṭā* can convey “middle” or “best/most excellent,” a semantic range that helps explain why the prayer is named separately. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** On either reading, the special mention awakens attention: people may be especially occupied or vulnerable to neglect at the time of the prayer being emphasized. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse does not invite a believer to speculate endlessly while neglecting the other prayers; it directs the community toward consistent observance and reverence. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]**

“Stand before God devoutly” translates *qānitīn*. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The commentators explain *qunūt* through several related ideas: obedience, humility, calm attentiveness, sustained worship, and a stillness appropriate to prayer. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī emphasizes obedience and devotion; al-Saʿdī describes a posture of humility, sincerity, and reverent concentration. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The physical standing matters, but the verse’s call is not merely to remain upright: the worshipper stands with heart and limbs directed toward God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The sources also connect the verse with silence during prayer. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Reports from Zayd ibn Arqam describe Companions once speaking to one another during prayer, then refraining when the command to stand devoutly was revealed; prophetic teaching clarifies that ordinary human conversation does not belong in the prayer, which is filled with remembrance of God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** This reading of *qānitīn* as quiet devotion complements, rather than replaces, its meanings of obedience and humility. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]**

*(digression)* Al-Qurṭubī develops a lengthy legal discussion about whether congregants should stand or sit when an ill imam leads prayer while seated, comparing reports from different occasions in the Prophet’s final illness. **[Qurṭubī]** The issue is a technical question of congregational practice and competing reports, not the central sense of this verse’s command to stand devoutly when able. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The placement of the prayer command between rules on marriage and divorce also gives the surrounding passage a devotional frame: worship is not isolated from social life. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** Family duties and financial rights are to be handled under the same awareness of God that governs prayer. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Guarding the prayer repeatedly trains attention, patience, and restraint—qualities needed when a person faces conflict or must honor another’s rights. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The report of the Confederates gives the majority identification a concrete setting: the battle delayed the Companions from performing ʿAṣr, and the Prophet’s wording names it as “the middle prayer.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** This report explains why many commentators connect special vigilance with that prayer, but it does not imply that prayer at another time is of lesser obligation. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** The related discussion of *qunūt* also insists that a worshipper’s attention is not merely bodily stillness: the tongue is occupied with recitation and remembrance, while ordinary conversation is set aside. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

Maʿārif notes that ʿAṣr is a time when many people are occupied with work, which can make the special emphasis on guarding it especially practical. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Yet the plural “prayers” continues to govern the full daily cycle: a believer should not preserve one prayer carefully while neglecting the others. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]** The readings of *qunūt* likewise add depth without cancelling one another: outward stillness, inward humility, obedience, and refraining from ordinary speech all describe a worshipper intentionally present before God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources differ over which prayer is *al-wusṭā*, though ʿAṣr is the majority identification in several commentaries; they also preserve multiple senses of *qānitīn*, from obedient humility to silence in prayer. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The singled-out prayer reminds believers that their obligations to one another are lived in the presence of God. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** To guard prayer is to keep returning attention to its source, while standing devoutly means that neither the body nor the heart treats worship as a casual interruption. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:239

239239
*“If you are in fear, then pray on foot or mounted. When you are secure, remember God as He taught you what you did not know.”*

**Meaning.** The verse addresses prayer under danger, when a person cannot maintain the ordinary posture, direction, or stillness of worship. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** It permits prayer on foot or while mounted, preserving the obligation even when an enemy, a predator, a flood, or another life-threatening danger makes the normal form impossible. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Jalālayn understands “on foot” as praying while walking; al-Saʿdī and the Study Quran likewise describe prayer while moving or riding when fear requires it. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The permission is proportionate to the danger. Under intense fear, the worshipper may pray facing whichever direction safety requires and indicate bowing and prostration by gestures, lowering the gesture for prostration where possible. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The details of the usual prayer are not simply abandoned; the person performs what can be done while being excused from what danger makes impossible. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The Study Quran notes that commentators also discuss shortening the number of cycles in extreme circumstances, with further detail deferred to the fear-prayer passage in 4:101–102. **[Study Quran]**

The sources distinguish this emergency prayer from the more organized form of the fear prayer in which a congregation divides into groups and alternates between worship and watch. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** That structured arrangement is treated elsewhere; this verse addresses the sharper case in which the person must pray while moving or mounted because danger is immediate. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī describes the relevant fear as a serious threat to life, not a minor inconvenience, and includes the risk of a pursuing enemy, a dangerous animal, or a threatening flood. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

There is a notable difference in how broadly the permission to pray while moving is applied. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** These commentaries read “on foot or mounted” as allowing the worshipper to pray while walking or riding, facing the direction safety permits and using gestures. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Qurṭubī]** Maʿārif takes a more restrictive position: if a person can remain stationary and gesture, prayer may be performed in that manner, but prayer while walking is not allowed; if actual fighting makes even that impossible, it permits delaying the prayer and making it up afterward. **[Maʿārif]** This is a real juristic difference about the limits of emergency prayer, not a disagreement over the duty to pray or the need to respect life-threatening danger. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]**

Al-Qurṭubī reports further disagreement about how many cycles a person must pray in extreme fear. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** Some early authorities allow one cycle or, if even that is impossible, a reduced gesture; others hold that the normal number should be completed as far as ability permits. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** *(digression)* These reports show the effort to adapt worship to danger, but the precise number is a juristic discussion rather than the central sense of “on foot or mounted.” **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

“When you are secure, remember God” signals a return to the ordinary form of prayer once the threat has passed. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Here “remember God” is explained as performing the prayer with its usual standing, bowing, prostration, direction, and attention; it also includes gratitude for safety and for the guidance that teaches the worshipper how to pray. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The exception is not a reason to let the emergency form become habitual when security has returned. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]**

The phrase “as He taught you what you did not know” directs gratitude toward revelation and instruction. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** People do not invent the prayer’s limits according to convenience; they learn from God how to worship in ease and how to preserve worship in danger. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Saʿdī also draws a broader lesson: knowledge is a gift that should increase remembrance and gratitude, and gratitude itself is a cause for further blessing. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The verse does not make safety and worship rivals. It grants concessions under severe threat, while retaining the act of prayer to the extent possible. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī rejects an interpretation that reads “when you are secure” merely as returning from travel, because the surrounding contrast is between fear during prayer and security afterward. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Thus the movement of the passage is practical: preserve prayer amid danger, then restore its full form when danger recedes. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]**

Al-Ṭabarī rejects a report that takes “when you are secure” to mean simply that travelers have returned from a journey and settled at home. **[Ṭabarī]** His reason is contextual: the verse contrasts fear, which permits an adapted prayer, with the return of security, when the normal form must again be observed even if the worshipper is still traveling. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The concession is therefore tied to danger, not to travel by itself; travel has its own rules elsewhere. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The Arabic pairs the worshipper on foot with the rider; al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī explain that “on foot” includes walking and that “mounted” covers the available riding animal or conveyance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The gesture may replace the ordinary bow and prostration when danger prevents them, and the direction of prayer may follow what safety permits rather than a fixed orientation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** These allowances are tied to necessity and ability, not to casual convenience. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Once the threat passes, the worshipper returns to the regular prayer as taught. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]**

**Interpretive note.** Most sources permit prayer on foot or mounted, with gestures and without requiring the usual direction under acute fear; Maʿārif restricts prayer while walking and allows delay during actual fighting. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The verse makes room for human vulnerability without treating worship as disposable. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** In danger, a person prays as able; in safety, the person returns to the form God taught and remembers the protection and knowledge received. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

## 2:240

240240
*“Those among you who die and leave wives behind should make a bequest for their wives: provision for a year without expelling them. If they leave, there is no blame on you concerning what they do with themselves honorably. God is Mighty, Wise.”*

**Meaning.** The verse provides for widows through residence and material support after a husband’s death. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Its central protection is explicit: the widow is not to be expelled from her home during the period described, and she is to receive *matāʿ*—provision or support—rather than being left without a place to live. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The phrase “if they leave” makes her departure voluntary; it does not give the heirs permission to drive her out. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

This one-year provision must be distinguished from the widow’s waiting period in 2:234. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The latter prescribes four months and ten days for a nonpregnant widow; this verse speaks of a year of residence and support in an earlier legal arrangement. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** Even on the view that the support or residence could continue beyond the waiting period, the woman was not required to remain unmarried for a full year: once her *ʿidda* ended, she could leave or enter a lawful new marriage. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

The word *waṣiyya* is read with more than one grammatical ending, allowing commentators to discuss whether the verse speaks of a bequest to be made by the husband or a prescribed provision owed to his widow. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī prefers the reading that presents it as a right established by God for the widow, not a benefit that depended solely on whether a dying husband remembered to write a will. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Jalālayn describes the provision as an obligation, while Maʿārif explains that in the early arrangement the husband was instructed to make a will for a year of housing and maintenance. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]**

The commentators differ over whether the one-year rule was later abrogated. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The majority cited by al-Qurṭubī, and the readings in Ibn Kathīr, al-Jalālayn, and Maʿārif, treat the year of waiting or maintenance as superseded by the four-month-and-ten-day rule in 2:234 and by the widow’s fixed inheritance share in 4:12. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī likewise describes an earlier right to a year’s residence and support, then explains that later rules reduced the waiting term and replaced the maintenance arrangement with inheritance. **[Ṭabarī]**

A different interpretation, reported from Mujāhid and favored by al-Saʿdī, says the verses can be read together rather than as contradicting one another. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** On this view, the four months and ten days remain the obligatory waiting period, while the widow may choose to stay in the marital home and receive support for the rest of the year; if she leaves, the family is not to blame. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran also notes that a right to residence and sustenance for a year need not contradict the shorter waiting period if she remains free to leave earlier. **[Study Quran]** Al-Qurṭubī records this view but regards it as an isolated position, whereas al-Saʿdī argues that the wording supports it. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

The disagreement concerns the later legal force of the year-long provision, not the verse’s refusal to permit forced expulsion. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Under either reading, the widow’s interests are treated as a serious claim: she is not to be deprived of shelter by the heirs’ convenience, and any choice to leave belongs to her. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The later inheritance share—one quarter when the husband leaves no child and one eighth when he does—also changed how her provision was secured. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The relationship between a personal share in the estate and a separate right to housing is part of the abrogation debate. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

“If they leave, there is no blame on you concerning what they do with themselves honorably” is interpreted as permission for the woman to leave by choice, and, after her waiting period, to adorn herself or marry in a lawful way. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** If she gives up the optional residence or support, the heirs are not responsible for her independent decision; they are not, however, entitled to use the clause to force her departure. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** “Honorably” keeps her actions within the law and distinguishes a lawful new beginning from a marriage contracted before the end of *ʿidda*. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The closing names, “Mighty, Wise,” affirm that these rules come from a power no family can overrule and a wisdom that accounts for grief, property, and a widow’s agency. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** God’s might warns those who would violate the widow’s rights, while His wisdom is visible in the balance between a defined waiting period and provision for her material security. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

*(digression)* Ibn al-Zubayr once asked ʿUthmān why the verse remained in the Qur’an if its ruling had been abrogated; ʿUthmān replied that he would not alter the placement of anything in the revealed text. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The report illustrates that a verse may remain recited even when jurists consider a particular ruling superseded. **[Study Quran]**

The command “without expelling them” is particularly important where the house and estate pass to other heirs. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The widow’s right to remain cannot be erased by relatives’ impatience, while her choice to leave is not a breach that makes them sinners. **[Ibn Kathīr]** On the continuing-right interpretation, leaving or remarrying before the year ends may end the additional support, but neither action changes the four-month-and-ten-day waiting rule. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources divide between the majority abrogation reading and a continuing optional right to reside and receive support for up to a year; all distinguish that issue from the four-month-and-ten-day waiting period. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The verse resists the idea that a widow’s shelter and future are merely matters for the heirs to decide. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** Even where commentators disagree over abrogation, the underlying concern remains visible: provide security, do not coerce departure, and leave the woman room to act honorably after her prescribed waiting period. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

## 2:241

241241
*“For divorced women there shall be a provision according to what is fair—a duty upon the reverent.”*

**Meaning.** The verse returns to a broad statement about the material care owed when a marriage ends: divorced women are to receive a fair provision, *matāʿ*. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** In its plain wording it is not limited to the narrow case in 2:236, where no dowry was stipulated and divorce preceded consummation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī therefore reads it as extending the benefit to every divorced woman, including cases addressed separately in the preceding verses. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The word *matāʿ* can denote a useful gift or provision—clothing, maintenance, a servant, or another benefit—not a single fixed sum named by the verse. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The surrounding rulings prevent this general direction from erasing distinctions among women’s rights. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** A woman divorced before consummation with no stipulated dowry receives the proportionate gift described in 2:236; if a dowry was fixed, 2:237 gives her half unless a party voluntarily remits a share. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Verse 241 broadens the moral and legal discussion rather than silently changing either calculation. **[Study Quran]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Saʿdī links the passages in this way: the first case has a gift measured by means, the second has the half-dowry entitlement, and a divorced woman whose marriage was consummated is also to be treated with generosity. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The commentators disagree about how far the universal wording makes a separate gift legally obligatory. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī favors the view of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr that every divorced woman is entitled to *matāʿ*, reasoning that earlier verses state particular cases and this verse supplies a general ruling. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records several positions: some authorities include all divorced women, others distinguish a woman who has already received half a specified dowry, and others understand this verse especially as concerning women whose marriages were consummated. **[Qurṭubī]** These are real differences in how the general wording is reconciled with 2:236–237, not disagreement that divorce must be handled honorably. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The meaning of “provision” itself is also discussed. **[Maʿārif]** If *matāʿ* means a parting gift, the earlier special rulings determine some cases while a further gift may be recommended in others; if it is read as the woman’s dower or maintenance, the amount and duration follow the rules for those entitlements. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī records the view that a stipulated dowry due after consummation is distinct from a discretionary gift, and al-Saʿdī says that a gift after consummation is recommended according to the majority while some scholars consider it obligatory. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse’s general encouragement should thus not be mistaken for a claim that all schools calculate every divorce payment identically. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]**

“According to what is fair” places a standard on both the amount and the manner of giving. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** A provision is to be recognizable as decent under the circumstances, not a humiliating token offered only to make a former wife go away. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Since the verse specifies no sum, capacity, custom, and the rights already settled by the marriage all matter in applying it. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The command echoes 2:236, where a husband’s means set the scale for the gift; the two passages together oppose both extravagance beyond ability and stinginess used as an excuse for cruelty. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

The word “duty” (*ḥaqqan*) is reinforced by “upon the reverent.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī takes the clause as establishing an entitlement for women, while al-Qurṭubī preserves debate over the legal force of the gift in particular classes of divorce. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Saʿdī notes that the provision is among the qualities of reverence whether one follows the position that makes it obligatory in the case at hand or the position that regards it as recommended beyond the specified cases. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The moral address does not reduce a woman’s claim to a favor dependent on a former husband’s mood; it calls the believer to fulfil what is due and to give beyond the minimum with good grace. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

*(digression)* Al-Qurṭubī also records disagreement over women who themselves initiate separation through *khulʿ* or a negotiated release: some jurists include them in the general provision, while others do not. **[Qurṭubī]** This is a subsidiary legal question; the verse’s direct concern is the fair treatment of divorced women and the recognition that separation carries material as well as emotional consequences. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

This broader encouragement must also be kept separate from the woman’s established dower. **[Maʿārif]** After consummation, Maʿārif explains, a stipulated dower remains payable in full; if none was named, she is owed the customary equivalent (*mahr al-mithl*). **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** Maintenance owed during a waiting period is another distinct obligation, not simply another name for a parting gift. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** These distinctions matter because a husband cannot use a general gift to cancel a fixed financial right, nor can the discussion of a dower erase the verse’s call to fair provision. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The commentators differ over whether the verse requires a separate *matāʿ* in every case and over how that provision relates to the fixed dowry and maintenance rules. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** They agree that divorce is not a license to leave a woman without what the law or fair dealing entitles her to. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Reflection.** A lawful separation still calls for a person to act with decency. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse asks the one ending a marriage to remember that a former spouse is not a disposable stranger and that reverence is measured in practical fairness as well as private devotion. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:242

242242
*“Thus God makes clear His signs to you, that you may understand.”*

**Meaning.** This short verse closes the sequence of instructions on divorce, waiting periods, dowries, nursing, and support with a reminder about why those rulings have been made plain. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The demonstrative “thus” points first to the preceding explanations: the rights spouses owe one another, the limits on taking a woman back or obstructing her, and the financial duties that remain when a marriage ends. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse is therefore not an additional divorce formula or a new payment rule. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** It directs the reader to understand the guidance already given and to recognize its purpose. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]**

Al-Ṭabarī explains that God has clarified what is incumbent on husbands and wives and what each owes the other. **[Ṭabarī]** The aim is that believers comprehend the divine limits, understand their obligations, and learn what brings well-being in both religious and worldly life. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** He connects this practical knowledge with putting relationships right: when each party knows the other’s claim and fulfils it, disputes need not be settled by force, resentment, or the stronger person’s preference. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The laws are thus not isolated technicalities; they order ordinary family life and protect people whose interests could otherwise be ignored. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

Ibn Kathīr reads “His signs” broadly as the rulings God permits and forbids, the duties He requires, and the boundaries and commands He has made clear. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The clarity matters because people need to distinguish a valid claim from a custom or demand that has no authority. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The preceding verses have repeatedly separated cases that might be confused: a widow’s waiting period is not the same as a year of optional support; a fixed dowry is not the same as a parting gift; and a husband’s right of revocation does not include permission to retain a wife in order to harm her. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Clear distinctions are part of the mercy of law, because they let people know which duties are fixed and where jurists have recorded disagreement. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The verb “understand” (*taʿqilūn*) calls for more than hearing the words. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Saʿdī says the purpose of explanation is that people grasp the rulings, preserve them, comprehend their meaning, and act upon them; he praises the laws for their clarity and their accord with sound reason. **[Saʿdī]** The verse does not invite a person to replace revelation with private preference. **[Ṭabarī]** Rather, reason is exercised by learning what has been disclosed, seeing how the rules fit together, and applying them faithfully to the situation at hand. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The formula “God makes clear His signs” appears in other passages of the Qur’an, so the closing can also carry a general reminder beyond the immediate subject. **[Study Quran]** In this context, however, its first reference is local: the detailed rulings just given are among God’s signs and guidance. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Jalālayn glosses the phrase as God explaining what has just been mentioned so that people may reflect and understand. **[Jalālayn]** The sequence therefore moves from specific legal instructions to a wider habit of thoughtful obedience: believers should not treat the rules as disconnected orders but consider the protection, fairness, and responsibility they establish. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

Because the verse is brief, it should not be made to settle disputes that the preceding commentaries themselves leave open. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The scholars differ on matters such as the legal status of *matāʿ* for every divorced woman, the obligation of a deceased father’s heir to support a nursing child, and whether the optional widow-support provision in 2:240 was abrogated. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The closing call to understand encourages careful attention to those distinctions; it does not require pretending that every juristic question has only one transmitted answer. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** At the same time, disagreement about secondary applications does not cancel the clear ethical demands shared by the sources: do not exploit a spouse, withhold a settled right, or use family power to cause harm. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

Al-Ṭabarī also connects understanding the rulings with the good of both this life and the next. **[Ṭabarī]** Proper knowledge can repair relations between people now, while faithful action earns reward in the return to God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** This places domestic conduct within a larger horizon of accountability. **[Jalālayn]** The same God who clarifies rights sees how they are upheld when there is no public audience, and the believer is asked to carry that awareness into private agreements and difficult separations. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The closing also encourages readers to reason across the cases rather than isolate a sentence from its setting. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The rules have repeatedly guarded against a stronger party manipulating a gap in procedure: a guardian may not obstruct a mutually desired lawful remarriage, parents may not use a child to injure one another, and a husband may not use revocation to prolong harm. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Those examples are drawn from the preceding verses, not added commands in 2:242 itself. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The call to understand asks the reader to notice how clarity about separate cases can preserve fairness in the whole relationship. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]**

**Interpretive note.** The verse summarizes and dignifies the preceding laws; its key emphasis is comprehension that leads to action, not a fresh legal ruling. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** To understand a law is to see both its boundary and the people it protects. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The closing reminder asks readers to bring thoughtfulness, not mere technical compliance, to the rights and responsibilities of family life. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:243

243243
*“Hast thou not considered those who left their homes by the thousands, fearing death? God said to them, ‘Die,’ then revived them. Truly God is Possessed of bounty for mankind, but most of mankind are not thankful.”*

**Meaning.** “Have you not seen?” is understood by the commentators as seeing through knowledge: the Prophet was not an eyewitness to this ancient event, but God made it known to him. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse recounts a people who left their homes in great numbers because they feared death. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** God then caused them to die and restored them to life, making the event a sign of His power over life and death. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The wording does not name the people, their town, the prophet associated with their revival, or the exact danger from which they fled. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The commentators preserve different explanations for why the people left. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Many reports identify an outbreak of plague; others connect their flight with an enemy or with fear of being killed in battle. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The Qur’an itself says only that they feared death, and the next verse’s call to fight makes the possibility of a military context relevant without proving that it was the sole cause. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī transmits the assessment of Ibn ʿAṭiyya that the detailed narrative reports have weak chains, and that the firm point is the Qur’anic account: a people fled death, God caused them to die and then revived them, and the event teaches that life and death are in His hands. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

For that reason, the commentarial details should be kept distinct from the verse. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** Reports give competing totals, locate the event in a particular village, name a prophet such as Ezekiel, or describe angels, scattered bones, and the manner of revival. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** These details are not established by the verse, and some belong to Israelite narrative traditions rather than the Qur’an’s own account. **[Study Quran]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* They may illustrate how later exegetes imagined the event, but they should not be repeated as certain history. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse’s own statement of resurrection is sufficient: the One who brought them back can raise the dead again. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

The story challenges the assumption that flight can guarantee safety from death. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Saʿdī says their escape did not save them from what they feared; the reversal of their intention displays both God’s power and the limits of human control. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]** This is not a command to seek danger or to abandon reasonable precautions. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** The later Prophetic guidance about entering or leaving a plague-stricken land comes through hadith and juristic discussion, not from a blanket rule that can be inferred from this narrative alone. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

*(digression)* Al-Qurṭubī and Maʿārif discuss the Prophetic reports on plague, including the instruction not to enter an affected area and not to flee from it once there; they explain that precaution and belief in divine decree are compatible. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** That legal discussion is significant in its own right, but it should not be confused with the verse’s direct account of the ancient people. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators use the story to frame the next command to fight, not to derive every later rule about illness from this verse. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]**

“God is Possessed of bounty for mankind” includes the revival of the people and the lesson made available to later generations. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** God’s favor is not only the preservation of life; it includes guidance that makes people reflect on mortality and return their hopes and fears to Him. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Yet “most of mankind are not thankful” warns that seeing signs does not automatically produce gratitude. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** Gratitude means acknowledging the gift and using one’s life in obedience, rather than treating survival as something owed or death as something that can be managed by evasion alone. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The placement of the story before “fight in the way of God” gives it a further contextual force. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** It reminds the believers that avoiding a prescribed duty out of fear does not control the appointed end of life, while the example of revival makes the resurrection credible. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that the account functions as a prelude to the command to fight; al-Ṭabarī likewise reads it as encouragement to persist rather than let fear decide obedience. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The lesson is not that every dangerous undertaking is required, but that fear of death alone cannot be treated as proof that one may reject a duty God has actually imposed. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The description “by the thousands” signals a multitude, but the reports disagree widely about the exact count. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī discusses the word *ulūf* as indicating a large number and rejects the need to settle the figure from the competing transmissions. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī records estimates ranging from a few thousand to tens or hundreds of thousands, which is another reason not to turn a disputed number into part of the Qur’anic account. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse’s point does not depend on whether the group numbered four thousand or far more: a crowd cannot evade the power of the One who gives life. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The verse affirms death and revival, while the cause, location, number, and identity of the people remain disputed reports; Qurtubi explicitly cautions that the story’s detailed chains are weak. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The story turns fear of death into reflection on the Giver of life. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Its closing contrast asks whether a person will answer divine favor with gratitude and faithful action, or remain among those who see a sign yet fail to respond. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

## 2:244

244244
*“Fight in the way of God, and know that God is Hearing, Knowing.”*

**Meaning.** The verse moves from the account of people who feared death to a direct command to fight in God’s way. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Most commentators understand the address as directed to the community of Muhammad, not as a command spoken to the revived Israelites. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī argues that the grammar and sequence do not require inserting an unspoken command from God to the ancient people after they were revived. **[Ṭabarī]** The Study Quran records another reading that connects the words to the story, while also explaining the direct-address reading as a general exhortation to believers to struggle for truth. **[Study Quran]**

“In the way of God” defines the purpose of the struggle. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī explains it as fighting in the religion God has guided the believers to, not in service of Satan or some rival aim. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī says the intended purpose is that God’s word be supreme and notes that “God’s ways” can be broad, though the immediate setting is armed fighting. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The phrase prevents the command from being reduced to pursuit of wealth, reputation, revenge, or personal anger. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** It also anchors the verse in its particular revealed context: the passage speaks of a community facing a real call to fight, not of permission for private violence against people unrelated to that conflict. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The order follows a pointed argument: the people in the preceding account could not avoid death merely by fleeing, and the believers are now told not to let fear alone turn them away from a duty. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī warns that those who abandon the encounter may still meet the death they feared, while those who live or die do so within God’s decree. **[Ṭabarī]** This reasoning is not fatalism and does not make prudence blameworthy. **[Qurṭubī]** The same passage elsewhere recognizes concessions in danger, and the commentators distinguish reliance on God from neglecting the means He has permitted. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The immediate rebuke is aimed at letting fear of death nullify an obligation once it has been prescribed. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

“God is Hearing, Knowing” brings both words and inward purpose under divine awareness. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī relates the reminder to the speech of those who claim that people killed in battle would have survived had they stayed home, and to the hidden unbelief or hypocrisy behind such claims. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī likewise says God hears what people say and knows what they intend. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The warning is not merely that public declarations can be overheard; it is that God knows whether a person’s stated courage matches the heart’s intention and subsequent action. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

Al-Saʿdī connects the verse with sincerity: the believer fights so that God’s word is highest, while God hears even an unspoken or concealed statement and knows what the heart contains. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** This knowledge can steady the one who acts sincerely, because the effort is seen and its hardship is not lost. **[Saʿdī]** It also warns against turning a noble cause into a cover for vanity or hostility. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The verse thus joins outward action to inward accountability; neither the act nor the intention is hidden from God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]**

The command also leads naturally into the next verse’s invitation to spend. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Saʿdī observes that the passage joins struggle with the body to expenditure of wealth, since the effort cannot be sustained by courage alone when the needy lack the means to participate. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The following “goodly loan” calls those with resources to support the cause and those in need; verse 244’s call to fight therefore does not isolate the individual combatant from the wider community. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

*(digression)* The commentators debate whether this command is a general address to the Prophet’s community or a continuation of the ancient story, and al-Ṭabarī gives a grammatical argument against the latter. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** That debate affects the immediate historical referent; it does not alter the shared emphasis on devotion to God, sincere purpose, and divine knowledge of words and hearts. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

The Study Quran notes that some readers extend “fight in the way of God” to a moral struggle for truth as well as physical conflict. **[Study Quran]** That wider resonance should not obscure the plain military setting of this passage, where the surrounding verses speak of armies, a river test, and a named enemy. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The command is addressed to the believing community, and al-Qurṭubī records that this is the majority interpretation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The contextual specificity matters: “in God’s way” limits the purpose of the action, and it cannot be detached from the revealed duty and conditions that give it meaning. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The command does not promise that every person who fights will return unharmed, nor does the preceding story promise that every person who avoids a battlefield will live longer. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Its reasoning is about obedience rather than control over outcomes: life and death are God’s, while the believer remains accountable for responding to a duty that has actually been given. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** This is why the reminder that God hears and knows follows the command—the visible act, the words used to excuse retreat, and the inward purpose all belong to the same moral account. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Interpretive note.** The majority reading addresses the Muslim community, while a minority links the command to the Israelites; all readings keep the struggle oriented to God rather than worldly advantage. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks a believer to align public commitment, inner intention, and action. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** To know that God hears and knows is both a warning against evasion and a reassurance that sincere effort is never unseen. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

## 2:245

245245
*“Who is it that will lend God a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him many times over? God withholds and outstretches, and unto Him you shall be returned.”*

**Meaning.** The question is a generous invitation: who will give wealth in God’s cause, trusting that God will repay with far greater reward? **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The expression “lend God” is a metaphor of honor and assurance, not a suggestion that God lacks anything or borrows from creatures out of need. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Everything already belongs to Him; the comparison to a loan assures the giver that what is spent sincerely is not lost but returned as reward in the Hereafter. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]**

The immediate context gives the invitation a practical setting. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The previous verse commands fighting in God’s way; al-Ṭabarī explains that the good loan includes helping a poor believer who wishes to take part but lacks the means, while al-Qurṭubī includes support for the needy and for the defense of the religion. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Saʿdī says the passage brings together bodily effort and expenditure, since both are needed for the community’s work. **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran records several compatible readings: the “loan” may refer to the effort and risk of fighting, to charitable spending, or to both. **[Study Quran]**

A loan is “goodly” when it is offered with a sound intention and a generous heart, directed to a proper need and not followed by reminders, insult, or injury. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī emphasizes that the giver acts in response to God’s invitation and in hope of His reward; the act is obedience, not a service God needs. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Maʿārif similarly explains that “loan” refers to good deeds and spending, while noting a secondary application to a real loan that relieves another person’s need. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse therefore measures generosity not only by the amount given but by the purity of motive and the care taken not to humiliate the recipient. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

“Many times over” leaves the reward in God’s hands rather than promising a fixed worldly return. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī says the multiplication has no stated limit, and Ibn Kathīr connects it with the image in 2:261 of a single grain producing many ears. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The promise is not a contract that the donor will become wealthy immediately or receive a calculable sum in this life. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** It assures the believer that God can multiply the reward according to His wisdom and generosity. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

“God withholds and outstretches” first refers to His control of provision: He narrows or expands what people receive. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The verse answers the fear that spending will necessarily make a giver poor. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The wealthy are tested by whether they assist those in need, while the person whose provision is narrow is also tested in patience and trust. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** That trust does not excuse waste or neglect of dependants; it frees the believer from treating wealth as an independent power that can secure life without God. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The Study Quran also notes a spiritual interpretation of contraction and expansion in the heart, but the ordinary sense of provision remains central in this passage. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]**

The final words, “unto Him shall you be returned,” place both wealth and its use within accountability. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The one who has been given abundance will answer for how it was used, and the one who had little will answer for how he responded to the limits placed upon him. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The return to God is also the horizon in which a gift made now can become an enduring gain, rather than a loss measured only by what left one’s hand. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

*(digression)* Some commentators also connect the word “loan” with lending directly to people in hardship and discuss rules for human loans, including the prohibition on making a stipulated increase a condition of repayment. **[Maʿārif]** **[Qurṭubī]** Those are separate legal discussions; the verse’s metaphor of lending to God should not be confused with an ordinary interest-bearing contract. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The image also supports social solidarity: a person with resources can help someone whose faith and willingness are present but whose means are not. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Al-Ṭabarī mentions assistance with the equipment or conveyance needed for the campaign, while al-Qurṭubī includes generosity toward the poor and needy. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Giving is therefore not merely an inward feeling; it makes another person’s good action possible. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The giver remains responsible for choosing a fitting purpose and treating the recipient with dignity, because an act followed by boasting or injury would contradict the description “goodly.” **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The wording “lend God” also honors the person who receives the gift: the needy believer is not presented as an inconvenient burden but as an occasion through which the giver may seek God’s favor. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī explains that divine speech uses a familiar human image of lending and repayment to draw people toward generosity, while God Himself is free of every need. **[Qurṭubī]** The promise is therefore not an ordinary debt with a due date or a stipulated worldly increase; the promised return belongs to God’s reward and wisdom. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** That assurance invites generosity without turning it into a claim to control when or how God provides. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Interpretive note.** The commentators differ on whether the “loan” is primarily charitable spending, support for struggle, or both; they agree that God is in no need and that sincere giving is rewarded many times over. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The verse turns generosity into trust: wealth is not diminished in the final reckoning when it is given sincerely for a good purpose. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The giver parts with something limited and entrusts its return to the One who controls both scarcity and abundance. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:246

246246
*“Hast thou not considered the assembly of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, ‘Raise up a king for us, and we will fight in the way of God.’ He said, ‘Might it be that, if fighting were prescribed for you, you would not fight?’ They said, ‘Why should we not fight in the way of God, when we have been driven from our homes and our children?’ But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned back, save a few among them. And God knows the wrongdoers.”*

**Meaning.** The verse introduces a story about a people who ask for a king so that they can fight under his leadership. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The word “assembly” (*malāʾ*) points to the influential leaders of the Children of Israel, while the Qur’an leaves their prophet unnamed. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Later reports identify him variously as Samuel, Simeon, or Joshua, but these names are not part of the verse and the commentaries do not agree. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* The story’s teaching does not depend on choosing among those identifications. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]**

The request appears against a background of defeat and dispossession. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The people say that they have been driven from their homes and children; the commentators explain this as their land being taken and family members being carried away or held captive. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī cautions that the wording is collective: the leaders who speak are not necessarily claiming that each one standing there was personally displaced. **[Ṭabarī]** Their stated aim is to fight in God’s way, and the request for a king is also a request for a recognized commander who can gather a divided force and direct its action. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The prophet answers with a question that exposes a gap between desire and commitment: will they still fight if the duty is actually imposed? **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** His warning is not a denial that their grievance is real; it tests whether their words are a settled promise or an expression of anger while defeat remains someone else’s problem. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī explains that the people can imagine battle while speaking from safety, but their resolve may weaken when they must face its risks. **[Qurṭubī]** The narrative thus distinguishes asking for a duty from accepting it once it arrives. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

They respond emphatically: their homes and children have been taken, so what reason would they have not to fight? **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Their answer sounds sincere, and the verse does not suggest that every person who spoke was deliberately lying. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Yet the next clause reveals that their spoken resolve was not enough to carry the whole group through the test. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** When fighting was prescribed, most turned away and only a few remained. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The contrast is one of the passage’s central lessons: a pledge made in anticipation is not the same as obedience when the cost becomes immediate. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The phrase “fighting was prescribed” indicates that the command came from God; it was not simply a king’s private demand or a self-appointed campaign. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The story therefore concerns a revealed duty in a particular historical setting, not a general license for any leader to send people into battle on any pretext. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The stated aim remains “in the way of God,” and the following verse will explain that the king’s authority is itself subject to God’s choice and wisdom. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]**

“God knows the wrongdoers” closes the account with a reminder that outward participation and private intention are both known to Him. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī explains the wrong as breaking the commitment they themselves had asked to undertake; al-Qurṭubī describes the majority as faltering when the reality of war confronted them. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The few who remained are not praised merely for boldness but for keeping faith with a duty they had acknowledged. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The warning also prepares the reader for the later river test, which further distinguishes those who obey from those who seek comfort at the decisive moment. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

The report does not provide enough information to identify every combatant, number the displaced families, or reconstruct the military history. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some commentators preserve extended stories about the prophet and the political history of Israel, but those details are transmitted reports rather than the Qur’an’s stated point. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The passage emphasizes three things that are explicit: the people ask for a leader, they profess willingness to fight, and most retreat when the duty arrives. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]**

The request for a king also has a practical political dimension. **[Saʿdī]** The influential people want one recognized leader so that disputes about command will end and the army can act together. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The story does not treat organization itself as blameworthy; rather, it exposes the hope that a new office or a forceful leader will automatically make a hesitant group courageous. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The warning from the prophet shows that structure cannot replace conviction, and the later retreat confirms that a command is meaningful only when those who sought it are prepared to obey. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The “few” who remain also prepare the reader for the next stage of the story. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī connects them with those who will cross the river with Talut, while the commentators use the subsequent test to show that their number will become smaller still. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse therefore moves from the broad public declaration—“we will fight”—toward a sequence of increasingly concrete tests of loyalty. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Interpretive note.** The prophet’s personal name and the surrounding chronology are disputed in later reports; the Qur’an leaves them unspecified and centers the contrast between professed resolve and actual commitment. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks readers to measure intention by what they are prepared to do when a responsibility becomes real. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** It warns against making a promise in anger or distress and then abandoning it once obedience demands patience and sacrifice. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:247

247247
*“Their prophet said to them, ‘God has appointed Saul as king over you.’ They said, ‘How can he have sovereignty over us when we have more right to sovereignty than he, and he has not been given abundance of wealth?’ He said, ‘Truly God has chosen him over you and has increased him amply in knowledge and body.’ God gives His sovereignty to whomsoever He will, and God is All-Encompassing, Knowing.”*

**Meaning.** The prophet answers the request for a king by announcing that God has appointed Talut, commonly identified in English as Saul. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The people object that he lacks the family standing and wealth they associate with rule. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** In their view, they themselves have a stronger claim to sovereignty; they measure the office by lineage and material abundance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** Their objection reveals how easily people can confuse inherited status with the qualities needed to discharge a public responsibility. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The prophet does not answer by denying that competence matters. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** He gives two qualities named by the verse: Talut has been granted breadth in knowledge and in bodily capacity. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The commentators explain knowledge as sound judgment, understanding of leadership, and—especially in this military context—knowledge of how to direct an army. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Bodily capacity includes strength and endurance useful for command and battle; it is not a command to judge leadership by appearance or size alone. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The story presents relevant ability, not wealth, as the answer to the people’s stated need for a commander. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]**

Al-Qurṭubī draws a broader political lesson from the verse: leadership is not established by ancestry alone, and the qualities of knowledge, religion, and strength are more relevant than family pedigree when judging fitness for office. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** This is an exegetical application of the story, not a complete constitutional code or a claim that every office has identical requirements. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The immediate point is that the Israelites’ preferred candidate cannot displace the one God has chosen and whose qualities suit the task before them. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

“God has chosen him over you” answers the challenge at its root. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The prophet is not claiming to have made the appointment by private preference; he attributes it to God’s choice. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The people’s wealth-based objection assumes that a ruler must be rich enough to establish a household or to display royal prestige. **[Jalālayn]** The verse redirects attention to God’s judgment of what the community needs, and it does not treat riches as proof of merit or poverty as proof of incapacity. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The statement “God gives His sovereignty to whomsoever He will” makes clear that kingship is ultimately not the private property of a lineage. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that the authority belongs to God, who grants it to whom He wills and knows who is fit for the task. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verse can be read as part of the prophet’s reply or as a divine statement reinforcing it; either way, it closes off the claim that ancestry alone can overrule the appointment. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

“God is All-Encompassing, Knowing” balances sovereignty with wisdom. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** His bounty is not exhausted by the family that expects an office, and His knowledge is not limited to public wealth or rank. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** He knows which people and circumstances require a leader with the capacities He has bestowed. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse therefore does not teach that the best leader is necessarily the strongest person or the most learned in every subject; it says that the capacities named here outweigh the people’s objection about fortune and lineage in this particular appointment. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

*(digression)* The commentators discuss whether Talut was a prophet, a king, or a commander appointed for this campaign, and they record different accounts of his occupation and ancestry. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** Those details are not necessary to the Qur’anic argument and should not be stated as certain. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The verse itself identifies the qualifications and the divine appointment; it does not name his trade. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]**

Some commentators report that Talut worked as a water carrier, tanner, or in another ordinary trade, but the accounts vary and the verse itself says only that he lacked abundant wealth. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Those reports should not be used to turn his occupation into a Qur’anic fact. **[Study Quran]** The point of the objection is clearer than the biographical detail: the people take limited wealth as evidence that he cannot rule. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]**

The phrase “in knowledge and body” should likewise be read in relation to the task. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ibn Kathīr includes sound judgment and knowledge of warfare as well as strength and endurance, while al-Qurṭubī notes that the phrase need not mean mere physical bulk. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse thus gives no warrant for choosing a leader by appearance alone; it joins understanding with the capacity to carry responsibility. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** Nor does the passage say that every political appointment is made by a prophet receiving direct revelation: this is the specific story of Talut’s appointment, which the verse explicitly attributes to God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**
