The verse does not condemn wealth itself, nor does it say that a ruler may ignore material capacity. **[Qurṭubī]** Rather, it rejects the assumption that abundance of money is the proof of fitness for this office. **[Ṭabarī]** The qualifications named are attached to the need at hand—knowledge to guide and bodily capacity to lead the force—while God’s choice remains decisive. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** This distinction keeps the passage from being turned into either a celebration of poverty or an endorsement of wealth as the sole test of authority. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The decisive contrast is between worldly criteria of wealth and lineage and the qualities named by revelation—knowledge and bodily capacity suited to the task. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The story challenges the habit of treating inherited position or wealth as a substitute for competence. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** It also warns that the community’s preferences are not a measure of God’s wisdom when a duty and a qualified leader have been made clear. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

## 2:248

248248
*“Their prophet said to them, ‘The sign of his sovereignty is that the ark shall come to you, bearing tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the House of Moses and the House of Aaron left behind, borne by the angels. Truly in that is a sign for you, if you are believers.’”*

**Meaning.** The people have questioned Talut’s appointment; their prophet now points to the return of the ark as a sign confirming the appointment and his own message. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Qur’an calls it *al-tābūt*, “the ark” or “the chest,” and says it will come bearing *sakīna*—tranquility or reassurance from God—and a remnant associated with Moses and Aaron. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** Its arrival is not presented as a substitute for Talut’s qualities; it confirms that the appointment is supported by God. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

Al-Ṭabarī explains *sakīna* through the sense of what settles the heart: a recognized sign in the ark that reassures the Israelites about the truth of their prophet’s statement. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī similarly explains it as something through which their hearts become calm and strengthened. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** Ibn Kathīr records glosses such as grace and mercy, while the Study Quran notes that commentators differ on whether the word refers to an object within the ark or to the tranquility its presence brings. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** These readings need not be forced into a single physical description: the verse’s clear point is that God provides a sign that reassures them and confirms the prophet’s word. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The phrase “a remnant of what the House of Moses and the House of Aaron left behind” is also left open in the Qur’anic text. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Commentators propose such items as Moses’ staff, fragments of the tablets, Torah material, or other sacred belongings, but the lists vary. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī explicitly concludes that the specific contents cannot be established from language alone and that no decisive report fixes the list. **[Ṭabarī]** Accordingly, those itemized descriptions should be treated as reports, not as details guaranteed by the verse. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)*

The same caution applies to the story of how the ark had been taken and returned. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** The commentators preserve elaborate accounts about the ark being captured, placed among idols, associated with illness, or carried back by animals and angels. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran observes that much of the surrounding detail in later commentary resembles Biblical or Talmudic material and is not narrated in the Qur’an. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī reports different explanations of “borne by the angels,” including direct carrying and angels directing the animals that draw it, but he favors the direct sense of the wording. **[Ṭabarī]** The disagreement shows why the verse’s statement—“borne by the angels”—should be distinguished from the many reported scenes used to imagine how it happened. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)*

The sign also responds to the people’s request for confirmation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** They had challenged the prophet’s announcement of Talut’s kingship; the ark’s return gives them a visible sign that the appointment is not a private preference. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The phrase “if you are believers” is understood as an invitation to accept the sign when it arrives, not a claim that the people’s earlier objection was itself a proof of faith. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The sign addresses their doubt about the prophet’s report and the authority of the king. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The ark’s meaning is therefore more than antiquarian curiosity. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** It represents a continuity with the sacred history of Moses and Aaron, and the return of something associated with them can settle the people’s hearts at a moment when they have disputed the legitimacy of their new leader. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** Yet the verse does not teach that a relic independently grants victory or that possession of a sacred object excuses disobedience. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** In the surrounding story, trust in God, obedience, and patience remain essential; the next verses will test the army’s willingness to follow the command. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]**

Al-Ṭabarī points out that the definite phrase “the ark” suggests an object already known to the Israelites, not an unfamiliar box whose identity is being introduced for the first time. **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators report that it had been associated with earlier generations and carried before an army, and that its loss marked a period of defeat; these are transmitted details surrounding the verse, not a chronology stated in it. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Study Quran cautions that much of the expanded story appears to draw on Biblical or Talmudic lore, so the safer reading stays with the Qur’an’s own claim that its return is a sign. **[Study Quran]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)*

The different explanations of *sakīna* also show why it is better to preserve the semantic center than to insist on one reported object. **[Ṭabarī]** Some reports imagine a spirit or unusual presence in the ark; other exegetes understand the term as reassurance, a recognized sign that calms the people. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* Al-Ṭabarī prefers the sense of something to which their hearts become settled, and says the various reported signs could all explain that effect without establishing one as certain. **[Ṭabarī]** This lets the verse speak of divine reassurance without turning a disputed description into doctrine. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The verse also does not require the reader to identify the ark with every later description of the Ark of the Covenant. **[Study Quran]** It gives the name, its signifying role, the tranquility associated with it, and the remnant connected with Moses and Aaron; it leaves the physical dimensions, precise contents, and route of return unstated. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The commentaries’ competing lists themselves demonstrate that those particulars were not securely fixed in the transmitted material. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** By preserving that boundary, the reading honors the verse’s claim without making the believer dependent on speculative history. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

**Interpretive note.** The verse clearly states the ark’s role as a sign and its association with tranquility and a remnant from Moses and Aaron; the precise objects and return narrative are disputed reports, often drawn from Israelite traditions. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** A sign can restore confidence, but confidence must lead to obedience rather than fascination with the sign itself. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The passage invites the reader to receive what God has made clear while remaining cautious about details the revelation leaves unstated. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:249

249249
*“When Saul set out with the hosts, he said, ‘God will test you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever tastes it not is of me, save one who takes a handful in his hand.’ But they drank from it, save a few among them. When he crossed it, he and those who believed with him, they said, ‘We have no power today against Goliath and his hosts.’ Those who knew they would meet God said, ‘How many a small company has overcome a large company by God’s leave! And God is with the patient.’”*

**Meaning.** After Talut leads the army out, he announces a test at a river. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The soldiers may not drink freely; a person who refrains remains with Talut, while a limited handful is permitted. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The exception matters: the trial is not a demand to ignore thirst completely, but a boundary testing whether the army can obey a command when water is immediately available. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The phrase “is not of me” is explained by al-Qurṭubī as meaning not of Talut’s company for this campaign, not as a declaration that every soldier who drinks has left the faith. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The test distinguishes who will follow the king’s instruction under pressure; it should not be expanded into a general prohibition on drinking water. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The permission to take one handful shows that a measured concession can coexist with a real command. **[Jalālayn]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The commentators discuss whether *ghurfa* means the act of scooping once or the small amount held in the hand, but both readings preserve the limit. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Qur’anic emphasis is not on an exact measurement in modern units; it distinguishes restraint from unbounded drinking. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Saʿdī explains the test as a means of separating the patient from the one whose desire overwhelms obedience, while Maʿārif emphasizes that steadfastness under a small, immediate trial prepares a person for the larger test of battle. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

Most of the army drink from the river, and only a few comply. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The sources preserve different reports about how many crossed with Talut and whether those who drank more than the permitted handful initially crossed before some withdrew. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some reports compare the faithful group with the number of the fighters at Badr, but the Qur’anic wording itself gives no total. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** It is safer to keep the focus on the contrast between obedience and excess rather than turn a transmitted number into a certainty. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ṭabarī]**

After the river, the words “We have no power today against Goliath and his hosts” express the army’s awareness of the enemy’s strength. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The commentators differ over whether these words came from those who had already failed the river test, from believers whose confidence still wavered, or from a group that later turned back. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Saʿdī preserves more than one possibility, while the Study Quran notes that those who were certain of meeting God answer with the reminder about the small company. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The narrative does not require us to pretend that every believer feels no fear; it shows how conviction can answer fear with trust and resolve. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]**

The response, “How many a small company has overcome a large company by God’s leave,” refuses to treat numbers as the final measure of success. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The phrase “by God’s leave” is essential: it does not promise that every smaller force will automatically win, but locates victory within divine permission and support. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** “God is with the patient” then identifies the quality required of the group—steadfast obedience, not merely confidence in its own strength. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

*(digression)* The Study Quran compares the river test with Gideon’s test in Judges, but describes the relationship as typological rather than a historical identification. **[Study Quran]** Later descriptions of the river’s exact location and the army’s totals likewise come from commentarial reports, not from the wording of the Qur’an. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The wording marks the test at several levels: a person who “drinks” freely is excluded, while the one who does not even “taste” the water is counted with Talut, except for the permitted scoop. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī notes that the wording makes even a small taste relevant to the order, while the exception preserves a narrow allowance. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** This is why the verse is not about whether water is ordinarily lawful or whether thirsty people should generally be denied relief; it is about a specific test announced by the commander on a particular march. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The commentaries also differ on the sequence after the test. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī’s preferred reading allows that some who drank more than the permitted amount crossed the river with Talut but later fell away when they saw Goliath’s force; al-Qurṭubī reports that many commentators identify those who crossed as the ones who had refrained. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The distinction affects who first said “We have no power,” but it does not alter the moral progression: the river exposes one level of resolve, and the sight of the enemy exposes another. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The text’s own sequence should be respected without forcing the competing reports into a single exact headcount. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The allowance of a handful keeps the test from being a demand for needless hardship. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The sources explain that the small amount was enough to ease thirst, while unrestricted drinking would show that the soldiers had put immediate desire ahead of the instruction they had received. **[Maʿārif]** **[Jalālayn]** In that sense, the measure is intentionally modest: the point is not to prove who can suffer the most, but who can keep a limit when an easy excess is within reach. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources agree that the river tests obedience and that only a small number remain steadfast; they differ over the precise number who crossed and who voiced the initial fear. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The small test of a handful of water anticipates the larger test of standing before an overwhelming army. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** The passage locates strength not in thirst, numbers, or equipment alone, but in disciplined obedience and patience under God’s command. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:250

250250
*“When they came forth against Goliath and his hosts, they said, ‘Our Lord, pour out patience upon us, make our feet firm, and help us against the disbelieving people.’”*

**Meaning.** The verse follows the river test with the moment the faithful group comes face to face with Goliath and his army. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** They do not begin by boasting about their courage; they turn to God in supplication. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** Their prayer has three linked requests: abundant patience, firmness in the encounter, and victory over the hostile force. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

“Pour out patience upon us” asks God to grant steadfastness in abundance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verb evokes a flow or outpouring, as if patience is a gift the believers need God to send down upon them when their own strength is not enough. **[Jalālayn]** **[Qurṭubī]** The prayer does not deny fear; it acknowledges the danger and asks for the inward capacity to meet it without abandoning obedience. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** In the preceding verse, the believers have already resisted the comfort of drinking freely and answered discouragement with trust; now the test moves from self-restraint to endurance in battle. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

“Make our feet firm” is explained as a request that their hearts be strengthened so their bodies do not flee. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The phrase joins inward resolve to outward steadiness: courage is not a boast but the ability to remain in the place where duty has put the believers. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** Their feet are not made firm by their own numbers or confidence; they ask God for help against panic and weakness. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The final request, “help us against the disbelieving people,” locates victory with God rather than with the army’s size. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** In the story, the enemy is Goliath and his force, and the prayer is made in the setting of a specific battle. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** It should not be detached from that context and turned into a general license to attack people outside the conflict described. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]** The believers ask for aid in a struggle they understand as being in God’s way, consistent with the command and purpose of the preceding verses. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]**

The prayer also demonstrates that trust and practical effort belong together. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The faithful have crossed the river, followed their leader, and reached the enemy; at the moment of encounter they still ask God for patience and aid. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Their supplication is neither passivity nor self-reliance. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** It recognizes that action is required while the result remains beyond human control. **[Saʿdī]** **[Jalālayn]**

The next verse reports that God granted them victory by His leave. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** That sequence links supplication to the outcome, but it should not be read as a formula promising that any person who recites these words will obtain a specific worldly victory. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse presents the prayer of this faithful group in this historical encounter; its broader lesson is how believers ask for the qualities needed to obey under pressure. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

*(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* Later accounts add details about the weapon David used to kill Goliath and about promises made to him by Talut. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Those details belong to reports about the subsequent event, not to the words of this prayer, and should not be represented as part of 2:250. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The Qur’anic focus here is the believers’ plea for patience, firmness, and divine help. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]**

The collective “they said” also highlights the role of shared supplication. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Their faith is not only an individual feeling; the small company asks together for a steadiness that will allow them to remain a community under strain. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The prayer transforms their awareness of being outnumbered into dependence on God, without concealing the seriousness of the danger. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

The opening verb, “they came forth” (*barazū*), is explained as their appearing in the open ground before the enemy. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** This is the moment when danger is no longer imagined at a distance: the two forces stand in view of one another, and the believers respond by asking for help rather than boasting about their strength. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]**

The three requests form a progression. **[Saʿdī]** First, they ask for patience to endure; then for firmness so that fear does not turn into retreat; finally, for victory that only God can grant. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The prayer does not ask that the enemy disappear or that the believers be excused from acting. **[Qurṭubī]** It asks for the inner and outward steadiness needed to fulfil the responsibility before them. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The next verse reports that they overcame their opponents by God’s leave, preserving the distinction between the believers’ effort and the source of victory. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The outcome therefore does not make the prayer an incantation with a guaranteed result in every later conflict. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** It shows how this group understood its dependence: they prepared, faced the enemy, and asked God to grant what their own resources could not secure. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The first request, for patience, concerns endurance through the trial; the second, for firm feet, asks that endurance remain steady when movement or retreat becomes possible. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The third request seeks help beyond what either quality can guarantee on its own. **[Saʿdī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The prayer thus moves from the inner capacity to persist, to the outward act of standing firm, to the result entrusted to God. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The verse records the prayer of the believers at the encounter: patience, firmness, and help from God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The prayer asks not merely for escape from hardship but for the strength to remain faithful within it. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Patience steadies the heart, firmness steadies the feet, and trust gives the community a direction beyond fear. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:251

251251
*“So they routed them by God’s leave, and David slew Goliath; and God gave him kingship and wisdom, and taught him of that which He willed. And were it not for God’s repelling some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted; but God is bounteous to the worlds.”*

**Meaning.** The preceding prayer for patience, firm footing, and victory is followed by its answer: the smaller company defeats Goliath’s force by God’s leave. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The text attributes the outcome to divine support rather than to a numerical advantage or to the soldiers’ independent power. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** “By God’s leave” does not turn the battle into a guarantee that every small force will prevail; it tells the reader how this particular victory is understood within the story. **[Saʿdī]** The verse’s sequence keeps together human action, prayer, and reliance upon God without confusing them. **[Saʿdī]**

The verse names David as the one who slew Goliath but does not describe the weapon, the manner of the encounter, or David’s age and occupation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Later reports tell of a sling, stones, a shepherd’s bag, a special stone, a promised marriage, and other dramatic details. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Some of these accounts are expressly described as Israelite material, and others belong to narrative reports rather than the Qur’anic wording; they should not be repeated as settled history. **[Ibn Kathīr]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* The secure point is the one the verse itself makes: David killed Goliath, and the result came within God’s decree. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]**

The next clause moves from the battlefield event to David’s later gifts: kingship and *ḥikmah*, often rendered wisdom. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Kathīr understands the kingship as the authority previously held by Talut, and the wisdom as prophethood; other commentators speak more broadly of the knowledge and judgment God bestowed upon David. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse does not give a timetable for the transfer of authority, nor does it name the prophet who had appointed Talut. **[Ṭabarī]** It presents David’s public authority and divine gift of wisdom together, without making political inheritance, family status, or wealth the criterion of God’s favor. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]**

The words “and taught him of that which He willed” leave the teaching open rather than providing an inventory. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Later commentators associate David with useful knowledge, sound judgment, eloquence, the craft of making coats of mail, or other gifts mentioned elsewhere in the Qur’an. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** These can illuminate the broad phrase, but none should be made into a complete list of what the verse means. **[Saʿdī]** The wording directs attention to God as the giver and to the scope of His will, not to speculative biography. **[Saʿdī]** It also places David’s success within a sequence of gifts: victory, authority, wisdom, and knowledge are all received rather than self-originated. **[Ṭabarī]**

The general statement about God’s repelling people through others broadens the story beyond the two armies. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** In the immediate context, the defeat of Goliath’s force prevents its domination of the Israelites; other commentators extend the principle to the way God checks oppression and corruption through the presence and actions of different groups. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse does not say that every conflict is righteous or that every victor has divine approval in every act. Its stated point is that without God’s restraining one group through another, corruption would spread through the earth. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr connects the formulation with the later verse about protecting houses of worship from destruction, showing that the principle can include the preservation of places where God is remembered. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The clause “but God is bounteous to the worlds” interprets this restraint as favor. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** It is not only the combatants who benefit when destructive power is checked; the wider community is spared the consequences of unchecked harm. **[Saʿdī]** The verse therefore does not celebrate violence for its own sake. It frames the particular victory as one instance of a larger providential ordering in which power is checked and communal life is protected. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** The exact social or political forms through which this occurs can differ; the Qur’anic statement is general, and the specific outcome in this passage remains God’s deliverance of Talut’s company. **[Ṭabarī]**

This verse closes a narrative sequence that has tested the people at several stages: they requested a king, disputed Talut’s appointment, faced the river, and then confronted a formidable enemy. **[Saʿdī]** **[Saʿdī]** The few who persevere are not described as flawless or self-sufficient; their prayer in 2:250 asked for the patience and firmness they needed. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Ṭabarī]** The conclusion thus places steadfastness beside divine aid: obedience and courage matter, but the victory is still “by God’s leave.” **[Qurṭubī]** The narrative gives readers a way to understand the relation between effort and outcome without pretending that strength, weapons, or numbers alone settle the matter. **[Saʿdī]**

**Cross-reference.** The wording about God checking one people by another is echoed in 22:40, where the same principle is linked to the protection of monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques. **[Ibn Kathīr]** That parallel helps explain why the verse moves from a historical battle to a statement about the earth more generally. **[Qurṭubī]** The next verse calls this account among God’s signs and links its truthful recitation to the Prophet’s mission. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

The wording “God’s repelling” has more than one authorized reading in the exegetical tradition: one form emphasizes God’s act of repelling, while another can express defense or mutual resistance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī treats the readings as converging in meaning, since God’s defense of one group can occur through the actions of another. **[Ṭabarī]** This linguistic point reinforces the theological point without requiring a reader to imagine that human agents operate independently of divine will. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]**

**Reflection.** The story asks readers to distinguish firm resolve from self-congratulation. **[Saʿdī]** The people pray, stand, and act, yet they credit God for the victory and recognize that their strength is not self-sufficient. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The broader statement invites a sober gratitude for the restraints that keep oppression from becoming universal, while warning against assuming that worldly power is proof of moral right. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]**

## 2:252

252252
*“These are the signs of God that We recite unto thee in truth, and thou art indeed among the messengers.”*

**Meaning.** “These” points back to the signs and events just recounted, especially the history of the Israelites and Talut’s company in the preceding verses. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī reads the reference across the connected account, from the people who fled death through the appointment of Talut and the defeat of Goliath. **[Ṭabarī]** The verse is therefore not an unrelated formula inserted after a battle story; it tells the audience how to receive the account that has just ended. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

Calling these events God’s “signs” means that they are proofs and indications, not simply entertaining episodes about the past. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Their truth, the pattern of divine help, and the way the story is recited all contribute to the verse’s argument. **[Qurṭubī]** The wording “We recite unto thee” places the Prophet as recipient of revelation rather than as a witness who personally observed the events. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** Maʿārif specifically treats the accurate reporting of this history as evidence of prophethood, since the Prophet was not learning it from the prior scriptures or from an eyewitness to the events. **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī likewise argues that the account is not a fabrication or a recitation taken from books; it is presented as God’s proof against those who knew the earlier scriptural histories. **[Ṭabarī]**

The phrase “in truth” qualifies both the content and its manner of transmission. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** It asserts that the revelation is truthful, not that every expanded story later attached to the passage has the same status. **[Study Quran]** That distinction matters here because commentaries preserve many details about Talut, David, and Goliath that the Qur’an itself does not narrate. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** A reader may learn that such reports exist, but should not confuse them with the revealed account that the verse calls true. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse’s claim is strongest when its limit is respected: the Qur’an confirms the events it states, while further particulars must be assessed separately. **[Study Quran]**

“And thou art indeed among the messengers” directly affirms Muhammad’s prophetic office. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The emphatic form answers those who denied that he was sent by God, and it follows naturally from the preceding phrase: God is the one reciting these signs to him. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Maʿārif links this verse with the next, which continues to speak of the messengers and of differences among their communities. **[Maʿārif]** Together, the verses offer reassurance in the face of rejection without implying that every community accepted its messenger. **[Study Quran]**

The account’s relevance is not exhausted by proving that the Prophet had access to otherwise hidden history. **[Saʿdī]** The preceding verses have shown claims to authority being tested, the difference between resolve and retreat, and a small group’s dependence on God. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Saʿdī draws practical lessons for the community from the sequence, but the verse’s immediate assertion remains that God’s revelation is true and that Muhammad belongs to the messengers. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ṭabarī]** The narration also encourages reflection on earlier prophetic communities, whose experiences can console later believers facing opposition. **[Study Quran]**

There is a difference between the historical claim made by the Qur’an and a modern demand for an exhaustive chronicle. **[Study Quran]** The verses provide enough to establish their moral and theological point: God appoints, tests, supports, and judges; human groups respond differently. **[Ṭabarī]** The names and numbers that are not given, the exact chronology, and the mechanics of every reported episode are not necessary to understand this affirmation. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** The lack of such detail does not weaken the verse’s claim; it keeps the reader’s attention on its signification rather than on speculative reconstruction. **[Saʿdī]**

The opening “these” can also be heard as a transition from this particular history toward the wider account of messengers in 2:253. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** The Prophet is told that what is being recited is a divine sign and that he is one of those sent to deliver God’s message. **[Ṭabarī]** It is not a claim that the community will never face disagreement: the following verse explicitly says that communities differed after clear proofs had come. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The affirmation of prophethood and the reality of human rejection therefore stand together in the passage. **[Qurṭubī]**

**Cross-reference.** The next verse continues with “those messengers,” while 3:44 and 12:102 similarly identify knowledge of past events as revelation rather than personal observation. **[Study Quran]** The specific cross-references are explanatory parallels; the claim in this verse itself is already complete in its assertion of truthful recitation and prophetic mission. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The verse also distinguishes revelation from mere access to old historical material. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī emphasizes that Muhammad was not a reader of the earlier books and did not witness these events, so their truthful narration is evidence for the source he names: God. **[Ṭabarī]** Maʿārif makes a similar argument about the story’s unexpected appearance in the Qur’an. **[Maʿārif]** This claim is about the Qur’an’s authority, not an invitation to judge every later retelling by the same standard. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The revelation itself is the criterion against which extra narrative additions must be weighed. **[Qurṭubī]**

The demonstrative opening also binds the evidence to the text just heard: “these” signs are the ones God is now reciting, not a set of independent legends that readers must recover elsewhere. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** The affirmation of the Prophet’s mission is thus joined to the act of recitation itself. **[Maʿārif]**

**Reflection.** A revealed narrative is meant to guide as well as inform. **[Saʿdī]** The verse invites the reader to hear history as a sign of God’s power and as a source of moral instruction, while keeping the line clear between the Qur’anic account and later embellishment. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Its final assurance reminds a messenger and a community that rejection by some listeners does not invalidate the truth of the message. **[Maʿārif]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

## 2:253

253253
*“Those messengers: We favored some of them above others. Among them are those to whom God spoke, and some He raised in ranks. We gave Jesus son of Mary clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. Had God willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them; but they differed, some believing and some disbelieving. Had God willed, they would not have fought one another; but God does what He wills.”*

**Meaning.** The verse affirms distinctions among messengers without withdrawing the shared prophetic dignity of them all. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Qur’an elsewhere commands belief in all God’s messengers and forbids rejecting some while accepting others; the distinction here concerns the favors and particular missions God gave, not a permission to despise any prophet. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī reconciles the verse with reports warning against ranking prophets by distinguishing God’s revealed preference from boastful comparisons made in argument. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The text does not offer a complete ranking or name every messenger who received a particular degree. **[Ṭabarī]**

“Among them are those to whom God spoke” is commonly understood as referring especially to Moses, whom God addressed directly. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The mention is one example of divine favor, not a statement that other prophets were excluded from revelation or that their prophethood was lesser in its essential truth. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī identifies Moses as the one spoken to in this clause; commentators also discuss whether other forms of divine address belong within its wider wording. **[Ṭabarī]** The following phrase, “some He raised in ranks,” is explained in different ways, including the special station and universal mission of Muhammad. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Such explanations illuminate the phrase without requiring the reader to infer a single exhaustive list from the verse. **[Qurṭubī]**

The verse then singles out Jesus son of Mary, to whom God gave clear proofs and whom He strengthened with the Holy Spirit. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The proofs are understood to include the signs associated with his mission, such as healing the blind and the leper and raising the dead by God’s permission. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** These are signs of Jesus’ prophetic commission, not independent powers that displace God as their source. **[Maʿārif]** The common identification of the Holy Spirit here is Gabriel, who supported Jesus; al-Saʿdī also prefers an interpretation involving the spirit of faith, while acknowledging the Gabriel reading. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** The Study Quran notes wider exegetical possibilities for the term across the Qur’an, so a commentary should not make one lexical gloss erase the interpretive history. **[Study Quran]**

The second half turns from prophetic distinction to communal conflict. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Clear proofs have been brought, yet those who came after the messengers did not respond uniformly: some believed and some disbelieved, and disagreements led to fighting. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Ṭabarī takes “those after them” broadly as the communities who followed the messengers, while reports also single out those after Moses and Jesus. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse does not specify one single war or one unbroken episode; it describes a recurring pattern in which revelation is followed by divergent human responses. **[Study Quran]**

The repeated “had God willed, they would not have fought” recognizes God’s power over history. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** It does not teach that fighting is morally approved simply because it occurred, nor does it say that divine guidance was unclear. The same passage says that proofs had come and that people differed in belief and disbelief. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Saʿdī reads the verse as affirming that God’s will governs causes and outcomes; the Study Quran places it among Qur’anic passages discussing why humanity is not made into one community by compulsion. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** This explanation preserves both divine sovereignty and the moral weight the text gives to belief, rejection, and conflict. **[Qurṭubī]**

The verse can comfort the Prophet as well as teach about earlier generations. **[Maʿārif]** The rejection he faced was not proof that his message lacked evidence; the earlier messengers also encountered communities divided in their response. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** This reading echoes 2:252, where the truthful account is itself presented as a sign of Muhammad’s mission. **[Maʿārif]** The consolation is not that opposition is harmless, but that the messenger’s responsibility is to convey what God reveals while the outcome remains within God’s will. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

The verse begins with “those messengers,” linking it to the previous affirmation that Muhammad is among the messengers and widening the horizon beyond the story of Talut. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** Its grammar groups prophets together before distinguishing particular favors; this order guards against reading special gifts as a separation from the common prophetic call to worship God. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The verse also repeats the possibility that God could have prevented fighting, which emphasizes that the conflicts were not beyond His power. **[Ṭabarī]** Repetition is not an endorsement of conflict but a reminder that the history of disagreement unfolds within divine sovereignty. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]**

The verse does not ask the audience to settle every theological question about comparative rank before understanding its immediate message. **[Study Quran]** It teaches that God’s favor is not distributed in identical forms: one prophet may receive direct speech, another a distinctive sign, another a wider mission, and another a particular form of support. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The source of these distinctions is God’s wisdom, not human speculation about hidden degrees. **[Saʿdī]** Reverence for the whole prophetic line remains essential even when the Qur’an names specific favors. **[Maʿārif]**

This is why the verse can speak of preference and still be followed by a command to believe in all messengers: differences in honor and mission do not create different sources of truth. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]**

**Interpretive note.** The ranking of messengers concerns God-given favors, missions, signs, and stations; it does not cancel the duty to believe in all prophets. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Holy Spirit is most often identified here with Gabriel, though Saʿdī records and prefers a faith-related reading. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** Knowing that earlier communities differed should make believers neither surprised by disagreement nor careless about truth. **[Maʿārif]** The verse holds together reverence for all messengers, gratitude for particular divine gifts, and recognition that people remain responsible for how they respond to clear guidance. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:254

254254
*“O you who believe, spend of that which We have provided you before a day comes when there will be no sale, no friendship, and no intercession. The disbelievers—they are the wrongdoers.”*

**Meaning.** The address “O you who believe” turns from the history of conflict to a command for the believing community. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** “Spend of that which We have provided you” presents wealth as a provision entrusted by God, from which people are to give before the opportunity for action ends. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī includes both obligatory dues and charitable spending, while al-Qurṭubī reports that some authorities understood the verse as zakat and others as encompassing both zakat and voluntary giving. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Saʿdī stresses that the phrase “of what We have provided” implies giving part rather than surrendering everything. **[Saʿdī]**

The immediate context has led some commentators to connect the spending especially with supporting the struggle described in the preceding verses. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī records this contextual reading and notes that expenditure could be obligatory when the duty is specifically required and voluntary in other circumstances. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī also mentions spending in God’s cause, giving charity to people in need, and paying what God has made due. **[Ṭabarī]** The broader wording, however, is not limited to one transaction or one historical battle; al-Saʿdī understands it to encourage spending along all good paths. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The interpretive range should be preserved rather than reducing the command either to a single military levy or to an unspecified act of generosity alone. **[Jalālayn]**

The deadline is “before a day comes” on which the familiar means of earthly exchange no longer function. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** A person cannot buy another chance to perform the neglected duty, trade for a better standing, or use wealth as a ransom in the manner of this world. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The commentators explain that the Day is the Day of Resurrection, when the period of action and earning has passed. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** This urgency is not an instruction to give recklessly; it is a reminder not to postpone the good one is able and obligated to do. **[Saʿdī]**

“No friendship” means that worldly affection or alliance cannot, by itself, rescue a person from accountability. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** It does not deny that righteous believers love one another or that companionship matters in this life; it denies that a friend can independently cancel God’s judgment. **[Qurṭubī]** The Study Quran connects the verse with other descriptions of worldly friends becoming unable to help, and with the statement that friends on that Day will be enemies except the God-fearing. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī likewise says the verse’s warning about friendship and intercession is especially directed to those who reject God, since the Qur’an elsewhere affirms righteous companionship. **[Ṭabarī]**

The mention of “no intercession” must also be read with the Qur’an’s other statements that intercession occurs only by God’s permission. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** The verse rules out a guaranteed or independent advocate whom a person can rely on as though intercession were a purchasable right. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī says the general wording is directed in this context to disbelievers, while believers may intercede for one another by God’s leave. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** Ibn Kathīr emphasizes that no one can ransom the self or rely on mere kinship to avoid the Day’s reckoning. **[Ibn Kathīr]** This qualification avoids treating the verse as a denial of every form of intercession affirmed elsewhere. **[Qurṭubī]**

“The disbelievers—they are the wrongdoers” closes with a statement about those who reject God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains their wrong as putting denial and disobedience where faith and obedience belong; the injustice is not in God’s judgment but in their own response to His provision and command. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The emphasis does not label every person who has ever delayed a donation a disbeliever; rather, it identifies the ultimate wrong of meeting God in rejection. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Saʿdī links the injustice to using God’s gifts for rebellion rather than for the purpose of worship and gratitude. **[Saʿdī]**

This command echoes the earlier description of believers who spend from what God has provided them and recalls the “good loan” image in 2:245. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** Giving is possible because God first gives; spending is thus an act of gratitude and preparation, not a payment that places God in debt. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī notes how the surrounding passages join the themes of fighting and spending, while the verse’s broader language remains applicable to charitable obligations and voluntary good. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]**

The three negatives have also been read with slightly different grammatical forms in canonical recitation: some readings make the nouns categorical, while others present them as statements about the Day. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** The difference does not change the main warning: worldly trade, friendship, and self-appointed advocacy cannot serve as an escape from judgment. **[Qurṭubī]** It is useful to preserve this distinction between what cannot be purchased or demanded and what God may permit by His mercy. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]**

The command’s position after the story of Talut gives the warning a practical edge: a community may be called to spend from its resources as well as to show courage. **[Maʿārif]** Yet al-Saʿdī’s reading preserves the broader scope, since the verse does not name only one recipient or one kind of expenditure. **[Saʿdī]** The reader is not told to give away all possessions; the limiting phrase “of that which We have provided you” keeps the command tied to responsible use of a gift. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks what should be done while action is still possible. **[Saʿdī]** Its warning is sober, but its form is also generous: the wealth being spent is described as something God has already provided, and only “some” of it is requested. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The reader is invited to combine timely giving with humility, remembering that neither wealth nor social connection can replace faith and obedience. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Qurṭubī]**

## 2:255

255255
*“God—there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting. Slumber does not seize Him, nor sleep. To Him belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth. Who is it that intercedes with Him save by His leave? He knows what lies before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge save what He wills. His Kursī encompasses the heavens and the earth, and preserving them wearies Him not. He is the High, the Great.”*

**Meaning.** This verse, known as the Verse of the Throne, gathers a series of affirmations about God’s unique divinity, life, sustaining power, knowledge, authority, and transcendence. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The opening “God—there is no god but He” excludes any rival object of worship; “the Living” and “the Self-Subsisting” describe the One whose life is not dependent on another and upon whom all else depends. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Saʿdī reads the names as establishing both the perfection of God’s attributes and the need of creation for His continuous care. **[Saʿdī]**

“Slumber does not seize Him, nor sleep” denies any interruption or fatigue in divine governance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** Human beings need rest because they are limited; God’s sustaining of creation is not interrupted when creatures sleep. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The phrase is not a comparison that makes God a body subject to human needs. It negates such limitation and affirms that His care is unceasing. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** The two terms are often explained as lesser drowsiness and full sleep, but their paired force is clear even without reconstructing a physical image. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]**

“To Him belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth” grounds the following mention of intercession in God’s ownership. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** No creature possesses an independent claim over God or can intervene against His will. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The rhetorical question—who intercedes except by His leave?—does not deny the possibility of intercession altogether; it denies that any intercessor acts autonomously. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī treats intercession as a favor God grants, not a power that forces His hand. **[Qurṭubī]** The order of the verse is important: sovereignty belongs to God first, and any permitted intercession is therefore subordinate to His judgment. **[Saʿdī]**

God knows what lies before and behind those who are addressed, while they grasp nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The commentators explain “before” and “behind” in several ways, including what is ahead and what has passed, or what is hidden from creatures and what they can observe. **[Qurṭubī]** The shared point is that divine knowledge encompasses all realities, whereas human knowledge is limited and granted. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Saʿdī]** This statement gives a further reason no one can presume to intercede or judge independently: God’s knowledge is complete, and every creature’s understanding is partial. **[Maʿārif]**

The word *Kursī* has been explained in more than one way. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some commentators transmit the view that it is a created footstool encompassing the heavens and earth; others discuss it as a figure for knowledge or divine authority. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Because the exegetes transmit differing explanations and discuss reports of unequal strength, the verse should not be used to assert a detailed cosmological picture as though its precise nature were agreed upon. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The secure meaning is that the *Kursī* is associated with a vast encompassing that underscores God’s majesty and the smallness of creation before Him. **[Maʿārif]** **[Saʿdī]**

“Preserving them wearies Him not” returns the reader to the opening description of God as Living and Self-Subsisting. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The heavens and the earth do not burden or exhaust Him; their continued existence depends on His sustaining power. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** The statement can be understood without imagining that God’s preservation resembles the tiring work of a creature. It denies weakness and affirms effortless sovereignty. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** The final names “the High, the Great” reinforce transcendence and majesty, closing the verse with the supremacy already implied throughout. **[Ṭabarī]**

A report about Moses and two jars is sometimes mentioned in discussions of this verse, but Qurṭubī calls that report unsound. **[Qurṭubī]** It is not needed to explain the verse and should be omitted from the account of its meaning. **[Qurṭubī]** *(weak)* More generally, reports that attempt to map the *Kursī* in exact physical dimensions or to describe divine attributes in human terms must not be promoted beyond what the sources establish. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse’s language affirms God’s incomparable sovereignty; it does not authorize speculative descriptions of His essence. **[Saʿdī]**

The verse also gives a foundation for trust. **[Saʿdī]** If God is the One who sustains all that exists, whose knowledge encompasses what creatures cannot know, and whose preservation is never weary, then worship and reliance belong to Him alone. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The preceding verse urged spending before the Day when worldly support fails; this verse identifies the Lord whose knowledge, permission, and authority govern that Day. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**

The verse’s progression is itself instructive. **[Qurṭubī]** It first names God’s life and sustaining power, then denies interruption, establishes universal ownership, limits intercession by permission, describes the contrast between divine and human knowledge, and concludes with encompassing majesty and effortless preservation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The sequence makes clear that no created being, even one granted an honored role, can rival God’s sovereignty. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]** The final pair of names, the High and the Great, gathers these claims into an affirmation of transcendence rather than a picture of spatial limitation. **[Saʿdī]**

Each clause also limits a different kind of imagined independence: no drowsiness interrupts divine care, no creature owns what exists, no intercessor acts without leave, and no created knowledge rivals God’s. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** This cumulative structure makes the closing statement about God’s greatness a conclusion supported by the whole verse rather than an isolated epithet. **[Qurṭubī]**

**Reflection.** The verse begins by removing rivals, proceeds by denying limitation, and ends with transcendence. **[Qurṭubī]** The reader is invited to seek help from God without treating intercession, knowledge, or worldly power as independent from Him. **[Saʿdī]** Its immense scope is paired with restraint: many details are discussed by commentators, but the central theological claim is clear and sufficient without speculative elaboration. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]**

## 2:256

256256
*“There is no compulsion in religion; right guidance has become distinct from error. So whosoever disbelieves in false gods and believes in God has grasped the firmest handhold, which never breaks. God is Hearing, Knowing.”*

**Meaning.** The verse opens with a direct statement that religion is not to be imposed by coercion. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** Ibn Kathīr explains that the clarity of guidance makes forced profession pointless: compelling a person to pronounce belief cannot itself create faith in the heart. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Saʿdī similarly emphasizes that the truth has been made distinct from error, so conversion is not to be produced by coercion. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** The verse’s reason is stated immediately: right guidance and error have become clear, and a person is called to recognize and choose the truth. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The commentators preserve different reports about the occasion of revelation, including accounts involving families among the Ansar and children connected with the Banu Nadir. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** These reports vary in their details and should be identified as transmitted explanations rather than as wording supplied by the Qur’an. **[Ṭabarī]** *(weak)* The verse’s meaning is not dependent upon selecting one of those stories. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī discusses the legal setting in which communities whose religious status was recognized were not compelled to abandon their religion, while also explaining that an occasion-specific report need not restrict a verse’s application to that single event. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The scope of the ruling has been discussed by commentators and jurists. **[Qurṭubī]** Some classical legal readings connect the verse especially with protected religious communities under the law of their time; others take its wording as a broader principle that faith is not created by compulsion. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** Saʿdī rejects the claim that the verse was abrogated and distinguishes fighting in a legal or political context from forcing a person’s inward religious belief. **[Saʿdī]** Qurṭubī records multiple positions, including abrogation claims and arguments against them, so these should be presented as historical exegetical debates rather than collapsed into one uncontested legal conclusion. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

“Whoever disbelieves in *ṭāghūt* and believes in God” describes a two-sided commitment: refusal of false objects of worship and affirmation of God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Al-Ṭabarī defines *ṭāghūt* broadly as that which transgresses against God and is worshipped besides Him; other commentators gloss it as Satan, idols, or a false authority that leads away from God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The term should not be narrowed to one named being when the sources give it a broader range. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The “firmest handhold” is a metaphor for a secure attachment to faith that does not break. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Exegetes explain it as belief in God, the testimony of divine unity, or the bond of Islam; these descriptions identify the same central commitment rather than competing objects. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The image contrasts the instability of false worship with a bond grounded in the living God. **[Maʿārif]** The clause “which never breaks” expresses confidence in the truth of that commitment, not a promise that believers will never be tested or experience uncertainty in ordinary life. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The closing names “Hearing, Knowing” return the matter to God. **[Ṭabarī]** He hears what people say and knows what their hearts intend; a coerced outward declaration cannot conceal inward belief or disbelief from Him. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** This also means that human communities should not claim access to a person’s interior state simply from an outward act that has been forced. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The verse should not be isolated from neighboring passages. **[Qurṭubī]** The preceding verse describes God’s authority over intercession and the Day of Judgment, while the next verse describes God’s guidance of believers from darkness to light. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Together they distinguish divine sovereignty from human coercion: God knows and guides, while people are accountable for the faith they truly embrace. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The disagreement about abrogation is especially important not to conceal. **[Qurṭubī]** Some exegetes transmitted a claim that later fighting legislation superseded the verse, while others treated it as still operative and understood it in relation to recognized religious communities. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī rejects the abrogation claim and says that a verse revealed in response to a particular event can still have broader application. **[Ṭabarī]** Saʿdī likewise refuses to make fighting synonymous with compelling belief: the verse concerns religious adherence, whereas conflict and political law are discussed under other conditions and texts. **[Saʿdī]** The interpretive record is therefore more complex than either a bare slogan or a claim that the verse has no legal history. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The phrase “right guidance has become distinct from error” is not a claim that every listener will find the decision emotionally easy. **[Saʿdī]** It says that the distinction has been made clear through revelation and proof, so a forced outward performance cannot substitute for inward conviction. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse then describes the believer not merely by a positive confession, but by rejecting false worship as well as affirming God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** This paired movement prevents the firm handhold from being reduced to a bare political label or a coerced public identity. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]** The ending returns the evaluation to God, whose hearing and knowledge exceed what a human authority can compel or inspect. **[Qurṭubī]**

The next verse’s description of God bringing believers from darkness to light follows naturally: guidance is offered and received, not mechanically imposed by an authority that can command the heart to believe. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** That connection strengthens the passage’s contrast between divine guidance and coercion. **[Saʿdī]**

**Interpretive note.** The reports about the verse’s occasion and the legal scope of its application differ; the stable textual point is that genuine belief is not manufactured by forcing a profession. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Reflection.** Guidance is not made more truthful by coercion. **[Saʿdī]** The verse calls the reader to clarity, rejection of false worship, and trust in God, while reminding human beings that God alone fully hears and knows what is believed. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

## 2:257

257257
*“God is the Protector of those who believe. He brings them out of darkness into light. As for those who disbelieve, their protectors are false gods; they bring them out of light into darkness. They are the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein.”*

**Meaning.** This verse follows the statement that religion is not imposed by compulsion with an account of guidance as a relationship of divine protection. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]** God is the *walī* of believers: commentators explain the word as protector, helper, guardian, or ally. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī stresses that God supports believers through aid and guidance; Saʿdī expands this to include nurturing them toward knowledge, certainty, obedience, and remembrance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

“Darkness” and “light” are commonly read as disbelief and faith, or misguidance and guidance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** The image describes movement: God brings believers out from what obscures truth into what clarifies it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]** Saʿdī includes ignorance, sin, heedlessness, and turning away among the spiritual conditions from which God guides people, while the light includes knowledge, certainty, faith, and obedience. **[Saʿdī]** The contrast should not be treated as a claim that believers are instantly free of every error; it describes the direction and source of guidance, not an absence of struggle. **[Maʿārif]**

The verse then contrasts God’s protection with the *awliyāʾ* of those who reject faith. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Qur’anic word *ṭāghūt* is rendered by Jalālayn as false deities, while al-Ṭabarī elsewhere explains the term broadly to include idols, devils, and whatever is worshipped besides God in transgression. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ṭabarī]** Qurṭubī records Satan as a gloss, and the Study Quran’s translation uses idols; the interpretive range points to false powers and allegiances that lead away from God. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The parallel phrase says that these false protectors bring people “out of the light into darkness.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Since many people addressed may never have embraced Islam, commentators explain “bringing out” not only as a reversal from prior faith but also as turning someone away from guidance to which they were being called. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Some early reports apply the wording to people who accepted Jesus but later rejected Muhammad; other exegetes say the verse’s language is general and applies to every community in which some believe and others reject. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The text does not require a single occasion or group to exhaust its meaning. **[Study Quran]**

Ibn Kathīr notes a rhetorical difference: light is singular, while darkness is plural. **[Ibn Kathīr]** This supports the exegetical image of truth as one, whereas falsehood branches into many forms and paths. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** The contrast is useful but should not be pressed into a claim that every disagreement among people is a form of disbelief. The verse speaks here about faith, rejection, and the direction of one’s ultimate allegiance. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The ending—“they are the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein”—states the consequence of the rejection described. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** It is not a license for human beings to pronounce final judgment on particular individuals whose inner state is known to God. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The passage emphasizes divine knowledge and accountability, following the assurance that God hears and knows in 2:256. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

There is an important difference between coercion and guidance. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse does not say that people are forced into faith; rather, God is the source of the light by which they recognize and follow it. **[Saʿdī]** The preceding statement rejects compulsion in religion, while this verse names the help and protection God gives to believers. **[Study Quran]** **[Qurṭubī]** It therefore invites gratitude for guidance and humility about its source instead of self-congratulation over one’s own insight. **[Maʿārif]**

**Cross-reference.** The imagery of God bringing people from darkness into light appears in 5:16, 14:1 and 57:9, while the opposition between a straight path and multiple misleading paths is expressed in 6:153. **[Study Quran]** These parallels reinforce the metaphor without requiring a speculative account of how guidance enters each heart. **[Ṭabarī]**

The singular “light” and plural “darknesses” sharpen the contrast in the verse. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Guidance is represented as a coherent direction toward truth, while falsehood appears in many forms that can draw a person away in different ways. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī’s explanation of darkness as what blocks the heart’s sight makes the metaphor epistemic as well as moral: guidance enables recognition, while disbelief conceals the evidence. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse’s pairing of divine protection and misleading protectors also warns against treating every claimed ally as a source of genuine care. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]**

The repeated verb “brings them out” is a vivid image of movement from one state into another. **[Jalālayn]** For believers, guidance is not merely information but a change in direction that God enables; for those who reject, false protectors draw them away from the truth they are invited to recognize. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The symmetry is not exact in source: God is the true Protector, whereas the false protectors have no real power to benefit or harm independently. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Maʿārif]** This contrast continues the previous verse’s distinction between God’s firm handhold and *ṭāghūt*. **[Study Quran]**

The universal metaphor should not be confused with the particular report about some people who first believed in Jesus and then rejected Muhammad. **[Ṭabarī]** That report is one application of the verse, not a limitation imposed by its wording. **[Qurṭubī]** The paired images remain applicable to the believer’s movement from error toward guidance and to the rejection that leaves a person in darkness. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

The final phrase “abiding therein” makes the warning serious, but the verse assigns knowledge of particular hearts and their final standing to God. **[Ṭabarī]** Its contrast is between the destinations of belief and rejection, not an instruction to treat neighbors or disputants as already judged. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

**Reflection.** The verse asks the reader to consider which allegiance is shaping perception. **[Saʿdī]** Divine friendship directs a person toward what is true and life-giving; false protectors promise support but lead toward confusion and loss. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

## 2:258

258258
*“Hast thou not considered him who disputed with Abraham concerning his Lord because God had given him sovereignty? When Abraham said, ‘My Lord is He who gives life and causes death,’ he said, ‘I give life and cause death.’ Abraham said, ‘God brings the sun from the east; bring it, then, from the west.’ Thus the one who disbelieved was confounded. And God guides not wrongdoing people.”*

**Meaning.** The verse presents Abraham in debate with a ruler who disputes his testimony about God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Qur’an does not name the ruler. Commentators commonly identify him as Nimrod, but the Study Quran notes that this identification depends on folkloric material rather than a sound prophetic report; the name should therefore be marked as a transmitted identification, not stated as Qur’anic fact. **[Study Quran]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* The verse’s argument remains clear without his name, genealogy, city, or the length of his reign. **[Ṭabarī]**

The phrase “because God had given him sovereignty” connects worldly authority with the ruler’s posture in the dispute. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Study Quran notes a grammatical possibility that the recipient of sovereignty could be Abraham, whose descendants are elsewhere described as receiving sovereignty, but says most commentators understand it to refer to the opponent’s worldly power. **[Study Quran]** The common reading makes the ruler’s authority a source of arrogance: a gift that should have led to gratitude becomes a basis for contesting the Lord who gave it. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]**

Abraham’s first statement identifies God as the One who gives life and causes death. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The ruler answers, “I give life and cause death.” Many commentaries explain this boast by saying that he ordered one condemned man killed and spared another, then called the spared man’s survival “life.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** This reported illustration is not part of the Qur’anic narration; its interpretive point is that political power over a sentence is not the same as creating life or governing death. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** Ibn Kathīr also notes the possibility that the ruler meant to claim creative power, and rejects any reading that gives the ruler a real share in God’s act of creation. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

When Abraham recognizes that the ruler’s reply equivocates over the meaning of life and death, he shifts to an argument that exposes the claim directly. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** “God brings the sun from the east; bring it, then, from the west” appeals to a regular cosmic sign that the ruler cannot control. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The second argument does not concede that Abraham’s first statement was inadequate; it tests the ruler’s boast on a level where there is no easy verbal substitution of pardoning for giving life. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The result is that the disbelieving opponent is “confounded,” understood as losing his argument and falling silent. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** The verse does not say that he accepted the truth, only that the proof overcame his claim. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The closing statement that God does not guide wrongdoing people explains the failure to reach guidance as a consequence associated with wrongdoing and rejection, not as a flaw in the proof. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The sources use the exchange to illustrate reasoned argument in defense of belief. **[Qurṭubī]** Abraham’s response is not an invitation to humiliate an opponent for its own sake; it aims to make the distinction between the Creator and a human ruler unmistakable. **[Saʿdī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Qurṭubī draws a broader lesson that debate can be permissible when it is grounded in knowledge and directed toward clarifying truth, while warning that argument without fairness can collapse into quarrelling and vanity. **[Qurṭubī]** *(digression)*

The verse’s core contrast is between God’s actual creative power and a ruler’s limited command over human affairs. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The ruler’s ability to issue an order does not make him a creator, just as possessing a kingdom does not make him its ultimate owner. **[Study Quran]** **[Saʿdī]** The passage therefore critiques the inference that political success proves theological truth. **[Maʿārif]** Authority is a test and a trust; it cannot cancel dependence upon God. **[Qurṭubī]**

Later narratives about the ruler’s genealogy, the mosquito said to have killed him, a tower reaching heaven, or a detailed exchange over food and tribute are not stated in this verse. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** They are transmitted tales of unequal reliability and are unnecessary to the proof narrated by the Qur’an. **[Study Quran]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* The account should remain focused on Abraham’s two arguments, the ruler’s failure to answer the second, and the moral diagnosis at the end. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Jalālayn]**

The phrase “Have you not considered?” is a rhetorical invitation to reflect, not necessarily a claim that the Prophet or his listeners witnessed this ancient debate directly. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that “seeing” here can mean knowing and contemplating through revelation. **[Ṭabarī]** That is consistent with the transition from the historical scene to its lesson about proof and wrongdoing. **[Study Quran]** The word translated “confounded” describes the opponent’s being silenced or deprived of an answer; it does not describe repentance. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Jalālayn]** The verse leaves the ruler’s later fate unstated and directs attention to the argument that defeated his claim. **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The phrase “because God had given him sovereignty” exposes a moral reversal: the ruler’s authority is a gift, yet he treats it as if it made him self-sufficient. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Maʿārif]** Al-Saʿdī describes the kingship as having misled the tyrant into arrogance, while the text itself leaves the ruler unnamed. **[Saʿdī]** The story therefore speaks beyond one historical opponent: the danger lies in using a limited worldly power to imitate or challenge the Creator. **[Study Quran]**

The account also corrects a category error: sparing someone who might otherwise be killed is an exercise of human discretion, whereas originating life and ending it by divine power belong to God. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The sunrise argument then moves from a contested use of words to an observable order the ruler cannot command. **[Saʿdī]**

**Reflection.** The passage warns against mistaking possession of power for independence from God. **[Saʿdī]** It also models the value of answering an equivocation with a clear argument, while leaving the final judgment of hearts to God. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:259

259259
*“Or like him who passed by a town fallen upon its roofs. He said, ‘How shall God give life to this after its death?’ Then God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him. He said, ‘How long hast thou tarried?’ He said, ‘I have tarried a day, or part of a day.’ He said, ‘Nay, thou hast tarried a hundred years. Look at thy food and drink; they have not spoiled. And look at thine ass. And that We may make thee a sign unto mankind. And look at the bones, how We raise them, then clothe them with flesh.’ When it became clear to him, he said, ‘I know that God is powerful over all things.’”*

**Meaning.** The verse gives a second example of resurrection after Abraham’s debate with the ruler. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** A traveller passes a ruined town, its structures fallen down, and asks how God will bring it to life after its death. **[Jalālayn]** The image of a town in ruin becomes an occasion for a sign about the possibility of restoration, while the verse does not identify the town or describe its history. **[Study Quran]** **[Ṭabarī]**

The person who asks the question is not named in the Qur’an. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]** Commentators identify him variously as Ezra or ʿUzayr, Jeremiah, or another figure; the accounts also disagree about the location of the town and the circumstances of its destruction. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** These identifications come from exegetical reports and, in some cases, Israelite narratives; they should not be presented as certain. **[Ṭabarī]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* Al-Ṭabarī stresses that the name is not needed to understand the sign, and Saʿdī likewise treats him as an unnamed man in his explanation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Saʿdī]**

Commentators also differ over the sense of his question. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī takes it as expressing doubt about how the ruined town could be revived, so God shows him an instance of life after death. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Saʿdī likewise reads the man as someone who questioned resurrection. **[Saʿdī]** Al-Qurṭubī, following Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s objection to treating a prophet as doubting God’s power, presents the question instead as wonder, grief, or a request to see how revival occurs. **[Qurṭubī]** The sources therefore do not warrant a flat claim that every commentator agrees on the man’s faith or prophetic status. **[Study Quran]**

The narrative states that God causes him to die for a hundred years and then raises him. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Jalālayn]** Asked how long he has remained, he answers according to what seems to him like a day or part of one; he is then told that a hundred years have passed. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ṭabarī explains that the man’s answer reflects his perception, not deliberate falsehood: the visible conditions around him give him no ordinary sense of the full interval. **[Ṭabarī]** The point is the contrast between human perception of time and God’s power to bring life after a long period. **[Study Quran]**
