The food and drink have not spoiled, while the verse also directs him to look at his ass and at the bones being raised and clothed with flesh. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The Qur’an does not name the food or specify the precise mechanics by which the animal’s bones are restored. **[Study Quran]** Reports that identify figs, grapes, juice, wine, or the particular state of the donkey differ among commentators; they are narrative details, not facts stated in the verse. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* Exegetes also differ on whether the bones belong to the man, the donkey, or both, and whether the donkey was dead or remained standing. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

The wording about the bones has variant readings, commonly explained either as raising and arranging them or as reviving them. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī treats the meanings as close: scattered bones are restored to their places, and life is returned after the body is reassembled. **[Ṭabarī]** The central point is not a technical account of bodily composition but God’s ability to restore what has decayed and to make a visible sign of resurrection. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The phrase “that We may make thee a sign unto mankind” makes the event more than a private reassurance. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The person’s experience is presented as a sign for people who encounter or hear of it, while the primary lesson is God’s power over death and resurrection. **[Jalālayn]** **[Study Quran]** Reports that he returned to find a particular son or grandchild aged, that a servant’s eyesight was restored, or that he encountered people who recognized him are not required by the verse and should be labeled as transmitted narrative if mentioned. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)*

The closing statement is translated either as “I know that God is powerful over all things” or, under a variant reading, as an imperative to “know.” **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Qurṭubī records disagreement about whether it is the man’s declaration after witnessing the sign or an instruction; in either case, the conclusion is a recognition of God’s power. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse does not require the reader to decide the man’s identity or reconstruct a full biography in order to understand its theological claim. **[Study Quran]**

The speaker who asks “How long hast thou tarried?” is not named in the verse. **[Qurṭubī]** Commentators suggest God, an angel, or another witness, but the disagreement does not alter the event’s point: the traveller’s own estimate is corrected by knowledge beyond his perception. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]** The verse likewise does not tell whether the town’s inhabitants are included in the phrase “give life to this,” or whether the ruined settlement itself stands as the visible sign; the surrounding mention of bones keeps the focus on restoration after death. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The narrative’s omissions help prevent the reader from confusing its demonstration with a complete historical chronicle. **[Saʿdī]**

The setting of a collapsed town also gives the word “death” a visible image before the reader reaches the details of the traveller’s own death. **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** The sequence moves from ruined dwellings, to the traveller’s misjudgment of elapsed time, to food and drink preserved, and finally to bones restored. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The several signs address different aspects of the same question, but the text does not require us to suppose that the traveller asked for every detail in advance. **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** The story moves from ruins and apparent finality to the visible possibility of renewal. **[Saʿdī]** The reader is asked to contemplate how little human perception can establish about what God is able to restore. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Study Quran]**

## 2:260

260260
*“And when Abraham said, ‘My Lord, show me how Thou givest life to the dead.’ He said, ‘Hast thou not believed?’ He said, ‘Yea, but that my heart may be at rest.’ He said, ‘Take four birds and incline them unto thee, then place upon every mountain a portion of them, then call them; they will come to thee in haste. And know that God is Mighty, Wise.’”*

**Meaning.** Abraham asks God to show him how the dead are brought to life. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** The wording asks about the manner of revival, not whether God has power to revive; Abraham immediately affirms, “Yea, I believe.” **[Jalālayn]** **[Saʿdī]** Most commentators therefore understand his request as seeking direct witnessing or reassurance, rather than as denying resurrection. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Qurṭubī explains that knowing something by report and seeing its manner directly are different kinds of assurance, while Study Quran similarly notes that the cause of the request is not stated with certainty. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Study Quran]**

The sources report several possible contexts: Abraham may have seen an animal’s remains dispersed among predators, may have sought a sign after his debate with the ruler, or may simply have desired to witness the manner of resurrection. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** These are explanatory reports, not details supplied by the verse, and should not be fused into one certain occasion. **[Study Quran]** Al-Ṭabarī accepts an account of an intrusive hesitation prompted by Satan and reads Abraham as asking to see the event so that the whisper would not trouble him again; he does not say that Abraham denied God’s power. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Qurṭubī rejects the claim of settled doubt, while Ibn Kathīr interprets the prophetic saying “we are more liable to doubt than Abraham” as a way of expressing the search for certainty, not as attributing unbelief to Abraham. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

God’s question, “Hast thou not believed?” elicits Abraham’s clear affirmation. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** His answer distinguishes faith from the additional calm he seeks: “that my heart may be at rest.” **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** Commentators variously describe this as increased certainty, the movement from knowledge by report to direct observation, or the quieting of thought through seeing the process. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The verse thus permits a believer to seek understanding and reassurance without equating every question about “how” with rejection of what is believed. **[Study Quran]**

The command to take four birds is followed by the instruction *fa-ṣurhunna ilayka*, whose interpretation has been discussed by the exegetes. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī and many early interpreters understand it as cutting or dividing the birds; others take the phrase as drawing them near or inclining them toward Abraham before the next action. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Saʿdī and Ibn Kathīr follow the cutting interpretation in their explanations, but the verse’s broader point does not depend on resolving every lexical nuance. **[Saʿdī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The four species are not named in the Qur’an, and the exact number of mountains is not specified. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]** Some commentaries list a rooster, peacock, crow, and pigeon, while other reports substitute different birds; those lists are not Qur’anic information. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* The command says to place a portion of the birds upon every mountain, then call them; they come to Abraham swiftly. **[Jalālayn]** **[Maʿārif]** The details some reports add about heads held in Abraham’s hand, feathers and blood flying separately, or exactly seven mountains belong to transmitted narrative and should not be treated as established by the verse. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]**

The demonstration echoes the preceding account of the ruined town. **[Saʿdī]** In both cases, God makes resurrection perceptible through a sign, while the final claim is broader than the particular event: God can restore life even when bodies or their parts have been scattered. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ṭabarī’s discussion of the variant readings for raising or reviving the birds likewise emphasizes the restoration of separated parts and the return of life. **[Ṭabarī]** The scene is therefore an answer to Abraham’s request for a demonstration, not a general ritual to be repeated by later believers. **[Study Quran]** **[Maʿārif]**

The final names “Mighty, Wise” complete the lesson. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** God is Mighty, so no obstacle can frustrate His power; He is Wise, so the act of giving Abraham a sign occurs by divine wisdom rather than as a spectacle without purpose. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Saʿdī]** The command to “know” that God is Mighty and Wise links the visible demonstration to a lasting conviction about the One who performs it. **[Jalālayn]**

The word “sought rest” or “that my heart may be at rest” does not mean Abraham’s conviction had been absent. **[Qurṭubī]** The commentators explain that the request concerns the felt stillness that comes with seeing what one already knows to be true, not the acquisition of faith after disbelief. **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Maʿārif]** The verse thus distinguishes the certainty of the proposition from the desire to witness its manner. **[Study Quran]** Reports that connect the request with the earlier debate involving Nimrod are possible contextual explanations, but they are not explicitly supplied by the verse and should not be treated as its only occasion. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]**

The birds’ coming “in haste” emphasizes that the result is not a still image of reassembled matter but living creatures responding to the summons. **[Ṭabarī]** **[Qurṭubī]** Commentators explain the manner as running or coming quickly; either way, the sign visibly answers the question about life returning after separation. **[Jalālayn]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The address to call them does not give Abraham an independent power of resurrection: it is God who gives the command, restores life, and makes the birds come. **[Saʿdī]** **[Study Quran]**

**Interpretive note.** The sources generally protect the verse from an interpretation of settled disbelief: Abraham affirms faith, while commentators explain his request as a desire for experiential assurance, increased certainty, or relief from an intrusive thought. **[Qurṭubī]** **[Ibn Kathīr]** **[Study Quran]**

**Reflection.** Faith can seek deeper understanding without rejecting its foundation. **[Saʿdī]** Abraham’s example makes room for the honest request to see and understand, while directing attention to God’s power and wisdom rather than to speculative details of the birds. **[Maʿārif]** **[Study Quran]**
